The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing Luder Aiello and Benjamin Berkenhout, with some Amendments: To which Amendments their Lordships desire the Concurrence of this House: Also, The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act to enable Darcy Danes Esquire, and Sarah Roundel/, to make Settlements, upon their Intermarriage, of their several Estates, notwithstanding their respective Minorities: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of^uppression the Town and County of Southampton, was presented to ^Smuggling, the House, and read; setting forth; That notwithstanding the many good Laws in force to prevent the Running of Goods, yet that Trade is still carried on; to the Discouragement of the fair Trader; and the lessening his Majesty's Revenues; and the very great Loss of the Petitioners: And praying, That some more effectual Method may be taken to put a Stop to it.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the ancient City of Winchester is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Master Shipwrights near London, Importing Subscribers thereunto, in behalf of themselves, and the foreign Oak, rest of the Shipwrights of Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the great Consumption in this Kingdom of the best British Oak Timber has caused a great Want for Ship Building; to the Prejudice of Trade: That this Evil may, in a great measure, be remedied, with Advantage to the British Commerce, if, in Exchange for our Manufactures, some Encouragement was given for bringing in foreign Oak Timber unsawed; for there is a Duty payable on importing it, which, with the great Freights that attend the Stowage of rough Oak Timber, makes it so chargeable, that very little is imported: The taking off that Duty will not prejudice the Revenue; but be an Increase thereof; And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, to enable his Majesty's British Subjects to import any unsawed, strait, and compass foreign Oak Timber, free from Duty, in Bi'itish-bu\\t Ships; and for such short time, as the House shall judge fit.

Resolved, That the Petition be rejected.

A Petition of William late Lord Widdrington was Late Lord presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Widdruigu* his real and personal Estate, to the Value of above One 1)ebts»^c* hundred thousand Pounds, being forfeited by his Attainder, has been sold, for the Use of the Publick: That, for Seven Years past, he has contracted several Debts, for the necessary Subsistence of himself and Family-:

That one Part of the said Forfeiture consists of an Estate of above Twelve hundred Pounds per Annum,* which, if the utmost Severity of the Law had passed upon him, would have gone immediately to his Children, being their Mothers Inheritance: That the Sum of Two thousand Four hundred Eighty-four Pounds and Ten Shillings, formerly granted him (for which he returns his most humble Thanks), had enabled him to discharge some Part of his Debts, and contributed to preserve him, and his Family, from sinking into the lowest Degree of Misery; to which, nevertheless, lie must soon, and unavoidably, be reduced, by his Want of Subsistence, and the remaining Burthen of his Debts; unless this House, in Compassion to his Distress, will please to grant him some further Relief: And praying, That his deplorable Circumstances may be taken into Consideration; and, out of his large Forfeitures, some Relief may be granted him towards paying the Remainder of his Debts; and for the future Support and Maintenance of him, and his unhappy Family. f

Mr. Gybbon, according to Order, reported, from the Malmsbury Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as Election, it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Malmsbury, in the County of Wilts, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the said Report and Resolutions are as follow: viz.

Upon the Petition of Giles Earle and John Fermor Esquires, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Trevor Lord Viscount Hilsborough, of the Kingdom of Ireland, and Sir John Rushout Baronet, to serve for the said Borough:

That the Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Aldermen and Twelve capital Burgesses.

That the Poll was,

For the Sitting Members, each - - - 8:

For the Petitioners, each ----- 5.

That the Petitioners Counsel alleged, They should add Two to their Poll; viz. Joseph Hancock and Richard Withers; who were refused, as having l>een amoved from being capital Burgesses in February last; whereas they insisted, that pretended Arnoval was made by a Minority of the Corporation; and was void:

That they also objected against T hree of the Sitting Members Voters; viz.against Charles Hudson and John Browning; as having no Right, because elected capital Burgesses by a Minority of the Corporation, in the room of Hancock and // ithers, who were not well amoved; and

Against Thomas Gingell, as being non compos, and thereby incapable of declaring his Vote at the Tinre of the Election.

That it was admitted, and it appeared by the Charter, That this Corporation consists of One Alderman,

T welve capital Burgesses, and Twenty-four Assistants:

That the Alderman, and the Twelve capital Burgesses, for the Time being, or the major Part of them, are the governing part of the Corporation; and by them the capital Burgesses are to be elected, out of the Twenty-four Assistants; and that any capital Burgess, or Assistant, is amovable by the Alderman, and capital Burgesses, for the Time being, or the major Part of them, quo ties res requiskrit, pro mule sc gerendo in ant alia justa

§ rationabil' de causa; and, when the Votes are equal, the Alderman has a double Vote.

That, as to Hancock and Withers,

Israel May said, That upon the Ninth Day of February last, Hancock and !Cithers were summoned immediately to attend a Court held in the Abby, at the House of Amy Hanley, Widow, by Adjournment from Saint Johns Hospital, to answer a Charge laid against then*; and, not appearing, a Second Summons w as sent, to answer a heavy Charge against them; and, not appearing the n, they were next Day taken, upon a War-

rant, and carried in Custody, to answer what should be objected against them.

Mr. Thomas Shearing said, That, at this adjourned Court, Withers was asked, by what Authority lie acted as a capital Burgess? And it was objected to him, That he did not, at the time of hia Election into Office, take the Oaths requisite by Law, and was therefore disqualified: To which he answered. He could not tell what Oaths he then took ;. but he took all that were administered to him.

James Baker said, That Withers received the Sacrament, at the Parish-Church, within a Fortnight after his Election; and took the Oaths at the next Quarter Sessions.

That it appeared, by the Evidence of Mr. Thomas Earle and Mr. Thomas Shearing, That the adjourned Court, in February last, amoved Hancock and Withers from being capital Burgesses, and elected Charles Hudson and John Browning in their stead; and that this Court consisted of the Aldermen, and only Five of Twelve capital Burgesses theni-i* being; of which Five, Thomas Gingell was one; And,

Mr. Shew ring' said Gingell was then* non compos, and could do nothing but laugh:

That the Admission of Joseph Hancock to be a capital Burgess was produced under the Corporation Seal, dated the 26th Day of Map 169g, jurat' coram Nich. Hayes, Alderman.

Mr. Thomas Earle said, That for 17 or 18 Years, Hancock did all Acts as a capital Burgess; and there was ho Objection to him till 1708, when the Court of King's Bench was moved for an Information against him.

It was said by Israel May and Nathanael Mathews, That Withers had, for 14 Years, acted as a capital Burgess; and that both he and Hancock had all along enjoyed all the* Privileges of capital Burgesses; and, as such, do now enjoy their Parts of the Burgess-Lands: That Hancock made a Return of Members to the last Parliament; and That both he and Withers were allowed to vote, and were taken upon the Poll, in 1709, without any Objection:

But William Collins, the Town Clerk, said, Hancock's Vote was queried in 1705 and 1709.

Mr. Skewring and Mr. Matthews said. That Seven of the capital Burgesses, present at the public Court held at St. Johns, opposed the Adjournment of that Court, and refused to go to the Abby; and only Four, and the Alderman, concurred to the Adjournment

Mr. Thomas Earle said, That, at the Election of Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament, the Poll of all the capital Burgesses present being taken, the Alderman declared the Numbers; and that the Sitting Members had the Majority; and, after that, without the Concurrence of the Majority of the capital Burgesses present, and without asking their Consents, the Alderman, of himself, adjourned the Poll to the Abby-house, to take the Vote of Thomas Gingell\ who, the Witness said, could not then speak articulately, nor was, at that time, in his Opinion, capable of doing a rational Act; and when he was asked, Who he voted for? he answered, Hilsbo-rough and Floyd, as well as he could speak:

Being cross-examined, he said, He had known the Alderman, of himself, adjourn Courts, and that to private Houses, without putting any Question of Adjournment, or asking the Consent of the Burgesses present; but it was looked upon to be irregular.

It appeared, That in Michaelmas Term, 7m Anna, the Court of Kings Bench made a Rule, That Joseph Hancock should, the First Day of the next Term, shew Cause why an Information, in the Nature of a Quo Warranto, should not be exhibited against him, for claiming to be Alderman of this Borough; and, upon shewing Cause, that Rule was discharged: And,

In Trinity Term following, a Rule for a like Information, Unless Cause, the First Day of the next Term, was made against Richard Withers, for claiming to be. 13

a capital Burgess; and, upon shewing Cause, that Rule was discharged: And,

Mr. Richard IIarcourt, who produced those Rules, said, That, by discharging the Rules Nisi, the Court oi King's Bench had affirmed the Titles of Hancock and Withers:

Mr. Harcourt also produced a Rule of Court, of Easter Term last, for a like Information, Unless Cause, against Gowen Hart, for claiming to be a capital Burgess: And said, The Objection to Hart was, That he took only the Oath of Office, at the time he was elected a capital Burgess-; and did not then take the other Oaths appointed by Law: And the Town Clerk, who administered to him the Oath of Office, made Affidavit, That he administered no other Oath to him, at that time Hart swore, lie took all the Oaths that were administered to him; The Court said, The Fault was in the Officer, and he ought to be punished for it; and discharged the Rule against Hart: And,

Mr. Harcourt said further, That, after Eight or Nine Years Acquiescence, the Court of Kings-Bench would never suffer an Information, in the Nature of a Quo Warranto, to be filed, for not receiving the Sacrament, according to the Corporation Act:

That new Rules might be prayed against the Persons before named; but none have been prayed, nor would the Court grant any for the same Facts.

Henry Robins said, That, Hancock and Withers voted, at this Election, foF the Petitioners; but were not taken:

And it appeared, by the Poll, That the Votes of Charles Hudson and John Brazening were taken for the Sitting Members.

That the Petitioners Counsel objected Bribery, and illegal Practices, by the Sitting Members, and their Agents: And called,

James Baker: Who said, That, Thomas Young applied to him, to get his Father-in-law [Withers) over to Lord Hilsborough's Side; and told him, That he knew a Secret, which would disburgess Withers; who would be ruined, if he did not comply; but, if he did comply, he should have a double Portion: And that Samuel Hudson swore, If Withers did not come over to his Lordships Interest, he would be ruined; but, if he did come over, he would be made for ever:

That Lord Hilsbomigh promised the Witness, he should be one of the Twenty-four, and one of the capital Burgesses, in the room of Gingell, who could not live long, if he would get Withers over to his Interest.

Johannah, Wife of Gowen Hart, one of the capital Burgesses, said, That Lord Hilsborough, within a few Days before the Election, the Sixteenth of March, as she remembered, offered her, at Mrs. Henley s Chamber, Two Purses, in which, he said, were One thousand Guineas, to get her Husband's Vote for him and Floyd, who was then another Candidate: And she telling his Lordship, That her Husband had promised his Vote^and was unalterable whenever he promised; his Lordship answered, lie would then be the Ruin of her Husband, and all his Family; and could disburgess him, and take away his Estate:

That, at another time before this, his Lordship had offered her Five hundred Guineas, to get her Husbands Vote.

William Hart said, That, about three Weeks before the Writs issued. Lord Hilsborough sent for him, and gave him Four Guineas to go down to Malmsbary, and promised to give a hundred Pounds to himself, and a Thousand Guineas to his Father, if he could get his Fathers Vote for his Lordship: And, the l)ay^before the Election, his Lordship renewed this Promise to him; and threatened,' if his Father would not comply, it should be swore against him, that he had not taken the Oaths; and that he should be displaced from his Office.

As to Hancock and Withers,

The Sitting Members Counsel insisted, That Hancock's Election to be a capital Burgess, in 1699, was by the Minority of the Body; and was therefore a Nullity:

That, upon that Election to be a capital Burgess, he disclaimed to be one of the Twenty-four Assistants, and resigned that Office; and another was elected Assistant, in his stead:

That, in 1704, being conscious his Election in 1699 was void, he desired to be re-elected, and was accordingly re-elected, a capital Burgess; but was‘then incapable, in regard he was not, at that time, one of the Twenty-four:

That, Withers taking only the Oath of Office, at the time of his Election into the Office of a capital Burgess; and not taking, at the same time, the other Oaths appointed by Law; his Election was absolutely void. And,

Thomas Younge, being called, said, he was the Person who officiated for the Town*Clerk; and, by Direction of the Alderman, swore Withers into the Office of a capital Burgess, in 170S:

That Withers then took no Oath, but the Oath of Office:

The Alderman did not direct any other Oath to be administered; nor did the Witness, as lie said, then know any other Oath was necessary:

That, at the adjourned Court in February last, he was examined upon Oath, to this Point; and Withers, being, at the Court, asked the Question, confessed, That, at the time of his Election* he took no Oath, but the Oath of Office:

Which confession was also confirmed by Philip Lloyd Esquire:

And Younge further said, That the Election of Withers to be a capital Burgess was at an adjourned Court held the Twelfth of November 1708; when were present only the Alderman, and Five capital Burgesses, though there were then in being Eleven capital Burgesses, besides the Alderman; and that Withers was elected upon the double Vote of the Alderman:

And the Witness produced that Poll; whereby it appeared, there were Two other Candidates besides Withers; and that the Alderman, and Five capital Burgesses, who. were all that were present, voted for if it hers only:

That all Courts have been adjourned at^the Pleasure of the Alderman; and it has been usual to adjourn them as well to private as to public Houses:

That, being cross-examined, he denied he had ever solicited Withers's Vote, or threatened to disburgess him.

William Collins, the Town Clerk, said, That he had been acquainted with the Borough Twenty Years; That the Alderman always, of himself, adjourned all Cotuts,

by his own Authority:

That, when all the capital Burgesses present at the late Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament had polled, the Poll was adjourned, at Lord Hilsboroug/is Instance, to take Gingelis Vote; and that Gin gel I, being asked by the Witness, Who lie voted for? answered, very distinctly. For Lord Hilsborough and Sir John liushout; and the Poll was declared after he had voted, and not before:

As to Hancock and Withers, he said, That, upon Hancock's claiming and insisting he was a capital Burgess, under his Election in 1699, Hancock then declared, He was no longer one of the Twenty-four; and afterwards James Tily, late Alderman, was elected to be one of the Twenty-four, in his stead:

That, in 1704, upon the Death of Arnold, one of the capital Burgesses, Hancock told them, He had not been well elected a capital Burgess, and desired to be elected de novo; for that his Election in 1699 was by a Minority; and thereupon he was, in 1704, re-elected a capital Burgess; but was not then one of the Twenty-four:

That the Rule of the Court of Kings Bench, for an Malmsbury Information against Hancock, Nisi causa, was for claim- E,lection* ing under his First Election in 1699; but, he shewing another Election in 1704, the Rule was discharged for that Reason, and no other:

That all the capital Bgrgesses were summoned to the adjourned Court in February last, which amoved Hancock and Withers; and that Withers did then declare,

He took only the Oath of Office at the time of his Election, and did not know it was incumbent on him to take any other.

And called,

Thomas Younge: Who said, That, about a Year ago,

Mr. Thomas Earle, one of the Witnesses for the Petitioners, and who appeared as an Agent for them in this Election, applied to him, in behalf of the Petitioner Colonel Earle, and desired him to solicit the Burgesses to be for the Colonel; and declared, He would, in a few Days, lodge in the Witness's Hands Two hundred Pounds apiece, and more, if that would not do, for as many of the Burgesses as he could get; and proposed the getting of Seven or Eight; but the Witness refused to concern himself in the Matter: And, at another time after this, he promised the Witness, That the Colonel would immediately give him a Place, under the Government, of a Hundred Pounds a Year, and it might, in a little time, be Five hundred Pounds a Year to him, if he would do as desired; and declared, That the Colonel had given him Authority for what he offered.

Charles Wallington said, That Mr. Shew ring solicited Votes for the Petitioners; asked his Vote for them; and promised him Two hundred Pounds for it; and that his Son should have the First Parsonage of a Hundred and Fifty Pounds per Annum that should be vacant in the Gift of the Crown: -

That this Evidence was confirmed by his Daughter,

Mary Wallington, who was present at th?^Offer:

Miles Martin said, That, some time before the Election, Mr. Showing declared, That he had, the Day before, offered Mr. Wallington Two hundred Pounds for his Vote; and that he would have it, or give more, the next Day.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Richard Withers was duly qualified to vote as a capital Burgess of the Borough of Malmsbury, in the County of Wilts, at the late Election of Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Joseph Hancock was duly qualified to vote as a capital Burgess for the Borough of Malmsbury, in the County of Wiltsf at the late Election of Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Trevor Lord Viscount Hilsborough, of the Kingdom of Ireland\ is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Malmsbury, in the County of Wilts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir John Rushout Baronet is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Malmsbury.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Giles Earle Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Malmsbury.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Fermor Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Malmsbury.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Daniel Pultcncy reported from the Committee, Expiring who were appointed to inspect uhat Laws arc expired, Laws, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued; That they had considered the Matter to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read:

And the Resolutions are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That in an Act made in the Fourth and fifth Years of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, intituled,

An Act for reviving, continuing, and explaining, several Laws therein mentioned, which are expired, or near expiring, there are several good Clauses and Provisions relating to Jurors; which Clauses and Provisions, were, by the said Act, to continue in force for Three Years after the First of May 1693, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; which said Clauses and Provisions were, by an Act made in the Seventh and Eighth Years of the said King William the Third, intituled, An Act for the Ease of Jurors, and better kegulating of Juries, continued for Seven Years frojtt

Act, of the Twelfth of Queen A?me, intituled, An Act for the reviving and continuing several Acts therein mentioned, for the preventing Mischiefs which may happen by Fire; for building and repairing County Gaols; for exempting Apothecaries from serving Parish and Ward Offices, and serving upon ‘Juries; and relating to the Returning of Jurors; continued, and put in force, for Eleven Years from the Expiration thereof; which, being near expiring, are fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act made in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled, An Act for exempting Apothecaries from serving the Offices of Constable and Scavenger, and other Parish and Ward Offices; and from serving upon Juries; which Act was to continue for seven Years, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament; which was, by an Act made in the First Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for reviving the Act, intituled, An Act for exempting Apothecaries from serving the Offices of Constable, Scavenger, and other Parish and Ward Offices; and from serving upon Juries; continued for the Space of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament; which Act was, by an Act, intituled, An Act for revivigg and continuing several Acts therein mentioned, for the preventing Mischiefs which may happen by Fife; for building and repairing Counly Gaols; for exempting Apothecaries from serving Parish and Ward Offices; and serving upon Juries; and relating to the Returning of Jurors; continued for Eleven Years, and to the End of the next Session of Parliament, which is hear expired; ought to be made perpetual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act made in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for explaining an Act for the better preventing the Embezzlement of his Majesty's Stores of War; and preventing Cheats, Frauds, and Abuses, in paying Seamen's Wages j and for reviving and continuing an Act for the more effectual Suppressing of Piracy; which was to be in force for Five Years, and to the End of the next Session of Parliament; be revived, and made perpetual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act made in the First Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for making the Militia of that Part of Cj^cat Britain called England more useful; and for obliging an annual Account to be made of Trophy-money; which was to continue only for Five Years, and to the End of the next Session of Parliament; ought to be revived.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of the Act made in the Filth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act against clandestine Running of uncustomed Goods; and for the more effectual preventing of Frauds relating to the Customs; as relates to such Foreign Goods, Wares, and Aicr-

A Petition of the Persons whose Names are subscribed, South Sea in behalf of themselves, and others, w ho have Stock Annuities, allowed thorn in the South Sea Company, in respect ot their several Interests in the redeemable Debts and Funds, was offered to the House: 1 .'

And the' Question being put, That the Petition be brought up to the Table;

It passed in the Negative.

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported, from the Stated Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of the State of the publick Credit; and of the State Cr rt' of the National Debt; the Resolutions the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at1 the Clerks Table: Where they were read; and are asTol* low; viz\ ,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Chmihitteef,

That, towards restoring the publick Credit, as well as the Credit of the South Sea Company, which hath suffered an immense Loss and Damage, by the many Frauds, Abuses, and Breaches of Trust, which were committed by the late Sub Governor, Deputy Governor, and Directors, of the said Company, and others in Confederacy with them, or some of them, so much of the Act of Parliament of the Seventh Year of his Majesty's Reign, as relates to the reducing, sinking, and annihilating, the full Sum of Two Millions of Pounds Sterling, Part of the capital Stock then belonging to the said Company; and so much of the same Act as imports, That a proportional Part of the Annuities, or yearly Funds, of the said Company, payable at the Exchequer, in respect of Two Millions, should, from and after the Feast of the Nativity of St. John Baptist 1722, be no longer payable; but should from thenceforth for ever cease and determine, for the Benefit of the Publick; be repealed, and made void: And that the said Two Millions shall again be revived, and added to the capital Stock of the said Company: And that- the said proportional Part or Parts of their Annuities, or yearly Funds, in respect of the said Two Millions, shall also be revived, and again made payable at the Exchequer, as if the said Act had not been made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the whole capital Stock of the South Sea Company, and the Shares of the respective Members and Proprietors of and in the same, be divided and separated into Two equal Parts or Moieties; and that One of the said Moieties of the said capital Stock shall be and remain capital Stock of the said Company; and One Moiety of their Annuities, or yearly Funds, in respect thereof, be still continued in the said Company, with all Profits and Advantages that may attend the same, according to the Laws and Statutes now in force:

And that the respective Members and Proprietors, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, shall have their proportional Shares in the said Moieties of the said capital Stock, and Annuities, of the said Company, and in all the said Profits and Advantages to attend the same:

And that the other Moiety of the said capital Stock, and of the said Annuities, or yearly Funds, be converted into Annuities, payable at any Rate, not exceeding Five Pounds per Cent. per Annum, until Midsummer Day 1727, and from thence at any Rate, not exceeding Four Pounds per Cent. per Annum, until Redemption by Parliament; the same Annuities to be payable out of the other Moiety of the said yearly Fund, which the Company shall receive at the Exchequer, and pay to the respective Annuitants, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns: And that the whole capital Stock now-belonging to the said Company, and the Annuities attending the same, may be redeemed by Parliament, according to the former Powers of Redemption, contained in the Act or Acts of Parliament for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards lessening the publick Debts and Incumbrances, all the Annuities payable, after the Rate of 12 ' Five

Upon the Petition of David Scott Esquire, complain-. ing of an undue Election and Return of Philip Anstruther Esquire, to serve for the said District of Bufghs;

That the Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

It appeared, by the Minutes taken at the Election That the Five Commissioners for this District of Burghs met at Kilrtnm/, the presiding Burgh; and proceeded to the Election on the Day appointed, the Thirteenth of April last, betwixt Eleven and Twelve in the Forenoon: That Three of the Five voted for the Sitting Member; and the other Two withdrew, and separated from the Meeting, without giving any Vote:

Which Proceeding was in the following Order; viz. Kilrenny — Robert Waddell for the Sitting Member: Anstruther Easter — Sir John Anstruther for the Sitting Member:

Pittemceem — James Melvill said, He would not vote: and then said, he would not vote here; when Mr. Rqjtt said, he would separate:

Anstruther. Wester — Philip Anstruther for the Sitting Member: i

Crail — Mr. David Scott went out saying, . Clerk will go with us; and required to be allowed to bring in another Clerk;

Which was denied; and the Separation was protested against: and Instruments were taken thereupon.

The Petitioner's Counsel owned a Majority for the Sitting Member; but insisted, That Robert Waddell\ one of inc Three for him was gained by Force; for which Reason the other two could not elect; and therefore the Election was void: That the same force had been offered to James Melvill, who was in the Petitioner's Interest: And, relying upon the Matter of Force to make the Election void, they called,

John Melvill, the Commissioner for Pittenweem: Who said, That Waddell, both before and after he w as chose Commissioner for Kih'tmtiy, declared his Apprehensions of Force to gain his Vote for the Sitting Member:

That, the Sixth of April last, when Waddell was elected a Commissioner, lie, and A felviU the Witness, went to the Petitioners House for Protection; and, next Day, they signed a Petition to the Sheriff for his Protection against the Sitting Member; but had none; and, lor fear they should be carried off, they gave Instruments declaring their Votes for the Petitioner; hild left "their Commissions, with him, for Safe Custody:

That, the Twelfth of April, they went to CVdil, which Tbw n was in the Petitioner's Interest; and, When they were fn Bed there, ih a Magistrate's HdUse, the Night be-foYe the Election, several of the Sitting Member's Friends, with some Persons in his Livery, came ill at the Window; and, with Pistols in their Hands, and Swords by their Sides, forced them to rise at Twelve a Clock at "Night, \o go to the Sitting Mfcrfiber at Kilrehhy; against which 'Force they protested:

Ordered, That the said Hugh Baillie, for his said Breach of Privilege, be taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

MR. Speaker acquainted the House, That, pursuant to their Order, he did, on the Twenty-fifth of December last, give Notice, in Writing, to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, at their public Office in London, of the Resolutions of the House, of the Eighteenth of the same December: Which Notice was as followeth; viz.

Gentlemen, 25th, 1722.

In Obedience to the Commands of the House of Commons, I am to acquaint you, That the said House did, on the Eighteenth of this instant December, come to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That Notice be given, or left at the publick Office of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, on the Twenty-fifth Day of this present Month of December, pursuant to the Act of the Third Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for redeeming the Duties and Revenues, which were settled to pay off Principal and Interest, on the Orders made forth on Four Lottery Acts, passed in the Ninth and Tenth Years of her late Majesty's Reign; and for redeeming certain Annuities payable on Orders, out of the Hereditary Excise, according to the former Act in that behalf; and for establishing a general yearly Fund, not ouly for the future payment of Annuities, at several Rates, to be payable and transferrable at the Bank of England, and redeemable by Parliament, but also to raise Monies for such Proprietors of the said Orders, as shall choose to be paid their Principal and Arrears of Interest in ready Money; and for making good such, other Deficicnces and Payments, as in this Act are mentioned; and for taking off the Duties on Linseed imported, and British Linen exported; That this House do redeem all such of the Annuities payable by that Act, after the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent, per Annum, as have not been subscribed into the capital Stock of the South Sea Company.

And this Resolution, thus signified by me, is to be suffieient Notice to you of the said Redemption, pursuant to the said Act of Parliament of the Third Year of his present Majesty's Reign.

I am, with great Respect, Gentlemen,

Your most humble Servant,

Sp, Compton, Speaker.

Upon the Petition of Sir Thomas Clarke Knight; and also the Petition of James Gatnurd, and others, lYeemen and Inhabitants of the ancient Borough of Hertford, in the County of Hertford, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Charles Ceesur Esquire, to serve for the said Borough:

That the Committee have examined the Merits ol this Election.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Inhabitants not receiving Alms; and in such Freemen only, as, at the time of their being made free, were Inhabitants of the Borough, or the Parishes thereof; the Number of the Freemen living out of the Borough not exceeding Three Persons.

The Petitioner's Counsel produced Evidence to disqualify 12.5 Voters for the Sitting Member; and to add lb to the Petitioner's Poll.

Touching which the Evidence was as follows: Eighty-three, who voted as Freemen, were objected to, as having no Right to vote: And,

Jonathan Smart, John Archer, John Late ford, Joshua Gilman, and Five others, gave Evidence for the Petitioner, That Thirty-nine of those Freemen were never Inliabitants within the Borough:

7'bat Three others wore neither Freemen nor Inhabitants at the time of the Election: And that the other Forty-one were not Inhabitants at the time they were made free:

Which Evidence, as to Thirty-four of those Voters, was contradicted by Ralph /ViUymott, the Town Clerk, Charles Saunders, Leonard Dell, William Balaam, and Six others; who were called on behalf of the Sitting Member, and averred the Qualifications of those Thirty-four Freemen as good Votes, in Contradiction to the Evidence winch had been given against thorn.

'Twelve others, who voted for the Sitting Member as Inhabitants, were objected to: And,

Which Evidence, as to Nine of those Twelve, was contradicted by the Evidence given, on the Sitting Members Part, by Robert Dew, John Hay don, Joh/i Woolmer, and Five others; who gave Evidence, That those Nine were Inliabitants within the Borough, at the time of the Election.

Thirty other Voters for the Sitting Member were objected to, as being only Certificate-men:

Which was proved, on the Petitioner's Part, by producing thp Certificates; and by the Evidence of Joshua Gilman:

And, on the Sitting Member's Part, it was proved by William Etheridge, John and Three others.

That Six of those Thirty had gained Settlements sinc^ their Certificates, or lived by Certificate from One Parish to another within the Borough.

To add Sixteen to the Petitioner's Poll, who voted for him as Inhabitants at the time of the Election, and were refused by the Mayor;

Evidence was given by Jonathan Smart, Joshua Gilman, Rostock Toller, and Tlwce others, on the Petitioner's Part, 'That Three of those Sixteen lived in the Castle; and that the other Thirteen were Inhabitants within the Borough at the time of the Election:

In Answer to which Evidence; the Sitting Member's Counsel produced a Survey of the Boundaries of the Borough, taken in the Year 1(121; by which it appeared^ That the Boundaries of the Borough go but to th# Castle Ditch: And,

Richard Younge and John Esquire, who

spoke for Forty years past, said, the Castle was always esteemed to be out of the Borough: And,

Mr. Willy mot f, the 'I own Clerk, said, That, at the Election preceding the last, the Castle was not insisted upon to be within the Borough.

As to the other Thirteen; John Woolmer, John William Etheridge, and Seven others, gave Evidence, on the Sitting Member's Part, That 'Three of them came into the Borough only upon Account of the Election, and went away again after it was over: That another was a Pauper; and another, who claimed as a Freeman, was relused his Freedom by the Mayor, because he served only Six Years of his Apprenticeship, and then left his Master; though his Master went with him to desire his Freedom, and declared himself satisfied with his Service: And,

That the other Flight were only Lodgers in the Borough at the time of the Election, and paid no Rates.

This Witness also said, he had looked over this Poll, and was sure there are above Fifty polled for the Sitting Member, and as many for the Petitioner, who were determined to have no Right by the last Resolution of the House; and were objected to at the former Poll; and were now again objected to at this Poll: And that the same Person who made that former Return is now Mayor again, and made the present Return.

That, upon Examination of the whole Matter, it appeared to the Committee, That the Burthen of the capital Debt, now due from the said City, with the growing Interest thereon, will disable the said City to perfect these Undertakings; and to carry on, and complete, several other necessary Works proposed to be done for the Service of the Town, and the Publick; unless the Term granted by the last mentioned Act be enlarged; and the same be made effectual, by subjecting the Brewers in the Confines to the Payment of the said Duty: Which is what is prayed for by the several Petitions referred to the Consideration of this Committee.

The House being acquainted, That the Committee of Privileges and Elections did, Yesterday, pursuant to the Order uf the House, proceed upon hearing the Matter, touching the Election for the Borough of in the County of Warwick ;but did not go through the same;

Mr. Gybbon, according to Order, reported, from the

Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Tanmorth, in the Counties of Stafford and Warwick,

and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's T able: Where the same was read: And the Report and Resolutions are as follow;

Upon the Petition of Richard Swyttfen and John Jatxis Esquires, complaining of an undue Election and Return of the honourable Willoughby and

Samuel Bracebridge Esquires to serve for the said Borough:

That the Petitioners Counsel wayed the Matter of the Petition, as to Mr. Jarvis; and admitted Mr. JWilloughby to be duly ejected.

That the Election was disputed between Mr. Suynfen

and Mr. Bracebridge; and the Right of Election was

controverted.

The Petitioners Counsel insisted, That Tamarorl is a Borough by Prescription; and that the Right of Election is in the Inhabitants pay ing Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms:

The Sitting Member's Counsel insisted. That the Right of Election is in the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot; and in such Freeholders who have Freeholds in the Borough, whether resident in the Borough or not.

That the Petitioners Counsel called Charles Wilcox, Fisher Littleton Esquire, Joseph Os-

borne and Richard Batman: M ho spoke for upwards of Fifty Years past; and said, some of their own Knowledge, others as they had heard ancient Inhabitants, who are since dead, declare, That, anciently, the Freeholders w ho were not Inhabitants in the Borough, did not vote in Elections: That the Freeholders were fivst brought in about Forty Years ago, to carry Sir 2 Thymic'* Election, by Peru ell his Steward, who was one of the Bailitfs; but they were then objected to, and opposed, by the other Bailiff, who refused to sign the Return; and they were also objected to, and opposed, by the Inhabitants; and were again opposed in the next Election; and then taken in a By-paper:

The Witnesses confessed, That the Freeholders had voted ever since; and had sometimes carried the Election by their making a Majority; but that the Inhabitants had always objected against their voting.

That the Sitting Member's Counsel called,

Samuel Twigg: M ho said, the Freeholders had voted in all Elections for Sixty Years past.

John Butler, and Samuel Bu spoke for Twenty Years past; and said, That, in all Elections in that time, the Freeholders had voted; and had sometimes carried the Election by their making the Majority.

Then the Petitioners Counsel admitted, That the Freeholders had voted since the Resolution of the House in 1698; but argued against their voting, as being an Innovation upon the ancient Right of the Borough, and inconvenient in respect of multiplying Freeholds: That the Sitting Member's Counsel denied, that any such Inconvenience appeared; and insisted on the Freeholders Right to vote; and that there was no Reason now' to vary the former Resolution of the House, of 17th of March 1698; when it was resolved, That the Right of Election was in the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot; and in such Persons as had Freeholds within the Borough, whether resident in tl)e Borough, or not.

Thereupon the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Tanneorth is in the Inhabitants, being Housholders, paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Aims.

Appendix, N* I.

Report, 1

Fo the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury, by Humphry Brent, one of the Commissioners of the Customs in Scotland) of Frauds in the Tobacco Trade.

May it please your Lordships,

In Obedience to your Lordships Commands, of thq 4th May last, signified by Mr. tValpole, to the Commissioners of the Customs, That it was your Lordships Pleasure I should survey the Ports, and see the new Surveyors put in a regular Method, in their respective Stations; I set out from Edinburgh the 30th of May last^ and did not return till the 18th of July, believing your Lordships might dispense with my Attendance at the Board, if I could be able, in my Survey, to make any Discovery of the Frauds complained of, in the several Memorials of the Merchants of Bristol, Liverpool, and Hlutehaven; an Inquiry which hath been often pressed, and recommended, by your Lordships.

I have, as 1 was commanded, seen every one of the Four new Surveyors stationed at their respective Posts, and given them the best Instructions I was capable of; by which, I humbly conceive, they will hereafter be able, if they are diligent and faithful in their Trusts, to prevent those gross Frauds, that, in the Progress of my Sur-Vol. 20.

vey and Inquiry, I found had been committed in the Tobafcctf Tobacco Trade. IraUe,

Upon my coming to Glasgow, Port Glasgow, ana Greenock, I acquainted the Officers with the several Complaints exhibited against them by the English Merchants, and earnestly pressed them to make a Discovery of the Frauds; offering them, at the same time, to intercede for their Remission, if they had been themselves guilty: From some, I had an Acknowledgment, That; a Turn of the Scale, when a Hogshead was milch damaged, had been given the Merchant, of about 16 Pounds Weight, besides the Allowances by Law; and from others, many Arguments, to make me believe the Rise of the Clamour proceeded from Jealousy in Trade; but none, as I remember, would say, but that all the Officers were Men of Integrity, and never privy to any Design in Prejudice of Jiis Majesty's Revenue. I must do Mr. Grahame, Collector of Port Glasgow, the Justice to say, he was of Opinion such great Quantities bf Tobacco could not be sent from Scotland into England without some unwarrantable Allowance at the Scale:

But I could not think these Answers sufficient; and therefore I entered upon a Work, which, I most humbly presume, will give a great Insight into the T Frauds.

The Merchants at Glasgow are the principal tm-‘ porters of Tobacco: The Places of Discharge are, Poi't Glasgow, the chief Port; and Greenock, its Member, but Two Miles from it: After the Duty is paid, or, for the most part, secured, at Importation, they sent, by Permit, all their Tobacco, in Lighters, to the Town' of Glasgow, for dressing, except where an immediate Exportation is intended; and from thence it is sent, by'

Permit, to any Part of the Kingdom of South or North Britain, for Exportation, or Home Consumption: I therefore directed the principal Officers of Port Glasgow, Greenock, and the Collector of Glasgow Town, to prepare me several Accounts, of different Years, of Tobacco imported, exported, sent Coast-ways, by Land-carriage, &c.; which appearing too voluminous, I have, instead of the Accounts themselves, which I am read/ to produce, annexed the Titles of them to my Report.

It is answered; .;

1st, That the Instances to be given of such Exportation are very few, and the Quantity inconsiderable; neither is it to be understood, how a Merchant in Scotland, in the fair Way of Trade, can find his Account in importing Tobacco there, then sending it to London, or Bristol, and from thence exporting it to foreign Parts, when the same might have been more easily done at the Place of Importation, with less Hazard and Expence.

2dly, That no Part of that great Quantity of Tobacco sent into England could have been the Damages, and 8 per ContS allowed at Importation; ~ for, as the Money paid for the Duties since the 1st of August 1716 is so inconsiderable, the Merchants of Scotland must, at least, have retained those Advantages, to answer their own Consumption.

Appendix, N° If#

May it please your Lordships,

We have received your Lordships Orders of Refer* ence, on the annexed Petition of sundry Merchants of Bristol, concerned in the Importation of Tobacco; and on the annexed Memorial of the Mayor, Aldermen, and other Merchants, of Leverpooky in relation to the Tobacco Trade; and also, on the annexed Me- morial of the Merchants of Whitehaven, relating to the'

Duties on Tobacco; wherein they set forth, That great Quantities of Tobacco are brought to South Britain from North Britain, and sold in some Places at a lower Price than is consistent with the Payment of his Majesty's Duties, and other necessary Charges of Importation; and at other Places, for less than the Duties; which Practice, they apprehend, must be carried on by Means of Frauds committed in Scotland, by undue Methods used in weighing the Tobacco, at Importation: And therefore the Petitioners desire, That such Accounts be laid before your Lordships, as may make the Fraud appear; and also propose, That the Duties on Tobacco imported may be lessened, as a Means to prevent the Persons concerned from committing the Frauds now used in the Tobacco Trade, by running, re-landing, and short-weighing, for the future; and that Power may be given to the Officers of the Customs, to examine Sailors, and others, upon Oath; allowing a reasonable Reward for Discovery of Frauds, in order to detect the same: Your Lordships directing us to consider the said Petition and Memorials; and to report the several Cases, with our Opinion;

We humbly report, That the Merchants of Bristol trading in Tobacco did, some time since, by their1 Memorial, transmitted to us by the principal Officers of that Port, represent the Hardships they laboured under in their Trade, occasioned by large Quantities of Tobacco brought thither, Coast-ways, from Scotland; alleging, That the same was sold for less than what they paid Duty and Freight; whereby the First Cost was intirely sunk:

That the Methods made use of in Scotland, as it was generally said, were such as these; viz. they make their Tobacco as heavy, or heavier, in Virginia, than other Traders commonly do; and, at the Importation, they are informed, the Land-waiters give them about Half of the Weight at the King's Beam; That, near as much as they enter, they export to foreign Pails,

and Numbers, by which the Tobacco is imported, are rased out, and the Hogsheads indorsed on the Cocquets, as rc-packed; whereas it is visible, the Package is the same, commonly, as at the First Importation:

And the said Officers of Bristol acquainted us, That they had examined into the said Affair; and it appeared to them, That York River Tobacco, when imported directly to Bristol, and all Duties paid in Money, stands the Merchant in 8d. per Pound, including all Charges; whereas the same Sort of Tobacco, when brought Coast-ways from Glasgow, is commonly sold at Bristol, free of all Damage, for 7 d per Pound, and under: That such Tobacco appears, by the Cocquets, to have the Duties only secured; which must render it f ])er Pound dearer to the Importer than when paid: The said Officers further certify, That they are informed the Sellers of the Tobacco from Scotland declare, it cannot be exported by Debenture, notwithstanding it appears, by the Cocquets, to be in time.

We further report, That on Receipt of the said Letter and Representation, we directed the Officers of Leverpoole and Whitehaven to inquire, and report to us, the Reasons w by such great Quantities of Tobacco w'ere brought to their Ports from North Britain; what Tobacco entered from the Plantations sold for, when the Duties were paid, or secured; and at wffiat Price Tobacco brought from Scotland was sold.

In Answer where to, the Officers of Leverpoole certified us, That the Tobacco Trade increases in North Britain, and lessens very much at Levcrpoole: That it is near lost at Lancaster and Whitehaven: That the Merchants of Levcrpoole say, they buy their Tobacco cheaper in Virginia than the Scotch do: That the Scotch w ill give any Price almost to have Tobacco; and the Leverpoole Ships many time come home halffreighted, or less: That the Prices of Tobacco imported into Leverpoole, Duties paid, or secured, are from 7 to 8 d.\ per Pound for Aronoco, and sweet-scented, from 9 d. \ to 10 d.\ per Pound: That the Merchants there now scarce sell any Tobacco within Land, as formerly: That what is consigned to Levcrpoole from North Britain, is sold at least 1 d. per Pound cheaper, besides the Carriage: That some of the Leverpoole Merchants have bought Tobacco in North Britain, paid Freight and Carriage, and can get more by it than by importing it from Virginia, anti yet sell it 1 d. per Pound cheaper than what they import: That the Scotch sell their Tobacco to Brest on, Manchester, and many Parts of Yorkshire, at least 1 d. per Pound cheaper than the Leverpoole Merchants can afford it, and yet pay 1 d. per Pound for Carriage.

The Officers of Whitehaven certified us, That the Trade of Glasgow is mostly carried on by Ships and Sailors hired from Whitehaven: That the Merchants of Glasgow generally give from \os. to 20 s. per Ton more Freight, than is given by the Merchants of Whitehaven: That the Scotch Cargoes outwards consist of great Quantities of English Manufactures, attended with the Charge of Land-carriage, from the inland Tow ns in South Britain to North Britain: And the said Officers certify, they are well assured the Scotch pay as great, if not greater, Prices for their Tobacco in Virginia and Maryland, than the English; and, of late Years, the Scotch Merchants have been the Occasion of making the Commodity dearer there than usual: That the Scotch send large Quantities of Tobacco over the Borders near Carlisle, as also through Northumberland, into South Britain, for the Supply of the Neighbourhood about Whitehaven, and almost all ' Places in the Northern Counties; where, after the Expence of Land-carriage, they sell it for 6 d. \ per Pound, and under; the Effects of which arc felt by the Mer-

portation: That the Masters of Ships, and Sailors, of Whitehaven, employed in the Scotch Service, do affirm, that the Merchants in Scotland seldom permit them to be present at the weighing of Tobacco at the Kings Scales; which, at Glasgow, as they further say, is in an inclosed Yard, where none are admitted, but who they think proper; and which makes the said Masters and Sailors, when they sell their Portage Tobacco, always insist of being paid for what it weighs when it comes into the Merchants Cellar^ and not at the King's Beam > And that, on dividing of Cargoes in Partnership, this Method of re-weighing is generally practised; and the Weight then taken, they say, exceeds that in the Land-waiters Book§; because a Portage Bill made out iflr, Scot hind does not amount to above -}ds, or -£ths, of a Portage Bill made out in England, on the like Number of Hogsheads, notwithstanding the y were sensible the Scotch make their Hogsheads in Virginia as heavy as -possible: The Officers of Whitehaven have likewise certified, That the Prices of Tobacco there, imported from the Plantations, aFe, when the Duties are paid,' or secured, generally from 7d. to 8 d. \ per Pound Weight.

From whence we humbly observe, That if appears, by the Accounts of the Officers, as well as from w hat is contained in the Petition and Memorials, that great Quantities of Tobacco are brought from North Britain to South Britain, and sold for less tiiarr the Duties i From whence it is plain, that such Tobacco had not paid the Duties; so that, unless some effectual Provison be made for tUS putting a Stop to so mischievous a Practice, the Tobacco Trade will be unavoidably lost to England, and the Revenue greatly diminished in-its Duties.

The only Remedy which the Merchants, who attended us on this Occasion, have proposed, is, That annual Accounts be laid before your Lordships, by the Commissioners of tlte Customs in North Britain, of all the Tobacco imported into North Britain since the Union; expressing the Number of Hogsheads; the Weights1 of the Tobacco entered; and how much-allowed for Damage not cut off; together with an Account of all the Tobacco annually exported from tlienee, during the same time:

And also an Account of all Tobacco sent from North Britain'to South Britain, Coast-ways, during the same time; orrwhat Vessel; and to what Place::

And that tire like Account be laid before your Lordships,' quarterly, for the future, to be compared, with the Accounts kept here, of Tobacco brought here fr.om North Britain since the Union; and the Account of Tobacco exported to Scotland the 2d or 3d Year before the Union; by which their Consumption may be computed; and by which, they say it will appear, if w hat they export to foreign Parts, and what they bring Coast-ways, exceeds the Quantity imported, the Crown is defrauded on so much, besides the Consumption in Scotland;

As to which Accounts, when prepared, they will only shew*, that Frauds are committed in the Tobacco Trade, in North Britain; which, we are humbly of Opinion, is sufficiently proved already, by the lore-going Reports from the Officers; but, at the Request of the Merchants, we thought proper to lay their Pro- posal before your Lordships:

But, as these Frauds are committed in North Britainf by the clandestine Running of great. Quantities of Tobacco, or by re-landing the same, or from the Want of due Care in weighing the Tobacco at Importation; and in regard the Management thereof is under the Commissioners

p Geo. I. 24° — -250 Januarii: iod

Commissioners in Scotland; we humbly offer, That the said Petition and Memorials of the English Merchants trading in Tobacco be referred to that Board, for their Care therein:

As to what the Merchants of Whitehaven propose, That the Officers of the Customs be impowered to examine the Sailors, and others, upon Oath; and to allow a reasonable Reward for Discovery of Frauds; we think it a Proposal of an extraordinary Nature, and, if it should be obtained, will not answer what is intended by it.

All which is huiribjy submitted to your Lordships Consideration.

That it appeared further to the Committee; That several Officers in the Port of Glasgow, in a Representation by them made to David Graham Esquire, inspector General of Tobaccoes imported into Scotland, allowed, That there had been, and were, great Abuses in the Importation of Tobacco into North Britain.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That great and notorious Frauds have been committed, upon the Importation of Tobacco into that Part of Great Britain called Scotland\ by not duly paying the Customs thereon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That great Quantities of Tobacco, on which the Customs have not been duly paid, have been brought, by Land-carriage and Coast-ways, from that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, into that Part of Great Britain called England, to the very great Prejudice of the Revenue, and great Loss and Damage to the fair Importers of Tobacco from Virginia and Maryland into England.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some speedy and effectual Remedy be provided, to prevent the like Frauds for the future.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That a Bill be brought in for preventing Frauds and Abuses in the Tobacco Trade*

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to prepare Heads for the said Bill.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Upon the Petition of Delves Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir William lieyte Baronet, to serve for the said Borough:

That the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of this Petition.

That the Petitioner's Counsel alleged, They should make a Majority for the Petitioner, by taking from the Sitting Member's Poll, and adding to the Petitioner's; and that they could make good the other Allegations in the Petition; but should not proceed upon those other Allegations, unless they were forced to it by the Sitting Member's Counsel.

That the< Right of Election was'first controverted:

It was agreed by the Counsel oh both Sides, That Warwick is a Borough by Prescription; and has, Time out of Mind, sent Members! to Parliament:

And the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That the Right of Election is in the Commonalty; viz. the Inhabitants at large: But,

The Sitting Member's Counsel insisted, That the Right of Election is in such Persons only, as pay Scotland Lot for Houses or Lands within the Borough,

Robert Taylor, being called, said, He had long known this Borough; and had polled at an Election there Forty-two Years since, when Mr. Booth was a Candidate; and, at that Election, all Housholders and Freemen were polled, without any Objection, whether they paid Scotland Lot, or no; and he said, several who polled then, did not pay:

That, at the next Election, about Thirty Years since, when Mr. Colmore was a Candidate, all Housholders and Freemen voted: That several of them did not pay; and that there was no Talk of Scotters and Lotters then, nor till Mr. Booth came a Second time:

Being further examined, he said, That, at the before-mentioned Election, when Mr. Colmore was Candidate, none but Scotters and Lotters were polled by the Mayor:

That Copies of the following Returns were produced;

16 January 1700, } All which are lhus:

And the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That polling Scotters and Lotters only, was contrary to the Rights of the Borough; and not agreeable to the before-mentioned Resolution of the House.

That the Sitting Member's Counsel urged, That the Word " Commonalty," in that Resolution, has been always understood in the Borough to mean such Persons only, as paid to Church and Poor; and that the Constant Usage ever since that Resolution, now near 100 Years, has been, to poll such Persons only, and no others: And they called,

IVm. Colmore Esquire: Who spoke for 50 Years past; during all which time, he said, none were ever polled, at any Election, but those who paid to Church and Poor: That all others, whether Freemen or Inhabitants, if they did not pay, were constantly refused; and that those who lived out of the Borough, if they paid to Church and Poor within the Borough, were alwrays admitted to vote: That he had been several times chose Member of Parliament for the Borough; and that, whenever he was Candidate, the Mayor did not admit any to poll who did not pay:

That, at the Election mentioned by Robert Taylor, after the Mayor had closed his Poll of Scotters and Letters only, Sir Richard Newdigate, One of the Candidates, and Alderman Booth, went together, and took a private Poll of some Freemen, and other Inhabitants:

He confessed, That Inhabitants who did hot pay Scotland Lot, had often demanded to be polled; but said, That no Mayor had ever, in the time of his Memory, admitted any to Poll who did not pay: And that the Rule, and constant Usage, has been, to go by the Poors Rates, with which the Parish Officers always attend the Elections; and none were ever polled, in his Memory, but such as were in those Rates.

Mr. Richard Lane said, He had known the Borough Thirty Years; had been twice Mayor, once when an Election happened: That none were polled by him, nor by any other Mayor* in the time of his Knowledge, but such only as paid to Church and Poor; and that such as. paid, though they lived out of the Borough; were never refused or disputed:

That, at ;the present Election, hot above Two or Three Inhabitants, who did not pay Scotland Lot, came to demand to be polled; and they were drunk, and were not minded.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Warwick is in such Persons only as pay to Church and Poor in the 9aid Borough.

That, the Counsel being acquainted with this Resolution, the Petitioner's Counsel admitted. That the Sitting Member has a Majority upon that Foot;

And thereupon,

A, 1722.

The Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Sir William Keyte Baronet is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Wamick.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out these Words "such Persons only $s pay "to Church and Poor in;" and, instead thereof, to insert the Words "the Inhabitants of:"

And the Question being put, That the Words " such " Persons only as pay to Church and Poor in" do stand Part of the said Resolution;

The House divided.

The Noes go forth.

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for die Borough of Warwick is in such Persons only as pay to Church and Poor in the said Borough.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Sir William Keyte Baronet is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Warwick.

Mr. Hungerfoi'd reported, from the Committee appointed to inquire into the Project, commonly called The Harburgh Lottery, and all other foreign Lotteries, now carrying on in the City of London, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the said Committee have, with the utmost Diligence, endeavoured to find out by what Authority, and by virtue of what Instruments, the said Lottery was erected; in order to lay the same before the House; and to make the said Lottery, and the Management Vol. 20.

thereof, the more intelligible: But the Committee,

finding the y should meet with great Difficulties in obtaining such Instniments; and the more, for that One of the Persons, who, as your said Committee was informed, was capable of giving your Committee a very material Account of the Creation of the said Lottery, was withdrawn; and your Committee being unwilling to enter into the Examination of any Instruments, or Writings, which might be interpreted to be Part of his Majesty's German Administration; have contented themselves to lay only before the House the printed Copy of the Scheme of the said Lottery, with some Remarks thereon; and the Examinations of Witnesses, viva voce, relating the reto:

That the Scheme proposes, that f. 1,500,000. Sterling, or 16,500,000 Guilders should be subscribed; and that it was to be drawn at Harburgh in 5 Classes, 100,000 Tickets being to be drawn in each Class, at £. 3. pei' Ticket: and that every^erson subscribing was to pay 12 s. or 6 Guilders, for each Ticket, before the drawing each class of the said Lottery.

That £. 200,000. of the £. 300,000. in each Class, was to be divided in Lots to the fortunate Adventurers; which amounts to 1,000,000; to be deducted out of the whole Sum which was to be paid to the fortunate Adventurers.

It will be necessary, in order to infonn the House how the other £, 500,000. wras to be disposed of, to acquaint them with such Knowledge as the Committee could gain of the Nature and Establishment of the Company; not being able to see the Instruments by which it was granted.

It appeared to the Committee, That a Sum of £. 1,000,000 was subscribed, for to carry on a Trade between Great Britain, and his Majesty's Geivnan Dominions; and that 2 per Cent. was agreed to be paid in upon the Stock so subscribed; of which, a Sum of £. 13,000. or more was actually paid in Money; and £. 7,000, or more, was secured by Notes; £.400,000. whereof was subscribed for at first: and £. 100,000. Stock was sold at £ 15. 3$'. per Cent.; of which 2 per Cent, only was paid in to the Company; and the rest disposed of as follow; viz. £. 13. 3^. perCent. which amounted to £.13,150; £. 10,000. of which was given to Mr. Ntcclai, and £. 3,150. to Mr. Joules, for-their Services: And as to the £.13,000. paid in Money, at 2 per Cent. for Stock, as aforesaid, and £. 7,000. in Notes, the Committee could get no Account w hat was become of it; not being able to see their Books: Nor can your Committee learn what Number of Tickets have been delivered out, or w hat Money thereupon has been received, or what is become of what they have received.

The Committee thought it necessary to lay this Matter before the House, to inform them what was to be done with the other £. 500,000.

In the First Place, 5 per Cent. upon £. 1,500,000. which amounts to £.75,000; was to be deducted for Management; which, being taken out of the said £. 500,000. leaves £. 425,000; which Sum was to be incorporated into the Stock of the First Company, and to make a Part of a Capital of £. 1,500,000. as they apprehend; of which they could get no positive Information: But, whether the former Capital wfas intended to be so great, or only to consist of this £. 425,000. and the £. 1,000,000. which was before subscribed; it appears to us that a plain Fraud was intended, in joining this real Sum with an imaginary Subscription of which 2 per Cent. only was paid in, or secured; and that, probably, embezzled:

As to the further Particulars of the Lottery; the Committee beg Leave to refer to the printed Copy of the Scheme, which is hereunto annexed (N° 1.)

And, in order to inform the House more fully of the Subject-matter of the said Lottery, the Committee have thought fit to lay before the House the most material Parts of the Examinations themselves: Which are as follow.

Mr. Benjamin Joules informed your Committee, That he, the Examinant, had not the written Scheme of the Harburgh lottery; for that Air. Ridpath, who is Secretary to the said Lottery, has all the Writings and Accounts relating thereto; but that he had a printed Copy of the Scheme of the said Lottery, which he delivered to the Committee, and is hereunto annexed; and said, He takes it to be a true Copy of the written Scheme, which, as far as he knows, has been always in Ridpath's Hands.

That, in the 6th Article of a Charter for Commerce, granted by his Majesty as Duke and Elector of Brunswick, there is a Grant given for setting up a Lottery; which Grant was made to several Gentlemen, in Trust for the Benefit of the Examinant That he has seen the original Charter: That it bore Date about the latter End of November 1720: and that it specifies the Lottery to be drawn at Hanover: That, the Grant of the Lottery was made to the Examinant, about this Time 12 Months:

That, when Sir Thomas Webster proposed to make the Examinant Recompence for his said Right in the Charter, as to the Grant of the Lottery; Sir Thomas said, That they were agreed to give the Examinant a Gratuity, and offered him £.10,000; and the Examinant made Answer, He would leave it to them; and did accept of the £. 10,000. for assigning his said Right; which Assignment was made to several Persons, in Trust for the Company:

That there were 5 Classes in the said Lottery; and that he was to receive the £. 10,000. at 5 several Payments, at £. 2,000. each Payment, before the drawing each Class of the said Lottery:

That the Payment of the Money is secured to the Examinant, by Articles in Writing, bearing Date the 16th October 1722, which he delivered to the Committee, under the Hands and Seals of the Persons, to whom the Profits of the Lottery are conveyed, in Trust for the Company; and that it appears thereby, that the Examinant was to be paid the £. 10,000. as before-mentioned:

That it likewise appears, by the Recital of the said Articles, that the Profits of the said Lottery, which are purchased of him for the Sum before-mentioned, was, by an Agreement made at Hanover, bearing Date the 14th November 1720, N.S. previously granted to the said Examinant Benjamin Joules:

Being shewn one of the Tickets of the said Lottery, N° 17, M. 211, to which the Examinants Name is printed as Treasurer;

Said, That the Tickets were issued by his Privity and Consent; and that he believes they were not delivered out numerically:

That he is not Treasurer to the Trustees for the Lottery; for that they act themselves as Treasurers, alternatively, in manner following; viz.

That there are Two Iron Chests; and that Two of the Trustees have each of them a Key, and the Secretory has another; and that the Trustees deliver over their Keys to the next that wait, and then they are answerable no longer.

That the Two Trustees and Secretary, when in waiting, had it in their Power to take out the Effects, that ,w«re in those Chests:

That there are 20 Trustees; but some of them are in Germany; and those that are here now, are Lord Barrington, William Sterling, Sir John Hartop, Benja. Smith, Chr. Fred. Kreinberg, Benja. Burroughs, John Ixmdon, John Thompson, Fiennes Harrison, Henry Bendish, Peter Hartop, # Foster, Win. Squire, Benja. Joules the Examinant, Edward Richter, John Manley, John Caszvall: That every one of the said Trustees have accepted the Trust, except Mr. John Matdey, Mr. Henry Bendish, and Mr. Foster, by signing the Counterpart of the Assignment of the Lottery; but that Lord Barrington, Sir John Hartop, and Mr. Henry Bendish, never acted:

That he believes, That all the Trustees he has named who have acted, have had the Keys of the Chests:

That there were to be printed .500,000 Tickets: and the Examinant believes most of them are printed: and that they are printed upon Tower-hill', and that the Examinant believes Mr. Billingsley did agree for the printing the m: That the Tickets were brought to the York Buildings House, and locked up in the Iron Chests by the said Trustees, who deliver them out, and receive the Money for them. That he does not know what Number of Tickets have been issued out, nor w hat Sums of Money received for Tickets delivered; for that he never saw' any Account of it:

That he believes, Mr. Ridpath keeps die Account of the Money received:

That if the Lottery should take place, the Stock would be worth 29 per Cent.: That the whole Stock is called £. 1,500,000. Stock; and that it was as large before the new Proprietors came in: That 2 per Cent, is paid in upon £.1,000,000; in Money, £. 13,000; in Notes, £. 7,000; which were paid to the Examinant as Treasurer to the Company:

Being examined by what Authority he was Treasurer, said, He w'as appointed Treasurer by the Charter of the King; and that his Name is in die Warrant of the King as Treasurer:

Being asked, how he came to take Notes; declared, He received Orders from some of the Directors to take them; and that the Notes are some of dieir own:

That the Notes are in the Custody of Ridpath; for that he, the Examinant, has accounted with the Company, and delivered the Account to him the said Ridpath.

Mr. Geo. Ridpath, Secretary to the Trustees for the Harburgh Lottery, being examined as to the Scheme of the said Lottery, said, That the Calculations of the Lottery agree with the Scheme that was approved by his Majesty:

That there is a Power to erect a Lottery by the 6th Article of a Charter granted by his Majesty, which was in order to clear the River Elbe.

That he cannot be positive who formed the Lottery;' but that he has heard, that Mr. Billingsley formed the Scheme of it:

Being asked, who wras the Person that first handed the Scheme to the Examinant; said, That he saw it in Company, but cannot tell who brought it to the Company: That Lord Barrington, and some others, w ere then present; and that it did appear to have his Majesty's Sign Manual, and Seal of the Electorate, when it was first handed to the Company, as a Company; but that the Examinant, previous to that, saw the Scheme in the Hands of Mr. Billingsley, whom he takes to be chief Project or; and that he is not certain it was the same Scheme as is printed; and that, then, it neither had his Majesty's Sign Manual, nor the Privy Seal of the Electorate:

That, when this Scheme was projected, the Profits of the Lottery were Mr. Jouless, by an Agreement made at Hanover, for which he was to clear and deepen the River Elbe: And that Lord Barrington, Sir Alexander Cairnes, Mr. Nicolai, Mr. Alderman Bay Us, Mr. Fiennes Harrison, and Mr. Mount, made that Agreement with him; which was confirmed by the Company, Nernine contradicente; and is entered in the Minutes: That Mr. Joules petitioned his Majesty for an Order to issue the Lottery; but that it was previously granted to him by a Vote of the Company:

That, since he was Secretary, there has been Minutes kept, which is since the Charter was granted for the Commerce Company, in which there is a Power to erect a Lottery:

Being desired to produce the Charters, Books, and Papers, relating to the Lottery; said, That he has not his Majesty's Leave to produce them; and desired the Committee would not put him upon Difficulties:

Being again asked, Whether he would not deliver the Papers; said, That he was very willing to deliver the Papers, if it was not for the Difficulties he has before mentioned; and that he is afraid those Difficulties

There being an Advertisement in Yesternight's St,

The Lottery will be publicity drawn at in the Manner of the State Lotteries drawn in England; except that, in this, the Prizes will be drawn first, and the 333,335 remaining Numbers will be the Blanks.

The whole Lottery will be drawn in Presence of some of the Trustees appointed by Ins Majesty' who, with all the Officers, will be sworn to see Justice done.

The Prizes and Numbers will be proclaimed twice, signed by Two of the Trustees,' and filed in the same Order they shall be drawn.

To the first-drawn Prize, in each Part, w ill be added

£. 101. Sterling, or 1,111 Guilders; and to the last-‘drawn Prize, in each of the Five Parts, wiif be added

£. 500. Sterling, or 5,500 Guilders.

If any of the subsequent Payments be not made by the Adventurers, according to the Scheme, the Money by them paid will be forfeited, and their Numbers will be disposed of to others.

After the Drawing of each Part, the Adventurers, in Office Hours, may check and settle their Tickets by the Trustees Books.

There will be a Stamp on the Tickets for each Payment.

The Adventurers may examine which of their Numbers are drawn, paying 6 d.Sterling, or 51 Stivers, for every Six Tickets so examined.

The Tickets will be printed on Paper made on Purpose for the Company, and signed by the Treasurer.

The Numbers will" be writ in Words at Length, and Figures; and the Tickets will have sufficient Checks to prevent Impositions.

The Prizes will be paid, within One Month after they arc adjusted, to such as have completed their Payments, without any Deduction; and, as soon as each Part shall be drawn, the Trustees will proceed to examine and certify them.

The Company will give £. 3* of their capital Stock to every' Blank.

That the Stock may be made more valuable, all the Profits arising from this Scheme of the Lottery', except 5 per Cent, for erecting, managing, mid drawing, the same, excepted in his Majesty's said Approbation, will be added to the Stock, to enable them to carry on a beneficial Trade between Great Britain, Germany, anti other Parts, pursuant to their Charter, and the Privileges therein granted the Company by his Majesty- m,

rlo the Three last-drawn Blanks will be added the Three following Sums; viz. to the First of the said Thrte, £.3,000, Sterling, or 33,000 Guilders; to the

Second, £. 7,600. Sterling, or 77,000 Guilders; and

to the last-drawn Blank, £. 10,000. Sterling, or 110,000 Guilders; according to the foregoing Scheme of tire whole Lottery.

That the Adventurers may be present, publick Notice shall be given when all the Numbers will be put into the great Wheel A; and the Benefits, in Five Parts, at Five several Times, into the lesser Wheel B; arid mixed as equally as possible.

After the Prizes shall be drawn, the Blanks will be drawn, proclaimed and published; that every one may be satisfied, that their Numbers were put into the Wheel.

The Prizes will be paid after the Drawing of each Part, within One Month after they shall be brought in, and examined, without any Deductions; except to complete £. 3. Sterling, or 33 Guilders, for every

Ticket.
