Mr. Bemlish, Mr. Manley, Mr. Hartop, Mr. Harrison,

Mr. Burroughs, and Mr. Squire, be of the said Committee; and to report to the Directors:

The Preamble to be as follows:

It having been reported to the Directors, That the English Ministers think it neither legal nor prudent to grant a British Charter to the Company, as the Gennan Charter now runs; the Committee, being very desirous, out of the Duty they have for his Majesty, and the due Regard they have to the Company, and this Undertaking, to remove all the Difficulties, that the English Ministers apprehend to be in the Way of granting k British Charter, on the Foot of the present German Charter, do propose the following Plan; which, though it will take from the Company one of the most valuable Privileges, which they have acquired by their Interest, and by a considerable Expence of Time and Money; yet ho[>e it may be accepted by the Company, in order to remove the aforesaid Difficulties, on the one Hand, which the English Ministers apprehend might arise to his Majesty's Administration, if a British Charter should be granted to the Company, whilst they remain possessed of that Privilege, in this difficult Conjuncture; and to prevent Uie great Discontents and Clamours, on the other Hand, that may arise, if this Undertaking should not proceed, for want of a British Charter, on which they

have

That they be continued z.Gei'man Company, with these lowers following, in their said Charter:

3d, With a Power for their sole or exclusive exercising and enjoying all other Privileges contained in their said present German Charter; and such farther Privileges as his Majesty shall be pleased to grant; except,

A PETIT ION of many of the Inhabitants of the Tobacco ancient Borough of Salop, who are concerned in Trade, making or trading in the Woollen Manufacture of those Parts, was presented to the House, and read; setting, forth. That we formerly sold great quantities of Cottons,"

Flannels, 8$c. for Virginia; which Trade, for some Years past, bath been dwindling away; the Cause whereof is now manifest, from what we observe in the Publick, relating to Frauds committed by the Tobacco Merchants in North Britain, by the great Quantities of Tobacco conveyed lfom North Britain into these Parts, and sold at excessive low Rates: And praying. That the House will be pleased to give a timely Check to these undue Practices; that so the-Government may receive its just Due; that Trade may return to its former Channel, and the Poor to their daily Labour.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Walpole reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commonalty, of the Borough and Town of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, in Common Council assembled, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, That, by the Act of Parliament mentioned in the said Petition, and passed in the 10th and 1 ith Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William ihs Third, several Duties upon Coals, and other Commodities, were thereby granted, for clearing,'tepairing, preserving, and maintaining, the Haven ana Piers of Great Yarmouth aforesaid, for the Term of 21 Years from the 24th Day of July 1699; and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; which Act is now expired.

That it further appeared to the Committee, That Unless the said Act be revived, and continued for a further Term of Years, the said Haven and Piers will fall to decay, and the Harbour be utterly lost; to the great Detriment of the Trade and Interest of the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, the City of Norwich, and the said Town and Port of Great Yarmouth.

Ordered, That J^eave I>£ given to bring in a Bill for reviving and continuing an Act, passed in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, for the clearing, repairing, preserving, and maintaining, the Haven and Piers of Great Yarmouth: And that Sir. Walpole} Mr. Townshend, Sir

Charles Turner, and Sir Erdmund Bacon, daprepare, rod bring in, the same. v

A Petition of the Mayor* Jurats, Freemen, and In- Dover and habitants, of the ancient Town and Port of Rye, in Sus~ sex, in behalf of themselves, and many Hundred of his WSr Majesty's faithful Subjects, was presented to the House* and read; setting forth, That the Port of Rye, in Sussexh is the only Harbour remaining on the Coast of Sussex and Kent, from Portsmouth to Dover: That the said Harbour lies very convenient for the Ships, which pass up and down the Chanel, to save themselves in Stress of Weather, and from the Enemy in time of War: That the said Harbour is opposite to Diepe, and other considerable Ports of France; and been of great JJse to the Navigation of this Kingdom; has often received the Ships of War, and many large Ships built in the said Port; as plainly appears from the Examinations and Report laid before the House the 28th January 1720: That the Flood-gates and Cross-walls, of late Years erected, have so much hindered the Flowing and Reflowing of the Sea, that there is not sufficient Back-water to drive out again the Slub, w'hich, by Force of the Tide, is constantly brought into the said Harbour, and so daily swerves up the same, that, unless Care be taken, it will be totally destroyed; to the great Prejudice of the Fishery of the said Port of Rye, whence the City of London hath a constant Supply: That the Method proposed by the Commissioners of his Majesty's Navy, and Masters of Trinity-house, delivered with the Report aforesaid, to let the Tide have its proper Flux and Reflux, w'ould not only preserve the said Harbour, but recover its ancient Depth of Water: And praying this House to take such Measures as will best conduce to so great and national a Good, as the restoring of this ancient Harbour, for the Safety of the Navigation of this Kingdom; which, without immediate Care, will be inevitably lost.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir Basil Dixwell Baronet, and other Assistants, incorporated for the Preservation of Dover Harbour, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of the said Petition; and report the same, as it shall appeal' to them, to the House.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, Freemen, and other Dittos Inhabitants, of the Town and Port of Hastings, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there is no Harbour remaining for the Convenience of Shipping on the Coast of Sussex and Kent, from Portsmouth to Dover, except that of the Town of Rye; and which is of late Years, gone to Decay, and daily swerves up with Slub; That, unless some Care is taken, it must soon be rendered useless: That the said Harbour hath been of great Use for Ships passing up and down the Chanel in stormy Weather; and that, since it hath gone to Decay, there have been several Instances of Ships perishing, and a great Number of Men losing their Lives; That, the said Harbour lies opposite to Diepe, and other Places of France; and hath been formerly the Preservation of many Ships from falling into the Enemies Hands in time of War; and hath often received great Ships belonging to the Royal Navy: That the Reason of the said Harbours going to Decay is, by the Commissioners of Sewers erecting Cross-walls, and making Sluices; which prevents the Flux and Reflux of the Sea; by means thereof there is not sufficient Backwater to drive out the Slub, which the Tide brings up; and the Loss of the said Harbour will not only be to the Prejudice of Navigation and Trade of this Part of the County of Sussex, but to the Ruin of the Fishery of this Town, on which it chiefly depends: And praying this House to take the same into Consideration; and that such proper Methods may be taken, as shall be thought proper for restoring and continuing; the said ancient Harbour, so much for the Advantage and Security of Navigation and Trade.

his Majesty's good and faithful Subjects was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Town of Winchelsea is situate on the South-west Side of a certain Chanel called Winchehea Chanel, that runs from the Harbour of Rye, close by the said Town, into the Levels of Brede, and other Levels; in which said Chanel, several Hovs, and other Vessels, of upwards of One hundred Tons Burthen, have, till very:lately, passed and repassed, loaded and unloaded, with great Quantities of Corn, Coals, Timber, and other Goods: That the Flood-gates, and Cross-walls, which have been erected of late Years, on the North-east Side of the 9aid Harbour, very much hinders the Flux and Reflux of the Sea: That there is not sufficient Back-water to carry out the Slub, that by Force of the Tide is constantly brought into the said Harbour and Chanel; so that the same daily swerves up, by reason none but small Vessels can pass up and down the said Chanel: That, if some speedy Care be not taken, the said Harbour and Chanel will be destroyed; to the Prejudice of Navigation in general, as well as the Trade of the said Town, and Places adjoining, in particular: That the Petitioners conceive, That if the Flood-gates were removed, and inside Walls made with a Bason to receive the Saltwater, to let the Tide have its ancient Course, it would preserve the said Harbour and Chanel, and bring them to their ancient Goodness, and Depth of Water; And praying, That the House will be pleased to take such Ways and Means, as they shall think proper, for the restoring of the said Harbour and Chanel to their ancient Goodness.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir Basil! Dinvell Baronet, and others, Assistants incorporated for the Preservation of Dover Harbour, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Mr. Gybbon, according to Order, reported, from the Dorchester Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as Election, it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Dorchester, in the County of Dorset, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which he read jn his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the said Report and Resolution is as followeth; viz.

Upon the Petition of Wm. Chappie Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Ed? mund Morton Pleydell Esquire, to serve for the said Borough:

That the Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Inhabitants of the Borough who pay to Church and Poor, in respect of their personal Estates; and in such Persons as pay to Church and Poor, in respect of their real Estates within the Borough.

The Poll was,

For the Sitting Member - - 147:

For the Petitioner - - - 138.

The Petitioner s Counsel com plained,*That great £ak; tiality had been used in making up the Rates, of late Years, contrary to the ancient Practice in the Borough; and that Persons were put in or out, just as it served a Turn in Elections: And they called,

Mr. Peter Templeman: Who said, That before the Year 1710, for 30 Years, to his Knowledge, the Parish Officers were constantly chose by the Parishioners, at a Vestry, in Easter Week; and the Rates were always settled by common Consent of the ParishioiTers assembled in Vestry, upon Notice given in the Church; but, about that Year, there being a great Contest, touching an Election, the Justices of Peace took upon them to nominate the Parish Officers, and make the Rates according to their own Interest; and have since continued to do so: -j

He also said, upon Inspection of the Rates for several Years past, That he found, in some Years, several Persons Names inserted with Blanks for Sums, or Cyphers instead of Sums.

That the Petitioners Counsel said, They should take 19 from the Sitting Member's Poll; and add to the Petitioner's Poll 8; Four of which were rated; and the

As to the 19 objected to; That the 4th, John Bartlett, is a Maltster of Sub-

Mr. Templeman said, That Four of them were but stance; has Two Tenements of his own; but is not Day Labourers, or Persons in mean Circumstances; and rated: That these Four came to Poll for the Petitioner; that their Rates were paid by others: He produced Two and the Mayor refusing the Two first, because they were Receipts, by which it appeared, that Edmund Watts not rated, and declaring he would poll npne, but those paid for those Four, and for Five others, in 1716; and who were in the Rates, the other Two, hearing that, did for the same Four, and Four others, in 1717: And said, not tender their Votes to the Mayor; but declared, they Mr. Trenchard. a little before his Death, declared. And, as to the other Fifteen,

Mr. Templeman said, That William Smith and John Ward were not Housekeepers, but Gentlemen's Servants:

That, upon inspecting the Rates, on this Occasion, he found,

That William Gawler was not rated till 1721; but the House he voted for was before rated in the Name of Richard Gawler:

That Joseph Bishop junior was not rated till 1721; and is not in the Church Rate:

That Gabriel Gould, Taylor, is not in the Church Rate for 1721; but is in the Poors Rates for that Year; and was not rated before:

That Nicholas Doule is not in the Church Rate for 1721; but is put into the Poors Rate for that Year; after the Death of his Father, who paid the Rates in his Dfe-time: And Mr. Templeman said, Doule the Father was a substantial Man, and so is the Voter his Son:

That Mr. Robert Brampton, a Clergyman, is rated for the Year 1721; but had been left out of the Rates several Years: He was not an Inhabitant at the time of the Election; is Incumbent on a Living 12 Miles off; has another Living within a Mile of the Town; is rated for personal Estate; and that the House he comes to is his Mother-in-law's House, as the Witness believed:

That Richard Hopkins was not rated before 1721: He rents a House of £. 10 a Year; is in good Business; and has been in the Town 2 or 3 Years:

That the First time Richard Rose was rated, was in the Year 1720; and he then paid only Half the Rate; but the Witness could not say, whether that Rate was for a whole Year, or for Half a Year:

That Mr. Richard Hutchings was upon no Rate before 1721: He has been Minister of the Parish, and lived there Twenty Years; has voted in all Elections, without Objection; but his Living was not more than £. 9. 6s. id. per Annum, before it received Two Augmentations, of £. 10. per Annum each, from the late Queen's Bounty: That James Hounsle was not rated till 1721; he is rated for Land, which was before rated in another Name: And the Witness said, He had heard that Jiounsle had bought it:

That Edward Stricldand is rated for Lands; but not before 1721:

That John Bamfylde was no Inhabitant in the Borough, at the time of the Election, but lived a Mile off: His Name is upon the Rate for 1721, but not before: And that the House he is rated for, is his Father-in-law's House:

That Mr. John Gundry is rated for Lands; but has none within the Borough: That he has lived there Five or Six Years; has 2 or £300 a Year Estate, but no Lands in the Borough: That he is rated for Lands, and voted for Lands:

That John Primmer s Name is not in the Rates: That the Lands he voted for go by the Name of John Collins' Land: That Primmer was objected to at the Poll, and allowed, upon producing his Title.

To add 8 to the Petitioner's Poll;

George Batt and Mr. Templeman gave Evidence, That Three of them were in former Rates, and voted, in the former Election, for Mr. Janssen; and were, since that,

Mr. Templeman said, The other Four offered their Votes for the Petitioner; and were refused by the Mayor.

It was proved, That these Four were rated, and paid their Rates.

That, on the Sitting Member's Part, it was denied, by the Counsel, that there had been any Partiality, or ill Practice, in making the Rates: And the Counsel alleged, That it had been usual for the Clerks, who ingrossed the Rates, to leave Blanks for Sums, which w ere Sways filled up in the Vestry, with Figures or Cyphers, as the Parishioners thought good: And,

As to the 19 objected to;

For the first Five of them, objected to as not paying their Rates, the Sitting Member's Counsel offered 110 Evidence; but alleged, They were not disqualified by the Petitioner's Witness: And,

As to the rest;

Wm. Glisson, Overseer of the Poor, said, That John Ward, one of them, is Journeyman to a Grocer in the Town; and his Wages are £.30 a Year, as he had heard: And,

Being examined, as to the other 13, Glisson gave Evidence, That they were all rated to the Poor, some in their own Names, some in their Tenants; and that those. 13 Voters paid the Poors Rates to him in the Year 1721.

Besides which Evidence, the Sitting Members Counsel observed, That several of these Voters were not disqualified by the Petitioner's Evidence.

Against adding Five of the Eight, which the Petitioner would add to his Poll, the following Evidence was given;

Wm. Glisson said, That Three of them were struck out of the Rates, in the Vestry, 3 Years since; because, the Vestry said, They were not able to pay; and they have never since been rated: He confessed they voted for Mr. Janssen; and said, That the 4th, John Bartlett, was never rated.

David Haydon said, Another of them, viz. John Hay* don, voted for his Brother Jonathans House, who has been in Possession Twenty Years, and paid the Rates; and that the Voter had no Title.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Edmund Morton Pleydell Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Dorchester, in the County of Dorset.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

And the Question being put, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Edmund Morton Pleydell Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Dorchester, in the County of Dorset;

The House divided.

The Noes go forth.

Resolved, That William Chappie Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Dorchester.

Mr. Chapman reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, in the County of Bucks, and of the Stage Coachmen, Carriers, and Waggoners, in behalf of themselves and many others, who have frequent Occasions of travelling upon the great Roads from Northampton to London, was referred; and also, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways between the House commonly called the Horseshoe-house, in the Parish of Stoke Gold big ton, in the County of Bucks, and the Town of Northampton; and also, of the Inhabitants of the several Parishes of Stoke Goldington, Gay hurst, alias Gol hurst, and Lathbury, in the said County of Bucks, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parishes; was referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them upon both Petitions; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said First Petition: And,

Vol. 20.

Tirringham Backxvall Esquire, and Mr. Charles Lanes being called, said, That the Road between the North Bridge in Newport Pagnell, and the said Horseshoe-house, which Road lies in the sakl Parishes of Lathbury,

Got hurst, and Stoke Goldbigton, in the County of Bucks, being Four very long Miles, is so very bad in the Winter Season, that it is dangerous to Passengers; and that great Sums of Money have been laid out in repairing the same, but have proved ineffectual; and if the Inhabitants should lay out, and do yearly, much more than they are obliged to lay out, and do, by Law, the same would not put and keep the said Read in good Repair; for that some Parts thereof is very bad, even in the Summer Season.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine the Mat^ ter of the Second Petition: And the Act of Parliament passed in the 8th Year of her late Majesty's Reign being produced; whereby several Tolls, therein mentioned, were granted, for repairing the Highways between the Horseshoe-house, in the Parish of Stoke Goldington, in the County of Bucks and Nwthamptcn; which Duties are to continue for the Term of One-and-twenty Years, from the First Day of April then next ensuing;

That the Accounts of the Receipts and Disbursements of the Money arising by the said Act were produced; which, we find, have been regularly passed, and the Money duly applied, according to the Directions of the said Act.

That it appeared to the Committee, That the Trustees appointed to put the said Act in Execution have borrowed several Sums of Money, upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, as they were, by the said Act, impowered to do; and that there is now a considerable Sum owing of the Money borrowed; which cannot be paid off' and the Road, by the said Act directed to be amended, effectually repaired, and so, as it may continue in good Repair in the Winter Seasons, for the Conveniency and Benefit of all Passengers, without the Term by the said Act granted may be prolonged, and thereby a sufficient Stock of Money raised for that Purpose; nor can the Road lying in the Parishes of Lathbury, Gayhurst alias Gothurst, and Stoke Goldington, Part of the great Road from London to Northampton, be put into good Repair, and so kept, without some Part of the Toll, by the said former Act granted, may be applied for that Purpose; which the Trustees impowered to put the said former Act in Execution do not oppose; provided the Term granted by the said Act passed in the 8th Year of her Majesty's Reign, may be enlarged.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term granted by an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways between the House commonly called the Horseshoe-house, in the Parish of Stoke Goldington, in the County of Bucks, and the Town of Northampton; and for repairing the Road from the North Bridge of Newport Pagnell, in the County of Bucks, to the said Horseshoe-house: And that Mr. Chapman and Sir Justinian Isham do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Prisoners of the King's Bench Prison Debtor# was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, Petition,

That die Petitioners, as Debtors, labour under unsufferable Calamities, their Wives and Children being reduced to Beggary: That, by reason of their Prison' being overcharged, such Numbers coming under the Lock, and for Want of Necessaries, groan under an additional Calamity: That fatal infection, as the Season advances, may necessarily arise amongst them; which, hitherto ..... have guarded the Nation from: That the Petitioners, most of us, have been Traders in the Nation; and our Misfortunes fell on us through a gradual Decay of Trade: That the Petitioners are willing to do every thing in their Power to content their Creditors, as they were ready to do, on the last Act of Insolvency ..... by the Texture of some of its Clauses, unhappily rendered so unbeneficial, that not above Seven were thereon discharged from this Prison: And praying, That, for the Raising of publick Credit, and Reviving of Trade; for the Benefit of the Creditors; and for rendering themselves and their Families useful again, in their several Capacities, to their native Country; the House will admit such a Bill of Insolvency, as may universally answer the aforesaid Ends.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors, whose Hands are there under-written, on behalf of themselves, and other Prisoners for Debt and Damages, in the Castle of Norwich, being the Common Gaol of, and belonging to, the County of Norf olk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That most of the Petitioners have lately been Persons of good Business and Trade in the World; but, by reason of the Badness of Trade, the low Prices of Commodities, and many other Losses which have befallen them, and not any ways able to pay their just Debts, or render such Satisfaction to their Creditors; but are willing to do all they can towards Satisfaction thereof; and forasmuch as several of the Petitioners, who have been kept in this calamitous Condition for some Years last past, well hoped that they should have been relieved by the late gracious Act designed for the Relief of poor insolvent Debtors, who were imprisoned for Debt and Damages: And praying to take their deplorable Condition into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to your great Wisdom, shall seem most proper and Convenient

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Yonge reported from the Committee appointed to inquire into the Printer and Publishers of a printed Pamphlet, intituled, " The Report of the Committee " appointed to examine into the Project commonly called " the Harburgh Lottery," That the Committee had examined into the Matters to them referred; and had directed him to report the same to the House; and be read \ (be Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows: viz.

That the Committee, upon the Examination of the following Witnesses, do find, as follows;

John Stagg, Bookseller, in Westminster-hall, said. That the printed Reports, which he sold, he had from Nathanael Dodd, Seller of Pamphlets, near Temple-bar.

Nathanael Dodd said, That he sent some of the printed Reports to Stagg; and that he had them from Richard Franklyn, a Bookseller, who assured him, That if they were called to Account about it, he would own himself to be the Proprietor and Publisher of it.

Richard Franklyn, being shewn the printed Report Vo l.20.

referred to the Committee, owned, That he was the Proprietor of it; and that the said Report was printed by his Direction; and that nobody was concerned in the Profit of it besides himself:

That the Copy was brought to him by an unknown Hand, inclosed with a Letter:

The Purport of which Letter was;

That, in printing the said Report, it would not only be a great Advantage to himself, but also agreeable to some in the Administration: He also declared, That he had not the said Letter about him; but believed, he might be able to find it at home, and to produce it to the Committee:

That the same Person who brought him the Copy so inclosed, had it back from him again; and said to him, That he hoped, if the thing sold well, he, the Examinant, would give him a Gratification; which he promised he would:

The said Franklyn further said, That he had a Thousand of the Reports printed; and that one Parker printed the same.

Henry Parker, Printer, in being

shewn the printed Report, owned, That he printed it for Mr. Franklyn, and had the Copy from him:

That, upon questioning Franklyn, whether he might not run himself into Danger by printing it, Franklyn answered, They were all safe; that, if they were called to Account for it, he would take it upon himself; and thereupon desired him to get it done with all Expedition:

That he, the said Parker', was to have but the common Price for printing it.

John Grocer, an Under-writer to Mr. John Pitt, said, That he writ Two Copies of the Report for William Norman, another Under-writer to the said John Pitt; who told him, That one of the Copies wa- for Mr. Blew, the other for one Purcevall; and Norman paid him for writing the m; and ordered him not to acquaint Mr. Pitt with it; for, should it be known, they should be turned out from being his Clerks.

James Blew said, That Norman had left a Copy of the Report with him to read; but that he had not so much as opened it, or read a Line in it; neither had any body else seen it; and that it had not been out of his Custody since the time he had it from him:

And he brought and left the said Copy of the Report with the Committee.

John Grover, being called in again, and shewn the said written Report, acknowledged, That it was his Hand-writing.

Henry Parker, being shewn likewise the same Copy, said, That he believed, that the same Hand that wrote that Copy, wrote the Copy from which the Report was printed.

David Richmond, one of Parker*& Servants, said, That he had seen the Copy the Report was printed from; and he believed, that the Copy shewn him by the Committee, was of the same Hand-writing.

Benjamin Brown, who composed most of the Report for Parker, being shewn the said Copy, confirmed Richmond and Parker's Evidence, in being positive, that the Copy then shewn him, w'as the same Hand-writing as the other Copy, which the Report was printed from.

IVm. Norman confessed, That he gave Directions to Grover, for writing the aforesaid Two Copies of the Report; which he paid him for; and that Mr. James Blew had one of them from him, and one Lewis Purceval the other: That Purceval told him, when he gave him the Copy, That it was for a Friend of his in Golden-square; and that Purceval promised him Half a Guinea for it.

Lewis Purceval said, That, upon s desiring

him to get a Copy of the Report for him, he applied himself to Norman, to procure a Copy for him, if he

could; and that be had One from him accordingly: And he, the said Purceval, promised him he should have Half a Guinea for it:

That he gave the same Copy toFranklyn, at the Fountain Tavern in the Strand, and had a Guinea of him for it: That he did not carry it to him inclosed With any Letter: That nobody was by when he gave it to him; for that a Drawer, whose Name he did not know, called Franklyn out of a Room to him:

That he said to Franklyn, That he hoped, that he did not intend to print it; and Franklyn assured him, That he would not, and he might be easy about that Matter; for, should he print it, and be called to Account for it, it would cost him more Money than the Profit of printing it would amount to.

Resolved, That Henry Parker, Printer, in Bishopsgate-street, having, by Direction of Richard Franklyn, Bookseller, in Fleet-street, presumed to print the Proceedings Of a Committee of this House, contrary to the Order of this House, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That the said Henry Parker be, for his said Breach of Privilege, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Resolved, That Nathanael Dodd, having presumed to publish in Print the Proceedings of a Committee of this House, contrary to the Order of this House, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That the said Nathanael Dodd be, for his said Breach of Privilege, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Ordered, That the said Report be received upon Friday Morning next.

A Petition of Samuel Seager, Charles Webb, Jonathan Nicholls, Edward Steers, and Stephen Wootten, on the behalf of themselves, and other Inhabitants of the Borough of Caine, in the County of JVilts, was presented to the House, and rfcad; setting forth, That the Petitioners, together with others, are Inhabitants of the said Borough of Caine, having a Right of Common there; and that, by virtue of a Resolution, passed in the House in the Year 1710, which declares, That the Inhabitants of the Borough have a Right of Common; and, being sworn at Ogborne Court, have a Right to elect Members to serve for the said Borough: That, at the last Election of Edmund Pike Heath Esquire to serve for the said Borough, thd Petitioners, and others, did intend to vote; but, notwithstanding the Right they have of voting, founded on the said Resolution, and although they then claimed to be polled for' the said Mr. Edmund Pike Heath, the Guild Stewards, who are the Returning Officers there, utterly refused to admit them to vote; whereby the Petitioners are greatly injured, and debarred of that Right which they justly claim, founded on the said* Resolution: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that thfey do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ordered, That the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting in Trustees the Estates of George Rennet Gentleman, and of Henry Rennet, his only Son and Heir, in the County of Devon, to be sold, for the Purposes therein mentioned, be read a Second time, upon Wednesday Morning next.

Ordered, That the House be called over upon Tuesday come Fortnight, the Twelfth Day of March next.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as shall not then attend their Service in Parliament, be taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to go out of Town, without Leave before obtained from this House.

Ordered, That no Leave be asked for any Member to go out of Town, but between the Hours of One and Two Of the Clock.

- - Mr. Gybbon reported* from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Shire o( Sutherland, with the Resolutions of the-Committee thereupon; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the Report and Resolutions were read; and-are as follows; viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir John Gordon Baronet, and the Petition of Colonel Robert Mrnro, and others, complaining of an undue Election and Return df Sir Wm. Gordon #aronet to serve for the said Shir#; That-the Committed proceededtO examine the Matter of tl>e$e Petitions. -* ' -: 1

That the Counsel for the Petitioner Sir John Gordbn alleged, that the Freeholders Roll had- been, in favour of ,thb Sitting Member, arbitrarily -and illegally made up by the Sheriff, contrary to Law; which ordains th&t Roll so be made up by the Freeholders at the Michaelmas Head Court: 1

They also alleged illegal and partial Proceedings in the' Election; and that, by taking from the Sitting Members Poll, and adding to the Petitioner's, thsy

But the Right of Election being first controverted; The Petitioners Counsel insisted, the Right of Election is in this Shire the same as in all other Shires in Scotland; viz, That none were capable to elect, for be elected, but such as were publickly enfeoft in Property or Superiority, and in Possession of a Forty Shilling Land, of old Extent, holding of the King, or Prince, distinct from the Few Duties in Few Lands; or Four hundred Pounds (Scots) of valued Rent; That Noblemens Vassals have no Vote: And,

That none but proper Wodsetters, having Lands of the Holding, Extent, or Valuation, foresaia, or Life-renters of like Holding, Extent, or Valuation, have Vote: And that this Right of Election, in the Terms before-mentioned, is settled and established by Two Acts of Parliament made in Scotland before the Union; viz.

The First Parliament of King Charles the Second, 1661, 35. AS: concerning the Election and Charges of the Commissioners from Shires to the Parliament:

The Third Parliament of the same King, 1681, 21. Act concerning the Election of Commissioners for Shires:

And by the Articles, and Act, of Union: And,

By the Act 120 Amide, Cap. 7. for better regulating Elections in Scotland.

That the-Sitting Member's Counsel admitted the General Law of Scotland, delating to Elections, to be as before stated; but insisted, That, by special Constitution, Law, and Usage,

The Right of Election in this Shire is upon a Foot different from other Shires: And,

That all Heretors, Fewars, Wadsetters, and Life-renters, in Possession, have Right to vote in the Shire of Sutherland, which is a new-erected County, not included in the old Law of Scotland relating to their Rights of Elections.

And the Sitting Member's Counsel produced;

Dated 140 September 1631, 70 Car. 1. A Copy of a Grant from the Crown:

Reciting, That John then Earl of Sutherland had surrendered into the King's Hands the heretable Right of Regality of Sutherland, and the heretable Offices of Sheriffdom and Crownerie of Sutherland, and all Liberties -and Privileges belonging, whereof the said Earl stood heretably infeoft; and for which the Crown was, by contract, to pay a Thousand Pounds Sterling to the said Earl, his Heirs Males, or Assigns, when the Crown should think fit; and till Payment, the Earl, and his Heirs Males, and Assigns, to enjoy the said heretable Regality and Privileges, with new Privileges annexed; ancf Infeoftments thereof were granted by the Crown; and Seisins followed: And,

The King, de novo, erects and incorporates the Shire of Sutherland in a free Sheriffdom; and grants the same, with all Liberties and Privileges, to the said Earl, his Heirs Males, and Assigns, till Redemption of this Grant; and, upon such Redemption, the Grant to determine, and be void: And,

Part of the adjacent Shire of Inverness is separated and divided from that Shire, and incorporated into this new-erected Shire of Sutherland for ever: And this Shire, thus new-erected, and the heretable Regality, and here-. table Offices, of Sheriffdom and Crownerie, are regranted to the said Earl, his Heirs Males,; and Assigns, in blanch Holding, at the annual Rents of Two Penies Scots, if demanded, till Redemption shall be made, as aforesaid: And,

Domock is made a free Burgh Royal, with Power to choose Commissioners to the Conventions of Boroughs; And,

The King gives and grants Power and Privilege of choosing Commissioners for the said Shire to all Parliaments, liberis baronibus, alusque inhabit antibus, infra dictum Sutherlandia vicecomitatum nunc preesentibus, eorunir yue successorihus orrwi tempore a futuro:

Which Charter, Infeoftments, and Seisins following thereupon, were ratified, approved, and confirmed, by Act of Parliament in Scotland, in the Year 1633: And, by the same Act, the Country of Sutherlana, with the additional Limits and Privileges aforesaid, is of new erected in a free and distinct Sheriffdom: And,

By another Act, passed in the Year 1641, reciting, That, there being then but Two Inhabitants within the said Shire holding Lands of the King, the hail remanent Heretors being either Vassals to the Earl of Sutherland\ or holding the ir'Lands of some other Superior; and so, according to the general Act, the Allowance of the Commissioner of this Shire could not be dividit, or imposit, for Payment and Satisfaction of his Charges and Expences, except the same be extended against the Heretors, Fewars, and Freeholders, within the said Sheriffdom, holding Lands of other Superiors: And,

Therefore, this Act made all Heretors, Fewars, Life-renters, and Freeholders, within this Shire, whether Vassals to the King, or holding their Lands of any other Superior whatsomever, according to the Stent of their Lands lying within the said Shire, liable to such Allowance to the Commissioner for this Shire:

And, to prove the constant and uninterrupted Usage to be, as alleged by the Sitting Member's Counsel; Copies of the following Returns were produced; viz.

lg* August 1639, % Barons and Gentlemen within the Sheriffdom of Sutherland; signed by Nine:

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of electing a Commissioner to serve in Parliament for the Shire of Sutherland is in the Heritors, Fewars, Wadsetters, and Life-renters, possessed of Lands in the said Shire, whether holding of the Crown, or of a Subject.

The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That none but proper Wadsetters had Right to vote.

The Sitting Members Counsel insisted, That, by the Special Law and Usage before-mentioned, in this particular Shire of Sutherland, new-erected, and different from other Shires, all Wadsdfters in Possession, whether proper or improper, have Right to vote.

The Petitioner's Counsel offered to produce Evidence, That improper Wadsetters voted for the Sitting Mem*

That, upon the whole, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

s Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Provision made by the Act of the Stli and 9th of King William the;Third, intituled, An Act for the more effectual Relief of Creditors, in Cases of Escapes; and for preventing Abuses in Prisons, and pretended privileged, Places; has not proved effectual within the Place comiponly called the Mint: And that further Provisions shpqld be piadq; and the same be expended to the Contrivers, Aiders, and Abettors, of and in the Offences mentioned in that Part of the said Act, which relates to pretended privileged Places.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That further Powers be vested in the Justices of the Peace for tlm County of Surrey for the more effectual

Execution of their Warrants, and Escape Warrants, within the said Place called the Mint.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some Provision be made for defraying the Charge of raising the Posse Comitatm, or any other Power that shall be requisite* to execute Process or Warrants within the said Mint.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That Assemblies of Persons, taking upon themselves to regulate and determine Matters within the said Place called the Mint, greatly contribute to the Support of the Disorders, and illegal Practices, committed therein; and that effectual Provision should be maJe against the Contrivers, Actors, Aiders, and Abettors, of and in such Assemblies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some proper Encouragement and Reward be given to the Prosecutors, upon their convicting such Offenders.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That the granting some Relief to such Insolvent Debtors as have been, for a certain 'Time to be limited, within the Minty and shall appear to be Objects of Compassion, under proper Regulations and Restrictions, may conduce to the dispersing the great Numbers that have resorted thither, and to the abolishing the pretended Privileges of the same Place. . v

May it please your Worships,

We, the unfortunate Gentlemen of this Place called the Mint, are unwilling to give the least Umbrage to your Worships Order, in the executing your Warrants upon Highwaymen, Thieves, Pickpockets, and Whores: But must mtreat yon, Gentlemen of this honourable Pencil, that, as our Case and Circumstances are des- perate and deplorable, and our Liberties but small, to the Maintenance of ourselves, Wives and Children; so, wre humbly hope this honourable Bench, as Gentlemen and Christians, will Commiserate our Cases.'

We are very sensible, that many Reflections are daily thrown upon 11s, without real Cause;'and \ve do assure your Worships, we will always obey your Warrants, as afore-mentioned': But, as our Lives, and the Miseries of Thousands, ought to move your Worships to Commiscratioti; as we are Gentlemen, Merchants, &c.; so we humbly hope, your Honours will excuse us, if any Accident should happen in Defence thereof; we being truly loyal and dutiful Subjects t6 his Majesty Kitig* George, and ready to sacrifice our Lives in Defence' his Sacred Person, and Government.; 1 4

Linlithgow Mr. Dundass reported from the Committee, to whom Town the Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Council,

Revenue. of Linlithgow, in the County of West Lothian, on behalf of themselves, and the Community of the said Town,

~ was referred, the Matter as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition*

Mr. Walter Hamilton appeared before the Committee; and said, That the Town of Linlithgow is engaged in, and stands charged with, considerable Debts, which were very much increased by the late Rebellion in North Britain, amounting now to the Sum of £.1,600. Sterling, or thereabouts; and that he knew very well what the Debt of the Town was, as also the Revenues thereof, having carefully searched the Towns Books, and taken an Extract from them of the Debt and Revenue; which he produced to the Committee.

That it appeared further, upon the Examination of the said Mr. Hamilton, That the publick Works and Buildings of the said Town are in a very decaying and ruinous Condition; and that there is wanting, for the public Service of the said Town, a Church to be repaired, which wants a new Roof) Provisiyeu*4o be

That, upon Examination of the whole Matter, the Committee find', That without some Provision be made for raising Money, the Dehts of the said Town cannot be discharged; nor the necessary Works and Buildings aforesaid Be begun, carried on, and completed, for the Service of the said Town; the annual Revenues of the said Town not being sufficient for those Purposes.

A Petition of James Earl of Barrymore, George Venables Vernon Esquire, Thomas Warburton Esquire, and Matthew Page Gentleman, was presented to the House, and j-ead; setting forth, That the Petitioners, being Proprietors of Rock Sait Pits in Northwich Collection-, in the County of Chester, have, for the greater Convenience and Encouragement of the Trade, and Dispatch of Shipping, frequently lodged and stored great Quantities of Rock Salt, in the Warehouses at Frodsham Bridge, in the County of Chester; and Bankey, in the County of Lancaster: That, by the Statutes for laying Duties upon Rock Salt, for the better Security of the Duty, Bond is to be given to his Majesty, upon the Delivery of any Rock Salt from the Pits: which Bonds nevertheless, are to be delivered up, and fresh Bonds given for the same Duty, upon Certificates fresh the proper Officer, That such Salt so lodged in the Warehouses, is stopped for Exportation; That the Petitioners, in the Months of September, October, and November, 1720, sent several great Quantities of Rock Salt, the Duty whereof amounting to £.561. i6y. 8d.: That in the Month of December, in the said Year 1720, there happened the greatest Flood, or Inundation, upon the Rivers Weaver and Mercy, occasioned by a high Spring Tide, and violent Wind, whereby those Rivers werd raised several Yards higher than had been known in the Memory of Man; and thereby all the Salt in the Warehouses was totally destroyed, and perished: to the great Loss and Damage of the Petitioners: That, inasmuch as there is a Provision made in the several Statutes for making a Satisfaction for the Duty to the Owners or Proprietors of such Salt, or. Rock Salt, as shall be lost, or perished, gt Sea, the Petitioners did apply to the Collector at Nmtliwich to have their said.Bonds delivered up; but lie alleged, lie could not deliver up their Bonds without an Order from the Commissioners of the Duties on . Westminster A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City and Liberty Paving. of Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed,

on behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of the said Inhabitants, was presented to the House, and read, setting forth, That by an Act of the 2d and 3d of the late King William and Queen Mary, the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty, among many other good Things therein enacted, are obliged to keep the Pavements before their Doors, to the Denter Stone, or Middle of the Street, in good Repair; twice, in every Week, between the Hours of Six and Nine in the Morning, to sweep the Streets, Lanes, 8$c. for the Rakers carrying away the Dirt and Soil; That, in Obedience to the said Laws, srreat Numbers of the Inhabitants have, at a very great Expence yearly, endeavoured to keep clean, and m good Repair, the Streets and Lanes aforesaid; and the Justices, in their Quarter Sessions, have frequently exerted themselves, by punishing Defaulters: That the Petitioners, as the Law now stands, are obliged to pave' Part of the Highway before their Doors; yet, the Sort of Stones to be used in that Work being not particularly directed, the Pavements are generally performed in a slight Wav, and little Regard had to the Level of the Streets: That, of late Years, this City and its Liberties, being very much improved by the Increase of its Buildings, the Inhabitants do suffer in their Pavements, by the Proprietors of the several Water-works, who frequently break up the Streets to mend their Pipes; as also by the Carts employed in carrying Bricks, Stone, Timber, and other Materials for building, by the great Addition of Brewers Drays, and all other Wheel Carriages: the Owners whereof, who all greatly contribute to the Wear and Tear of the Pavements, do not, in any Proportion, contribute towards making good the same: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Sandys reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to prepare Heads of a Bill for preventing Frauds and Abuses in the Tobacco Trade; and to consider of the Duties and Allowances upon Tobacco, and what Abatements or Regulations may be made therein; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the said Resolutions are as follow; ws.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be but One Commission of the Customs for the whole United Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Importer of Tobacco from the British Plantations shall pay down the old Subsidy of One Peny Pound, with an Allowance only of Five /;cr Ce/tf. as usual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the other Duties, amounting, together, to Five Pence, and One-third of a Peny, per Pound, shall be paid down, or Security given for the Payment, within Eighteen Alonths.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of all former Encouragements, Allowances, and Discounts, Twenty-five per Cent, or One-full-fouvth Part of the said last recited Duties, shall be deducted and allowed, upon the Entry of the Importer.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Importer, not paying down the said Duties, shall be chargeable, from a certain time after Importation, with an Interest at a certain Rate per Cent. per. Annum, until the same is paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Allowance be made for damaged Tobacco; but the Importer shall have Liberty to separate such da-

Yo iu 20.

maged Tobacco; and the Officers of the Customs shall cause the same to be burnt and destroyed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, upon the Exportation of Tobacco into any foreign t Parts, the whole Duty paid inward, or secured, shall be drawn back.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That farther Encouragement be given to such as shall discover fraudulent Drawbacks upon Tobacco exported.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That any Tobacco, coming Coast-wise from one Port to another in Great Britain, may be detained by the Officers of such Port, upon Suspicion, until proof be made, that the Customs and Duties of such Tobacco have been paid, or secured; and, in case such Suspicion be found groundless, the said Officers to be liable to Costs and Damages.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in case any Tobacco, coming Coast-wise from one Port to another in Great Britain, shall have been taken on board in any foreign Part, or from on board any Ship or Vessel at Sea, or in any Place, other than the Port whence it was certified, such Tobacco, and the Value, to be forfeited.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Sandys, Sir Nathanael Gould, Mr* Walpole, and Air. Lowndes, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven- Ways and night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, Means, to consider further of Ways and Aleans for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee, who layer's, Ac, were appointed to examine Christopher Layer, and Conspiracy, others; and to whom the several Papers and Examinations, relating to the Conspiracy mentioned in his Majesty's Speech, were referred; which was ordered to he taken into further Consideration Tomorrow Morning; be taken into further Consideration upon Friday Alornino; next.

And then the House adjourned till Friday Alorning next, Nine of the Clock.

House, That since the Report from the Committee appointed to examine Christopher Layer, and others, in relation to the Conspiracy mentioned in his Majesty's Speech, was made to the House, a Letter from the Bishop of Rochester, in the said Bishop's own I land-writing, had been found upon his Servant, who attended him; And that his Majesty had commanded him to lay the said Letter before this House.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer also acquainted the House, That, William JFood, the Bishop of Rochester's Coachman, having been examined upon Oath, it appeared, That the Times of the said Bishop's coming to, and going out of, Town, were set down in a Day Boole of Accounts kept by the said William Wood, as they are mentioned in his Depositions, in the Appendix to the Report; and that Mr. Thomas Moore, the Bishop's Chaplain, had got the said Book into his Possession, and carried it away, upon a promise to return it, as is sworn against him; and that the said Mr. Moore, having been examined before a Committee of the Lords of the Council, and required to deliver the said Book, as being Part of the King's Evidence, had denied his having it, or knowing any thing of it:

Resolved, That, upon Consideration of the Report, and the several Papers and Examinations relating to the Conspiracy, it appears to this House, That a detestable wnd horrid Conspiracy has been formed, and carried on, by Persons of Figure and Distinction, and their Agents and Instruments, in Conjunction with Traitors abroad, for invading these Kingdoms with foreign Forces; for . raising insurrections, and a Rebellion at Home for seizing the Tower and City of London; for laying \iolent Hands upon the Person of his most Sacred Majesty,* and the prince of I Tales; in order to subvert bur present happy Establishment in Church and State, by placing a Popish Pretender upon the T hrone.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Christopher Layer, in his several Examinations before the Lords of the Council, and the Committee of this House, has grossly prevaricated; suppressed the Truth; contradicted himself; and endeavoured, as far as in him lies, to disguise and conceal the said horrid and detestable Conspiracy.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That John Plunlei has been a principal Agent and Instrument in the said horrid and detestable Conspiracy; and has carried oti several treasonable Correspondences, to procure 12

That it likewise appeared, by several Statutes, Provision is made, That if Salt, or Rock Salt, be lost at Sea, by the sinking of die Ship, or be token by Enemies, or be lost ut Sea by violent or stormy Weather, or by being thrown over-board, for preserving Men's Lives, or the Vessel in which such Salt is shipped; the Owner of die Salt shall, upon Proof before the Justices of the Peace, at the Quarter Sessions, of the Loss of such Salt, receive a Certificate thereof, by which they are intitled to buy the like Quantities, Duty-free: That those Statutes, mentioning only Losses at Sea, cannot be extended to Losses that happen on Shore.

And it npijcared, by a Minute of the Treasury, upon the said Report from the Commissioners for die Salt Duties, That it was ordered no Suit should be commenced upon the said Bonds; so that the Petitioners might have time to apply to Parliament for Relief.

Mr. Broderick reported from the Committee appointed Address on. to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, L*»y«r'»> &e upon the Resolution of 'Thursday last,. That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; w'hich they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons, in Parliament assembled, do humbly bee Leave to approach your Royal Person, with Hearts full of Concern and Horror, for the detestable Conspiracy formed against your Person and Government.

We lament, with Indignation, that any of our Fellow Subjects, who enjoy, in common with us, the many and signal Blessings of your Majesty's mild and just Administration, should so far give themselves up to Delusion, aa to conspire against publick Liberty, against their own Security, and against the only Bulwark of all that is dear and valuable, your Majesty's Person, and the Protestant Succession in your Royal Family.

We see, with Astonishment, that Persons of Figure and Distinction, who ought to have been the best Judges, and most zealous Defenders, of your beneficent and mild Reign, by which alone their Fortunes and Dignities can be made secure, should be so far infatuated, as to head and abet a monstrous Conspiracy to destroy your Majesty, their Country, and themselves; that Honour,

Faith, and the most solemn Ties of Religion, should bo violated in Favour of a Popish Fugitive, known only foe his blind Bigotry, and Attachment to Rome.

As we have, with sensible Sorrow, and just Resentment, discovered these vile Practices; so will we tako care, that the wicked Authors may not, by any Contrivance or Practice whatsoever, escape Punishment; but that all Conspirators may, by the Justice of Parliament, be for ever hereafter deterred from engaging in such traitorous Attempts.

We congratulate your Majesty, and all your good Subjects, that you have escaped the black and unnatural Designs of the worst of Men; and that Almighty God has, by this happy Discovery, given you, and your Royal Family, a fresh Instance of his singular Care and Protection,

For us, your faithful Commons, who feel with Joy and Gratitude the inestimable Blessings of your Reign; who are sensible of the glorious Advantages of Liberty,

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors within the Prison of Ludgate was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, many of them, been considerable Traders,- and are, all of them, Citizens and Denizons of this opulent City of London; but, by great Losses sustained in their several Dealings, are now become not only intirely useless to the common Weal of the said City, but alike also to themselves and Families; all of whom are become either grievous Chatges to their several Relations, or Burthens to various Parishes in this said City; the Petitioners having, by their long Confinement, consumed those little Effects, which

Vol. 20.

Martiv. 173

Losses, and Decay of Trade, had left, and their Creditor^ had refused to accept; by which means they have now left no other Support, but the Charities of well-disposed Persons; and, moreover, since the Consequence of the late grand National Calamity, the South Sea Scheme, hath so fatally and generally been discovered ill the Ruin or Decay of so many wealthy Families, not only of our Gentry, Merchants, and considerable Dealers, but even of several among those of the first Rank in Honour and Estate; to the great Stop and Decay of Trade in general: The Petitioners do also most humbly pray, That they may have Liberty to shew, though the late Act, intituled, An Act for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, did abundantly express the Pity and Tenderness of the then Legislative Body of these Realms; that as the Numbers of the Prisoners thereby relieved were, in Comparison, none, to the Multitudes that were left to remain in their distressed Conditions, there being but 16 out of 130 odd within the said Prison of Ludgate, who received the Benefit thereof; yet those remaining, as the said Petitioners do most humbly conceive, are proper and designed Objects of the said Relief:

And praying a Bill may be brought in for their Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Nobility, Justices of Peace at Severn® the General Quarter Sessions held for the County of ^ndae* Worcester, with the Clergy, Gentlemen, Freeholders, and divers other Inhabitants within the said County, the 15th Day of January 1722, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there is no Convenience of passing the River Severne with Coaches,

Horses, Waggons, and other Carriages, between Worcester and Btxcdley in the said County, but by Boat; which; of late Years, has been neglected, to the great Hindrance and Prejudice of all Travellers, and other neighbouring People that reside near the said River, and to the Loss of the Lives of several Persons, and their Effects; and also the great Check and Denial to Trade, in a Country so well stored with Corn, Hops, Cyder, and Fruit; which would be of vast Use to those Parts of the Kingdom that lie on the North-east Side of the said River: And whereas the Noblemen, Gentlemen, Free1 holders, and other Inhabitants within the said County of Worcester, have entered into a voluntary Subscription, for raising a Sum of Money towards building a Bridge over the said River Severne, at some convenient Place between Worcester and Beu'dley, for the safety of all Persons that have occasion to pass and repass the said River; but some Difficulties arising in the purchasing of Lands for the Roads that must lead to the said Bridge, and for the Repair thereof when built; which cannot be accomplished without an Act of Parliament: Anrf praying Leave to bring in a Bill for Erecting and Building of a Bridge, to prevent the Inconveniences which the Inhabitants of the County, and otiiers, at present labour under.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Mr. Speaker acquairited the House, That the House, on Wednesday last, attended his Majesty with their Address: To which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I return you my Thanks for this dutiful and loyal Address: It is agreeable to the many Instances of Zeal and Affection to me, which you have, upon every Occasion, expressed: The just Resentment and Indignation you have shewn against this Conspiracy, will, I doubt not, give intire Satisfaction to all that sincerely wish well to our present Establishment; encourage the Friends to my Government; and deter the Enemies of our common Peace from renewing these rash and desperate Attempts.

Thanks on Resolved, Nomine contradicente, That the Thanks of

Answer. this House be presented to his Majesty, for his most gracious Answer to their Address.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, do return the Thanks of this House to his Majesty.

Regulating Mr. Godfrey reported from the Committee, to whom Journeymen the Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Commonalty, Shoemakers. Qf Mystery of Cordwainers, of the City of London, and other Masters using the same Art and Mystery, was committed, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon 5 and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report and Resolutions were read, and are as follows; viz.

That the Committee-have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined several Witnesses; and find the Matter to be as follows;

Charles Reynolds, a Master Shoemaker, said, That he has delivered several Materials for making of Shoes to his Journeymen, who have immediately pawned them; and that he never had any Satisfaction for the same: That he has had several good Soles exchanged, and bad ones worked up in the Room of them; and that he found at one Calcot*s, a Pawnbroker s, about 50 or 60 Pair of Shoes cut out, and ready to be made up: That there were pawned in the Three Bowls in Hounds-ditch, and the Seven Stars in Petticoat Lane, as many Shoes, as he believes, \yould fill a Cart:

That the Workmen sometimes buy the Neck Part of the Hide, and work it up, and make it look as well as good Leather.

Mr. Ridout said, That he has had several Pair of Shoes, and Materials for making Shoes, paw ned at the Three Bowls in Houndsditch, and the Seven Stars in Petticoat Lane, and the One Bond in Houndsditch:

That he found at the Seven Stars, Three Pair of Shoes pawned that belonged to him; and that the Pawnbroker would not let him have them, unless he would pay the Money first for which they were pawned: That it is a constant Practice for the Journeymen Shoemakers to pawn their Work, and never redeem it: That the Pawnbrokers have told him, That they would take in Shoes and Leather to pawn, although they knew them to be the Goods of, or belonging to, the Master of the Person that paw ned them.

Wm. Hall said, That he has been a very great Sufferer by the Exchange of his good Leather for bad; and that some Gentlemen have told him, That their Shoes were not worth Half a Crown:

That he seldom had the same Materials worked up, as he delivered out to his Workmen:

That no Man ought to work at the Shoemakers Trade, without he has served Seven Years Apprenticeship to that Trade.

John Share said, That the Journeymen have told him, That the Masters cannot make good Shoes, but the Journeymen can:

And that he has had several Parcels of Materials for making of Shoes changed; and that he caught One of his Men, within this Fortnight, that had changed his good Leather for bad.

Abraham Hazard said, That he only makes Shoes for Women: That it is common for the Journeymen to pawn their Lace, and find upper Leathers, and Silks: That he had a Man that pawned a pair of Wedding Shoes, which he valued at £3.; and he paid Five Shillings to have them' out again: That the same Person pawned them twice afterwards; and he was forced to have another Pair made by another Hand.

That the Petitioners had divers other Witnesses to prove the Truth of the Petition.

That, upon the whole -Matter, the Committee came -to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That the Petitioners have fully made out the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That great Frauds and Abuses are committed by Journeymen Shoemakers, m and about the Cities of London and Westminster, Borough of Southwark, and Parts adjacent, by selling, pawning, and exchanging, Leather, and other Materials delivered to them by their Masters, to work up into Boots, Shoes, and Slippers; to the great Loss and Discredit of the said Masters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Pawnbrokers of London, Westminster, Borough of Southwark, and Parts adjacent, give great Encouragement to the said Journeymen to defraud their Masters, by buying, changing, or lending Money to Journeymen, on Shoes, cut Leather, or other Materials for making of Boots and Shoes.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Pawnbrokers, and Journeymen Shoemakers, ought to be restrained from the like Practices for the future.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for preventing Journeymen Shoemakers selling, changing, or pawning. Boots, Shoes, Slippers, cut Leather, or other Materials for making Boots, Shoes, or Slippers; and for better regulating the said Journeymen: And that Mr Godfrey, Mr. Bernard, Mr. Lochvood, Mr. Montagu, and Lord Carpenter, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of George Kelly, Clerk, Prisoner in the Tower of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, since the Petitioner hath been allowed the Use of Pen, Ink, and Paper, by Order of the House, and also Counsel and Solicitor to advise with him, he hath proceeded to prepare for his Defence against the Bill for inflicting certain Pains and Penalties upon him: And the Petitioner being advised, that the proper time for his being heard against the said Bill will be at the Second Reading, which is appointed on Monday next, and the Evidence against the Petitioner are thdn to attend, the Petitioner finds it impossible to be ready at that time, by reason of the Length and Variety of the Charges alleged against him: That Mr. Michael Bmninghmn Surgeon, and Messieurs Bask and Borgonio Merchants, who reside at Paris; and Mr. Gordon, Banker, at Boloign, in France; are material Witnesses for the Petitioner; but the said Persons cannot, as the Petitioner apprehends, be compelled to leave their Affairs, and make a Journey to England, to give Evidence at the Bair of the House: And praying, vrhat the Second Reading of the said Bill may be put off till Monday Sevennight; and that he may then be heard by himself and Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the said Bill; and that the Depositions, upon Oath, of the said Mr. Birmingham, Mr. Bask, and Mr. Burgonio, to be taken at Paris, before a Public Notary, or before some or One of the British Residents there; and also, that the Deposition of the said Mr. Gordon, to be taken, upon Oath, before the chief Magistrate of the Town of Boloign, or a Public Notary there; may be admitted to be read at the Bar of the House, as Evidence for the Petitioner.

Resolved, That the said Petition be rejected.

The Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Sevennight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bills to continue the Duties for Encouragement of the Coinage of Money; and for the Relief of William late Lord Jf idrington; and to suppress the Harburgh Lottery; and to prevent any foreign Lotteries from being carried on in this Kingdom; and to oblige the Persons concerned in the Management of the said Harburgh Lottery to make Restitution and Satisfaction for the Monies they have received from the Contributors to the said Lottery.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Gybbon, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Shrev shury, in the County of Salop, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon: And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the Report and Resolutions are as follows: viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir Richard Corbett Baronet, and Orlando Bridgman Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Corbett Kynaston and Richard Lyster Esquires to serve for the Borough of Shrewsbury, in the County of Salop:

That the Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That the Right of Election is only in the Burgesses inhabiting in the Borough, or in the Suburbs thereof, paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms or Charity:

And the Sitting Member s Counsel insisted. That the Burgesses in general, whether Inhabitants or not, had Right to vote; and that the last Determination of the House w as so.

That, on the Petitioners Part, Copies of Two Returns were produced; viz.

i° Maria, and 2" Phil. 8y Maria; Per ballivos burgi, Villa, fy Franches', Villa Salop', ac homines burgenses, ac commorantes infra Vill' 8$B pradictum tantes: And,

The Resolution of the House, 20th December 1709; when it was resolved, That the Right of Election for this Borough is only in the Burgesses inhabiting in the Borough, or in the Suburbs thereof, paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms or Charity.

That the Sitting Members Counsel observed, that Resolution was founded upon the Evidence of Two Witnesses only, contrary to antient Returns then produced:

And they insisted on the last Determination of the House, as to the Right of Election; viz.

27th May 1714; when it was determined, That the Right of electing Burgesses for this Borough is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough:

And they produced Copies of Twenty-three Returns; viz.

That the Sitting Members Counsel also produced an Exemplification, under the Great Seal, of an Act of Parliament made in the 23d Year of the Reign of King Henry the 6th, upon the Petition of the Bailiffs and Commons of the said Town, establishing divers Ordinances and Constitutions assented to by them for the good Rule ami Governance of the said Town for the future:

By the 16th Article whereof, the Auditors of tire Accounts of the Bailiffs, and other Town Officers, are appointed to be annually chosen by the Commons of tire Tow n; who are to assemble, for that purpose, on a Day certain, upon the Ring of the common Bell, which the Bailiffs are to cause to be rung; and the Burgesses, to be chosen to Parliament for the iuturc, are to he chosen by the said Commons, in Form as the said Auditors shall he: And,

Mr. Thomas Phillips, one of the Aldermen of the Town, said, For 30 Years past, the Burgesses of all sorts, as well Country Burgesses as others, voted in all Elections to Parliament, without any Objection, till 1709; and after that they tendered their Votes:

That the Auditors are now chosen, under the Charter of King Charles the First, by the Common Council of the Town: That, upon making up the Accounts, the Bell is rung; and sometimes Country Burgesses have come there: That inhabiting Burgesses have a Cow's Pasture in the Quarry, which foreign Burgesses have not: That foreign Burgesses pay no Tolls; and, if a. foreign Burgess comes, and inhabits in the Town, lie has all Privileges equal with any other Burgess:

Which Evidence, as to Out Burgesses voting till 1709, was confirmed by liobert, I Food, Richard Cheshire, and Maurice Lloyd:Who spoke for about 40 Years past;

and said, That, at all Elections, Proclamations were made for all Burgesses to come and poll, without distinguishing inhabitant, or not inhabitant, Burgesses:

And it was proved, That Arthur Tonga and Richard Finch, who gave Evidence in the controverted Election in 1714, That, for 35 or 36 Years past, the Out Burgesses voted, without Objection, till, the \ car 1709> were now not able to travel; the First, because ol his great Age; and the other, being laid up with the Gout.

Mr. Thomas Phillips, being examined, said, That

the Inhabitants of all those Vills and Parishes had always

voted, and were taxed to the Land Tax, with the Town; and that the Mayor exercised the same Jurisdictions there, in all' respects, as within the Borough; and that, in his Time, several Mayors (who are to reside in the Town), had, during their Mayoralty, lived in those Vills; and that the Inhabitants of the Parish of Holy Crons and St.Giles had constantly voted under the Resolution of 1709:

Being cross-examined, he said, That, about Five Years since, some Persons, who lived in thoee Vills, were turned out of the Common Council, as not living in the Body of the Town; the Validity of which Amoval was disputed in the Court of King's Bench; and Issue was joined, but no Tryal had, thereupon.

A PETITION of the poor Prisoners detained in the Sheriffs Ward in Bodmyn, in the County of Cornwall, In behalf of themselves, and of many Thousands more, under the like Confinement, in divers Parts of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have fallen under divers Misfortunes; and having been confined, some of us upwards of Twenty-five Years; by means whereof, we are utterly excluded, and rendered useless to the Public, as well as to ourselves and Families, unless timely relieved, by making, or causing to be made, an Act, or some other Provision, as may tend to the Relief of the said Petitioners, notwithstanding the several Acts made for Relief of poor insolvent Debtors, by reason of the Narrowness of the Sum, and Limitation of Time: And praying, That a Bill may be brought in for their Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Antrim Sif Nathanael Gould reported, from the Committee East India appointed to inquire into the Nature of a Subscription, Company. said to be carrying on by several of his Majesty's Subjects, to promote an East India Company now erecting in the Austrian Netherlands, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was lend: And the said Report and Resolutions are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of Fact.

That Mr. Samuel Procter attended the Committee, and informed them, That he was at Ostend about Three Years ago; and that several Subjects of Great Britain were then there; viz. Mr. Francis Acton, Mr. John JValkcr, Linen-draper; Mr. Dodd, Linen-draper; Captain Nash; Mr. Waldo, Second Supercargo under Mr. Holland; Captain Jackson, who has since taken a House at Ostend, and resides there; Mr. Supercargo to the Ship Wirtemburgh; and Captain;

who, he believes, were all concerned in the Trade carried on from Ostend to the East Indies; and that several of them did appear to be Managers at the publick Sale of Goods brought thither from the East Indies:

That the said Mr. Procter further said, That, at the time he was at Ostend, there were several English Ships in that Harbour arrived from the East Indies; and that Three of the said Ships were English built; and that he observed, that there w ere many English Sailors on board those Ships.

he had concluded the A (fair for the erecting an East India Company in the Austrian Netherlands; and that he informed Air.
