Air. James Colebrooke and Mr. John Ruck attended the Committee, and produced several original letters, some dated at Brussels, and others at Vienna, from the said Mr. John Colebrooke, Brother to the said Air "Which Letters w>ere read; whereby it appears Air. John Colebrooke has been soliciting for the Establishment of an East India Company in the Austrian Netherlands; and that he, from time to time, informed the said Mr. James Colebrooke, and Afr. of the several Steps

and Proceedings taken, in order thereunto: And, particularly, by Letter dated at Vienna the qth January 1722;

" That the Octroy, for the East India Company in " Flanders, was signed; and nothing was wanting but " inserting the Names of Seven Directors, of the Em- " peror's naming; which had been deferred, in order " to get some Information from the Low " which was then come."

And it appears further, by the said Letters from the said John Colebrooke, That lie was very solicitous to prevail with the said James Colebrooke, and his Partners, to be concerned in the said Stock, which, he intimated, was resolved to be to the Amount of Ten Aliilions of Florins; and, further to encourage them to be concerned therein, proposed it as an Affair that would be very profitable; assuring them, that the Direction would depend entirely on the concerned; and that the Duties on the Goods w ere not to exceed Four per Cent.:

That the said Air. James Colebrooke and Air. Ruck laid before the Committee Extracts of several of their Letters, in Answer to those sent by the said Air. John Colebrooke to them; whereby it appears, that they constantly rejected all Offers of being concerned in the said Company: And particularly, by their Letter dated the 3d July 1722, they say;

" That, supposing a real Profit were to be made by " the intended Company to be erected in the Netherlands, they should not, as they were Englishmen, join

" with a foreign Interest, and raise their own private u Fortunes, by hurting and prejudicing their own " Country."

The several Memorials and Representations presented to the House, relating to the erecting of the said Company; and referred to the Consideration of this Committee; were read:

Amongst which is a Afemorialfroni Monsieur Del IIer~ mitage, the States General's Minister residing here, dated the 26th March 1723, to the Lord Viscount Townshend; wherein was inclosed a Representation, or Remonstrance, from the Dutch East India Company, to the said States, complaining of the Attempts made to establish an East India Company in the Austrian Netherlands; and representing, that the setting up of such a Company is directly contrary to the Treaty of Peace made at Munster, in the Year 1648, which was afterwards confirmed by that of the Barrier; and further, representing the repeated Instances made by the said States General to the

Emperor,

0° Aprils.

Emperor* That his Subjects continue to press on the Design for this Trade; and have obtained from the Emperor, a Grant for a Trade from Ostend to the East Indies; and the said Minister farther signifies the Apprehensions the States General had of the ill Consequences which might happen from an Infraction of those Treaties; did continue to press his Imperial Majesty to a strict Observation thereof; especially considering, that those Articles have been religiously kept; and that the Subjects of the Spanish, now Austrian, Netherlands, have never been permitted to trade to the Indies: And the said Minister further acquaints the Lord Townshend\ Thpjt, by Order from the States General, he was to pray his Majesty, That he would be pleased, in pursuance of his Guaranty and Engagements, to direct his Ministers, at the Courts of Vienna and Brussels, to second, in his Majesty's Name, very vigorously, the Remonstrances that had been made on this Subject.

That, by the Lord Townshend's Letter, dated the 5th of April 1722, in Answer to Monsieur Del'Heritage's Memorial, his Lordship, by his Majesty's Command, assured him, That not only the solemn Engagements which his Majesty had taken upon him, but also the strict Friendship and Affection which his Majesty had for the States General, did, and would always, incline him to support the Rights of that Republick:

And that his Majesty, having considered the Reasons in the Remonstrance, found them to be very clear; and that his Majesty hoped, w^hen they shall come to be set in the best Light before the Emperor, that his good Faith, his Justice, and his Equity, would engage him to replace Matters upon the old Foot:

And the Lord Tcnvnshend did further assure the said Minister of the States, in his Majesty's Name, That his Majesty would cause such vigorous and cordial Instances to be made as their High Mightinesses desire.

And then the Committee, upon the Whole, came to the Resolutions following; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That several Subjects of Great Britain have been concerned in promoting and carrying on a Trade from the Austrian Netherlands to the East Indies; and negotiating an Establishment of a Company for that Purpose; to the great Prejudice of the Trade of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill effectually to prevent his Majesty's Subjects from subscribing, or being concerned in encouraging, or promoting any Subscription, for an East India Company in the Austrian Netherlands; and for the better securing the lawful Trade of his Majesty's Subjects to, and from the East Indies.

The First of the said Resolutions being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradieente, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That several Subjects of Great Britain have been concerned in promoting and carrying on a Trade from the Austrian Netherlands to the East Indies; and negociating an Establishment of a Company for that Purpose; to the great Prejudice of the Trade of this Kingdom.

Ordered, Nemine contradieente, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill effectually to prevent his Majesty's Subjects from subscribing, or being concerned in encouraging or promoting any Subscription, for an East India Company in the Austrian Netherlands; and for the better securing the lawful Trade of his Majesty's Subjects to and from the East Indies: And that Sir Nathanael Gould, the Lord William Pazvlet, and Mr. Hungerford, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The said Trustees also humbly shew unto this honourable House, That, as they first proceeded to the Sale of the Hobshold Goods, and other personal Estates, of the said late Directors, and others, as being most liable to spoil or damage; so they have begun to dispose of their Leasehold Estates, as being some of them at large Kents, and untenunted; and so rather Charges on the particular Estates to which they belonged, than an Advantage:

That they have also proceeded to the Sale of some of the real Estates of the said late Directors, and others, whereon no Claims have been entered; or whereon the Claims, so entered, have been heard and determined; and are now ready to sell several others of them; and, in order to thfe bale of the Residue of the said Estates, have directed the respective Titles to the same to be abstracted; and have given Orders to their respective Receivers to transmit to them exact Particulars of the several Estates within their respective Receipts; so that by such Abstracts and Particulars, they may know what Interest they have in, and what is the Nature and Value of, the several Estates to be sold, or disposed of.

The said Trustees beg Leave to observe, That as at the time of their making their said former Report to the then House of Commons, by reason of several Difficulties therein set forth, they could not then make any certain Computation of what the said real Estates might be worth, or what the clear Produce thereof might be; so they are still incapacitated to make any certain Computation thereof; because, as they have great Reason to believe, several Coutrivances were formed to advance the annual Rents of several of the said Estates, before the same were purchased by the said late Directors, and others; which being purchased by them when they had not Leisure to take due Care in examining into their real Values', they might be deceived: And many of the said Estates having been contracted for at exorbitant Prices, since the First Day of June in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty, from which time the Estates of the said late Directors, and others, were vested in the said Trustees; and small Parts only of the Purchase-money paid by them; it remains yet a Doubt, whether the said Trustees will.be obliged to complete such Purchases; which if they should not be compelled to, would prove a considerable Addition to the Estates vested in the said Trustees.

They beg leave, lastly, to report to this honourable ‘House, That they are now in a great Forwardness towards dealing with many of the said late Directors; which they had ere this completed, could they have employed their lime wholly to that Purpose: But great Numbers of the Claimants having, with great Earnest-pegs, applied to them for the early hearing their several

Claims; especially such as were made upon Account of Trusts; they were obliged to comply with such Applications; and to deviate from the Rule they first proposed, of going through with their several Affairs, and examining into the several Claims on their respective Estates, in a regular Course; which they now hope, that, for the future, the; shall be better able to follow.

Mr. Gybhon, according to Order, reported, from the Wells Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as Election, it appeared to them, touching the Election for the City of JVells, in the County of Somerset, and the Resolutions

of the Committee thereupon; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follows; viz.

Upon the Petition of the honourable George Hamilton Esquire, and Wm. Piers Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return ot Thomas Eduards and FrancisGwyn Esquires, to serve for the said City:

The Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Mayor, Masters, Burgesses, and Freemen, of the City:

But the Qualification of the Freemen was disputed.

It was agreed, That a Person serving Seven Years Apprenticeship to a Freeman, or being the eldest Son of a Burgess, born after his Father's Admission to Burgesship, or marrying a Daughter or Widow of a Burgess, was qualified to be a Freeman: And,

The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That all Persons, having any such Qualification, had a Right to vote;

But the Sitting Members Counsel insisted, That the Consent of the Mayor and Common Council was necessary, previous to Admission to Freedom; which was denied by the Petitioner's Counsel:

To which Point, the following Evidence was given on the Petitioner's Part:

The Journal of the 30th of May 1716, in the then controverted Election, was produced; when it was resolved by the House:

That the By-law jnade by the governing Part of the Corporation of Wells, in 1712, pretending to inflict One hundred Pounds Penalty on the Mayor that nominates or makes any Burgess without the Cousent of the major Part of the Corporation, and Fifty Pounds Penalty on any Burgess that takes the Oath appointed to be taken by the Burgess, or that use, claim, or challenge, any Freedom, or Privilege of a Burgess, without such Assent, w*as arbitrary and illegal.

Humphrey Cordxvent, Master of the Taylors Company, said, He was admitted without Consent of the Corporation: That such Consent was never asked, nor was necessary: That he was sworn a Burgess, and was of the Corporation so tong as he voted as they would have, him; and, when he would not, they turned him out of the Common Council; but that he remains a Burgess, and camfe in by Redemption:

He also said, That all Freemen, admitted into any of the Companies of the City, had a Right to vofei and voted in all his time, whether they were sw'orn Burgesses, or not: That nobody can be sworn a Burgess by the Corporation, before he is admitted of One of thi Companies: That the previous Consent of the Mayor and Common Council w as not necessary to any such Admission: This Practice he spoke to, of his own Knowledge, for 40 Years past: And said. That, till lately, there was no Distinction made between Freemen admitted into any of the Companies, and sworn Burgesses:

That both have the same Privileges, in all respects; and that the late Attempts to confine the Right of Voting to sworn Burgesses, was looked upon, by the People, to be arbitrary and illegal.

On the Sitting Members Part;

To prove. That none could be admitted to Burgesship, or to Freedom of any of the City Companies, without previous Consent of the Mayor and Common, Council;

The following Evidence was produced; viz.

310 Eliz. A Charter granting Power to the Mayor and Conmlon Council, to make Laws and Ordinances, agreeable to the Laws of the Realm., for good Government of the Burgesses and Inhabitants; and for Direction of Artificers; and otherwise for the publick Utility of the City: And,

Several Bodies of Ordinances and Laws made and established by the Mayor and Common Council, pursuant to the said Charter, against admitting any Persons into any of the Companies aftermamed without Examination, and Proof, before the governing Part of such Company, of serving Seven Years Apprenticeship; and without presenting such Person to the Common Council, and having their Consent, previous to such Admission, under Penalties on the Masters and Wardens of the Companies; and declaring all Admissions to the contrary to be void; viz.

22 Mar. 1649, Tor the Mercers Company, ratified by both Justices of Assize:

14 September 1665, For the Company of Taylors, confirming Ordinances, made 340 Eliz.

9 February 1673, For better Government of the Tam tiers, Glovers, arid Butchers:

20 Feb mary 1694, For better Government of the Clothiers, Woobcombers, Stocking-makers, 8$c.

14 August 1707, For the Cordwainers Company: And,

14 August 1707, For the Company of Blacksmiths, <§c. Hammermen:

1 Mar* 1668, An Order in the Convocation Book of the City, That no Master, or Wardens, of any Company, should admit any Person into such Company, without first having Approbation and Allowance thereof, from the Mayor for the Time being; and that the same be presented by him to the Common Council, for their like Consent and Approbation; upon Pain of forfeiting, for every Offence, Twenty Shillings; and every Admittance, otherw ise, to be void:

And divers Instances in the Corporation Books, were produced, of Applications made to the Common Council, for Leave to be admitted into some of the Companies; and giving such Leave, accordingly; in the Years 1669, 1670, 1672, 1687, 1O94, 1695, 1707, and 1719; the Two last of which were the Petitioners.

Mr. John Gutch, who has been Town Clerk almost 22 Years, and was born in the Town, said, That, in all his time, the Usage has been, for Persons to apply, by themselves, or by the Master of some Company, to the Common Council, for Leave to be admitted into that Company, previous to such Admission; and that all Admissions, with* out such Leave first had, are called clandestine Admissions, and are looked upon to be illegal; and that Persons, having a Right to Freedom, make that Right appear to the Common Council before Admission, or any Leave for it:

That some late Admissions, though clandestine, have been confirmed by the Common Council, and the Persons admitted to vote, for Peace-sake only; but that, regularly, Leave of the Common Council, for Admission, ought to be first had; and, when these Admissions, last mentioned, were confirmed, the Common Council insisted, That, for the future, Application should be made to the Corporation, previous to any Admission, according to the ancient Usage:

Being cross-examined, he said, That, at the Election before the last, several Persons were allowed to vote, who were admitted to Freedom, without the previous Consent of the Corporation.

Thomas A nicy spoke, for 50 Years past, to this Usage of applying to the Common Council, for Leave to be admitted into some Company, previous to such Admission; and said, Those who were taken into any Company without such previous Consent of the Corporation, had no Right, and were not admitted, to vote in Elections to Parliament.

Mr. JVm. Goldfinch, being called, on the Petitioners Part, said, The Generality of the Town exercised their; Vol. 20.

Trades, without being swftrn Burgesses, and without Welfs Consent of the Corporation; but that none exercised any Trade, without being of some Company; and that Freemen were not denied any Privilege, which Burgesses had, except voting in Elections to Parliament.

Then the Committee came to this Resolution;

AN ingrossed Bill, from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting the Estates of Sir Gcrvas Clifton Baronet in Trustees; and to enable him to take an Estate for Life, by way of Purchase, in several Settlements intended to be made of his Estates, on the Marriage of Robert Clifton Esquire, his Son and Heir apparent; was read the Third time.

A Petition of several Half Pay Officers, who, through Execution of unavoidable Misfortunes, have been obliged to fly for

Refuge to the Mint, was presented to the House, and A n ' read; setting forth, That several of the Petitioners afQ driven to great Extremity through Means of the Debts contracted by their poor Wives and Children, whilst they were upon Service abroad, and other unavoidable Misfortunes; their Half Pay being scarce able to keep Life and Soul together, much less to pay Debts: That the Petitioners being ruined and undone, by several Ways and Means; some by Loss of Sight, Limbs,

Deafness, old Age. and Infirmities, contracted in their Service; others, who, through Zeal to serve their Country, expended their Fortunes, as Volunteers, at several Battles and Sieges, before they had any Commission given them; which were the Causes of their unhappy Circumstances; that the Petitioners were obliged to make over their Half Pay, others the small Stipend allowed them by Friends, to raise Money to furnish their little Habitations and Lodgings* in order to have the Comfort of their Families with them, under their melancholy Confinement in the Mint; for, though the Petitioners are no Prisoners in the King's Bench yet are, by being debarred of their Liberty, rendered as dead to the World, as if they were actually in Prison:

That the Petitioners have nothing more at Heart, than the Payment of their just Debts; and many of them have a Prospect, at the Death of Friends, or some other Ways, to answer their Intentions, had they their Liberty, or Time to wait for some happy Change in their Fortunes; which may be thought the more reasonable, considering how few on the Half Pay List are under these melancholy Circumstances: And praying, That your Honours will be pleased, by a Clause in some proper Bill, to grant the Petitioners the Term of Seven Years for the payment of their Debts, or what other Term of Time as to your Honours shall seem meet.

A Petition of Richard Pcndrill, John, Thomas, William, Ditt«. and Maiy Pcndrill, and others, whose Names afe subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are the Descendants of William Pcndrill, John, Richard, Humphrey, and George Pen-drill, Charles Giffard, Francis Yates, and his Wile, Thomas Whitegrare, of Mostly, Colonel William Carlos, and Francis Reynolds, of Carlton, in the County of Bedford; who were eminently instrumental in the Preservation of the Person of his most Sacred Majesty King Charles the Second, after the Battle of Worcester; the Merits of which Services have been remembered with Royal Protection in every Reign: That the Petitioners, far from engaging in, or abetting, any of the unnatural Rebellions or Conspiracies against the established Government, and detesting such wicked Principles, have ever behaved themselves wdth all loyal and dutiful Allegiance to his present Majesty King George, and his Royal Predecessors; and, in Consideration of the said Services of the Petitioners Ancestors, and of the Petitioners demeaning themselves peaceably, and as faithful and obedient Subjects, all Prosecutions against them, on account of being Papists, have been, from time to time, stayed, by the Royal Favour and Protection of his most Sacred Majesty, and his Predecessors: That the Petitioners have never done any thing to forfeit such Favour; and abhor all Thoughts of so doing; and do assure this honourable House of their constant Fidelity and Obedience to his Majesty, and the Succession of the Crown, as by Law established, in the Royal House of Hanover: And praying, That, in regard to their Ancestors Fidelity, and eminent Services to the Crown, in the Preservation of the Sacred Person of his late Majesty King Charles the Second, on which depended the Restitution of the Royal Family, and the Restoration of the Government, by Law appointed to be for ever annually

A PETITION of the poor insolvent Debtors, Prisoners in Durham Gaol, in the behalf of themselves, and of many Thousands in England, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That whereas the Petitioners being many in Number, most of which, having suffered many Years Imprisonment, without any Redress of Grievance, could by no means be suffered to reap the Benefit of his Majesty's late Act of Grace for such insolvent Debtors, by reason of its taking Date so soon, x>r rather so far backward; and being so very strict for being without the Limits of the Gapl, though with a Guide, that, out of Eighteen just and lawful Prisoners, only Six reaped the Benefit thereof: And praying. That your Honours would be pleased to commiserate these our great Afflictions, and deplorable State and Condition, by redressing all these our Grievances, by a further Act of Grace to the same Effect.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is sitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House; and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speakers, Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is sitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning to Four in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster i and that lie do see the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House.

Ordered, That no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

AP ET IT IO N of John Prise Esquire, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, and Jatr.es JValhvyn Esquire, stood Candidates at the late Election of One Citizen to serve in this Parliament for the City of Hereford\ in the room of JVnu Mayo Esquire, deceased: That Mr. JValhvyn was guilty of notorious Bribery, by giving several Hundreds of the Freemen Two Guineas apiece, and other Sums of Money, for their Votes; by which Means, and other indirect Practices, by polling foreign Freemen, and others who had no Right, he procured himself to be returned; although the Petitioner was duly chosen by a Majority of legal Voters, and ought to have been returned; And praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Gcot'ge Lord Carbury, of the Kingdom of Ireland, and Thomas Bennett Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That at the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Westbury, in the County of Wilts, the Petitioners, and James Bertie and Francis Annesley Esquires, stood Candidates: That Samuel Gibbs, the Mayor, polled divers Persons, who had no Right, against the Petitioners; and refused several who had a Right to poll for them, and he denied a Scrutiny, though it was demanded; and Mr. Bertie and Mr. Annes ley, and their Agents, used divers illegal and corrupt Practices, in procuring Votes; and they are returned; although the Petitioners were duly chosen: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition he referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Sir Richard Fouler Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, and Sir Humphry Houorth Knight, were Candidates at the last Election for Knights of the Shire for the County of Radnor; and that Sir Humphry, with his Agents, and in Confederacy with Henry Haworth, Nicholas Tayler, and others mentioned in the Petition, procured a Majority upon the Poll by their illegal Practices; and Sir Humphry is returned, although he is not qualified in Estate; and many of the Voters were, by Bribery and Menaces, deterred from voting, and who would have voted for the Petitioner; and Sir Humphry also treated the Freeholders, in several Places within the said County, after the Testa of the Wri?, contrary to Law; and in Prejudice to the Petitioner's Election: And praying the Consideration of the House, and Relief therein.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the Hou§e.

A Petition of Sir Nicholas Williams Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, at Vox.. 2'J.

Januarii". 227

the Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this Parliament for the County of Carmarthen, the Petitioner, and Edward Rice Esquire, stood Candidates; but the Sheriff, who was under the Influence of Mr. Rice, appointed the Election to be at Llandilo, a small Village, near Mr. Rices House, not capable to receive and lodge One-third of the Freeholders; which Inconvenience ho was told of, but he persisted in his Appointment: That the Election began on the 19th of Apr. 1722; and was continued, by Adjournments, to the 24th of April, on purpose to tire out the Petitioner's Electors; and then, after all the Freeholders who appeared for Mr. Rice had polled, adjourned to the 25th, without the Petitioner's Consent: That the Sheriff, and his Under Sheriff, proceeded very arbitrarily in taking the Poll, by polling many illegal Voters for Mr. Rice, and refusing to poll many good Votes for the Petitioner; and committed many other Partialities, in favour of Mr. Rice: That, during the Time of Election, the Petitioner, and his Friends, were frequently insulted in Court by Mr. Rice, and his Friends; and his Agents often brought great Numbers of rude Persons armed with Swords and Clubs; and more especially on the Evening, the said 24th of April, some short time before the Adjournment; at which time they assaulted and wounded divers Persons; and would not disperse, though the Proclamation against Rioters was, by Order of divers Justices of Peace there, read; which Riot, of Mr. Rice his own making, he pretends, was the Cause of the Sheriffs closing of the Poll; and the said Sheriff hath returned Mr. Rice; in Prejudice of the Petitioner: And praying such Relief in the Matter as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Ralph Jenison, of Elswick, in the Cotinty of Northumberland\ Esquire, Was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner and William Wrightson Esquire, stood Candidates at the late Election of a Knight of the Shire for the said County, in the room of Algernon Seymour Esquire, now Lord Piercy, called up by Writ to the House of Peers; and the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes; but Mr. Wrightson, and his Agents, by Menaces, Riots, Bribery, and 'other indirect Practices, procured several to vote for him who were not qualified, and caused others to absent themselves that would have voted for the Petitioner; by which Means, there appearing to be in the Poll Books a greater Majority, the Sheriff hath returned Mr. Wrightson; in Wrong to the Petitioner: And praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ereskin produced a Commission, as Delegate for St. Andrews; but there was another Commission produced for Alexander Bell; who insisted, That he was lawfully Delegate for that Borough: That the Petitioner produced a Commission, as Dele- gate for Cowper, from the Magistrates and Town Council, and signed by the Common Clerk, with the Seal of the said Borough, and having all other Formalities, as usual: That Ensign ,fames Ereskin, Brother to the said Captain, produced likewise a Commission pretended

The Lord Pinch reported, from the Committee ap- Address On pointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented 1)1 e King* to his Majesty, That they had drawn up an Address ac- Speech* cordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as foHoWeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, thU Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled; beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty upon your safe and happy Return into these Kingdoms; and most humbly desire your Majesty to accept the unfeigned Thanks of this House for your Majesty's most gracious Speech from the Throne. As your Majesty is pleased to tbuncf the Grandeur of your Crown in the Security of the Liberties of your People, and your Glory in promoting their Prosperity ;. so they, in Return, must be excited by all the Ties of Duty and Gratitude, to build their Happiness upon the firm and unshaken Principles of Loyalty and Affection to your Majesty's most Sacred Person, and Government.

It is the greatest Satisfaction to your Majesty's faithful Commons, to find that the Loyalty of their Resolutions, and the Justice of their Proceedings, in the last Session of Parliament, have been attended with all the happy Consequences they expected from them, and now* have been rewarded with your Majesty's Royal Approbation.:

We beg Leave to assure your Majesty, that we shaft readily and chearfully raise all such Supplies as shall be necessary to support the Honour of your Majesty's Government, and secure the Tranquillity of these Kingdoms.

We are highly sensible of your Majesty's* Goodness to all your People in recommending, particularly at this time, to our Consideration, the publick Debts of the Kingdom; which are so heavy a Load, and so nitich a national Concern, that we should be wanting to ourselves, if we did not assure your Majesty, that we will use our utmost Endeavours to improve and augment the Sinking Fund, and thereby put the national Debt into a Method of being gradually reduced and paid, without any Violation of publick Faith, or Infringement of privath Property; and, as your Majesty is pleased to encourage our attempting so great and noble a Design, so we are fully persuaded, that the Wisdom and Steadiness of your Majesty's Government will enable us to perfect this great Undertaking.

We assure your Majesty, that we know of no other Safety, under God, for our Trade and Wealth, Liberty and Property, religious and civil Rights, but the Security of your Majesty's most Sacred Person and Go-

- yernment,

The said Address being read a Second time;

ResolvedNanine contradicente, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to his Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know his Majesty's Pleasure, when he will be attended by this House.

Lime Regis A Petition of William Smith Esquire, was presented to

Election. the House, and read; setting forth, That, the 24 of March 1721, came on the Election for Burgesses to serve - in this Parliament for the Borough of Lime Regis, in the County of Dorset; and Henry Holt Hailey Esquire, John Burridg, Thomas Parish Esquires, and the Petitioner, stood Candidates: That Robert Burridg Esquire, Mayor of the said Borough, and Father of the said John Burridg, hath returned him and Mr. Hailey as Burgesses duly elected for the said Borough; though the Petitioner apprehends Mr. Burridg is not qualified in Estate to serve, and insists on it; and many were admitted by the Mayor to poll for the said John Burridg, who had no Right to vote; and many, who had a Right, were not suffered to vote for the Petitioner; who, had he not been guilty of such partial Proceeding, should, with Mr. Henley, have had a Majority of legal Votes of the said John Bumdg; and ought to have been j returned, instead of him: And praying the House to ' take the Premises into Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Petition be-referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House;

Anglesea A Petition of Owen Meyrick, of Bodorgan, in the

Election. County of Anglesea, Esquire, was presented to the

House, and read; setting forth, That, at the last Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in Parliament for the County of Anglesea, Richard Lord Bulkley, and the Petitioner, stood Candidates; and the Lord Bulkley, despairing to have a Majority of the Freeholders at the Election, did, a little before the same, greatly increase the Number of Efeeholders, by executing several illegal Conveyances, of &bout 45s.per Annum, to his Tenants and Servants, and other Persons; and, by Menaces and Bribery, and other undue Practices, and Promises, procured divers bad and good Votes, who otherwise would have polled for the Petitioner; and the Sheriff of the said County hath returned the said Lord Bulkley as duly elected; though the Petitioner was so, and ought to have been returned: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Linlithgow A Petition of George Douglas Esquire, was presented &c.Election. to House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, and Danitl Weir Esquire, stood Candidates at the late Election of a Member to serve in this Parliament for the District of Burghs of Linlithgow, Lanerk, Selkirk and Peebles; and the Petitioner was duly elected, and ought to have been returned: That the Town Council of Linlithgmv, in whom the Right of Election is, consists of Twenty-seven, of whom, not less than Fourteen are a Quorum: That Walter Hamilton the present Provost of Linlithgow, and Sheriff Depute, took upon himself, in an arbitrary and illegal manner, by Threaten-

ing, and Force of Arms, to beat and intimidate the Majority of the Majority of the said Counsellors, who were in the Petitioners Interest, from entering into the Council Chamber of the said Town; and on the 12 of April 1722, did proceed, with several Counsellors, under the Number of Fourteen, to the Election of a Commissioner for the said Burgh: That 14 of the Counsellors, who were the Majority, being hindered from entering the Council Chamber, as aforesaid, immediately retired to a House in the Town, and made Choice of Baily Smith, as the Commissioner from Linlithgow, to vote in the Election of a Member to the ensuing Parliament: That, the 13 of April 1722, the Election, being the Election Day, Hamilton placed 30 or 40 armed Men upon the Stairs, with Orders to stop the said Baily Smithy if he should dare to enter the Room of Election; and, accordingly, Smith endeavoured to go into the Council Chamber; but was stopped, and beaten and wounded, by said Hamilton, and his Mob, in such a Manner, that his Life was in Danger, of his Bruises, and Loss of Blood; upon which Protestation was made; and the Commissioners for Selkirk and Peebles voted for the Petitioner; and the Commissioner for Selkirk produced a Letter from Baily Smith, signifying his being duly chosen for Linlithgow; and that he voted for the Petitioner; so that Three of the Commissioners voted for him; and he ought to have been returned; but Provost Hamilton, upon an illegal Commission, pretending he was chosen Commissioner for Linlithgow, who, with the Commissioner for Lanerk, rejected Smith's Commission; and have returned the said Daniel Weir; in Wrong to the Petitioner, and in Violation of the Constitution of Parliament: And praying the immediate Consideration of the House herein, and such Relief as shall be thought just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Electors, and by divers other illegal and unwarrantable Practices, hath procured himself to be returned; in Prejudice of the Petitioner: Arid praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Edward Hughes Esquire, wag presented Weobley. to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Peti- Election, doner, and John CarpenterJL$<\me, with Nicholas Philpot, and John Birch Serjeant at Law, were Candidates at the late Election of Members to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of Weobley, in the County of Hereford; and the Writ coming to the Under Sheriff of the said County, he made out a Precept, and directed it to John Davies and Walter Green, Constables of the Borough, who were the only proper Returning Officers, and sent a Messenger with it from Hereford to Weobley; who, when he came there, was prevailed on to carry it back again to the Under Sheriff; who kept it dll next Day, and then brought it himself; but, instead of delivering it to the said Two Constables, he gave it to John Moor and Thomas White, whom the Sitting Members, or their Agents, had procured to be sworn in Constables, between the time of sending back of the Precept, and its Return, by Edward Witherston and Tho. Carpenter Esquires, Two Justices of the Peace, who came to Weobley, out of their Division, for that Purpose; although the legal time of electing Constables there is at a Court Leet, held at Michaelmas: That Davies and Green demanded the Precept of the Under Sheriff; but he gave it to the pretended new Constables, after he had read it in the Town-hall, at the Election, before the Four Candidates: That the legal Constables proceeded in the Election; and on a Poll, the Petitioner had a Majority; and they declared him duly elected; and tendered a Return to the Under Sheriff' which he 3 refused;

A Petition of William Goldzvyer, Samuel Hookey Joshua, Stevens, John Hancock, Thom. Jeanes, and John Bursty, Burgesses of the Borough of Christ Church Twyncham, in the County of Southampton* in behalf of themselves, and divers others, Burgesses of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Borough is a Borough by Prescription, consisting of a Mayor, Burgesses resident inthp Borough, Out-burgesses, and Inhabitants, called the Populace: That, on the 8th of September, annually* the Mayor and In-burgesses did use to meet in their Town-hall, and there nominate Three Persons of their Body to be presented to the Populace* on the 14th of the same Month, for them to choose One of those for Mayor for the ensuing Year, who had constantly beert sworn into his Office at the following Michaelmas Leet: That, on the 8th of September 1718, John Stevens was so duly chosen Mayor, and expected to have been sworn in as such at the next Michaelmas Court Leet; but, by Contrivance of some of the Inhabitants, and the Lord of the Leet, no Court was held, as usually, that Year, though often applied for: That afterwards, in April 1719, a Court Leet Was held and the said John Stevens then offered* and demanded, to be sw orn but the Steward of the Court refused to sw>ear him, and suddenly broke up the Court, after he had sworn the Serjeant at Mace, and some other Officers, who were presented by the same Jury: That James Stevens, who Was Mayor in the Year next preceding, gave up his Accounts, as usually, and never after pretended to act as Mayor, and died in April 1719; so that from September 1718 there was not any Person acting as Mayor in the said Borough; notwithstanding which, on the- 8th of September 1719* some few Burgesses met in the Street, anti there put Francis Gwyn Esquire in Nomination for Mayor for the Year ensuing, though they had no Mayor who presided, as was always usual; and was sworn Mayor at next Ali-'chuelmas Court Leet; and made One James Colgill his Deputy, who had been a principal Manager in these Affairs: That a Quo Warranto was brought, in the Kings Bench, against these unjustifiable Proceedings; and, in Michaelmas Term 1720, a Verdict was given against Mr. Gwyn and Colgill, and Judgment was entered of Ouster; but before any Benefit could be had as to instating or swearing the said John Stevens, he died: That, in order to restore the Borough to its Privileges, the Petitioners, and others, petitioned his Majesty for a Charter of Incorporation; which was referred to the Attorney and Solicitor General, the 6th of February 1720; and Mr. Gwyn, and those in his Interest, also petitioned his Majesty, That if the prescriptive Right of the Borough was lost, it might he restored by Writ Mandatory; which Petition w as also referred to the Attorney and Solicitor General; and, upon their Report, That it was most advisable for his Majesty, if he thought ... to grant a Charter, in which respect might be had to the former Privileges of the said Borough: That, upon this Report, Mr. Gwyn, and others, petition to be heard by his Majesty in CouncilOn the 17 October 1721, when all Parties w ere heard, it was ordered. That a Charter should be granted; but it is not yet obtained; yet Colgill, in September 1721, after he had joined in the Petition for his Majesty's Writ Mandatory, ^ook upon himself to preside as Mayor;

Carpenter Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, with Nicholas PhiIpot Esquire, and Serjeant Birch, were Candidates at the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Weobly, in the County of Hereford; the Under Sheriff directed a Precept to John Davies and Walter Green, Constables of the said Borough, who were the only proper Returning Officers, and dispatched a Messenger with it from Hereford to Weobly; but the Messenger, instead of giving it to the paid Two Constables, was prevailed upon to carry it back to the Under Sheriff; who, the next Day, brought it to Weobly again; and then gave it to John Moor and Thomas White, Two Persons whom the Sitting Members, or their Agents* had procured to be sworn as Constables, between the time of the Precept's being sent back to Hereford, and its return to Weobly, by Two Justices of Peace, who came out of their Division for that Purpose: That the said Green and Davies demanded the Precept of the Under Sheriff, and he refused to give it them; but, on the Election-day, came to the Town-hall, read the Precept, and then gave it to the pretended new Constables: That the legal Constables then proceeded to an Election; and on a Poll, the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes; and they declared him duly elected; and executed a Return, and tendered it to the Under Sheriff; but he not only refused to take it, but, on the contrary, took a Return, made by the pretended new Constables, of the said Mr. Philpot and Serjeant Birch; and many other unwarrantable Practices were used; in Prejudice of the Petitioner: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and re*

port the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A PETITION of above Two hundred distressed Debtors in the Prison of Wood-street Compter, London, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands in the several Prisons in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting, forth. That the Petitioners have long groaned under most oppressive Confinement, obnoxious to the most loathsome Miseries of life, without Hope of Liberty from their hard-hearted Creditors, who have had their All: And praying the Compassion of the House may expend to them, as it has done to a Multitude of unhappy Persons, who sheltered themselves in the Mint from their Creditors: And as a neighbouring Parliament are, at this Juncture, dispensing Relief to the Miserable in their Kingdom, the Petitioners hope a British Senate will have a regard to relieve them.

A Petition of the Prisoners in the King's Bench Prison was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That it being the Justice of the House to relieve the Oppressed, they apply for Redress; their unhappy Affairs rendering them incapable wholly to satisfy their merciless Creditors, though they have their All; so that the Petitioners Numbers daily increase; and the Length of their Captivity proves fatal to many of them, by Death, for want of common Necessaries; and 'tis un-christianly malicious in their Creditors, to confine in Gaol; alien they have sewed all their Debtors Effects, without any Support; a Practice not used in any Christian Country but our own; and which, they hope, the House w ill prevent: That, since an Act passed last Session for Relief of some Persons in the Mint, who sheltered themselves there, and consumed the just Property of their Creditors, in Opposition to Law; the Petitioner* pray the Relief of die House, who have suffered Loggary and Imprisonment under the Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The House* according to Order, took into Consideration the Report from die Committee, to whom the Pedtion of the Commissioners appointed by an Act of Parliament, made in the Sixth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for rebuilding the Parish Church of St. Martin in the Fields, in the City of Westminster, at the Charge of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred:

And the Report was read; and is as followeth;

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 23d instant, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and lind,

That the Commissioners, in pursuance of the said Act* have had several Meetings for rebuilding the said Church; and that all the Care and Diligence has been used by them, as possible, in the Application of the Monies thereby granted; but the several incident and unforeseen Expences, in carrying on the said Building/ has rendered the same, by the moot exact Computation of skilful and experienced Workmen, insufficient of being finished by the Provision that is now allowed by Parliament:

And, upon the Examination of Surveyor,

it further appeared to the Committee, That the said Commissioners had contracted and agreed with several Artificers and Workmen for rebuilding the said Church, at lower and more reasonable Rates than are usually given and paid to Persons concerned in Cases of the like Nature; and Advertisements were printed in die publick Papers for that Purpose; and, by the several Accounts of the Commissioners, and the Surveyors, produced and laid before the Committee, it appeared what Sums of Money have been raised by the said Act of Parliament, and how applied; and that a further Sum is still necessary to be raised, in order to finish and complete die rebuilding of the said Church.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for completing the rebuilding the Parish Church of St. Martin in the Fields;

A PETITION of the Prisoners of the Gaol in Debtor* Bristol was presented to the House, and read; Petition, setting forth, That, by the unavoidable Accidents of human Affairs, well known to the House, the Number of insolvent Debtors daily increase in the said Gaol, and are mere Objects of Alisery and Want; and the Length of Confinement has proved fatal to many of them by Death; and, though their Creditors have all their Effects, they will not release them, nor keep them in Gaol; an Act unheard of in any Christian Country but our own: But since this House has passed a Law for Relief of several Persons, who sheltered themselves in the against Law, to cheat their Creditors; the Petitioners, who have submitted to the Lawr, pray such Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Mr. Daniel Pulteney reported from the Committee Labourers i» appointed to consider of the Laws now in being relating Husbandry, to Labourers, and Servants in Husbandry; and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; That the Committee had considered the said Laws; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same in at the Clerks Table; Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Provision made by an Act, of the Fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, An Act containing divers Orders for Artificers, Labourers, Servants of Flusbandry, and Apprentices, for compelling Persons to serve in Husbandry, not being worth Ten Pounds in Goods and Chattels, be extended to Person* having Effects of greater value.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Powers be given to Justices of the Peace, to compel unmarried Men, not having any Child or Children, who are out of Service, or who work only by the Day, or the Week, and are bred to, or occupy themselves only in, Husbandry, to serve, and be retained, by the Year.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Persons hiring, or retaining, by the Year, Servants in Husbandry, be obliged to register, with the Minister of the Parish, the Names and Wages of such Servants, and the Time contracted for, or agreed upon;

And also the Names of the Persons signing the Testimonial required by the said Act: And that the Discharges of sqch Servants be also registered.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That further Provision be made for more effectually obliging Servants in Husbandry to be retained, and serve, by the Vear; and that no Person be discharged before the Expiration of the said Term, without the Consent of a Justice of the Peace, testified under his Hand; and that such Consent be registered in the same manner as Contracts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some more effectual Method be provided for obliging the Justices of the Peace to assess the Wages of Servants and Labourers mentioned in the said Statute of the Fifth of Queen Elizabeth; and also for the better Preventing of any Agreement, Promise, Gift, or Payment of Wages, contrary to such Assessment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Power be given to Justices of the Peace to compel the Payment of such Wages as shall appear to have been agreed on by any Contract, registered ais aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Power given by the said Act to Justices of the Peace, to grant a Writ of Capias to the Sheriff, for attaching fugitive Servants, be extended to Labourers in Husbandry leaving their Work unfinished.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some further Provision be made for punishing Servants within the said Statute, who shall be idle and disorderly, or otherwise misbehave themselves in their Services.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon* agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the Company of Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen, of the River of Thames, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act, 11 and 12 Willi. 3/. for explaining former Acts, and better ordering and governing the said Company, Power is given to their Rulers to make such Orders as shall be approved by the Lord Mayor and Aldermen of London, and confirmed by the Lord Chief Justice of either Bench, under certain Penalties, by Distress and Sale of the Offenders Goods, without Power of Commitment for want of a Distress; and the most turbulent and unruly Offenders have no settled Habitation; and no Distress can be made; so that the Abuses daily increase, and the Petitioners want Power to redress them: That, by an Act, 40 Anna', a Clause in a former Act, restraining the taking Apprentices under Sixteen Years of Age, is repealed; so that great Numbers of dissolute Watermen, for a small private Gain, take a greater Number of Apprentices than they can either employ or maintain, lodging them in their Boats all Night, for want of any other Habitation, w hereby they generally run into Pilfering and Robberies; and they also take Boys so very young, that they have not Strength or Capacity to manage either the Oar or Boat; whereby many Mischiefs* happen to Passengers: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making effectual the said former Acts; and for amending or repealing such Parts thereof as shall be thought proper; and to provide proper Remedies against the publick Mischiefs happening by reason of the Defects thereof.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and' report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards lessening the publick Debts and Incumbrances, the Annuities payable after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, and charged on the general Fund by'fc. Clause in the Act of Parliament, of the Fifth Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for granting to his Majesty an Aid, by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1719, other than, and except, such of them as have been subscribed into the Capital Stock of the South Sea Company, be redeemed, and paid off, at Lady-dap 1724.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the Principal, and Interest after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, payable for or on the se^ veral Standing Orders made, or to be made, for, or in respect of, the Blank Tickets only in the Lottery for One Million Four hundred thousand Pounds granted for the Service of the Year 1714, which shall remain due, and in A n ear, at Lady-day 17 24, other than, and except, so much thereof as has been subscribed into the Capital Stock of the South Sea Company, be then paid off, and discharged.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of the Monies arisen, or to arise, at or before Lady-day 1724, of or for the Surplusses, Excesses,

Or Overplus-monies, commonly called the Sinking Fund, and then remaining in the Exchequer, as*.will he necessary to redeem, and pay-off, the said Annuities, Principal and Interest; and also to redeem the Two Annuities, which, by the Act, of the Ninth Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for redeeming certain Annuities, payable by the Cashier of the Bank of England at the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent, per Ann. were enacted to be redeemed at Lady-day 1724; shall he issued, applied, and disposed of, for completing such Redemptions and Payments, as aforesaid, in the First Place; and, subject thereto, to the same Uses as they are now appropriated to by any former Act or Acts of Parliament.

Rcsobctd, That it is the Opinion of tills Committee, That, towards lessening the publick Debts and Incumbrances, the principal Sum of One Million Seven 1 Kindred and Seventy-five thousand and Twenty-seven Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpeny, now owing to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, in lieu of certain Exchequer Bills formerly by them delivered up, and cancelled; and which, by an Act of Parliament, of the Third Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for redeeming several Funds of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, pursuant to former Provisoes of Redemption; and for securing to " them several new Funds or Allowances, redeemable by " Parliament; and for obliging them to advance further " Sums, not exceeding Two Millions Five hundred thou- " sand Pounds, at Five Pounds per Centum, as shall be found " necessary to be employed in lessening the national Debts " and Incumbrances; and for continuing certain Provisions " formerly made for the Expences of his Majesty's civil " Government; and for Payment of Annuities formerly " purchased at the Rate of Five Pounds pa' Cent.', and for (c other Purposes in this Act mentioned; was to be attended with an Annuity of Eighty-eight thousand Seven bun- " dred Fifty-one Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence " Halfpeny, being after the Rate of Five Pounds perCent. per Ann.; and to be redeemable by Parliament upon a

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, and Commonalty, of Herring the Town and Port of Hastings, in the County of ~Su$* tishery. sex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That the greatest Dependence of the Inhabitants of the said Town is on the Fishery; which is brought to a low Ebb; and chiefly the Herring Fishery; the Dealers therein being under great Discouragements, by reason of large Quantities of shotten Herrings, that are yearly taken after the Feast of St. Andrew, when they are nnwholsome Food, and carried to Market; which prevents the Sale of those that are taken and cured at the proper time of the Year: That many thousand Families, who live upon the Sea Coast of this Kingdom, wholly depend upo^i the Fishery; and the Preventing of this pernicious Practice for the future will be a great Encouragement to the Fishery: And praying. That a Iaiw may be made to prevent the Taking of Herrings, for the future, after the Feast of St. Andrerc, except w hat is used for Bait at Sea only.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, Fishermen, and other Ditto. Inhabitants of the Town and Port of Folkestone, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Smacks or Stow-boats have been, from their First Beginning, very pernicious to Fishery in general; and, upon many Complaints made against them, they are under certain Restrictions; hut now are so increased, that, under Pretence of fishing for Sprats, they use Nets of so small Mash or Moak, that they take the smallest Fry ot Fish; and also great Numbers of shotten Herrings, when they are out of Season; and sell the same, when unfit to be eaten; to the Impoverishment of the fair Fisherman: And praying, 'Ihat no Herrings may be taken by the said Smacks, or otherwise, from the iot‘i of November until April,-yearly, save only for Baits.

A Petition of confined Debtors, to the Number of near Two hundred, in the Poultry Compter, London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a great N umber of the Petitioners were, by the Strictness of the late Act for Relief of insolvent Debtors, as well as by the Smallness of the Sum limited therein, obliged to remain Prisoners; arid, since then, many more by Misfortunes in Trade, and not a few by the South Sea Scheme, are added to their Number: That their extreme Poverty, loathsome Confinement, and continual Want of Necessaries, makes them fit Objects of Compassion; which they the rather hope for from the House, because, in the last Session of Parliament, they so suitably relieved the poor Shelterers in the Mint, whose Case could not be so wretched as the Petitioners: And praying, that a Bill may be brought in for the relief of insolvent Debtors in all the Gaols of the Kingdom, under such Restrictions as the House shall think fit.

Ordered That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ditto. A Petition of Captain John Bromfield, Wm. Harrison,

John Man, and Robei't Nicholas, in behalf of themselves, and several hundred of poor Debtors, in the Marshalsea Prison, in Southwark, and also in behalf of all others in the like miserable Circumstances, in general, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That many of the Petitioners have been trading Men, and others in the Service of the Government; and, by great Losses and Misfortunes, are reduced to the last Extremity, having languished several Years in the worst of Gaols, where they have no allowance but Water; and, though they have tendered their All to their Creditors, yet they are still kept starving, in close Confinement, worse than Death, and their poor Families are also become burthensome to their respective Parishes: And praying such Relief as a British Parliament shall think fit to give.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

'with it the greatest publick Advantage, and adds most to the national Stock: That the Shoals of Herrings come yearly, early in the Summer, round the Orkneys, and so along the Coast of North Britain, up to the Southward, till, in the beginning of September, they always strike on the Coast of Norfolk; where is chiefly the Rendezvous of the Fisher-boats, and the Curing of Herrings; and many Hundreds of Boats, and Thousands of Men, are annually employed there, in Catching and Curing of Herrings; and, besides all that are transported to the other Parts of the World, about Thirty large defensible Ships are yearly sent, with Red Herrings, to the several Parts of France, Italy, and Sicily, in the MediterraneanThat when the Shoals of Herrings are passing up the North Seas, they are always full, large and fat, and then only fit to pickle; and then only are best to make Red: That they continue full till past the Middle of October, w hen they begin to shoot their Spawn; yet such shotten Herrings as are taken belore Martinmas, which is the longest time the Fishing has been reckoned to extend, have been made Red; and, when so cured, have found Vent, at low Rates, principally at London, and on the Coast of Yorkshire, in Holland, Flanders, and Spain; and such are caught in the deep Sea, with large Boats, and long Nets, many of which are near Half a Mile in Length: That, towards the End of November, and in December, yearly, the shotten Herrings, which are then very dry and small, come in vast Abundance on the Coast of and

Essex; and, of late Years, have been there taken in such Quantities, with small Expence, that though they are little Worth, and produce but little Advantage to the Takers, yet they depreciate the Value of full Herrings; and, it is to he feared, may lessen the Shoals, which, going down the British Channel, and round Ireland, fill again, and come periodically by the Orkneys, up the North Seas: That, if some Provision be not made to preserve the said Trade from this Mischief, it must, in few Years, be lost; there being Herrings enough caught yearly, before the Feast of St. Martin, when only they are good and merchantable, to supply the Demand in every Market of the World: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the taking of Herrings on the Coast of Britain or Ireland, unless for Bait only, between the l ith of November and the First of May, yearly.

Mr. Bertie reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Third Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways from that Part of Counter's Bridge which lies in the Parish of Kensington, in the County of Middlesex, to the Powder-mills, in the Hoad to Staines; and to Cranford Bridge, in the said County, in the Road to Colnebrook; was referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as folloueth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 12th Day of , examined

the Mattel' of the said Petition: And,

Upon the Examination of Reginald Marryott, John Offley, Esquires, and Mr. Albert it appeared to

the Committee;

That the said Highways were in so bad and ruinous a Condition before the Commencement of the former Act, the Trustees, in order to make the Road passable the then next Winter, were obliged, pursuant to the Power thereby given them, to borrow a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls: That, by reason of the Badness of the said Roads at first, the Trustees were obliged to borrow of several Persons, and at several Times, the Sums of £. 6,400. and also f. 2,500. for Gravel bought in order to put the said Road into a good Condition; and, if the Trustees were to pay. off the Monies arising by virtue of the said Act, the Roads must then, inevitably, go to Decay, and become very dangerous to Passengers, before the Expiration of the said Term, for want of an annual Supply to keep the same in Repair; and even then, according to the nearest Calculation that can be made, there will be a Debt remaining of about f. 2,500.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term granted by an Act, passed in the Third Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways from that Part of Counter's Bridge which lies in the Parish of Kensington, in the County of Middlesex, to the Powder-mills in the Road to

Staines; and to Craiiford Bridge, in the said County, in the Road to Colnebrook; and for making the said Act more effectual: -And that Mr. Bertie, and the Lord Rowlett, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Lade reported, from the Committee, to whom Regulating the Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, Watermen, of the Company of Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen, of the River of Thames, on behalf of themselves and others, was referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the said Report and Resolution were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and took into Consideration the several Acts of Parliament for constituting and regulating the said Company; and particularly the Act, of the 11 th and 12th of King William the Third, mentioned in the Petition; whereby Power is given to the Petitioners for making Orders and By Laws for the better governing the said Company, to be approved of by the Court of Lord Mayor and Aldermen of London, and afterwards confirmed by the Lord Chief Justice of either Bench, under the Penalties therein contained:

That the Penalties inflicted by the said Act, are to be levied by Distress and Sale of the Offenders Goods, without any Power of Commitment, or corporal Punishment, in Default of Distress.

That the Petitioners, to prove the Defects of the said Act of Parliament and By Laws, produced several Witnesses; viz. (

Malt is Ryall and John Hill, Watermen: Who said, That most of the turbulent and unruly Watermen are neither llousholders, nor such as have any settled Habitations; so that no Distress can be made of their Goods; whereby the said Act is eluded, and the Offenders escape with Impunity; although the Mischiefs arising thereby daily increase: And,

Mr. Church, Clerk of the said Company, produced a List of 120 Watermen, w ho have several Servants, and yet have neither Boat nor Effects.

It further appeared to the Committee, That, by an Act, passed in the Fourth Y'ear of the late Queen Anne, for better governing the said Company, a Clause, in a former Act, to restrain the taking Apprentices under the Age of Sixteen Years, is repealed:

To which the Petitioners complain as a Grievance.

Maltis Ryal and John Hill said, That great Numbers of dissolute Watermen, for a small private Gain, take a greater Number of Apprentices than they can employ or keep, lodging them in their Boats all Night, having no other Habitation for them; and frQin thence they often run pilfering; and, frequently, take Boys of Ten or Twelve Years of Age, who have not Strength to row', or manage an Oar; and a great many of them are almost out of their Time at Sixteen Yrears of Age:

That, since repealing the said Clause, the Number of Watermen are increased above 4,000; and they produced a Li6t of the Watermen and Lightermen, and their Servants, with their Places of plying, amounting to 9,74).

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations ot their Petition: And that the House be moved, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better regulating the Company of Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen, of the River Thames; and for inflicting corporal Punishment on the Breakers of their By La'vs, where no Distress can be made, and restraining them from taking Apprentices without Limitation.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for better regulating the Company of Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen, of the River Thames And that Mr. Ijade and Mr. Hungerford do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Henrit Blake Esquire, being examined, said, He had sat in Three Parliaments for this Borough; had known the Borough Fifty Vears: That he always understood, and had been informed by ancient Persons, now dead, that the Right of Election ivas in the Guild Stewards and Burgesses, exclusive of all others; and no Pretence to the contrary was ever set up, or heard of, before 1700; when, und afterwards, in 1705 and 1710, some Commoners, who were not Burgesses, pretended to vote; but they were always denied by the Stewards and . Burgesses:

That all Burgesses, after their Election, and taking the Burgesses Oath at Caine, take the Oaths of Fidelity to the Government at OgburnCourt; w here they are presented by the Guild Stewards, or bring their Certificates of being duly elected Burgesses at

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for die Borough of Caine, in the County of Wilts, is in the ancient Burgesses of the said Borough only.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of returning Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Caine, in the County of , is in the Guild Stewards of the said Borough.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Gybbon also, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Pi ivileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Westbury, in the County of Wilts, with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read: And the said Report and Resolutions arc as follow;

'Upon the Petition of George Lord Carbury, of the Kingdom of Ireland, and Tho. Bmmett Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of the honourable James Bertie Esquire, and Francis

Annesley Esquire, to serve for the Borough of Westbury, in the County of Wilts:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in every Tenant of any Burgage Tenement, in Fee, for Life, or Ninety-nine Years determinable on Lives, or by Copy of Court Roll; paying a Burgage Rent of Four Pence, or Two Pence, yearly; being resident within the Borough; and not receiving Alms.

That the Petitioners Counsel alledged, There had been undue Practices for the sitting Members: That the Petitioners had a Majority of legal Votes; and ought to have been returned:

And, in order to prove a Copy of the Poll, called William Bourne:W ho produced, as a Copy of the Poll,

a Paper; w such, he said, he received that Evening from one Mr. Blezc, a Stranger to him: That he believed it to be signed by the Mayor, because he knew the Mayors Hand; but did not see him sign it; nor could he say any thing to the Truth of it, having never examined it with the original Poll; but that soon after the Election, he saw this Paper in the hands of Mr. , w'ho died

about Five Weeks since.

That, the Committee not thinking fit, upon this Evidence, to receive the Paper produced as a Copy of the Poll, the Counsel for the Petitioners acquainted the Committee,

Carnwath's was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, forfeited Es- That he, being unhappily engaged in the late Rebellion ute*" in the Year 1715, was, soon after, attainted of High Treason; wheretijton his Estate, extending to £. 864. per Annum, became forfeited; the greatest Part whereof was forfeited to the Superiors, who had Right thereto by the Act, of the First Year of the King, intituled, An Act for encouraging Superiors, Vassals, ^'C.; the remaining Part has been sold by the Trustees, for the Use of the Publick, for the Sum of £.5,100.: That the Petitioner, being thoroughly sensible of his Majesty's Mercy, has, since his Attainder, continued to live as a dutiful and obedient Subject; but, by reason of the said Attainder, is deprived of a necessary Subsistence for himself, and Three Children now living; and, being obliged to contract several Debts, is reduced to the utmost Extremity: And therefore praying, That the House will make some Provision for the Maintenance and Support of himself and Children, as the House shall think fit.

Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House, That the Contents of the said Petition had been laid before his Majesty: And that his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint the House, That he had no Objection to any Relief that this House may think proper to give the Petitioner.
