Resolved, That is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Duties upon Coffee and Tea, granted, by one Act of Parliament made in the Sixth Year of the Iteign of his late Majesty King William the Third; and by another Act of Parliament made in the Third Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne; and by another Act of Parliament made in the Tenth Year of the Iteign of her said late Majesty Queen Anne; for several Terms of Years, in the said respective Acts mentioned; and which have since been continued by several Acts of Parliament, and made perpetual, subject to Redemption by Parliament; shall, from and after the 24th Day of June 1724, cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Duties upon Cocoa-nuts imported from the British Plantations, granted, by an Act of the Sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third; and by an Act of the Third Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne; for several Terms of Years, in the same respective Acts mentioned; and which have been since continued by several Acts of Parliament, and made perpetual, subject to Redemption by Parliament; shall, from and after the 24th Day of June 1724, cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of the said Duties so to be determined, an Inland Duty be charged upon all Coffee and Tea sold in Great Britain, by Wholesale or Retail; and upon all Chocolate made or sold in Great Britain; to be paid by the respective Sellers of such Coffee and Tea, and by the respective Makers or Sellers of such Chocolate.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon all Coffee sold in Great Britain, be after the Rate of Two Shillings per Pound Weight, Avoirdupoise; and in that Proportion for a greater or lesser Quantity; over and above all Customs and Duties which shall remain payable to his Majesty for the same, upon the Importation thereof

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon all Tea to be sold in Great Britain, by Wholesale or Retail, shall be after the Rate of Four Shillings per Pound Weight Avoirdupoise; and in that Proportion for a greater or lesser Quantity; over and above all Customs and Duties which shall remain payable to his Majesty for the same, upon the Importation thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon all Chocolate to be made or sold in Great Britain shall be after the Rate of One Shilling and Sixpence per Pound Weight Avoirdupoise; and in that Proportion for a greater or lesser Quantity, to be paid by the respective Makers or Sellers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the 24th Day of June 1724, no Chocolate ready made, or Cocoa-paste, shall be imported or brought into Great Britain from any Part or Parts beyond the Seas.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Inland Duties to be raised and levied upon Coffee, Tea, and Chocolate, be appropriated and applied to the same Uses and Purposes, as the former Duties upon Coffee, Tea, and Cocoa-nuts, to be repealed and determined, are appropriated and applied.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Subsidies, and additional Imposts, which shall remain payable to his Majesty, for all Tea imported, upon the Importation thereof, be after the Rate of lour Shillings for every Pound Weight Avoirdupoise, instead of the present Method of paying the said Duties, according to the reduced Value, by the Price at the Candle.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Subsidies, and additional Imposts, which shall remain payable to his Majesty for all Coffee imported, upon the Importation thereof, be after the Rate of Seven Pounds for every Hundred Weight, containing One Hundred and Twelve Pounds Weight Avoirdupoise, 20

instead of the present Method of paying the said Duties, accocting to the Value sworn by the Importers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Subsidies, and additional Imposts, which shall remain payable to his Majesty for all Cocoa-nuts imported from the British Plantations, upon the Importation thereof, be after the Rate of Fifty Shillings for every Hundred Weight, containing One Hundred and Twelve Pounds Weight Avoirdupoise, instead of the present Method of paying the said Duties, according to the Value sworn by the Importers.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Kelsall, and Mr. Jamnb, do prepare and bring in, the same.

The Lord Morpeth reported from the Committee, to Paving.' whom the Petition of several of the Inhabitants of the City and Liberty of Westminster, and of the Out Parishes within the Bills of Mortality, in the County of RFiddlesex, was referred, That they had examined the Afatters to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same w as read t ‘

And the Report, and Resolutions, areas follow; viz.

Upon the Examination of Sir Henry Dutton Colt, and Sir John Vanbrugh.....find;

That the publick Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the said City and Liberty, and the Out Parishes within, the Bills of Mortality, have, of late Years, been very much neglected, and ill paved; and that a proper Care has not been taken of the Levels and Declivities; am! the Steepness and Depths of the Channels make it extreme difficult and dangerous for all Wheel-carriages that pass through 'the same:

That the Dirt and Soil, for'Want of being properly taken and curried away; lie so-thick,' all over the Pavements,

o

Circulation of Foreign' Gold Coins.

Insolvent Debtors.

to Geo. I.

ments, that the Streets are become now scarce passable for Foot-passengers.

That, upon Examination of the whole Matter, and Consideration of the several Laws, now in Force, for the Paving and Cleansing of the Streets within the City of Westminster, and Liberties thereof, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That one of the Causes of the Badness of the Pavement of the Streets is, the not observing a due Level.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That one other Cause of the bad Pavement of the Streets is. That each Inhabitant is. obliged to pave before his own House, without being limited either in the Time, Materials, or Method of doing it

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whilst the Pavement is under the Direction of the respective Inhabitants, it will be always subject to the Inconveniences complained of.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,: That the Laws nows in being, for paving and cleansing the Streets* are insufficient to remedy the said Incon-, ycniences.

i Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Inhabitants he exempted from the Charge of paving and cleansing before their respective Houses; und from the Penalties incurred by neglecting the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the future, the Expence of paving and cleansing the Streets be defrayed by a Pound Rate upon the Inhabitants.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards the Ease of the Inhabitants, and in Aid of the Pound Rate, a Tax be laid on all Persons who keep Coaches, and on all Wheel-carriages shod with Iron.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Commission be appointed, with proper Authorities and Restrictions, to execute such Powers as shall be judged proper for the belter paving and cleansing the Streets.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,-That the several Laws, now in being, relating to the paving and cleansing the Streets, so far as they relate to Die City of Westminster, and Suburbs thereof, be repealed.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second lime, were; upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upoil the said Resolutions: And that the Lord Morpeth, Mr. Strickland, and Mr. John Chetwynd, do prepare, arid bring in, the same. "

A Petition of several Merchants, and other Traders, on behalf of themselves, and Thousands more, in arid about the City of London, was presented to the House* and read; setting forth, That great Quantities of foreign gold, and English broad Pieces, arc offered in Payment to the Petitioners, in the comma*! Course of Trade, and on Inland Bills of Exchange; which if they refuse to take, they are prevented receiving their just Debts; and, when the Petitioners have received such Gold, they cannot pay away the same for Customs, Excise, or any other Taxes; which is a very great Difficulty and Hardship upon them, and a great Obstruction to Trade, and the due Circulation of Money: And therefore praying, That English broad Pieces* and all foreign Gold, may be prohibited passing in Payment, or else may be taken for Customs, Excise, and all other Brariches of the publick Revenue; or that the House will afford them such other Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon this Day Sevennight.

A Petition of several Bargemasters constantly employed in navigating on the River of Thames, living at Oxf ord, Abingdon, Henley, Reading, Martow, Wallingford, Staines,

Chertsey, Ditton, Moisey, and Kingston, and other Places situate on the said River, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That whereas a Bill was brought into this House, the last Session, for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water from certain Streams, or Rivers, that run by or near the Villages of Drayton and Cora ley, in the County of Middlesex; the Petitioners were then informed, That, if the said Design should have been put iit Execution, as wfas then proposed, it would have been prejudicial to the Navigation of the River of Thames \ but that they are now truly informed of the Ways and Means whereby the Adventurers propose to carry on their Undertaking, and put the same in Execution: And beg Leave to represent. That they are assured, that, if the Adventurers shall be permitted to put their Design, in Execution, in the Manner they have now proposed to do, it will greatly improve the Navigation of the said River Thames; and in Consequence, will be not only beneficial to the Petitioners, but also to the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Inhabitants thereof, and of all the Counties through which the said River runs:

And therefore praying, That such Encouragement may be given to the said Undertaking, as this House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Freeholders, Landholders, and other Inhabitants, of the County of Middlesex, w hose Names are subscribed; and also the Petition of certain Adventurers for supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with Water; were referred; be received.

A PETITION of the Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, of the several Parishes, wherein the Road from the City of Rochester, leading through Maidstone to Stile-bridge, in the County of Kent, lies, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read 7 setting forth, That the said Road is Fifteen Miles in Length; and, by reason of the many heavy Carriages frequently passing through the same, is become very ruinous; and many Parts thereof are almost unpassable during the Winter Season, and great Part of the Summer Season: That the said Roads are so very bad, that the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, through which the same lead, cannot, by the ordinary Laws of the Kingdom appointed for repairing the common Highways, effectually amend and keep the same in Repair, in, such a Condition as Passengers may pass through the same with Safety: Therefore the Petitioners pray, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bili for repairing the said Roads from the City of Rochester, leading through Maidstone to Stile-bridge, in the County of Rent, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Two of the Commissioners appointed to put the said Act in Execution, being examined, said. That the Trustees for repairing the Road between Croydon and East Gnn-sted have laid out a considerable Sum of Money in amending the Road between Godstoneund Blindley Heath* being Five Miles of the most ruinous Part of the said Road; which is now in good Repair, and very commo* dious for all Passengers to travel the same:

That from Blindley Heath to East Grinsted is between Four and Five Miles; and the said Road, which yet remains unrepaired, is very dangerous to all Passengers; and lies in the Parishes of Godstone and Horne, in the County of Surry; and that, according to the best Estimate they can make of the Charge of repairing the said remaining Part of the same Road, it will amount to the Sum of £. 1,500. or thereabouts; and that, if such Suni were advanced and raised for that Purpose, the said Road might be sufficiently repaired "and amended within the Space of Two Years:

That the said Witnesses further said, That only the Sixth-part of the Sum, borrowed on the Credit of the said former Acts, being allowed to the Trustees for amending the said Road from Croydon to East Grinsted, the Road aforesaid cannot be effectually repaired by the Provision made by the said Acts of Parliament, without a further Sum be advanced for that Purpose.

The said Fran. Green, Thomas Moor, and Tho. Ma-shew, said, That there are Two Miles of the great Road beyond the Town of East Grinsted, leading to a Place called Highgate, at the Entrance into Ashdown Forest, in the Parish of East Grinsted; which has been, for many Years, in a very ruinous Condition; although the Inhabitants of the Parish of East Grinsted have laid out great Sums of Money for putting the said Roads in Repair; and duly levied the utmost Rates, as by Law" they were obliged to do; and, unless some other Provision be made, the Roads w ill be so bad, that they will be impassable.

That the Petitioners laid before the Committee Articles of Agreement, dated the 15th of September 1720, made between John Newnham Esquire, and the Inhabit , tants of East Grinsted; whereby Mr. Newnham obliged himself, for the Consideration of the Sum of £.360. to be paid at the Times therein mentioned, to repair the said Road, from the End of East Grinsted to the Gate called Highgate on Ashdown Forest, for One Year; and to keep the same in Repair for Seven Years; And a Rate of 4 C Six

8 2 £ Mar lit. A. 1723.

Six Pence in the Pound was collected upon the Inhabitants of East Gmated for Three Vears, for the reimbursing, and discharging, the Monies agreed to be paid to the said Mr. Newnham by the said Agreement; and, accordingly, he has received the whole sum of £360.; yet the said Road is still in a ruinous Condition; and a considerable sum will be wanting to put the same into Repair; Materials proper for that Purpose being not to be had near the said Hoad.

That, upon Examination of the w hole Matter, it appeared to the Committee, That the said Roads, from Blindley Heath to East Grinsted, cannot be sufficiently amended, and kept in Repair, by the Provision already made by Parliament; nor can the Road from East Grin-sted to Highgate aforesaid be amended, unless some further Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending the Roads from the Stones End, in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surry, to a Place called Highgate at the Entrance of Ashdown Forest, in the Parish of East Grimted, in the County of Sussex, by enlarging the Terms granted by Two former Acts, the one of the Fourth, and the other of the Sixth, Year of his Majesty's Reign: And that Mr. Pelham and Mr.

A Petition of Joseph Hinxman Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner being a Candidate for the Borough oi Christchurch Twyneham, in the County of Soutkanfpton, the 22d of February last, to serve in this Parliament for the said Borough, in the room of Francis Gxvyn Esquire, who lately made his Election to serve for the City of Wells, one Jams Bullock, who took upon him to act as Mayor, with some new-made illegal Burgesses, refused to admit the Petitioners Voters into the Town-hall, the Place of Election; and ordered those that were in to withdraw, before the Precept was read; and then proceeded to Election, in a very illegal manner; yet a Poll was demanded; and the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned as duly elected; but the said Bullock bath returned Edward PrideuxGwyn Esquire; in Prejudice of the Petitioner: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Proviso was offered, to be added to the Bill, That this Act shall not extend to make good any Deed, Will, or Lease, made, and not inrolled, of the want of Inrolment whereof Advantage hath been taken, by any Action or Suit commenced, or lawful Entry made on the Day of but every such Deed, Will, or

Lease, shall remain of such Force only, as the same would have had, in case this Act had never been made:

The said Proviso was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to excuse Persons prosecuted for neglecting to take the Oaths, or registering their Names, and real Estates, in case they, before Judgment, submit to take the Oaths, or register their Names, and real Estates, and pay the Cosits of the Prosecution:

And the Clause was once read:

And the Question being put, That the Claris^ be read a Second time;

It passed in the Negative.

And other Amendments were made by the Housee in the Body of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendment^, be ingrossed.

Northamp- A Petition of the Inhabitants of Dunchurch and Thur-

toa Road. laston, in the County of Wamide, was presented to the

House, and read; setting forth, That the ancient Road from Coventry to London lieth through the Fields of Thurlaston, and Town of Dunchurch; and still remains the great Post Road from Chester to London \ but, of late Yews, the Stage Coaches and Waggons have quitted the said great Road; and, by Connivance, have been suffered.to pass over the Lands of the Duke of Montagu, who is Lord of the said Manor of Dunchurch, lying upon the Heath of Thurlaston; to the Prejudice of the Petitioners, who have right of Common there; which will be lost, if the Bill depending in the House, for amending of the Road from Mtridon-hiLl to Northampton, should pass into a Law: That there now is a Turnpike at Stony Stratford for amending the said great Road to Dunchurch; but, by reason of the Length thereof, being about 21 Miles, and the Scarcity of Materials, the said Road cannot be so effectually amended as it ought to be: And praying a Bill may be brought in for erecting One or more new Turnpikes on the said ancient Road; or if the said Bill, now in the House, should take place, proper Clauses may be inserted, for continuing the Road through Dunchurch, and thereby securing the Petitioners said Right of Common.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairing the Road leading from Meriden-hiU, in the County of Warwick, to the Town of Northampton, is committed.

Reign, intituled, An Act for the better Regulating of Pilots for the Conducting of Ships and Vessels from Dover, Deal, and the Isle of Thanet, upon the Rivers of Thames and Medway \ together with a Clause for further Explanation thereof, in an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for the further preventing his Majesty's Subjects from trading to the East Indies, under foreign Commissions; and for encouraging, and further securing, the lawful Trade thereto; and for further regulating the Pilots of Dover, Deal, and the fcle of Thanet; which is near expired; be further continued from the time of the Expiration thereof, for the Space of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament.

MR. Onslow reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor and Magistrates, and several other Inhabitants, of the Town of Guildford, in the County of Surrey; and also of several Persons living upon or near the great Road between the Town of Guildford, and the Town of Kingston upon Thames; was referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same inliis Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the said Report was read; and is as followed; viz.

That the Committee have taken into Consideration the said Petition, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 6th Instant; and examined the Matter thereof.

That it appeared to the Committee, by the Act of Parliament, passed in the Fourth Year of his Majesty's Reign, for amending the Roads from the City of London to East Grinsted., in the County of Sussex; and to Suttou and Kingston, in the County of Surrey; which was to continue for the Term of One-and-twenty Years, to commence from the 25th of March 1718; and by a subsequent Act, passed in the Sixth Year of his Majesty's Reign, for enlarging the Term granted by the said former Act, for the further Term of Two Years; That the Proportion allotted for the Repair of the Roads from London to Kingston, in the County of Surrey, is a Fourth Part of the Monies arising by the said Turnpikes*

6

Martii. A. 1723.

William Watkins Esquire, Surveyor General of his Majesty's Roads, and living near the great Road mentioned in the Petition, being examined* said* That he had surveyed the Roads from the Town of Kingston to Burton Common, in the County of Surrey, on account of his Majesty's passing through the same to Guildford; and that it is very ruinous, and almost impassable, in some Places; and especially from Kingston to Sandy Chappel:

That it is so bad from Cobham to liedhill, that Passengers are frequently obliged to go through a Warren; and the Examinant 1ms been forced to employ 40 or 50 Men to lay Bavins, and other Materials, to make it passable for his Majesty, when he went to Guildford: That 12d. in the Pound, besides the Statute-work, would not be sufficient to put the said Road in Repair; nor is it capable of being amended, but by a publick Expence:

That the Examinant, being a Justice of Peace for the County of Surrey, has found, That the Statute-work has been constantly done in repairing the said Roads:

That the Road from Putney to Kingston lies intirely upon a Gravel, and is easily put in Repair; for there is not any Part of it bad but the Hill; and there has been nothing done to that, except in the last Year; for that the Examinant would keep in Repair all that Part of the Road for £.30. a Year, for Ten Years to come:

That Travellers generally cross over the Thames at Putney, and go through the King's Road; therefore the Road from Putney to London is much less used.

Mr. John How said, That the Road from Kingston to Esher is much worse than any Part of the Road from London to Kingston:

That the Examinant has lived at Esher 33 Years; and has been twice Surveyor of the-Highways for that Parish; and they Constantly have done the Statute-work; but even that, and Six Pence in the Pound, will not be half sufficient to repair the same; there having been Six Pence in the Pound levied for that Purpose, and carefully applied; and the Road, notwithstanding that, remained in a very ruinous Condition:

That the Examinant, and his Servants, have been frequently called up, in die Night, to help Persons m Distress by the Badness of the Roads:

That the Carriers belonging to his Majesty, that go through that Road to Portsmouth, have been so mired, that he has been called by the Guards, to their assistance; and that 15 Horses could not draw a Carriage out, which Five Horses might have drawn, if it was not from the Roads bring so founderous.

That, upon Examination of the whole Matter, it appeared to the Committee, That the ordinary Means appointed by the Laws and Statutes of this Realm are not sufficient for the effectual repairing foe said Road from Kingston to Burton Common; nor are foe Inhabitants, in which foe ruinous Places of the said Road do lie, of Ability to repair the same; except 9ome other Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom foe Bill for amending the Roads from the Stones End, in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of 1Surrey, to a Place called Highgate, at the Entrance of Ashdowne Forrest, in the Parish of East Grinsted, in the County of Sussex, by enlarging the Terms granted by Two former Acts, one of the Fourth, and foe other of foe Sixth, Year of his Majesty's Reign, is committed.

That they do make Provision in the said Bill for repairing the bad and ruinous Places in the great Road between Kingston upon Thames and a Common called Burton Common, about a Mile beyond the Town of Ripley, in foe County of Surrey.

Mr. Gybbon, according to Order, reported, from the"Launceston Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it Election, appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Dunheved, alias Launceston, in the County of Cornwall, with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the Report, and Resolutions, are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of John Wilks Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Alexander Pendarvcs Esquire, and Doctor John Friend, to serve for the Borough of Dunheved, alias Launceston, in the County of Cornwall:

That the Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

That the Right of Election was controverted.

The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That this Borough w as first incorporated in the Time of Philip and Mary;

That the Right of Election was founded on their Charter; which incorporated the Mayor, and Eight Aldermen, all named to be Inhabitants; and gave Power to them, or the major Tart of them, to admit Inhabitants to be Burgesses, or Freemen; which are synonymous Terms in the Charter:

That the Right of Election is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Freemen, being Inhabitants at the time they were made free, and not receiving Pay of the Parish.

The Sitting Members Counsel insisted, That this is an ancient Borough, and, before their Charter, sent Members to Parliament Timeout of Mind: That the Charter confirmed all their ancient Rights and Privileges; and neither did nor could alter the Right of Election, which was in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Freemen sworn before the Mayor and Aldermen, or the major Part of them, whether such Freemen were Inhabitants, or not, at the time of Admission, and who do not receive Alms or Charity from the Parish:

That the Charter is dated the Fifteenth of February, in the Second and Third Years of Philip and Mary; which constitutes and grants, That the Borough or Town of Dunheved, alias Launceston, should, for the future, for" ever be a free Borough; and incorporates the Burgesses of the said Borough per nomen major*' communitaf burgi de Dunheved, alias Launceston; and erects, establishes, and creates, them a Body Corporate and Politick, to have perpetual Succession by that Name:

The First Mayor and Aldermen are named to be Inhabitants; all their ancient Rights, Customs, and Privileges are confirmed, except their Election of Portreeves, who are abolished by this Charter:

The Power granted, by this Charter, to elect free Burgesses, is in the following Words; Concedimus pra faf majdri communitati dicti burgi de Dunheved, alias-Lauft&ston, 8$ successoribus suis, quod iidem major com-4 G muni las

The Sitting Members Counsel offered to prove, That foreign Burgesses had joined in Returns to Parliament, since the Charter of Philip and Mary; which the Petitioner's Counsel admitted to have been done in and since the Reign of King James the Second; but insisted, That foreign Burgesses had no Right; and that this Charter of Philip and Mary was the First Charter of Incorporation of this Borough, and the only Charter under which the BurgesSes acted; and observed, That all precedent Grants or Charters, therein recited, were only Grants or Charters of Confirmation of Privileges, and none of them Charters of Creation or Incorporation.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Members called the following Witnesses; viz.

William Warren &nd Beijja Vigors: Who said, That, to their Knowledge, in all Elections, for Fifty Years past, the Out Freemen voted, and were never objected to, though they did not live in the Corporation at the time they were made free.

James Wakeham said, That, to his Knowledge, for 30 Years past, the Out Freemen voted, on all Sides, without Objection, though many of them never lived in the Corporation: That lie served his Clerkship to Mr. King., the Town Clerk, deceased; and had heard Mr.

To prove a Right to Freedom by Servitude; and to add Five to the Petitioners Poll, upon that Foot; the Petitioner's Counsel called,

William Stokes: Who said, He was Sixty-seven Years old; had known the Town all his Life: That the ancient Usage always was, to admit to Freedom Persons who had served Seven Years Apprenticeship to Freemen in the Borough; and he gave an Instance of One, in 1684, who, being refused, brought a Mandamus against the Mayor; and, thereupon the Corporation, after advising and consulting together, admitted him; and, after that, none were denied, till of late, that the Corporation having taken upon them to refuse ail but their own Party, and to swear those they admit never to be against the Mayor and Aldermen.

Thomas Kingdon and Robert Pcarse said, It had always been usual to admit to Freedom Persons that had served Seven Years Apprenticeship; and there was no Refusal of such till the late Differences about choosing Members of Parliament:

And Pearse said. That, upon an Election Twenty-four Years since, the Mayor admitted to Freedom several Persons who would promise to vote as the Corporation would have them; and refused all others.

The Five Persons, who the Petitioner would add to his Poll, upon this Foot of Right by Servitude, were Ca-rezv Tmgcomb, John Gudding, Shadrack Gezven, Nichr , White, and Dan. Eyme.

The Indentures of their Apprenticeships were produced and proved; and also their Seven Years Servitude to Freemen in the Borough: And,

John Carpenter said, They all tendered their Votes, at this Election, for the Petitioner; and he knew, that Four of them had demanded their Freedoms several Years before the late Election.

Henry White: He knew the other, Nicholas White, had demanded his Freedom of Two Mayors.

William Stokes said, That Tmgcomb had often demanded his Freedom of the Corporation; and was always refused, because he w'as not of the right Party, and for no other Reason; for he produced his Indenture, and they all knew of his Servitude:

That it had been usual for the Grand Jury to present Persons, who bad served Seven Years Apprenticeship, for not taking up their Freedom; and upon such Presentments, they were always admitted, or amerced for Refusal.

The Sitting Members Counsel denied, That any Servitude gave a Right to Freedom in this Corporation, other than for the Exercise of Trades, and Enjoyment of particular Liberties and Immunities; but gave no Right to the Privilege of Franchise of voting in Elections to Parliament; which depended upon the Charter; and insisted, That, according to the Constitution and Charter of this Borough, as before staled, the Admission to Freedom is perfectly discretionary in the Mayor and Aldermen, who may admit or refuse as they please: The Petitioner's Counsel agreed, That the Mayor and Aldermen had a discretionary Power to admit Inhabitants who had no Right; but denied, that they had any power to exclude Persons who had a Right, gained by serving Apprenticeships.

That the Sitting Members Counsel called,

William Warren: Who spoke for Fifty Years past; and laid, That the Consent of the Mayor, and Majority of the Aldermen, w'as always necessary to Admission to Freedom; and that there was no Right acquired by Servitude, or otherwise; nor any Way to gain Freedom, but by Consent of the Corporation: That himself was born n the Vol.20. '

Town, and was the eldest Son of a Freeman; but never j.auncestoa could obtain Freedom, because the major Part of the Al- Election, dermen w ould not consent, though some dlid.

Ben. Vigoj's, Wm. Warren, and James Wakeham: The Two first of w'hich spoke for Fifty Years past, the other for Thirty; and said, They never knew', rior understood, that any Person had a Right to Freedom by Birth or Servitude; and gave Instances of both Sorts refused wit!jin Sdven Years past; and said, The Answer which the Corporation gave to the Claimers, w'as, That there was no Right to Freedom: These Witnesses said, They thought there w as no Right; and that the Admission to Freedom must be by the Mayor, and Majority of the Aldermen, for the Time being; and they also gave Evidence, that neither of the Five Persons, who the Petitioner would add to his Poll, appeared, or demanded to be polled, at this Election, though after all the Voters present had voted.

Three Proclamations were made, at distinct times, as usual, for other Voters to come in, if there were any not polled.

To qualify Five of the Voters objected to, the Sitting Members Counsel called,

Benjamin Vigors: Who said, He remembered the Time, when Hugh Pyper Esquire came from Plymouth to live at Launceston, about Thirty Years since; that he lived in the Town, with his Family, at his ow n House there, at the time he was made free; and lived in the Towm also during his Mayoralty, w'hich was about Ten Years after:

That Arthur Porter lived in the Town, with his Father-in-law Philip King, at the time he was made free; w'hich was about a Year after his Marriage with Kings Daughter:

Being cross-examined, he said, He was not present when either Pyper or Porter were admitted to Freedom; and that he knew' the Times only by Information received in those Years; the First of which, he said, wras about 30, and the other about 20 Years since, though he could not name the King s reign.

That he was present when John Roberts Clerk was admitted to Freedom, about Nine or Ten Years since; that Roberts wfas, at that time, Usher to the Minister of the Town; and then lived, as an Inhabitant with the Minister, in his House in the Town:

This Evidence was confirmed by Wm. Warren and James Wakeham; and Warren said, He was present in Court at Poi'ters Admission to Freedom: And,

Arthur Laxvrence confirmed the Evidence, before given, of Roberts Inhabitancy when he was made free; and said,

He was also present, and admitted to Freedom at the same time with Roberts.

Ben. Vigors, James Wakeham, Arthur Laxvrence, and Wm. Webber, being severally examined, said, That John Abbott gave his Vote very distinctly for the Two Sitting Members by Name; but, speaking low the First time, was bid to speak higher; which he did, the Second time, loud enough for the w'hole Court to hear him:

That Samuel Ball, being demanded to poll, said, he gave his Vote for Mr. Pen dances, and for Doctor John Elliott; and then immediately, in the same Breath, said, I mean for Doctor John Friend:

That there was no Objection made to Ball's Vote for Doctor Friend: Webber took the Poll for the Mayor; and Lawrence said, there^was no such Candidate as Doctor John Elliott at this Election; and that he never heard of any such Man in his Life.

Wm. Warren gave the same Evidence as to Abbott's Voting.

The Petitioner's Counsel, on their Reply, insisted;

That the Objection to Larke, as being admitted by a Minority of the Corporation, was insufficient; for, in Cases of Right to Freedom, the Mayor acted not judicially, but ministerially; and then it was his Duty to admit, and not necessary to have a Majority of the Corporation; which was requisitein the judicial Capacity, upon the Elections to Freedom where there was no Right: And,

Henry White, being called, said, That Larke served his Apprenticeship to his Father, who was a Freeman; and, for 25 Years past, had exercised the Privelege of Freedom, and voted in all Elections.

Robert Pearse said, Richard Carpenter was made free about 30 Years since, several Years before he- went to Gravesend; that he lived at that time with his Mother in Launceston, and has voted in many Elections of Mayors.

That the Committee had taken into Consideration the said Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough and Hundred of Ryegate, in the County of Surrey, and Places adjacent; and examined the Matter thereof:

That Mr. John Cherrington, who had been Surveyor of 4he Highways for the Parish of Horley, and Robert Skinner, of Ryegate, being examined, said, That the Lane leading from the Borough of Woodliatch, in the Parish of Ryegate, by Salmons Cross, to Sidlow Mill, in the said Parish, is about a Mile in Length: That Horshill Lane is about Two Miles and Half long: That Bonners Lane is Two Miles long: and Pctridge Lane is Half a Mile in length;

That the said Lanes are publick Highways, leading from several considerable Parts of the County of Sussex, towards the City of London:

That the Inhabitants of the Parishes in which the said Roads respectively lie, have constantly done the Statute-work; and there has been a Collection of Six Pence in the Pound, which has been applied towards amending the said Roads; and yet they are in a very bad and ruinous Condition, and dangerous to Travellers passing through the same; and are, in some Places, almost impassable:

That great Numbers of Waggons, belonging to the Farmers and Inhabitants of the Hundred of Ryegate, go to Croydon Market, and pay to the Turnpike erected there, though they pass through no part of the Road amended, with the Money arising the reby:

That the Roads afore-mentioned cannot be effectually repaired and amended by the ordinary Means provided by the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, unless some other Provision be made for that Purpose:

That the Committee had also taken into Consideration the Petition of the Inhabitants of Ebisham, in the County of Surrey, and of great Numbers of Gentlemen resorting thither; and, pursuant to the Instruction of the House, of the 18 Instant, examined whether the Road mentioned in the Petition be a Publick Highway, or only a Private or Permission Road:

That, upon examining Mr. Corbett, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Surrey, Mr. Ralph Mitchell, Jolui Sumner, and several other Witnesses, it appeared to the Committee, That the Road between Non such Park arid Worcester Park, in the County of Surrey, is not a publick Highway.

To the honourable the House of Commons;

The Report of the Trustees nominated and appointed to put in Execution the several Trusts and Powers mentioned and contained in an Act of Parliament, made and passed in the Seventh Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for raising M$ney upon the Estates of the late Sub Governor, Deputy Governor, Directors, Cashier, Deputy Cashier, and Accomptant, of the South Sea Company, and of John Aislabk Esquire, and likewise of James Craggs senior, Esquire, deceased, towards making good the great Loss and Damage sustained by the said Company; and for disabling such of the said Persons as are living to hold any Office or Place of Trust under the Crown, or to sit or vote in Parliament, for the future; and for other Purposes in the said Act expressed.

The before-mentioned Trustees crave Leave humbly to represent, That, since the last Report they laid before this honourable House, of the Effects of their Doings and Proceedings in the Execution of the Trusts in them reposed, the Values of the respective Estates of John Aislabk Esquire, and of the late James Craggs, senior, Esquire, which were then unsettled, and lay depending before, the Justices of his Majesty's Courts of King's Bench and Common Pleas, and the Barons of his Majesty's Court of Exchequer, for their final Determination, have been adjusted by them: That the Sum of Forty-five thousand One hundred and Twenty-six Pounds Five Shillings and Seven Pence was, by the said Justices and Barons, decreed to be paid, and accordingly hath been paid, by Mr. Aislabk, to the Cashier of the South Sea Company, as the clear Value of the Estates, real and personal, which belonged to him, or any in Trust for him, after a Deduction made thereout of the Value of the Estates he had on the First Day of October 1718:

That the Sum of Sixty-eight thousand Nine hundred and Twenty Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Four Pence Halfpeny was, by the said Justices and Barons, decreed to be paid, and accordingly hath been paid, by the Administratrixes of the said Mr. Craggs's Estate, to the Cashier of the South Sea Company, as the clear Value of the Estates, real and personal, which belonged to the said Mr. Craggs, or any in Trust for him, at his Death, after a Deduction made thereout of the Vglue of the Estates he had on the First of December 1719.

The said Trustees crave Leave to take Notice, That, they having, in pursuance of the Directions of this honourable House, mentioned in their last Report, caused Interrogatories to be exhibited before the Barons of his Majesty's Court of Exchequer, for the Examination of William Tdlard, Arthur Ingram, William Morley, Samuel Read, Richard Horsey, Stephen Child, Esquires; Sir Wm. Hammond, Sir Jacob Jacobson, Knights; Hugh Raymond, Charles Joye, Peter Delaportc, Francis Eyles, James Edmundson, Esquires; Sir Robert Chaplin Baronet; John Gore Esquire; Sir Wm. Chapman Knight and Baronet; Tho. Reynolds Esquire; Sir John Blunt Baronet; Sir liarcourt Masters Knight; Ambrose Page and William Astdl Esquires; most of the said Persons, so interrogated, have put in their respective Answers to the said Interrogatories; and these Answers have been carefully examined and compared with the Inventories and Accounts delivered by the said Persons; and the Trustees are proceeding to exhibit Interrogatories for the Examination of the rest.

The Trustees do further represent to this honourable House, That William Tillard, Colonel Hugh Raymond, Thomas Reynolds, Arthur Ingram, John Gore, Francis Eyles, Peter Delaporte, Richard Horsey, Stephen Child, Esquire; Sir William Hammoml, Sir Jacob Jacobson, Knights; Samuel Read and William Morley Esquires; being the several Persons whom they, in their former Report, mentioned; they were proceeding to liquidate and adjust all Matters which have respectively passed the above Examinations; and, since that time, released to the said

Trustees their respective Estates, and complied with all the Directions of the said Act of Parliament; and that there does not appear to the Trustees any Reason to doubt, but that the said Persons have made a fair Discovery of, and delivered up, all their Estates and Effects:

That the said Trustees have settled and adjusted the Accounts of the said several Persons; and have paid them, respectively, the Balances due to them, on their Parliamentary Allowances, with Interest thereon, iromthe 29th Day of September 172?, to the time of such Payment, pursuant to the Directions of the Act made for that Purpose.

They beg Leave likewise to represent to this honourable House" That they have adjusted Accounts with the Executor of the late Mr. Grigsby, and have paid him the Balance that appeared to be due on the Allowance made to the said Mr. Grigsby, with such Interest as aforesaid; and that, Mr. Edmundson having complied with the Direction^ of the Act of Parliament, so as to intitle himself to the Sum allowed him by the said Act, they have paid him the same, with Interest, as above.

The said Trustees crave Leave to take Notice, That they have examined into the Accounts of, and Claims upon, several others of the Persons, whose Estates are, by the first-mentioned Act, vested in the said Trustees, so as to be in a s;reat Forwardness towards clearing

O O

them.

The said Trustees do further most humbly represent to this honourable House, That the time for entering those Claims on the Estates vested in them having, sineb their making their last Report to this honourable House, been prolonged, there have been entered before thenri Fortyffour new Claims; and that the Amount of the Sums thereby claimed is about Twenty thousand Pound#.

They were in Hopes, That the Times allowed by the last Act of Parliament made for hearing and determining Claim8 on the Estates of the late Directors, and others, would have proved sufficient for going through that Work; but they are now apprehensive, that, notwithstanding their constant Application, they shall not be able to do it within the Term prescribed by that Act

They beg Leave to acquaint this honourable House, That they have inquired into upwards of Six hundred Claims; on all which they have made their Reports, from time to time, to the Court of Directors of the South Sea Company, except some few, which, either through the great Importance or Intricacy thereof, or their depending on long Accounts, and other Matters lying on the Claimants to make out, remain yet unreported.

As the said Trustees, in their last Report, could only take Notice they had begun to sell itye real Estates in them vested; they now crave Leave to inform this honourable House, That they have made a considerable Progress in that, as well as other Branches of their Trust; and have hereunto annexed an Account, containing, First, The Amount of the real Estates sold; Secondly, The Amount of the personal Estates sold, and got in; Thirdly, The Amount of the Monies paid, as well on Claims, and for the Allowances made by Parliament, as others ise; distinguishing therein each particular Person s Estate, as far as the same can, at present, be done.

Mr. Fairer, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider further of that Part of his Majesty's Speech, which relates to the National Debt, the Resolution^ which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk's Table: Where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the permitting his Majesty's British Subjects trade-ing to the Greenland Seas to import, in British Ships, navigated according to Law, Oil, Blubber, and Whale-fins, taken and caught in the said Seas, without paying any Duties for the same, during the S pace of Seven Years, will very much contribute to the regaining the Greenland Trade; and will encourage the Navigation, and promote the Consumption of the Manufactures, of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty of Three Pence per Pound upon Whale-fins, granted by an Act made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the late King William the Third, and continued by subsequent Acts, and made perpetual, be not collected during the said Term of Seven Years.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Farrcr, Sir John Eyles, and Mr. Scrope, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of John Elwick, of London, Merchant, Claims before was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, South Sea That he, being possessed of Receipts for Money paid in, iustees* on the First and Second Money Subscriptions taken by the South Sea Company, delivered them up, in order to be allowed Stock for the same; and, being, at the same, time, intitled to One thousand Pounds in the Third Money Subscription, he acquainted the Company's Cashier therewith; and desired, that might be likewise carried to his Account: After which, an Act passed, prescribing the Manner, and limiting the Time, for claiming Stock for Money Subscriptions; which the Petitioner was not apprised of, till after the Time for claiming was expired; and is now informed, by the said Cashier, That, his said Stock not being regularly claimed, according to the said Act, he can have no Relief, but by Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That the House will give him such Relief, as to them shall seem meet.

That the Committee proceeded, in the First Place, to take into Consideration the Petition of John Thompson, James Colebrooke, Agneta Johnson, and Dorothy Johnson, in behalf of themselves, and other Persons who were possessed of several Navy and Victualing, Transport and Ordnance, Bills, and Army Debentures; the Principal and Interest amounting to £, (1,024. 19A'* 7 A or thereabouts: And, upon die strictest Examination, do find the same to be as follows;

Mr. Henry Johnson, from the Navy Office, attended die Committee, with several Books and Papers of the 7

said Office; wherein it appeared, That the Navy Bills, claimed by the Petitioners, w'ere made out for Service done, and Goods delivered, for the Use of the said Office:

And also, the same Person, pursuant to the Order of the said Committee, produced an Account of the Ser* vice performed, or Goods delivered, for which the said Bills were made out, pursuant to the said Contracts, accordingly:

The said Person gave the Committee an Account how their Books were made up of all the Debts of the said Office, that were owing in the Year 1711; which Books were delivered over to the South Sea Company, pursuant to an Act of Parliament for that Purpose.

Mr. John Bishop appeared, from the Victualing Office, with the Books and Papers of the said Office; wherein it appeared, That the Victualing Bills, claimed by the Petitioners, were made out pursuant to several Contracts made with the said Office:

And also, the same Person, by Direction of the Committee, produced an Account of the Contracts, pursuant to which, the said Bills were made out; and that the Service, for which they were made out, was performed: And said also, That an Account of these Debts was delivered over to the South Sea Company, in the Year 17111, pursuant to an Act of Parliament for that Purpose.

Mr. John Elliott, from Mr. Jett's Office, appeared/ with the Books and Papers, wherein several Army and Transport Debentures were entered, claimed by the said Petitioners; and gave an Account also, That the Books, wherein these Debts were stated, were delivered in to the South Sea Company, in the Year 1711, pursuant to an Act of Parliament.

And also, Mr. Peter Crankc appeared to the Committee, from the Commissioners who manage the Transport Service, to give an Account of the Services done, for which the said Bills and Debentures, belonging to fthat Service was performed.

That Mr. Read attended, with the Books of the South Sea Company; wherein it did appear. That the Navy, Victualing, Transport, Bills, and Army Debentures, claimed by the Petitioners, were in the several Book® delivered to the South Sea Company, in the Year .1711, from the respective Officers; and that the said Bills and Debentures were, at the Committee, examined and compared with the said Books; and did all appear to be stated in the said Books, except One Bill of Seven Pounds, which was not produced; and that the said Bills and Debentures were not subscribed into the Capital Stock of the said Company, by reason of the Proprietors not claiming them within the Time limited by Law.

That Mr. Colebrooke, and Mrs, Johnson, gave the Committee an Account, That the Reason why the said Bills were not wrote into the Capital Stock of the South Sea Company in 1711, was by reason that these Bills were either mislaid, lost, or occasioned by Mistakes in the Powers of Attorneys, to whom Assignments of such Bills were made, and the Parties living at distant and remote Places from Londm; which was the Occasion that these Bills were not subscribed into the Stock of the South Sea Company within the Time limited by Act of Parliament.

That it appeared to the Committee, That the Sum due to the Petitioners, by Certificates from the several Offices, and by the Account delivered by Mr. Read from the South Sea Company, amounted to £.3,628. 19$. 2f d. Principal, and Interest to the 2.5 th of December 1711; and that there is due to them Twelve Years Interest, from the 25th of December 1711 to the 25th of December 1723.

A Petition of several of the Inhabitants, Housekeepers* of the Borough of limit on, in the County of Devon, not paying Scotland Lot, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have an undoubted Right to vote for Members to serve in Parliament; and constantly enjoyed the same ever since the restoring the said Borough* which is above Eighty Years since, without any Opposition, until the Year 1711, when the then House of Commons determined the Right of Election to be in the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot only; and the Petitioners have, ever since, been refused their Votes, though they have always demanded them; and Returns have been made accordingly: That the Petitioners presume the said Resolution was taken for want of sufficient Information of their Rights: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

The House, Uncording to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration the Report, from the Committee of the whole House, to tvhorti the Bill for permitting his Majesty's British Subjects to import, from the Greenland Seas, in British Ships, navigated according to Law, Whale-fins, Oil, and Blubber, Duty-free, during the Term therein mentioned, Was committed:

And the Amendments, made by the Committee, to the said Bill, were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That the Act shall not extend to give Liberty to import Whale-fins, Oil, or Blubber, Duty-free, unless the commanding Officer of the Ship importing the same shall first make Oath before some of the Commissioners, or principal Officers, of the Customs, in the Place of Importation, That all the Whale-fins, Oil, or Blubber, so imported, was, bona fide, the Fins, Oil, and Blubber, of Whales caught in the Greenland Seas by the Crew of such Vessels only, whereof the Captain, and One-third Part, at the least, of the Mariners, were British Subjects: And the said Clause was twice read; and amended; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for amending the Roads from the Stones End, in Southwark, to llighgate, at the Entrance of Ashdown Forest, in the Parish of East Grinsted, in the County of Sasser; and from Kingston to Burton Common; and also the Lane leading from Woodhatch to Sidlmo Mill, and the Lanes called Horshills and Bonehurst, alias Boners, and Peteridge Lanes, in the County of Surry; by enlarging the Terms granted by Two former Acts, one of the Fourth, and the other of the Sixth, Year of his Majesty's Reign; without any Amendment. And also,

Examination The Lords have agreed to the Amendment, made by of Drug*,&c. this House, to One of their Lordships Amendments, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better Viewing, Searching, and Examining, of all Drugs, Medicines, Waters, Oils, Compositions, used, or to be used, for Medicines, in all Places where the same shall be exposed to Sale, or kept for that Purpose, within the City of London, or Suburbs thereof, or within Seven Miles Circuit of the said City.

A PROCLAMATION. GEORGE R.

WHEREAS our Parliament stands prorogued to Thursday the Twenty-fourth Day of this instant September: We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Twenty-fourth Day of this instant September, be further prorogued to Thursday the Twelfth Day of Nor ember next ensuing the Date hereof, to be then held at Westminster: And we have given Orders to our Chancellor of Great Britain to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do hereby

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: And that his Majesty was pleased to soy, That he had ordered the Lord Chancellor to declare, in his Nam:- and Words, the Causes of his Majesty's meeting his People in Parliament at this time: And that thereupon the Lord Chancellor acquainted both Houses, 'I hat he had received a Speech from Lis Majesty on the Throne; which the Lord Ch uicellor read; and of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I am persuaded you share with me in the Satisfaction I feci at the prosperous Situation of Affairs: Peace with all Powers abroad, at home perfect Tranquillity, Plenty, and an uninterrupted Enjoyment of all Civil and Religious Rights, are most distinguishing Marks of the Favour and Protection of the Divine Providence: And these, with all their happy Consequences, will, I doubt not, by the Blessing of God upon our joint Endeavours, be long continued to my People.

The same Provision by Sea and Land, for the Defence and Safety of the Nation, will continue to make us respected abroad, and, consequently, secure at home: The same Attention to the Improvement of the publick Revenues, and to the Ease and Encouragement of Trade and Navigation, will establish Credit upon the strongest Basis; and raise such a Spirit of Industry, as will not only enable us, gradually, to discharge the National Debt, but will likewise greatly increase the Wealth, Power, and Influence, of this Kingdom.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Officers to prepare, and lay before you, Estimates of the Expences for the Service of the ensuing Year; And as they do not exceed what has Vo l. 20,

further declare our Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Twelfth Day of November next, be held, and sit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and Commissioners of Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminster, on the said Twelfth Day of November next.

Given at our Castle of IVindsor, the Twenty-second Day of September, in the Eleventh Year of our Reign.

been found, by Experience, to be absolutely necessary for the Security of the Kingdom, I make no Question^ but I shall have your ready Concurrence in raising the Supplies, in such manner as shall be most easy to my People.

There is One thing that I cannot but mention to you, as deserving your particular Consideration: It is too manifest, that the Funds established for the finishing the Works at Greenwich Hospital, and providing for a competent N umber of Seamen there, cannot, in time of Peace, be sufficient to answer the Expences of this great and necessary Work: It is therefore very much to be wished, that some Method could be found out to make a further Provision for a comfortable Support to our Seamen worn out in the Service of their Country, and labouring under old Age and Infirmities.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

You must all he sensible how much our present Happiness is owing to your Union, and steady Conduct: It is therefore wholly unnecessary to recommend to you Unanimity and Dispatch in all your Deliberations: The Zeal and Abilities you have, on all Occasions, shewn, in supporting the Interest of your Country, even under the greatest Difficulties, leave me no room to doubt of ihy having your intire and effectual Concurrence in every thing that can tend to the Service of the Publick, and to the Good of my People.

That his Majesty's faithful Subjects are highly sensible of the Blessings they enjoy under his Government, in a full and quiet Possession ot their Rights, Liberties, and Properties; and that this House will use their utmost Endeavours, That the happy Consequences of these Blessings may, by the Divine Assistance, he transmitted to the latest Posterity: To assure his Majesty, That this House will proceed, with all possible Chearfulness and Dispatch, in raising such Supplies as shall be necessary for the Honour and Safety of the Nation; and consider of the most proper Methods for the farther Improvement of the publick Revenues, and of the Trade and Navigation of the Kingdom.

A Petition of Sir Nicholas Williams Barohet, was present- Carmarthen cd to the House, and read; setting forth. That, at the Elec- Election, tion of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this Parliament for the County of Carmarthen, the Petitioner, and Edward Rice Esquire, stood Candidates; but the Sheriff who was under the Influence of Mr. Rice, appointed , the Election to be at Llandilo, a small Village, near Mr.

Rices House, not capable to receive and lodge One Third of the Freeholders; which Inconvenience he was told of; but he persisted in his Appointment: That the Election began on the 19th of April 1722, and was continued, by Adjournments, to the 24th of April, on Purpose to tire out the Petitioners Electors; and then, after all the Freeholders, who appeared for Mr. Rice, had polled, adjourned to the 2,5th without the Petitioners Consent:

That the Sheriff, and his Under Sheriff, proceeded veiy arbitrarily in taking the Poll, by polling many illegal Voters for Mr. Rice, and refusing to poll many good Votes for the Petitioner; and committed many other Partialities in favour of Mr. Rice: That, during the tirfle of Election, the Petitioner, and his Friends, were frequently insulted in Court by Mr. Rice, and his Friends; and his Agents often brought great Numbers of rude Persons, armed with Swords and Clubs j and, more especially, on the Evening, the said 24th of April, some short time before the Adjournment; at which time they assaulted and wounded divers Persons; and would not disperse, though the Proclamation against Rioters was, by Order of divers Justices of Peace there, read; which Riot, of Mr. Rice his own making, he pretends, was the Cause of the Sheriff's Closing of the Poll; and the said Sheriff hath returned Mr. Rive; in Prejudice of the Petitioner;

And praying such Relief in the Matter, as the House shall think fit.

Mr. Thompson reported from the Committee appointed Address on Yesterday to draw up an Address, to be presented to his *be K*ng'» Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty the Thanks of this House for your Majesty's most gracious Speech from the Throne: And, as your Majesty's fatherly Tenderness for your People, and the unspeakable Comforts of an easy Government, demand the sincerest Tribute of Duty, your Majesty's faithful Commons do now oiler to your Majesty the most unfeigned Assurances of Gratitude and Loyalty, with that becoming Zeal and Affection that is particularly requisite at this time.

We beg Leave to congratulate with your Majesty on the prosperous Situation of Aflairs at Home and Abroad; a Subject not only of Content, but of Joy: And we should be wanting to ourselves, and insensible of our own Prosperity, if we did not feel the same Satisfaction in reaping the Fruits of your Majesty's great Wisdom, that your Majesty hath in employing it to direct and guide us to our ow n Happiness.

Peace with all Powers Abroad, Plenty and Tranquillity at Home, with a full and quiet Enjoyment of every thing that is dear and valuable to us, are peculiar Marks of your Majesty's Government; which that they may be for ever rcmembred, this House will use their utmost Endeavours, by the DivineAssistance, to transmit the happy Consequences of these Blbssings to the latest Posterity, as Monuments to Futurity of the Glories of your Majesty's Reign.

To support the Interest and Credit of our Country, is to pay the most acceptable Obedience to your Majesty:

And therefore this 1 louse w ill proceed, with all C'hear-fulness and Dispatch, in raising such Supplies as shall be necessary for the Honour and Safety of the Nation: We will labour to discharge, gradually, the national Debt, by the Improvement of the publick Revenues; to increase our Wealth, by the Advancement of our Trade; and to establish our Strength, by the Encouragement of our Na-13 vigation;

Captain IVm. tire shine produced a Commission as Delegate for St. Andrews; but there Was another Commission produced for Alexander Bell-, who insisted, That lie was lawfully Delegate for that Borough: That the Petitioner produced a Commission, as Delegate for Con par, from the Magistrates and Town Council, and signed by the Common Clerk, with the Seal of the said Borough, and having all other Formalities, as usual: That Ensign James Ereskine, Brother to the said Captain, produced, likewise, a Commission, pretended from Coupar, without Form, or Persons that had any Right to appoint a Delegate for that Borough: That it was disputed, whether Captain Ereskine, or Bell, was the lawful Delegate for St. Andrew*; and whether the Petitioner, or Ensign Ereskine, was Delegate for Coupar; The said Binny, Preses of the Meeting, arbitrarily, and in Combination with the Common Clerk of his own Borough, ordered the Commission for Captain Ereskine to be entered, as lawful, without examining it, and without looking upon BelFs Commission; though the Delegates for Perth and Dundee gave their Votes against that Proceeding; but Binny after gave his own Vote, and ordered Captain Ereskine's Vote to be marked, for removing Bell; and then, pretending the Votes were equal, gave the casting Vote himself; and Mr. Bell then voted for the Petitioner: That, after this, Binny and Captain Ereskine rejected the Petitioner's Commission for Coupar, and allowed Ensign Ereskine's; and, to awe the Delegates of Perth and Dundee, and the Petitioner, a considerable Number of Men in Arms Were placed at the Door of the Town-house, where the Delegates met: That the Delegates for Perth and Dundee, and the Petitioner, as Delegate for Coupar,

voted for the Petitioner; so that he had Two undisputed Votes to One, or, in the worst View, Three Votes to Two, to serve far the said District; and yet the Common Clerk of Forfar hath certified to the Sheriff, as if Captain William Ereskine was duly elected; and the Sheriff hath returned him: And praying the Justice of the House in the Premises; and that such false Return may be amended.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Geo. Deane Esquire, was presented 16 the House, and read; setting forth, That, at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the

Borough of Taunton, in the County of Somerset, in the room of John TreJichard Esquire, deceased, the Petitioner, and Abraham Elton Esquire, stood Candidates; at which Election, the Petitioner had a great Majority of qualified Votes, according to the last Resolution of the House; and ought to have been returned; but Edward Cadby, Mayor of the said Town, who, before the Election, declared he would not return the Petitioner, though he had never so great a Majority, shewed the greatest Partiality on behalf of Mr. Elton, refusing many legal Voters, who offered to vote for the Petitioner; and admitting many to vote for Mr. Elton, who had no Right; and closed the Poll,

Without Proclamation, contrary to the Petitioner's Request; and denied a Scrutiny; and, by other arbitrary and corrupt Practices, the said Mayor hath returned Mr. Elton; in Wrong to the Petitioner r And praying Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said, Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Resolved, That an humble Address he presented to his Majesty,- That he will be graciously pleased to give Directions, That an Estimate of the Rebuilding and Repairs of Ships of War, at his Majesty's Yards, over and above what is proposed to bn done on the Head of Wear and Tear, and is not included in the Ordinary Estimate of the Navy for the Year 1725, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty s most honourable Privy Council.

A Petition of Adventurers, whose Names are subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That great Numbers of New Houses have been, of late Years, built within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent thereunto; and the Inhabitants thereof are greatly increased: That, by reason thereof, the Rivers and Waters, brought into the said Cities for the Use of the Inhabitants, are not sufficient to supply them with Water for their ordinary Occasions: And praying the House will give such Encouragement to the said Undertaking, as they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House: \

And it is referred to Colonel Bladen, Mr. Pultency, Master of the Rolls, Lord Wm. A Petition of several of the Inhabitants, Housekeepers Of the Borough of Honiton, in the County of Devon, not paying Scotland Lot, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting fordi, That the Petitioners have an undoubted Right to vote for Members of Parliament for the said Borough; and have constantly enjoyed the same ever since the restoring the said Borough, which is upwards of 80 Years since, without the least Opposition, till 1711, when the House did determine the Right of Election to be in the Inhabitants of the said Borough paying Scotland Lot only: That, at the several Elections since the said Resolution, the Returns have been made according to the Majority of the Payers of Scotland Lot only, though the Petitioners have made a constant Demand of their Right, and have desired to sign the Returns; which the Returning Officers have refused, alleging it was contrary to the last Resolution: That, at the late Election on the 1 oth Instant, the Petitioners would have voted for the present Sitting Member, the honourable Wm. Yonge Esquire, had there been any Poll; and did desire to sign the Return; but were refused, as formerly: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition he referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ludgershall A PETITION of Thomas Webb, Serjeant at Law,

Elec lion, Was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That, at the late Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Ludgcrshall, in the County of Wilts, John Webb Esquire, Borlace Webb Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates: That Roger Hutchence, Butcher, a Person appointed by, and dependent on, John Webb Esquire, presided, and acted as Bailiff, at the Election; and the said John Webb and Borlace Webb did, by themselves and Agents, corruptly give divers Sums of Money to several Voters, for their Votes; and, by Threats, deterred others from voting for the Petitioner; and, some short time before the Election, fraudulently made a great many Conveyances of Tenements, within the said Borough, to the Relations and Servants of the said John Webb, in order to qualify them to vote for him; and, by the Partiality of the said Bailiff, they were polled, and many others, who had no Right, and were objected to; arid many that had a Right were not suffered to poll for the Petitioner; by which, and other unfair Practices of the said Bailiff, lie hath returned Mr. John Webb and Borlace Webb, as duly elected, though the Petitioner had a Majority of good Votes: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee?, That they do hear the Matter of the said Petition upon this Day Three Weeks, the Sixteenth Day of December next.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors confined in his Majesty's Prison of the Fleet was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners recollecting the many Instances of Favour and Compassion that unhappy Sufferers have received from a British Parliament; That many of us are reduced to this Condition, by unavoidable Losses in Trade, and such other melancholy Accidents that attend human affairs: We humbly hope the House will esteem us proper Objects of Compassion Yol. 20.

and Relief: We desire to surrender the Remains of our shattered Fortunes into our Creditors Hands, and to leave ourselves destitute of every Accommodation, provided we may be restored to Liberty, the most valuable Enjoyment of Life and w hen we have made a faithful Discovery of all our Effects, and delivered them up to our Creditors, under the same Penalties that Bankrupts are liable to, in case of Concealment: And praying the House to order such a Bill for their Relief' as shall be thought most proper for that End.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

ShcUcrers Mr. Bernard reported from the Committee, to whom from Debt it was referred to enquire into the Matter of a Complaint in Wapping. majje to the House of great Violences and Outrages committed by evil-minded Persons, got together in the Hamlet of IVa])ping, Stepney, under the Pretence of being Shelterers for Debt, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Complaint; and that it appeared to the Committee, That very great Violences and Outrages have been committed by several Persons got together in the Hamlet of Wapping, Stepney, and Places adjacent, under Pretence of sheltering themselves for Debt; and that the Committee had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk'sTable: Where the said Resolutions were read; and arc as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That further Powers be vested in the Justices of the Peace, throughout that Part of Great Britain called England, for the more effectual Execution of their Warrants, and Escape Warrants.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some Provision be made for defraying the Charge of raising the Posse Comitutus, or any other Power that shall be requisite to execute Process, or Warrants.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Assemblies of Persons, taking upon themselves to regulate and determine Matters within the said Hamlet, and Places adjacent, contribute to the Support of the Disorders, and illegal Practices, committed therein; and that effectual Provision should be made against the Contrivers, Actois, Aiders, and Abettors, of and in such Assemblies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some proper Encouragement and Reward be given to the Prosecutors, upon their convicting such Offenders.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the J louse.

Ways and Sir Charles Turnefc according to Order, reported, Cleans. from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they bad directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: WJiere the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, which, by former Acts of Parliament, have Continuance to the 24th Day of June 1725, be further continued, in that Part of Great Britain called England, from the Twenty-third Day of June 1725 until the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1726, for and upon all Malt which shall be made, and all Mum which shall be made or imported) and.all Cyder and Perry which shall be made, for Sale.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of the Duties on Malt made and "consumed in Scotland, an additional Duty of Six Pence shall be paid for every Barrel of Beer or Ale brewed by the common Brewer, or any other Person or Persons* who; doth or shall sell, or tap out, Beer or Ale, publickly or privately, in Scotland, from the Twenty-third Day of June 1725 to the Twenty-fourth Dajqof June 1726*; and in that Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in further Satisfaction of what ought to be paid for the Duties on Malt, the Allowance given by an Act, of the First Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, or by any other Act or Acts of Parliament, for the Encouragement of the Exportation of Corn, shall, from and after the Twenty-third Day of June 1725, cease, determine, and be no longer paid, for any Corn or Grain exported from Scotland, or brought from thenee, and exported from England, before the Twenty-fifth Day of June 1726.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.
