O IR Edward Knatchbull reported from the Committee, lO to whom the Petition of the Inhabitants of St. John Baptist, and Town of Margate, and of the neighbouring Parishes of St. Peter the Apostle, St. Laurence Minster, Mo nekton, Burchington, and St. Nicholas, at Wade, in the Isic of Thanet, and County of Aeto; was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows: viz.

That the said Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and do find, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, the same to be as follows; viz. ' ,

Roger Laming said, That the Timber Pier of Margate has been erected and built, Time out of Mind, for the Defence of the said Town from the Sea: That he has known the said IJier upwards of Sixty Years: That he is Master of a Vessel; and always paid certain Droits or Duties on landing or putting on board, within the said Pier, several Commodities.; which Duties have constantly been applied to the Support and Repair of the said Pier; and which Droits or Duties have been, Time immemorial, paid once a Year to the Pier-wardens of the Town of Margate, who are yearly elected to that Office:

That the Pier of Margate is the most commodious Place to ship off the Command other Produce of the Isle of Thanet, to London Market; and that the several Estates in the said Isle would be much less in their Value, and the Town drowned, should the said Pier be let go to Ruin:

That several Inhabitants of Margate, who are Hoy-men, have lately disputed, and refused to pay, the said accustomed Duties, which have been confirmed by several Orders and Decrees of the Lord Wardens of the Cinque-Ports; One whereof was produced to the Committee, bearing Date in 1615; under whose Jurisdiction the said Town of Margate is, although the said Duties are paid them by the Farmer:

That, about 34 Years ago, the said Pier was almost lost, and it cost about £. 500. to repair the same:

That they do not collect the said Duties of any Vessels, but such as lade and unlade at the said Pier; and that if the old accustomed Duties were paid, as usual, they would be sufficient to support and keep the said Pier in Repair: That he never knew any Suits commenced for any of the Duties that are in Arrear:

That the said Pier is a great Preservation and Safeguard to Merchant Ships, in time of War, from the Enemy's Privateers lurking about the North Foreland; who take them as they sail from the River to the Downs.

Valentine Jewell produced the Book of Account of the said Pier; whereby it appeared, That, one Year with another, for seven Years last past, the Duties amounted to about £. 140. or £. 150. a Year.

Mr. Brooke said, That several of the Inhabitants, which are Hoymen, have refused to pay the said Duties, alleging the re is no Law to compel them to it.

And the Petitioners produced many other Witnesses to prove the Matter of the said Petition; but the Committee did not think fit to trouble the House with the Report of any further Examinations.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, to enable the Pier-wardens of the Town of Margate, in the Isle of Thanet, more effectually to recover the ancient and customary Droits for the Support and Maintenance of the said Pier: And that Sir Edward Knatchbull, Sir Robert Fumes e* Sir George O.renden, Mr. Attorney General, Mr. Milks, and Mr. Onslow, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Regulating A Petition of many Citizens of the City of London, in London"3 behalf °* themselves, and their Fellow Citizens, was pre-Vol. 20.

sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners finding the Animosities and Divisions between'

Citizen and Citizen, and also between the Magistrates and Commons, of the City of London, grown to such a Height and Flame, that they are obliged to seek Relief from the House, to prevent their utmost Confusion; and: beg Leave to state their Case:

That the Citizens to serve in Parliament, the Lord Mayor, and Sheriffs, with some other Officers, are chosen by the Liverymen of London; the Aldermen, Common Councibmen, and some other Officers, are chosen, in their respective Wards, by the Housholders paying Scotland,

Lot; and the Petitioners apprehend all their Disorders spring from the annual Election of preceding Officers:

At the Elections by the Liverymen, Numbers of People, that have no Right to vote, break in, with Noise and Violence, upon the legal Electors; and poll, in their own or borrowed Names; and personate absent Electors, as often as they think they may, without being detected ;* and, at the late Election of a Sheriff, in the room of Sir,

Felix Feast, deceased, many Hundreds appear to have polled, without any Colour of Right; and, at the preceding Election, even the Sheriffs of London, without Example, concealed the Numbers of the Poll for each Candidate, though the Liverymen, several times, demanded the same:

That, for want of a Law, Nonjurors, and Persons receiving Charity, have demanded, and been admitted, to vote: That, at the Elections by the Wards, frequent Contests arise: The Unfreemen contend, That they con-, tribute to the Charges of their respective Wards; and that thereby, and by Law and Custom, have a Right to vote in the Election of Ward Officers: But this the Freemen will by no means allow: Nor will the Unfreemen intitle themselves to vote, by a Purchase of their Freedoms; alleging, That thereby they restrain themselves from disposing of their Estates by their Wills; and yet carry on considerable Branches of Commerce within the said City; yet are exempt from all Offices therein: That it has also been contended, That such Freemen as are Housholders, paying to the Church and Poor, ought to be deemed to have paid their Scot, and so be intitled to vote for Ward Officers: But others contending, That paying of Scot was not paying of some, but a general Contribution to all the publick Taxes and Charges upon the City of London, or the Inhabitants thereof; and this Dispute, coming before the Court of Aldermen, was, upon inspecting the City Charters and Records, and great Deliberation thereupon, decided by an Adjudication, That paying Scot was a general Contribution; but the Common Council, not approving this Adjudication, brought in a Bill, tending to appoint a different Sort of Qualification, and to oblige the Mayor and Aldermen, by Forfeitures, to declare, under' their Hands, the Names of each Voter they should disallow, and thereby become subject to the numerous Actions of such rejected Voters; so that, the Mayor and Aldermen disliking the Bill in general, fresh Causes of Dissention appear between the Aldermen and Commons:

And praying the Relief of the House for preserving the Liberties and Peace, and quieting the Minds of the Citizens; and for punishing all Intruders upon their Rights and Privileges; and settling their Elections upon a just and lasting Foundation,

Mr. Lade reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the Companyx>f Watermen and Lightermen of the River of 0

Thames, on behalf of themselves, and others, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report, and Resolution, were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of this House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and took into their Consideration the several Acts of Parliament for constituting and regulating the said-Company; and particularly the Act of the 11th and 12th of King William the Third, mentioned in the Petition; whereby Power is given to the Petitioners for making Orders and By Laws, for the better governing the said Company, to be approved of by the Court of Lord Mayor and Aldermen of London, and afterwards confirmed by the Lord Chief Justice of either Bench, under the Penalties therein contained:

That the Penalties inflicted by the said Act are to be levied by Distress and Sale of the Offenders Goods, without any Power of Commitment, or corporal Punishment, in Default of Distress.

That the Petitioners, to prove the Defects of the said Act of Parliament, and By Laws, produced the following Witnesses; viz.

Maltis.Ryall and John Hill: Who said, That most of the turbulent and unruly Watermen are neither Householders, nor such as have any settled Habitation; so that no Distress can be made of their Goods; whereby the said Act is eluded, and the Offenders escape with Impunity, although the Mischiefs arising thereby daily increase: That there is 120 Watermen, who have several Servants, and yet have neither Boat or Effects.

It further appeared to the Committee, That, by an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the late Queen Ann, for better governing the said Company, a Clause in a former Act, to restrain the taking Apprentices under the Age of 16 Years, , is repealed:

To which the Petitioners complain as a Grievance.

7 Mollis Ryaliand John Hill said, That great Numbors of dissolute Watermen, for a small private Gain, take a greater Number of* Apprentices than they can employ or keep; lodging them in their Boats all Night, having no other Habitation for them; and from thence they often fun pilfering; and frequently take Boys of 1 o or 1* Years of Age, who have not Strength to row*, or manage an Ogr; and a great many of them are almost out of their Time at 16 Years of Age:

That, since repealing the said Clause, the Number of Watermen is increased above 4,000: And they produced a List of the Watermen and Lightermen, and their Servants, with their Places of plying, amounting to 9,717.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their said Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better regulating the Company of Watermen, Wherry-men, and Lightermen, of the River of Thames: And that Mr. Lade and Mr. Onslow do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the poor distressed Prisoners for Debt in the low Gaol ot Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That some of the Petitioners have been imprisoned 5 Years; and all of them now languishing, not only by reason there is no publick Allowance to the Prisoners, but by reason of the Closeness of the Prison, which incapacitates them from working; so that they must inevitably starve, unless speedily relieved: And praying, That a Bill may pass, to oblige their Creditors an accept of all their Effects; and that the Petitioners may have their Liberty.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

the County of Devon, not paying Scotland Lot, in behalf of themselves, and many others, with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the said Report and Resolution arc as follow; viz.

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and heard Counsel for the Petitioners; and, against them, Counsel for the Inhabitants of the said Borough paying Scotland Lot.

It was agreed by the Counsel on both Sides, That this is a Borough by Prescription, and has, Time out of Mind, sent Members to Parliament: And,

The Petitioners Counsel insisted, That all the Inhabitants, Potwailers; that is, every Inhabitant in the Borough, who had a Family, and boiled a Pot there; had a Right of voting in Elections to Parliament;

Which was denied by the Counsel on the other Side; who insisted, That those only had a Right to vote who paid Scotland Lot within the Borough.

To prove that the Potwailers have a Right of Voting, the Petitioners Counsel called,

Mr. William GUI and Mr /Thomas Hare, who both pay Scotland Lot: The First of them spoke for 24 Years past, and the other for Forty; during which Time, they said, That in all Elections, the Potwailers were constantly admitted to vote till 1711; and then they w ere not objected to on either Side, neither upon the Poll, nor upon the Scrutiny, if they did not receive. Alms; and that it had been always taken and understood in the Borough, That the Potwailers had a Right to vote, equal with the rqst of the Inhabitants, whether they paid, or did not pay, Scotland Lot; and used to sign the Returns: And they gave Evidence, particularly, as to the Return in 1705, That several of those who signed that Return did not then pay Scotland Lot: And said,

That, at ail Elections since 1711, the Potwailers attended,'and constantly demanded their Right to vote, and sign the Returns.

Sir Walter Yonge Baronet, who had served in many Parliaments for this Borough, said, That the Potwailers were always allowed to be good Votes on all Sides, in all Elections; and were never objected to on any Side; nor were they objected to in the Country, either upon the Poll, or upon the Scrutiny, in 1711; but were, by every body, admitted to be as good Votes as any, if they did not receive Alms.

The Journal, of the 28th of May 1701, was produced, when it was agreed, in the then controverted Election between Wm. Courtney Esquire and Sir Walter Yonge, That the Right of Election was in the Potwailers not receiving Alms:

Against which, the Journal, of the 3d of February 1710, was produced, when, upon the Double Return, and the Petitions of James Sheppard Esquire, and Sir Walter Yonge, and the Potwailers, complaining of that Return; in which Election, Mr. Sheppard had the Majority of the Scotland Lot Men, and Sir Walter Yonge had the Majority of the Populace;, the House, differing from the Opinion of the Committee, as to the> Potwailers voting, determined the Right of Election to be in the Inhabitants of the Borough paying Scotland Lot only: Upon which last Determination, and the Evidence, then given, the Counsel for the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot did now rely; and did not think it-necessary to produce any other Evidence, to support that. Resolution. . .: .;

The Committee came to this Resolution; ..

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve.in Parliament for the Borough of Iioniton, in the County of Devon, is in the Inhabitants, Housekeepers, within the said Borough, commonly called Potwailers, not receiving Alms of the Parish.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Sandys, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the List of all unrated Goods and Merchandizes, which are usually imported into this Kingdom, and pay Duty, ad valorem, upon the Oath of the Importer, the Resolution they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and agreed unto by the House; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the additional Duty of Twenty Pounds per Cent. ad valorem, imposed upon Drugs imported, by an Act made, in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for Thirty-two Years, and since made perpetual, subject to Redemption by Parliament, shall, from and after the 25th Day of June 1725, cease and determine.

The said Resolution, being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen, who are to prepare, and bring in, a Bill for rating all such unrated Goods and Merchandizes as are usually imported into this Kingdom, and pay Duty, ad valorem, upon the Oath of the Importer, That they do prepare, and bring in, a Clause or Clauses, pursuant to the said Resolution.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, t8 consider further of the Bill to prevent Violences and Outrages being committed by any Persons, under Pretence of sheltering themselves from Debt, or any Process of Law, either within the Hamlet of Wapping, Stepney, or elsewhere within that Part of Great Britain called England.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A PETITION of the Commissioners, Gentlemen, Nino

Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, within the Navigation. County of Northampton, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on the behalf of themselves, and others, Borderers upon the River Nine, alias Nean, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, an Act passed for making the said River navigable; in which Act there is a Clause, That no Act should be done to make any Part of the said River navigable, until the Commissioners should have first actually agreed with some Person or Persons, jointly, to make all the said River navigable from Peterborough to Northampton; by which Clause, the said Act is rendered ineffectual; but that the Petitioners have Reason to believe, they shall be able to agree with several Persons to make the said River navigable by Parcels: And, there being some other Defects in the said Act, they pray, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for altering and amending the same, in such manner as this House shall think fit.

Manchester Sir John Bland reported, from the Committee, to Road* whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, living in and near the Road leading through Stockport, in the County of Chester, to the Chappel in the Frith, and Buxton, in the County of Derby, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the said Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House, bearing Date the 16th of December last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition: And the Petitioners, to make good the Allegations contained therein, produced Witnesses; viz.

John Mottram and Samuel Sherlock: Who, being severally examined, said, That the Road lying between the Top of Sherbrpokhill, in the Hamlet of Buxton, and Chappej in the Frith, in the County of Da by, leading through Stockjm't, in the County of Chester, and the Town of Manchester, in the County of Lancaster, in the Winter-season, is, in many Parts very deep, and bad, although the Statute work has been done in most Parts thereof; and that Materials proper to repair the same lie at a great Distance from many Parts of the said Road:

371

That somie Part of the Road is sb very bad And ruinous, that it is dangerous for Travellers to pass and repass; and that Wheel-carriages cannot pass through the same, in the Winter-season; and that if the Inhabitants of the Parishes wherein the bad Parts of the Road lie, were to do Three times the Work required by Law, it would not effectually repair the same.

That the Committee examined both Witnesses, as to the Road being narrow: And they said, That some Parts thereof, are so very narrow, that Coaches and Wheel-carriages cannot pass through the same with Safety.

Mr. Pulteney reported, from the Committee, to w hom Stanford the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, and of the other Bridge. Gentlemen, and Freeholders, and Inhabitants, within the East Riding of the County of York, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, upon such Examination, it appeared to the Committee;

That the County Bridge called Stafford Bridge, over the River Darwenl, in the great Road leading from the City of York to Bridlington, is of Wood, very ruinous, and incapable of Repair; and hath been so presented by the Grand Jury at the Quarter Sessions: And,

That it will be more for the Service of the County, that the said Bridge should be taken down, and'a new Stone Bridge built more convenient, at a small Distance below the said ruinous Bridge, where the said River is much narrower; and that the Charge of building such new Bridge will be much less to the County than the Expence of supporting the said old Bridge; and that this Advantage may be easily gained to the County, by altering the Road to the present Bridge, and disposing of that Ground, and purchasing Ground necessary for a Road to the new Bridge desired:

Which new Bridge may be so contrived, as not to be any Prejudice to the Navigation of the said River, and be of great Advantage to the Countiy.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Justices of the Peace for the East Riding of the County of York, to take down the County Bridge called Stans ord Bridge, and to build a new Stone Bridge at a more convenient Place, over the River Darxvent, in the said Riding: And that Mr. Pulteney, Sir IVm. Strict land, and Mr. Thompson, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the poor Prisoners in Ousebridge Goal, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they are confined in a most dismal Place, 12 l oot under-ground, with wet Flag-stones under theijii, and where no fire can be had; and they are ready to starve; their merciless Creditors, though they know they have had all they have, threatening to have their Bones, since they cannot have their Money: That the Petitioners return Thanks to the House for their good Intention in passing an Act for Relief of insolvent Debtors last Session; and hope, all objections will be removed in this Session; and that Gentlemen, Merchants, and others, who were deprived of the Benefit of the last Act of Grace, by the Smallness of the Sum, and the backward Commencement of the Act, may have their Liberty; And praying, That the House will take their deplorable Condition into Consideration, and give Leave for a Bill to be brought in to relieve all insolvent Debtors in general.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

whom the Petitions of the Commissioners, Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, within the County of Northampton, on the behalf of themselves, and others, Borderers upon the Uiver Nine or in the said County; and also the Petition of the Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Northampt; were referred; the Matter as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk's Tabic: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

1 he Committee, pursuant to the several Orders of the

House, have examined the Matters of the said Petitions; And the Petitioners, to make good the Allegations of their several Petitions, produced an Act, passed in the Parliament holden in the 12th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for making the said River navigable from Northampton to Peterborough; wherein is a Clause, That no Person or Persons whatsoever should attempt, or do any Act whatsoever, to make any Part of the said River navigable, until the Commissioners therein named should iirst have actually agreed with some Person or Persons, jointly, to make all the said River, from Peterborough to Northamptonnavigable.

Then the Petitioners called Witnesses;

Sir Gilbert Pickering, and Mr. Who,

being examined, said, 'That the Commissioners could not proceed in making the River navigable, by reason of the Restraint in the before-mentioned Clause in the said Act:

That the River is about 50 Miles in Length; and that Gentlemen, and others, who have Lands near the River, are very desirous to have the same made navigable, by reason such Navigation will drain their Meadows:

And the Witnesses said farther, f hat the Expence and Charge of making all the said River navigable will be so very great, that no One Undertaker will contract with the Commissioners for that Purpose: But if the Commissioners had Power given them to contract with. several Undertakers-for making the same navigable by Parcels; then the said River may, in time, be made navigable, as intended by tire former Act; which will he of publick Benefit; but at present the said Act is of no Use.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making more effectual an Act, passed in the Parliament holden in the 12th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for making the River Nine or Nen, running from Northampton to Peterborough, navigable: And that Sir Justinian Mr. Cartwright,

and Colonel Montagu, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Prayers.

York Cloth CIR William Strickland reported from the Committee, Manufac- O to whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, ture. Gentlemen, Freeholders, Cloth-makers, and others, of the West Riding of the County of York, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwardsdelivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the Report and Resolution are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, the same to be as follows; viz.

James Walker said. That be has seen several Pieces of Cloth, of about 24 Yards, stretched 3 or Yards at a time, which makes it a great deal narrower; has known an Action brought for overstretching of Cloth, but does not know what was recovered: That he has seen several Pieces of Cloth that had noSeals on; the Milman never being sworn, is the Reason he often stamps them wrong; and the Seals are generally pulled off; so that the Cloth is often stretched, and the Number of Yards are not known: That the Seal ought to be generally the Rule of Payment: That he could never get the Merchants to pay for the Seal: That the present Act does not prevent the Seal being taken off: That the Clothiers are willing the re should be a Seal or Mark set upon their Cloths, declaring the Length and Breadth; for which the Clothier would be answerable, if a sworn Measurer were appointed; Vql. 20.

Januarii. 377

That formerly the Clothiers registered their Cloth; but this has not been practised these 30 or4o Years last past.

Joseph Fenton said, That he has sold the Merchants 49 Yards and a Half of Cloth in a Piece; which, when it has been returned to him, has measured to 57 Yards: That the said Cloth is not above Half the Price, when so stretched; neither is it merchantable to Foreigners; and has had several Pieces of Cloth returned so stretched; and that the said Cloth shrinks very much, when worn in wet Weather.

William Ware said, That Cloth has been unreasonably used by Overstretching; That he had a Piece of Cloth stretched Six Yards: That it is a general Practice to stretch Cloth beyond the Act; and has known several pay the Fine, according to the Act, for so doing: That, if a Penalty be laid to prevent the taking off the Seal, it will prevent the stretching of Cloth.

George Franklynsaid, He had a Piece of Cloth of 42

Yards and Half stretched to 50 Yards and Half, when returned to him a Week after: That he could not sell it to any Advantage, it being stretched beyond Nature: That he has had several Pieces of Cloth stretched about Six Yards; and that it is a common Practice so to do; which is a great Abuse to that Manufacture: That if a Seal was affixed by the Milman, of the Number of Yards, it would very much tend to remedy the Grievance complained of.

William Jackson said, He has seen several Cloths pulled 3 or Yards beyond the Act: That it is a common Custom so to do: That Cloth is sold in the open Market to the Merchants; and the Merchants Servants measure it; and, by that Admeasurement, pay the Clothier for it; which sometimes fall short, by that means, of the Measure it was first delivered by the Clothier; and then the Merchant has it stretched again about 6 or 7 Yards; That he has sold several Cloths, and several Yards have been taken off, and he has been abated in the Payment.

Scudamore Lazenby, Merchant, said. That the Stretching of Cloth is not. the only Abuse; but it is the Narrowness of it, and also the bad Spinning: That the Law against these Abuses has not been put in Execution, as it ought to have been: That it lies upon the Merchants to be Informers; and so the Clothiers lie under a great Disadvantage: That, there has been no Cloths stamped or sealed for several Years: That the sealing the said Cloths will be no Detriment to the Trade, but will prevent the Stretching thereof: That it will not be any Detriment, if Cloths were made longer than they are; and that the Merchant hath no Objection against the Seal of the Milman being affixed; which will not be of any Prejudice to the Clothiers: That he never knew any Merchant prosecuted for Cloths being 50 Yards long, or upwards: That the Cloths ought to be 5 Quarters and a Half broad, and they are not above 5 Quarters: That Foreigners demand their Cloths to be Six Quarters broad: That it may be stretched to that Breadth; but it debases the Manufacture: That, if Cloth be made above 30 Yards, it pays as much to the Milman as if it was 46 Yards: That it cannot be stretched when once it is taken off the Tenters.

Manwaring Arthur sa.\A, Th&t several Abuses areused . in Overstraining of Cloths, which makes it not worth so much as it would be: That, if the Laws were put in due Execution, it would prevent the said Abuses: That it will be no Detriment, if a Seal should be affixed to the Cloths; which of late Years have not been done: That the Informers have an Opportunity to see the CIoths, when on the Tenters, if they be stretched beyond the Act; That there is no other Way to ascertain the Length of Cloths, but by the Clothiers themselves, when watered; That sometimes the Clothiers give in their Cloth, a Yard or Two more than they really are, to the Merchants:

That in Flanders the Merchants pay no more Custom for a Cloth of 40 Yards than for a Piece of 20 Yards; and they desire it may be sent over without being sealed; and that a Piece is sometimes cut into Four here before it be sent over.

Mr. Walker and Mr. Lazenby said, That it would be an Advantage to the Yorkshire Cloth, if the Dressers thereof were obliged to dress with Teazles-, but that they now dress them with Wire Combs; which very much tears the Wool, and damages the Cloths; and that, if the Yorkshire Clothiers were put on the same Foot with the Gloucestershire Clothiers, it will be an Advantage to the Woollen Manufacture.

The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That by the 21st Act, made in the Parliament of Scotland, the Third Parliament of King Charles the Second, concerning the Election of Commissioners for Shires, none had Right to vote, but those who were publicly infeoft in Property or Superiority, and in Possession of a Forty Shilling Land, of old Extent; or Four hundred Pounds, valued Rent.

Upon this Head, the Petitioner's Counsel objected to James Grahame, and several others of the Sitting Member's Voters.

It appeared by the old Retour, and Charter, and Sasine proceeding thereupon. That the Lands for which Mr. Grahame voted, were one Fifth Part of a Ten Pound Land called Kilmaheio: And

The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That this Right to a Part gave Persons no Right to vote, because the Lands were not retoured to such a Proportion as put them in the Terms of the Act of Parliament:

Which was denied by the Sitting Member's Counsel; who insisted, That where the Valuation appeared to be sufficient, as in this Case, that gave a Right to vote, though the Lands were not retoured.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Conveyance of undivided Shares of the Superiority of any Lands in the Shire of Dumbarton, in order to multiply Votes, or split an Interest in such Superiority, amongst several Persons, with a View to enable them to vote, is contrary to the Act of Parliament, made in Scotland in 1681, intituled, An Act concerning the Election of Commissioners for Shires.

Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the District of Burghs of Invert try, Elgin, Cullen, and Bamf with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the Report, and Resolutions, are as follows; viz.

Upon the Petition of John Campbell Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of William Frazer Esquire, to serve for the District of Burghs of Inverury, Kintore, Elgin, Cullen and Bamf:

The Committee proceeded to examine the Merits of this Election.

It appeared, by the Minutes of the Election, That Three of the Delegates from these Five Burghs voted for the Sitting Member, and Two for the Petitioner:

But it was disputed who was the legal Delegate from Bamf-, whether Mr. George Barclay, who voted for the Sitting Member; or Mr. Robert Steuart, who voted for the Petitioner.

And it was admitted by the Counsel on both Sides, That the Merits of this Election turned upon that Question.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Adventurers for making a Canal, from below Uxbridge, to some Place in or near Oxford Square, in the Parish of Saint Mary la Bone, for supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with Water; and for making the same, and also the Rivers Colne and Cowley, from Watford to the said Canal, below Uxbridge, navigable; was referred:

And the said Report, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House, took the said Petition into Consideration; and, upon Examination of several Witnesses, do find the same to be as follows; viz.

George Osmond said, That he took the Level of the new-intended River from Cowley Stream, below Uxbridge, to the Pavement of the Lord Harco Hall-door, in Oxford Square', and found the Descent of the new-intended River, to the said Hall-door, to be Ten Foot Nine Inches and Nine Tenths; which Hall-door is Three Foot Five Inches above the intended Pavement of the Street; and is, from Cowley Stream to the Pavement in Oxford Square, 14 Foot Two Inches and Nine Tenths: That there is a Fall, from Uxbridge to the Thames, of 105 Foot, and, from Saint Giles's Pound to Fleet-ditch, 84 Foot, Pescent:

That he, with Four others, took the Level by several Stations, and never moved the Level till the said Five People agreed the Thing was just, and entered their several Accounts in Books for that Purpose: That he had taken the Level Six several times: That the Meander was taken by him, and one John Eaden; and they find it to be about 19 or 20 Miles: That it is proposed to continue the Water at an equal Current, at Three Inches to a Mile, at 30 Foot wide: That the new River is Three Inches Six Tenths to a Mile, supposed to bring 1,500 Tun in an Hour; and, by Act of Parliament, to be Ten Foot wide: That less than Three Inches Declivity in a Mile, will bring about 1,500 Tun an Hour from Ux>. bridge: That the intended Reservoir is to be Four or Five Foot deep; which may be cleaned at any time, it having so great a Descent: That the intended River is to be about 30 Foot wide, and Four Foot and a Half, or Five Foot, deep, for Boats to pass by one another: That there will be no Shoals in the said River, the Current thereof being so equally divided, that there will be no Obstruction to any Barges being drawn by Men or Horses:

That it is intended that several convenient . Bridges shall be built, for the Use of the Country, and Passengers: That the Meander will do no Prejudiceto. any House, Garden,

Avenue, or Court-yards, of any Person: That there will be Five Foot Descent, from the Bottom of the Reservoir, to the Pavement of the Street at Oxford That the Water will rise Six or Seven Foot all roupd Oxford Square:

There are 3 Mills upon Cawley Stream; the middle one is . to be taken away, and the Two other . Mills to be made Overshot Mills; which will do more Work than the Three now do, and frill thereby be made the capital Mill*

That Mr. Jones and Captain Perry, with himself, took an Inspection of the River Thames, and Cowley Stream: That a Report thereof was made, by Mr. Jones and Captain Perry, to the Mayor and Court of Aldermen of the City of London: That if the whole Cowley Stream was taken in, it would not be diminished above 5 Tenths of an Inch; and that, if 1,500 Tun an Hour be taken out, it will not diminish the Depth of the Water above the Thickness of a Five Shilling Piece: That it will be no Damage to the Barges, nor to the River: That the River is grown wider, for want of the Landholders keeping up their Banks; which, in many Places, is the only Occasion of the Waters being shallower in Summer-time: That if the Bargemisters find any Inconvenience, by the Loss of their Tonage in Carriage, the Proprietors to build them a Lock at Newloch, at the Approbation of the Lord Mayor and Court of Aldermen.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take Supplying into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to London wttk whom the Petition of several Adventurers for supplying Water* the Cities of Loiulon and Westminster, and Places adjacent, with Water, presented to the House the Nineteenth Day of November last, was referred:

And the said Report, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the said Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House, have examined the Alatter of the said Petition; and do find, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, the same to be as follows; viz.

John Golding said, That he had taken a Level from that Part of the Cowley Stream that is below Uxbridge, at a Tail of a Mill called Adam Love's, or Little Cawley Mill, and found that Mill Tail to be above 23 Foot higher than the Corner of a Wall in Marybone Fields, commonly called the Duke of Chandos his Wall, which is one of the highest Places in Afarybone Fields.

William Dean said, That he took the above-mentioned Level, at several short Stations, of about One hundred Yards Distance, with a very good Instrument, it being made with double Telescopes; and found the Fail to be more than Twenty-three Foot.

Air. George Shelvocke said, That he had also levelled the Ground from the Tail of the above-mentioned Mill to the Corner of the Duke of Chandos his Wall in Marybone Fields; and found the said Alill Tail to be twenty-two Feet odd Inches higher than the Corner of the said Wall; and that he had levelled the same by or near the Alcanders that the intended Canal is to make; and that the intended Canal w ill go on the Brow or Sides of the Hills altogether, only where it crosses the Brent, and Two other small Rivulets; and that there is no Hill to obstruct the Passage thereof.

Wheeler Hardesty said, That he had measured the Ground, where the intended Canal is to be made, by its several Meanders; and that it will be under Twenty Miles long; and that he measured it by a Chain, commonly used in measuring of Land, of Four Pole long: And said the Canal w ould go on the Brow s or Sides of the Hills.

John Greenaway, Bargemaster, of Reading, said, He had used the Navigation of the River of Thames for above 25 Years: That the executing the Design of the Petitioners will be no Damage to the Navigation on the River Thames, provided they make a proper Lock on the said River; but, on the contrary, a great Benefit, as he instanced in several Particulars; and that such a Lock would not endanger the spoiling any Lands by overflowing them, inasmuch as it need raise the Water hut Three Foot high; and be placed were the Banks are Six Foot high, and more.

Thomas Dagnatt, Millwright, said, That he had altered Seven or Eight Alills in Hertfordshire, within these Fourteen Years last past, from Undershot to Overshot Alills, which afterwards ground as much Corn, and made as good Flour, as they did w hen they were Undershot: He further said. That he. could alter any Mill from Undershot to Overshot at any Plac^f whatsoever, where they had Fall enough for carrying off the Water that works it; and that he had lately built an Overshot Mill, for one Air. James Fordham, between the Towns of Hertford and /Fare, that had a Four Foot Head of Water, and a Wheel of Sixteen Feet in the Diameter; and that that Mill wall do as much Work as any Undershot Mill he ever heard of: That the usual Way of making a proper Fall for carrying off the Water, where he has changed Undershot Alills to Overshot, is, by deepening the River.

Mr. James Fordham said, That, at that Mill, with a List of One Inch and a Half, he could grind 1,500 Bushels of Wheat per Week.

John Golding and Wm.Dean informed the Committee,

That they had both levelled the Fall of the Cowley Stream from the Mill Tail above-mentioned to a certain Point of Land called Drayton Point; and they found the Fall thereof to be above Twenty-two Feet: And* John Golding being asked whether he had not heard, that the Mills on the said Stream have sometimes wanted Water; he said, That he had heard, thlt those Mills have sometimes wanted Water in the Summer.

The Adventurers propose, That the Mills, when made into Overshot, shall be made in the same manner as Fordiiams Mill abovesaid is; and that they shall be so placed, as that the whole Cowley Stream shall first give each of them a constant Four Foot Head of Water; and that the Residue only of the said Stream shall be brought on for supplying the Cities of London and Westminster; and that they design to turn the Water of the Heatham Stream into the Stamvell Stream; by which, this last will have a large Increase of Water for the supplying his Majesty's Gardens and Park at Hampton Court.

in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, as a Malt

made and consumed in Scotland, and to be levied as in

England', and if the said Duty of Three Pence per Bushel

shall not effectually raise and answer the said Sum of

Twenty thousand Pounds in net Money, after all Charges

and Deductions, that the Deficiency he made good, and:

raised, by a Surcharge upon all Makers of Malt, in that

Part oi Great Britain called Scotland, in proportion to the said deficiency.

A Petition of the major Part of the Aldermen of the Regulating City of iMndon, was presented to the House, and read; ^cd^9 irf setting forth, That, of late Years, rriany evil Practices, and unhappy Disputes, have arisen within the said City, greatly tending to disturb the good Order and Government thereof; which, the Petitioners apprehend, cannot be determined, but by the interposition of Parliament: That the Petitioners have taken a Copy of the Bill, now depend- ing in the House, for regulating Elections within the City of London; and for preserving the Peace, good Order, and Government, of the said City; and are of Opinion, that the same is not only consistent with, blit will also establish a lasting Foundation of, the ancient and true Rights and Privileges, both of the Magistrates and Citizens of London; and tend to restore Peace and Tranquillity within the said City: That they observe there is a Clause in the said Bill, touching the Right of passing Acts, or By Laws, in Common Council: This Dispute was never moved by any of the Commons, till the Times of the unhappy civil Wars; nor attempted since, till lately; and then, that nothing might be wanting, on the Petitioners Part, to end the same amicably, they did, on the 20th of March 1723, by their Recorder, propose to the Commons in Common Council assembled, that a proper Application should be made to any of the Courts in Westminster-hall, or else to the Parliament, to determine the Controversies between them; but the Commons did not think fit to comply, or take any step towards it; whereby the Government of the City, if not timely prevented, must inevitably run into the utmost Confusion:

And praying, That they may be heard by their Counsel, for the said Bill; it being the only Remedy, as they conceive, to put an End to the Disputes between them; or such other Means be found out, $s the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Petitioners be heard, by their Coun- . sel, for the said Bill, when the said Bill is read a Second time.

Ordered, That the Clerks of the several Livery Com- Livery of panies of the City of London, do lay before this House London, the particular Grants, or Constitutions, by which they were made Livery Companies, together with the present Numbers of their Liverymen respectively.

That the Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House, took into Consideration the said Petition And, to make good the Allegations therein contained, the Petitioners produced the Act, passed in the Fourth and Fifth Years of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne; whereby it appeared a Duty was laid upon all Coals shipped, or put on board any Ship or Vessel, in the Pier or Harbour of Parton, for the Term of Eleven Years, for and towards enlarging, deepening, cleansing, maintaining, and repairing, the said Pier and Harbour: And the Petitioners called,

Henry Gilpin: Who said, He has used the Sea for many Years, and has known the Harbour of Parton for about Ten or Twelve Years: That he went into the said,

Harbour about Eight or Nine Years ago; he has seen Twelve or Fourteen Ships in the said Harbour at a time:

That now, there being but little of the bid Pier standing, it is very dangerous for Ships to go into the same, there being no Security for Shipping, as forrherly there was;

Ships are now held only by their own Anchors,‘which is not altogether so safe: That the said Harbour is so very much decayed, that it must of necessity be rebuilt; and, if rebuilt, the same will be & very great Advantage to the Coal Trade thereabouts: That, if the said Harbour was built Two or Three hundred Yards off from the old one,

Ships would lie very safe in the said Harbour, which at present they'cannot do.

AN ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for enabling Elizabeth Rushout, Lady of the Manor of Over Swell, in the County of Gloucester, to inclose all and every the Lands lying within the said Manor or Parish of Over Swell, in pursuance of several Agreements therein mentioned to have been made between the said Elizabeth Rushout, and the Rector of the Parish aforesaid, and between the said Elizabeth and the Church warden and Parishioners of the said Parish; and to establish the said Agreements; was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the List of all unrated Goods and Merchandizes, which are usually imported into this Kingdom, and pay Duty, ad valorem, upon the Oath of the Importer, was referred:

And the said Resolutions, were read; and are as follows; viz.

1. Resolved\ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Archtlia, or Spanish Weed, for Dyers Use, the Hundred Weight, containing One hundred and Twelve Pounds, be Eighteen Shillings and Four Pence.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Ashes called Weed-ashes, the Hundred Weight, containing One hundred and Twelve Pounds, be Ten Shillings.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of jointed Babies, the Dozen, be Forty Shillings.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Bags called Runnet-bags, the Dozen, be Four Shillings.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Balls for Children, the small Gross, containing Twelve Dozen, be Twenty Shillings.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Bark of Oak, the Hundred Weight, containing One hundred and Twelve Pounds, be Ten Shillings.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Beads of Jet, the Pound, be Five Shillings.

8. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Beads of Horn, the small Gross, containing Twelve Dozen, be Five Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, instead of redeeming at Midsummer, now next ensuing, according to the Notice which hath been already given in that behalf, the Annuity of Eighty-eight thousand Seven hundred Fifty-one Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpeny, payable to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, by virtue of an Act passed in the Third Year of his Majesty's Reign, being after the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent, per Annum, on the principal Sum of One million Seven hundred seventy-five thousand Twenty-seven Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpeny, owing to the said Governor and Company, in lieu of certain Exchequer Bills, formerly by them delivered up, and cancelled; and that, instead of giving Notice to the said Governor and Company, and redeeming, according to the Power of Redemption contained in the said Act, an Annuity of One hundred thousand Pounds, payable to them by virtue of the same Act, being after the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent.per Annum, for the principal Sum of Two Millions, owing to the said Governor and Company, for the like Sum in Exchequer Bills by them delivered up and cancelled; the said Annuity of Eighty-eight thousand Seven hundred Fifty-one Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpeny, and the said Annuity of One hundred thousand Pounds, for the said principal Sum of One million Seven hundred seventy-five thousand Twenty-seven Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpeny, and Two millions, shall be continued to the said Governor and Company, to the Twenty-fourth Day of June, iwhich shall be in the Year of our Lord 1727; but that, from and after the said Twenty-fourth Day of June 1727, the said Annuity of Eighty-eight thousand Seven hundred Fifty-one Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpeny shall be reduced to an Annuity of Seventy-one thousand One Pounds Two Shillings and Three Pence Three 5 K Farthings;

Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House, That he had a Message from his Majesty to this House, signed by his Majesty; and further acquainted the House, That he was commanded by his Majesty to lay before this House Copies of several Reports, and other Papers, relating to the Masters ih Chancery: And he delivered his Majesty's Message to Mr. Speaker; and delivered the said Copies Of Reports, and other Papers, in at the Clerk's Table.

His Majesty's Message was read by Mr. Speaker; and is as follows; viz.

George R.

His Majesty, having Reason to apprehend, that the Suitdfs of the Court of Chancery were in Danger of losing a considerable Sum of Money, from the Insufficiency of some of the Masters, thought himself obliged, in Justice and Compassion to the said Suitors, to take the most speedy and proper Methods the Law would allow, for enquiring into the State of the Masters Accounts; and securing their Effects, for the Benefit of the Suitors: And his Majesty, having had several Reports laid before him, in pursuance of the Directions he had given, has ordered the said Reports to be communicated to this House, that this House may have as full, and as perfect, a View of this important Affair, as the Shortness of the Time, and the Circumstances and Nature of the Proceedings, would admit of.

And the said Reports, together with some of the Papers referred to in them, were read; viz.

Report, N# i. dated December 16th, 1724;

Containing an Account of the Charge upon the Masters and Usher of the Court of Chancery, in Securities and Money belonging to the Suitors of the Court, and the remaining Balance of Cash in each of their Hands, not including the Demands upon Mr. Dormer and Mr. Borret; and an Account of the Circumstances of the Offices of those Two Masters; and also, an Account of the Particulars of the several Effects which each Master, and the Usher, had produced, to answer their several Balances; with Observations upon the said Accounts:

Report, N° 2. dated January the 6th, 1724;

Concerning securing the Effects, and Balance of Cash, in the several Masters Hands; and what had been done in order thereto:

A Paper annexed to the last mentioned Report, signed by Mr. Wm. Kynaston, 28th December 1724;

Explaining an Item of £. 7,575. in his Account, viz.

That £. 6,000. thereof, being Part of the Money of the Suitors of the Court, in Mr. Rogers', Mr. Kynaston's Predecessor's, Hands, at the time of his Resignation; was retained by him, and still remained in his Hands, and never paid over to the said Mr. Kynaston; and that £. 1,575. the Residue thereof, was paid, and accounted for, by him, out of the Money belonging to the Suitors of the Court, into the Hands of Peter Coltingham Esquire, Secretary to the Lord Chancellor, for the Use of the said Lord Chancellor; and also explaining other Part of his the said Mr. Kynaston's Account: And also,

A Paper annexed to the same Report, signed by Mr. Thomas Rennet, 1724, December 28th;

Explaining i\n Item of JT. 9,075. in his Account; viz.

That £. 7,500, Part thereof, being Part of the Money Vo 4* SO.

The Commissioners for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of don and Westminster, and the Suburbs thereof, having represented to his Majesty,

That, in pursuance of several Acts of Parliament already made for that Purpose, Oqe Church hath been, for some time ‘finished, and consecrated; and Three Chapels have been1 converted into Parish Churches, and sdsp consecrated; and that Seven other Churches are built, or building, and near finished; for which Eleven Churches, convenient Districts have been also laid out, and appointed to be the Parishes respectively belonging to the same; and his Majesty being truly sensible of the great Necessity there is of new Churches, and of new Divisions of Parishes, in and about the said Cities and Suburbs; and very desirous to provide for the spiritual, as well as temporal, Welfare of all his Subjects; and being also firmly persuaded, that nothing will more effectually engage Almighty God to send down his Blessing upon his Crown and Peop'e, than a due Zeal for the Honour and Service of Religion; has thought fit to re*; commend to the House of Commons, in an especial manner, the providing a suitable Maintenance for the Ministers, who shall be appointed to perform Divine Service in the Eleven Churches aforesaid, by such Ways as may eflertuady answer the Ends aforesaid, according to his Majesty's Royal Purpose and Desire.

That the Committee have, according to Order, taken the said Petition into their Consideration; and, upon Examination of the Matter thereof do find, as follows; viz.

Ben. Jackman, of Kensington, being examined, said, That the Hoads from Counter's Bridge to Piccadilly are in a very bad and ruinous Condition; and that Half their Statute-work is applied to the Uxbridge Turnpike; and, if the whole Statute-work was applied to their Roads, that, and Six times as much move, would not be sufficient to repair the same.

Richard Biixl spoke to the same effect; and that there is Eight Miles of the Road that want to be amended; and that the Uxbridge Turnpike only amends One Mile and a Half of the Road in the Parish, for the Half-part of the Statute-work which is allowed them.

JVm. Burchett, of Chelsea, said, That the Road from Fulham Ferry, and North End to Knightsbridge, is very bad: That there are Iluts in the said Road Three Foot deep: That the Inhabitants of Chelsea pay Nine Shillings for every House: And

Every Farmer that rents Fifty Pounds a Year does Six Days Statute-work in the Year: And that he has talked with several Persons of Chelsea, Fulham, and other Parishes, who are very desirous to have a Turnpike erected.

David Morgan, of Chelsea, said, That the Roads are very bad; and, about a Month past, he saw Two Gentlemen on Horseback, at Chelsea Common, almost smothered in Dirt; and has seen several Market Carts stopped, and not able to get along.

Abraham Odell, of Fulham, Surgeon, said, That the Road between Fulham and Knightsbridge is very bad; and has seen Carts set between Hyde Park Cornier, and the Stones End; and that there are Iluts in the Road betw een Chelsea and Hyde Park Comer Foot deep; and that 20 Days Statute-work will not be sufficient to amend the said Road.

That several Persons have lately received Damage by passing through the Roads between Little Chelsea and Fulham; and particularly, a Man that is now under his Care, that broke his Leg by a Fall; and another Person likewise under his Care, being much hurt by a Fall from his Horse in the said Road: That the Roads cannot be repaired by the Statute-work.

Thomas Scott, Master Brick-maker, of Fulham, said, That he keeps several Teams for the carrying of Bricks; and the Road is so very bad at this time of the Year, that the Team cannot draw; and though it will cost him Four times as much as any other Person, if a Turnpike should be erected, yet he is willing to pay the Toll; and that the Roads can't be amended by the Statute-work, if it was Four times more than it is.

John Jones, of Fulham, High Constable, said, That the Roads are very bod; and the Ruts are, in some Parts, Three Foot deep: That Three empty Drays have been stopped at Little Chelsea, and Ten Horses put at Length to draw them out, one by one: That Three Weeks ago he travelled the way with a Chaise, and a Pair of Horses, between Piccadilly, and Hyde Park Corner; and by the badness of the Way, one of the Horses had like to have been smothered in the Dirt:

That the Road is bad from Chelsea Town to Stone Bridge; and several Travellers have received Damage by going that way: That the Roads are so very bad between Kensington and Chelsea, that they are almost impassable: That, by reason of the badness of the Road, the Commissioners of the Land Tax have not been able to get to Chelsea to pass their Accounts: That the Road from Kensington to Counters Bridge, is so very bad, that Persons are obliged to go through fVt2llam Green, which is a Mile about.

That the Roads cannot be amended by the Statute-work. Samuel Hoppcrton, of Fulham, said, That the Road from North End to Knightsbridge, and near Hyde Park, is very bad; and that they are obliged to go through Chelsea; and that the Road cannot be repaired by the Statute-work.

Mr, William Chelwynd reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, capital Burgesses, free Burgesses, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of the Devizes, in the County of Witts, and of the Inhabitants of the several Parishes of Rowdstreet, Urchfont, and Bishops Catlings, near the Devizes aforesaid, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of the Inhabitants and Landholders of the Village or Tythe-itig of Echilhamptoiu in the Parish of Atcamngs, and County of Wilts; was referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Petitioners produced to the Committee an Act of Parliament, made in the 5th Year of the Reign of the late Queen Arme, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways between Sheppard's Shord and the Devizes, and between the Top of Ashlington Hill and Rowdford, in the County of Wilts; which said Act was to continue in Force for the Term of One-and-twenty Years, to be accounted from the passing thereof; which Term is near expiring:

That an Account was laid before the Committee of what Money had been advanced on the Credit of the said Act, and what has been paid off; whereby there appears, That the Sum of £, 1,641. 1 2d, has been borrowed;

whereof only ^.291. 19 s. 2d. is paid off; so there still remains due, and a Charge upon the Turnpike, at this time, the Sum of £. 1,350.; which cannot be discharged by the Toll to be collected by the Turnpike, while the Act continues.

That, to prove the Condition of the Road mentioned in the First Petition, the Committee examined,

John Paradice, Henry Alford, and John Alerrit: Who said, That there being such a Debt upon the Turnpike, as aforesaid, all the Money arising by the said Act will be applied towards discharging the said Debt; so no Part thereof can be laid out in amending the Road directed to be repaired by the said Act, during the time it continues:

They also said, That that Part of the Road which lies within the Borough of the Devizes, is so bad, that several Carriages have been broke, going into the 1 own; and that the Inhabitants have done their Statute-work; but, if they were to do, and pay, twice as much as the Law requires, it would not put that Part of the Road in good Repair:

And the same Witnesses also said, That the Road between Stert Stone, near the House called the Shepherd and his Dog, in the Parish of Stert, and the Top of Ashling-ton Hill, in the Road in the former Act mentioned, through the said Parish of Stert, and Ashlington, being about Half a Mile in Length, is so very ruinous, that the same is dangerous*to Passengers; and although the Parishioners have done, and paid, more than required by Law, yet the same has not been sufficient to put that Pan #f the Road into such Repair, as that Passengers may pass and repass, in the Winter season, with Safety.

That it appeared to the Committee, That, in regard all Passengers and Carriages coining into the Town of the Devizes one Day, and going out the next Day, are, by the former Act, obliged to pay the Toll at their cofor VOL. 20,

ing in and going Out, it has been a grdai Prejudice and Hindrance to the Inhabitants thereof.

Then the Comrftittee proceeded to examine the Matter Of the Second Petition; arid examined the same Witnesses:

Who said,

That the Road from Echilhampton to Alcanings Water is so very bad, that it is dangerous to all Passengers; and that the Inhabitants cannot repair and amend the same, by what they are obliged to do, and pay* as the Law now stands.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term granted by an Act, passed in the 5th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Arme, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways between Sheppard's Shord and the Devizes, and between the Top of Ashlington Hill and Rowdford, in the County of Wilts; and for explaining the said Act; and making the same more effectual arid extensive: And that Mr. William Chetwynd, and Mr* Haskins Stiles, do prepare* and bring in, the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Subsidy of Tonage, imposed by an Act of the Twelfth Year of King Charles the Second, for his Life, hnd since, by several Acts, continued for ever, subject to Redemption by Parliament, on old Rags, Junks, and old Fishing Nets, imported for making Paper: and all other Subsidies, Rates, and Duties, by any other Acts of Parliament, payable thereon; shall, from and after the Twenty-fifth Day of March 1725, cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duty of Two Shillings per Bushel, for all Apples imported, granted by the Act of the Eighth Year of his Majesty's Reign, for Three Years, be further continued for Seven Years.

Niue Navi- A PETITION of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Bur-gation. jijL gesses, of the Town of Northampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Inhabitants of the said Town, till within Two Years, or thereabouts, were entirely destitute of Water for their common Necessaries, except such as was brought in Carts, or on Men's Shoulders; and the said Town was once laid in Ashes, chiefly, as they apprehend, for want of Water: That now the said Town is sufficiently supplied with Water, at the great Expence of Wm. Wykes Esquire, by the Help ofan Engine placed at a Mill near the said Town, called Nun Mill, standingon the River Nine: That the Petitioners find, by the Votes the House, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill for making more effectual an Act, passed 120 for making the River Nine, or Nen, running from North'ton to Peterborough, navigable; which Bill will bean irreparable Damage to the Inhabitants of North'ton, if the Undertakers be permitted to meddle with the said Mill, or any Part of the Water-works, whereby the said Town o f North'ton may be exposed to Flames for want of the said Water: And praying, That a Saving Clause may be inserted in the said Bill, for preserving the Right and Property of the said Mr. Wykes; or else, that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill for making more effectual an Act, passed in the Parliament holden in the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for making the River Nine, or Nen, running from Northampton to Peterborough, navigable, was committed, be received.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, Free- Nine holders, and Inhabitants, of the Town of Northampton, Navigation, in behalf of themselves, and several Hundreds of the Inhabitants of the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill for making more effectual an Act,

12 'Anna, for making the River Nine, or Nen, navigable from North'ton to Peterborough; which Bill may be of such Damage to the Petitioners, that no Satisfaction can be made them, if the Undertakers be at Liberty to meddle with a Mill called Nun AIM, standing on the said River; at which Mill Willi Esquire, at his own Charge, hath lately erected an Engine for supplying the Inhabitants of North'ton with Water, which before they were in great Want of, but now are thereby plentifully supplied with, and a great Quantity reserved, and so disposed, that in case of Fire, it may be let into almost any part of the Town, in a few Minutes, for their Security: And praying, That there may be a Saving Clause in the said Bill, That nothing therein may extend to prejudice the said Mill, or Works; and that Mr. Wykes may enjoy the same, as he now doth; or else, that the said Bill may not pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill for making more effectual an Act, passed in the Parliament holden in the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for making the River Nine, or Nen, running from Northampton to Peterborough, navigable, was committed, be received.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the City importing of Bristol, in behalf of themselves, and others, was pre- Plantation sented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Naval Store*. 'French, at Moville, on the River Messisipi, have begun

*to make Tar, Pitch, and Rice; and by an Act,

8* Georgii, for giving further Encouragement for the Importation of Naval Stores, the Inhabitants of his Majesty's Colonies in America are put under great Restrictions in making Tar; so that 'tis not possible for them to comply with the said Act; and thereby the Bounty intended on the said Commodities will cease, and the Planters be disabled to carry on the Tar Trade; and, consequently, this Kingdom must be supplied therewith by the French; to the Prejudice of the Trade and Navigation of Great Britain: And praying. That the House will grant such Relief, that such a Branch of our Trade may not be lost to the Nation.

A Petition of Bartholomew Tate Esquire was presented Nine toi to the House, and read; setting forth, That, Leave be- gatiou. ing given by the House to bring in a Bill for making more effectual an Act for making the River Nine or Nen, navigable, the Petitioner hath a Mill, called Nun Mill, standing on the said River, near the Town of Northton; which he hath lett, upon a very long Lease, to William Wykes Esquire, at a very considerable Rent, in order to supply the Inhabitants of the said Town with Water; and wrhere he hath lately placed an Engine for that Purpose:

That, if the Undertakers of the intended Navigation should be permitted to meddle with that Mill, it may prove a great Detriment to the same: And praying, That a Saving Clause may be inserted in the said Bill, That nothing therein may extend to prejudice the said Mill, or Works, or Mr. Wykes' Right thereto.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill for making more effectual an Act, passed in the Parliament holden in the 12th Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for making the River Nine or Ac//, running from North ton to Peterborough, navigable, was committed, be received.

County of Cumberland, Esquire, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz. "

John Gale Esquire said, That he has known Barton Harbour and Pier, in the Petition mentioned; for about 40 Year9 last past; and that, when he first knew it^ there was no Houses* but only a Salt-pan, thereupon:

That in the 4th and ^th Years of the late Queen, an Act passed for enlarging the said Pier and Harbour, by granting a Duty of lour Pence per Ton upon all Coals shipt there, for defraying the necessary Expence of the said Harbour and Pier: And the Trustees, in the said Act named, whereof the said Mr. Gale was one, entered into a Contract with the Petitioner for cleansing the said Harbour, and building the said Pier; but knows not any further the Contents of the said Contract

And the Petitioner, Mr. I/mplagh himself, being required by the Committee to produce the said Contract, he said. He had it not in Tow n, but believed it was in the Country: And, being required by the Committee to

Produce an Account of his Expences concerning the said >ier, he said, He could not do it; nor did, he produce any Evidence to prove the same:

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That Thomas Lamplugh Esquire has made good the Allegations of his Petition;

It passed in the Negative.

Ordered, That the said Petition be rejected*

Thomas Bradshaw said, That lie has seen in Mr. Chad-'fields Warehouse above 17 Barrels, of Gunj»ovvder at a time, besides several Hand-granades, and other combustible Matters: That he has seen in Air. Edmund, Duke of Buckinghamshire and Nonnanby, an Infant, by his next Friend, Charles Earl of Orrtiy

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of the Custody of the Great Seal of Great Britain;

The Petition of the Plaintiffs and Defendant Sheweth,

That, in Easter Term last, your Petitioners brought this Suit against the Defendant, for Relief, touching a Lease made by the said late Duke of Buckinghamshire and Normanby, in the Year 1705, of the Manor of Mulgrave, and Alum-works, in Yorkshire, for the Term of 19 Years:

That, by the Order annexed, dated the 23d of July last, it was ordered, That a Commission should issue the last long Vacation, for Examination of Witnesses; and that Publication pass the First Day of Michaelmas Term last; and that the Plaintiff be at Liberty to set down the Cause to be heard some time the said Term: That a Commission hath issued accordingly; and both Sides examined Witnesses thereat; and Publication hath long since passed, in order to the Hearing; That the said Lease will expire at Lady-day next; and your Petitioners are advised it will be absolutely necessary to have this Cause heard; so that proper Directions may be given, in relation to the said Lease, Agreements and Covenant^ therein, and Matters about it, before the said Lease expires; for otherwise your Petitioners Estate, and Alum-works, will greatly suffer: That the said Defendant is likewise desirous, and willing, that this Cause may receive a speedy Hearing, if your Lordships shall please; for that the Defendant conceives he is intitled to cut down the Underwoods

2 2d February 1724.

Let this Cause be set down to be heard upon Tuesday the Second of March next, in the Afternoon; the Clerks in Court of both Sides having signed their Consent: Give Notice forthwith. J. Mull, C. S.

Jeff. Gilbert, C. S.

My Lady,

Now the Hearing is over, and determined contrary to both your Grace's Expectation and my own; that is to say, Your Grace was very positive, that I should not have the Value of the Underwoods; and I was as positive, that the Alum could not be recovered from me; what remains therefore is, to deliver up Possession in such a manner as shall make us both easy: And, in order thereto,

I am willing to refer the Quality, Condition, and Value, of all the Stocks and Utensils, to Two, Three, or Four, indifferent Persons; and whatever the same is short, in any kind, I will immediately pay the Value; and whatever the same is over in Value, I will accept of your Grace the Price that the Appraisers shall agree upon, or remove the same before Lady-day, if it be your Pleasure not to pay such Value: But if some Method of this kind be not agreed upon, our Disputes will branch out into more Difficulties than we at present can foresee; and, till I can be at some Certainty in these Points, I hope you'll pardon me, if I say, That the Possession must remain where it is, except it should be rent from me through the Sides of my Privilege; which I always told your Grace I would never depart from; at the same time assured you, that every thing fair should be done by me: And, by this Proposed, your Grace will see I am not at all altered in my Resolution. I am obliged to be at the Assizes in the Country; and, for that Purpose, got Leave of the House Yesterday, to be absent for Ten Days: I go in the Morning; and write this to apprise your Grace thereof; being ready to meet you any time this Day, in order to settle the Points in Question, that I may not be charged with Delay, now* the Quarter-day is so near at hand; but, if nothing be done by your Grace herein, I hope you w ill not blame me, if every proceeding in my Absence fall under a Consideration of a Breach of my Privilege. I am, with great Duty and Respect,

Your Grace's most obedient Servant,

3d March 1724. John Ward.

appeared to them, touching the Election for the County of Anglesea, and the Resolutions of the'Cornmittee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read:

And the said Report and Resolution, being read a Second time, are as followeth; viz.

Upon the Petition of Owen Meyricke, of Bodorgan, in the County of Anglesey, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of the Right honourable Richard late Lord Bulkeley, Viscount Cashells, in the Kingdom of Ireland, to serve for the said County: That the Committee have examined the Merits of this Election:

D , CFor the said late Lord Bulkeley 217: The Poll was, |For ^Petitioner - - - - 148.

That the Petitioner's Counsel objected to One hundred and Eleven of the said late Lord Bulkeley s Voters.; viz.

Sixty-two, as not qualified, by their. Estates, to vole; and Forty-nine, as influenced by Bribery, or Menaces. That, on the First Head, they called,

Win. Lewis Esquire: Who said, he knew all, or the far greater Part, of the Voters in the County; and had made it his Business to speak xyith, and inquire concerning, them: And he gave Evidence of their Declarations and Confessions to him, as follows; viz.

That Five had only Leaseholds for Years:

That Twenty-one had Freeholds by Purchase within 12 Months before the Election, or by Conveyances executed within that time, by Lord Bulkeley, or others, to qualify them to vote:

That Eleven had no Freehold:

That Tw o voted for Lands, of which the Mortgagees were in Possession:

That another was only a Mortgagee for Years: And, That the Freeholds of Fifteen w ere under the Value of Forty Shillings per Annum:

He also said, That Two were not rated: And,

That three others were rated under the Value of Forty Shillings per Annum; and the Rates were produced.

Richard Thomas said, That Two others confessed to him, they had no Freehold.

That on the Head of Bribery, and corrupt Practices, Win. Lewis Esquire gave Evidence, That other Voters had confessed to him, That they voted for Lord Bulkeley for the following Reasons; viz.

Six, for Money given by his Lordship; and Two, for Money given by his Lordship's Direction:

Twenty-eight, for Gifts, or Promises of Rewards, by his Lordship, of Timber for Repairs, Fewel, Marie, or the like:

Another, for Remittance of Arrears of Rent, by his Landlord, a Friend of Lord Bulkeley:

Five others, because of Threats by his Lordship: And,

Another, because of Threats by his Agent. And,

Mr. Hugh Lewis said, Another was guilty of corrupt Practices in the Election.

Thomas Evans, being examined, gave Evidence, That Five others had confessed, they voted for Lord Bulkeley, because of Gifts, or Promises of Rewards, by his Lordship, of the like Nature as before-mentioned.

That, on the other Side, the Counsel, for supporting the Election and Return, insisted, That the Testimony of Mr. Lewis alone, as before given, touching Persons not qualified, by Estate, to vote, was not sufficient to disqualify so many Voters, who generally had sworn to their Freeholds at the Election: Add, against what he said, they called,

Wm. Lewis, of Tryselwyn, Esquire: Who gave Evidence, That Five of those objected to for want of Freeholds, had sufficient Freeholds at the time of the Election, and for several Years before. And,

Wm. Owen Esquire, and Mr. Hugh Price, being examined, gave the like Evidence, as to Thirteen others objected to on the same Head; and that Two others were taxed at the Value of Forty Shillings per Annum.
