Rules, Orders, and Regulations.

Any of the Rates aforesaid, or any thing contained in this additional Book of Rates, is not to extend to alter the Method prescribed by Law for ascertaining the Yaluesupon such unrated Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, imported, as are of the Growth, Product, or Manufacture. of the East Indies, China, or other the Parts withing the Limits of the Charters granted to the united Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies:

Or,

To the charging any Duty upon such Sort of Wood, Plank, or Timber, wrought or unwrought, or any of the Goods called Lumber, which are to be imported Dutyfree, by virtue of the Act made in the Eighth Year of Ids present Majesty's Reign, on the conditions therein mentioned, during the Continuance of the said Act;

Or,

To the charging any Duty upon such Drugs, or other Goods used in Dyeing, which are to be imported Dutyfree, by virtue of another Act made in the Eighth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, on the Conditions therein mentioned:

And whereas it may happen, that, several Goods and Merchandizes may be imported, which are omitted to be rated in the Book of Rates made in the Tw elfth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second; or in this additional Book of Rates; or in some particular Act of Parliament; in such case, the Value and Price of such Goods and Merchandizes for the Old Subsidy, other than of those of India, Persia, or China, shall be ascertained by the Oath or Affirmation of the Merchant, in the Presence of the Customer, Collector, Comptroller, and Surveyor, or any Two of them: And the better to prevent Frauds, and that all Merchants may be upon an equal Foot in Trade, the Collector and Comptroller, or other proper Officers of the Customs, may open, view, and examine, such Goods and Merchandizes paying Duty, ad valorem* and compare the same with the Value and Price thereof, so sworn to, or affirmed: And if, upon such View and Examination, it shall appear, that such Goods or Merchandizes are not valued, by such Oath or Affirmation, according to the true Value and Price thereof, according to the true Intent and Meaning hereof, that then, and in such case, the Importer or Proprietor shall, on demand made, in Writing, by the Customer or Collector, and Comptroller, of the Port where such Goods or Merchandizes are entered, deliver, or cause to be delivered, all such Goods and Merchandizes into his Majesty's Warehouse at the Port of Importation, for the Use and Benefit of the Crown; and, upon such Delivery, the Customer or Collector of such Port, with the Privity of the Comptroller, shall out of any Money in the Hands of such Customer or Collector, arising by Customs, or other Duties, belonging to the Crown, pay to such Importer or Proprietor the Value of such Goodp and Merchandizes, so sworn to, or affirmed, for the said Old Subsidy, as aforesaid, together with an Addition of the Customs, and other Duties paid for such Goods, and of Ten Pounds per Centum to such Value; taking a Receipt for the same from such Importer or Proprietor, in full Satisfaction for the said Goods, as if they had been regularly sold: And the respective Commissioners of the Customs shall cause the said Goods to be fairly and publickly sold for the

Articles exhibited by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, in the Name of themselves, and of all the Commons of Great Britain, against Thomas Earl of Mecctesfeild, in Maintenance of their Impeachment against him for High Crimes and Misdemeanors.

Whereas the Office of Lord Chancellor of Great Britain is an Office of the highest Dignity and Trust, upon the impartial and uncorrupt Execution whereof the Honour of the Crown, and the Welfare of the Subjects of this Kingdom greatly depend: And whereas Thomas > Vol. 40,

Earl of Macclesfeiid,. in or about the Month of May in the Year of our Lord 1718, by the great Grace and Fa- impeach^ your of his Most Excellent Majesty, was constituted and ment. appointed Lord Chancellor of Great Britain; and ,did thereupon take the usual Oath for the due Execution of that high Office; whereby he did swear well and truly to serve our Sovereign Lord the King, and his People, Poor and Rich, after the Law s and Usages of this Realm; and such other Oaths as have been accustomed; and the said Earl continued in this great Office until about the Month of January in the Year of our Lord 1724; and, in Right thereof, was entrusted with the Nomination and Admis* sion to the Offices of Masters of the Court of Chancery; which Masters of the said Court are Officers of great Trust, sw'orn to serve the King and his People, and associated to the Lord Chancellor, for his Assistance iti the due Administration and Execution of Justice in the said Court: And whereas his Majesty, upon the said Earls being appointed to the Office of Lord Chancellor, did, of his Grace and Bounty, bestow upon the said Earl the Sum of Fourteen thousand Pounds, or some other great Sum; and did likewise grant unto George Parker Esquire, now commonly called Lord Parker, eldest Son, and Heir apparent, of the said Earl, a yearly Pension of Twelve hundred Pounds, payable out of his Majesty's Receipt of the Exchequer, during the joint Lives of his Majesty and the said Lord Parker, determinable upon his Majesty's making a Grant to the said Lord Parker, in Possession, of the Office of One of the Tellers of his Majesty's Exchequer, for the Term of his natural Life; which Office, being of the yearly Value of Fifteen hundred Pounds, or upwards, has been since granted by his Majesty unto the said Lord Parker, for his Life; who, in or about the Month of July, in the Year of our Lord 1719, was duly admitted to, and doth still enjoy, the same; and the said Earl, during the time of his continuing Lord Chancellor of Great Britain, did not only enjoy the usual Salary, Fees, and Profits, belonging to his Office, of a very great annual Value, but also did continue to receive an annual Pension of Twelve hundred Pounds, which his Majesty, in or about the Month of June in the Year of our Lord 1716, had granted to him, and his Assigns, during his Majesty's Life; and did likewise receive from the Crown a further annual Allowance of Four thousand Pounds, and many other Advantages; yet the said Thomas Earl of Macclesfield, not being satisfied with this large and ample Revenue, nor regarding the Obligation of his Oath, or the Duty of his high and important Office, but entertaining wicked and corrupt Designs and Views, to raise and procure to himself excessive and exorbitant Gain and Profit, by divers unjust and oppressive Practices and Methods, herein after mentioned, whilst he continued in the said Office of Lord Chancellor, did illegally, corruptly, and extorsively, take and receive, to his own private Use, the following, or some other great Sums of Money:

Article XIXth.

That whereas his most sacred Majesty, out of his fatherly Goodness to his People, did, in or about the Month of November last, direct an Inquiry to be made into the Accounts of the Masters of the said Court of Chancery, to the Intent that proper Methods might be taken for the Security of the Suitors of the said Court; the said Thomas Earl of Macclesfield, being then Lord Chancellor of Great Britain, and One of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, in order to obstruct the same, and to prevent a parliamentary Inquiry into the State and Condition of the Offices of the said Masters, in Breach of the several great Trusts reposed in him, did give Advice and Encouragement to thp said Masters, to assist and supply each other with Monfey and Effects; and did represent to the said Masters, that it would be for their Honour and Service to appear able and sufficient; and that, if they made a bold Stand now, it might prevent a parliamentary Inquiry; or to that Effect; and did persuade several of them to make false Representations of their Circumstances to his Majesty, by adding a Subscription to their respective Accounts delivered to the said Earl, to be laid before his Majesty, to the Effect following; viz. That they were able to answer the Money and Securities in their Hands; and were willing to pay the same to such Persons as were intitled thereunto; although the said Earl knew, or had good Reason to believe, that several of the Masters were not then able to answer the Balance of their Accounts; nor are they yet able to satisfy, or make good, the same: And, when the said Masters were afterwards required to produce the Cash and Effects of the Suitors in their Hands, some of the said Masters, according to such Advice and Encouragement given by the said Earl, did supply others of them with Cash and Effects, to make a false Show and Appearance of their Ability and Readiness to Answer the Balance of their Accounts.

A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and Vestry, of the new Parish of St. John, Clerkcnxcell, in the County of Middlesex, in the behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in the Bill now depending in the House, for the better effecting the pious Intention of building Fifty new Churches in and about London and Westminster*, Provision is to be made for the Maintenance of the Minister and Curateof the said Parish: That the said Parish contains about 760 Houses, about 350 whereof are inhabited by poor Persons, none of which pay to the Poors Rate, and many of them receive Relief of the Parish; and the whole Rents of the rest of the Houses, which are charged in the Poors Rate, amount to but about £.5,000.per Annum; and the Poors Rates within the said Parish, for several Years past, have amounted to , 2s. 6d. in the Pound: And praying. That, out of the

Fund appropriated by Parliament for the Endowment of the said new Churches, such suitable Allowance may be made towards the Endowment of the said Church of St. John, Clerkemcell, as to the House, considering the mean Circumstances of the said Parish, shall seem meet.

Mr. Pultency took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Pultency reported from the Committee, That they had made some Progress in the Bill; and had heard Counsel upon the Petitions of the Vestrymen and Inhabitants of the Parish of St. George the Martyr; and on the Petition of the Inhabitants in and a!>out Bloomsbury, in the Parish of St. Giles in the Fields: and had al&> heard Counsel for the Clauses in the Bill, that were objected to by the Petitioners; and that the Committee had directed him to move, That they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill.

Fifty New A Petition of the united Company of Merchants of Churches. England, trading to the East Indies, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the old East India Company did convey to the Petitioners, and their Successors, a Piece of Ground in the Hamlet 0i Poplar, in the Parish of Stepney, whereon the Old Company had, above ,50 Years before, erected several Alms-houses, and a Chapel, which cost them about £. 5,000.; and they, and the Petitioners, have, ever since, constantly placed such poor Seamen in the said Alms-houses, as had suffered in their Service; and allowed them a sufficient Maintenance, and also to the Minister, to perform Divine Service in the said Chapel, for the Benefit of the said Alms-people, and such others as should resort thither: That the Petitioners have lately discovered, by a Clause in an Act, 10° Annce, for confirming to the Principal and Scholars of Kings-htdl, and College of Brazen-nose, in Oxford, the Purchase of the Advowson of Stepney, and other Churches; and for settling the same, to the Benefit of the said College; and, by a Clause in another Act, 11* Anna, relating to the Building of 50 new Churches, the said Principal and Scholars claim a Right to present to all Churches and Chapels that then were, or thereafter should be, erected within the Parish of Stepney; and, by a Clause, in the Bill now depending in the House, relating to the said new Churches, the said Claim seems to be confirmed: That the Petitioners being informed, that, if the said Chapel , was converted into a Parish Church, a considerable Sum would be saved to the Publick thereupon, they entered into Treaty with the Commissioners for building the .50 new Churches, and also with some Persons authorized by the College aforesaid; betwixt whom it was agreed, That the Petitioners should have the First Presentation for a Clerk to the said intended new Church; the said College to have the Two next Presentations; and the Petitioners the next single Presentation; and so, by Turns, for even after, the College to have Two, and the Petitioners One Presentation; And praying, That a Clause may be inserted in the said Bill, to confirm and establish the Agree- , ment aforesaid; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for better effecting the pious Intention of building 50 new Churches, or so many of them as shall be built by the Funds already granted; and for settling the Right of Patronage thereof; and separating the Parishes belonging to the same, and the Revenues thereof; and preserving the Right of the present Incumbents of old Churches; and for the Endowment of Eleven new Churches, therein mentioned, out of Part of the Fund appropriated by Parliament to that Use, and by a Pound Rate; and for regulating the Choice of Lecturers; and for making the Parish Clerks of the new Churches Members of the Corporation of Parish Clerks already erected; is committed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, iThat the several Glauses for Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of tips Kingdom; and for taking off several LHlties on. Merchandizes exported; in an Act, paf^ed in t he Eighth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty Kintr George, intituled, An Act for Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom; and p *' for taking off several Duties on Merchandizes exported; and for reducing the Duties upon Beaver-skins, Pepper, Mace, Cloves, and Nutmegs, imported; and for importation of all Furs, of the Product of the British Plantations, into this Kingdom only; and that the Two Corporations of Assurance, on any Suits brought on their Policies, shall be liable only to single Damages, ;and Costs of Suit; ought to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George, intituled, An Act to prevent the clandestine Running of Goods, and the Danger of Infection thereby; and to prevent Ships breaking their Quarantine; and to subject Copper Ore, of the British Plantations, to such Regulations as other enumerated Commodities, of the like Production, are subject; ought to be continued; except the Clause obliging all Ships or Vessels to perform Quarantine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thai the Two last Clauses/or the more effectual preventing Frauds relating to the Customs, and Frauds in jchixing Silks withStuffs to be exported, in an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for continuing of some Laws, and Reviving of others, therein mentioned, for Exempting of Apothecaries from serving Parish and Ward Offices, and upon Juries; and relating to Jurors; and to the Payment of Seamen's Wages; and the Preservation of the Naval Stores, and Stores of War; and concerning the Militia, and Trophy-money; and against clandestine Running of Goods; ought to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for the better preventing Frauds committed by Bankrupts, ought to be continued.

Churches. bitants of the Hamlet of Poplar and Blackwall, in the Parish of Stepney, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and divers other Inhabitants of the said Hamlet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed the Chapel at Poplar is intended to be made a Parish Church, and to be provided for by a Bill now depending in the House: That the Inhabitants of the said Hamlet are willing to pay, in proportion to their Abilities, towards the Maintenance of a Minister of the intended new Parish: But the Place, through the Decay of Trade for many Years, being burthened with Poor, the Rents of Houses very low, and the Lands exempt, by an ancient Modus, from any Part of the Charges; the Petitioners therefore pray, That such a Proportion of the Fund appropriated by Parliament for the Endowment of the new Churches, may be allowed them, as, together with a Pound Rate, may be a sufficient Provision and Support for the Minister of the intended Parish; or to grant them such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for better effecting the pious Intention of building Fifty new Churches, or so many of them as shall be built by the Funds already granted; and for settling the Right of Patronage thereof; and separating the Parishes belonging to the same, and the Revenues thereof; and preserving the Right of the present Incumbents of old Churches; and for the Endowment of Eleven new Churches, therein mentioned, out of Part of the Fund appropriated by Parliament to that Use, and by a Pound Rate; and for regulating the Choice of lecturers; and for milking the Parish Clerks of the new Churches Members of the Corporation of Parish Clerks already erected; is committed.

A PET ITION of the Inhabitants of the Parish of Deptford, in the County of Kent, was presented Churches, to the House, and read; setting forth. That, in the new District for the new Parish Church at Deptford, are near 900 Houses, many whereof are filled with Two, Three or more, Families, who are of so mean a Condition, that,

400 of those Houses are exempt from paying to Church and Poor; and the greater Part of the other Houses are lett at so lowRents, that not aboveTen pay above jC.zo per Annum: That their Cesses arise principally upon Land, which, paying Tythes, is intended, by a Bill depending in the House, to be exempt from paying the Pound Rate towards the Maintenance of a Minister; so that 'twill be impossible to levy, for that Use, any large Income, without being very grievous to the Inhabitants: That the trading Part of Deptford mostly depends upon the Sea Business, and the Service of his Majesty, and the Publick, in the Dock-yards, and Man of War, and Yachts, the Payment of whose Wages is generally deferred to some distantTimeafter it becomes due; and very much affects their Tradesmen: That the Poverty of the Town is of late sensibly increased, and is likely more to increase, by the building new Docks nearer to London; Removal of Persons who frequent the Exchange; new Buildings nearer London; and the daily Additions of Poor, by Widows and Orphans of Seafaring-men: For all which Reasons, and many more, they pray, That a bountiful Proportion may be allowed, out of the Fund granted by Parliament, towards the Maintenance of the Minister of their new Church.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for better effecting the pious Intention of building Fifty new Churches, or so many of them as shall be built by the Funds already granted; and for settling the Right of Patronage thereof; and separating the Parishes belonging to the same, and the Revenues thereof; and preserving the Right of the present Incumbents of old Churches; and for the Endowment of Eleven new Churches, therein mentioned, out of Part of the Fund appropriated by Parliament to that Use, and by a Pound Rate; and for regulating the Choice of Lecturers; and for making the Parish Clerks of the new Churches Members of the Corporation of Parish , Clerks already erected; is committed.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from his Majesty to this House, signed by his Majesty: And he delivered the same to Mr. Speaker , who read the same to the House:

And the said Message is as follows;

George It.

The Necessities of his Majesty's Government having rendered it impracticable for his Majesty to make any considerable Retrenchments in the Expences of his Civil List; and having engaged his Majesty in some extraordinary Expences, which, he is persuaded, his loyal Commons will believe, have been employed, not only for the Honour and Dignity of the Crown, but for the Interest and Prosperity of his People; his Majesty hopes, from the known Zeal and Affection of this Parliament to his Person and Government, That he may be enabled to make use of the Funds lately settled for the Payment of the Civil List Annuities; and for replacing the same to his Majesty in the most advantageous manner, and, upon

the Credit thereof, to raise a Sum of Money sufficient to redeem those Annuities, and to discharge the present Debts contracted in his Civil Government.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take his Majesty's most gracious Message into Consideration.

Ordered, That his Majesty's said most gracious Message be referred to the said Committee.

To the 14 th Article; the Earl saith, That Henry Edwards Esquire, in this Article mentioned, succeeded to the Office of Mr. Dormer about the 18th Day of May 1721; but, by reason of the Disorder the said Office was then under, and the great Danger of a Loss therein, the Earl had given up and quitted all the Advantage which might accrue to him upon the Disposal thereof, and left it intirely to the other Masters to raise what Money they could thereby; which was agreed to be all applied towards making good any Deficiency or Loss which might happen to the Suitors of the Court concerned, ifc that Office; and thereupon the Sum of <£.5,000. was raised, by the Disposal of the said Office to Mr. Edwards, and was applied accordingly: And the said Earl believes the Debt from William Wilson, in this Article mentioned, was assigned, by the said Mr. Dormer, to the said Mr. Edwards, inTrust, and to the Intent, that he should pay, apply, and dispose of, the said Debt, or such Part thereof as should, from time to time, be by him got in, and deceived, of and from the said William Wilson, in such manner as the Court should order and direct; or to that Effect: After which said Assignment, so made, the Earl believes, that the said Mr, Edwards used great Endeavours to obtain Payment and Satisfaction of the said Debt from Mr. Wilson: But, finding alibis Endeavours fruitless; and that the said Wilson had long before stopt Payment, and was in no Condition of paying his Creditors the Whole of their Debts; but that he was willing, And had offered, to come to a Composition, and to pay them, in Proportion, the utmost he was able; the said Mr. Edivards, thereupon, about the 30th Day of June in the Year of our Lord 1722, preferred his Petition to the said Earl, as Lord Chancellor; setting forth, in Substance, the state of the Case, as before-mentioned: And praying, That it might be referred to one of the Masters of the Court, to see if such Composition, so proposed by the said Wm. XV.

To the 15th Article; the Earl saith, That about the Month of February in the Year of our Lord 1720, he gave Orders to his Secretary to' write to the several Masters of the Court of Chancery, to bring in their Accounts of the Cash, Effects, and Securities, in their Hands, belonging to the Suitors of the Court; and believes he did so; but denies that the same was done with any un just Purpose, or with any Thought to terrify the said Masters to make any Contribution towards.satisfying the Demands upon the said Office of Fleetwood. Dormer; but believes, what they did contribute they paid, freely and voluntarily, and out of their own Money; and therein, as the said Earl believes, did no more than follow a Precedent of the like Nature, on the Failure of Dr, Edisbury, formerly a Master of the said Court: And the said Earl saith. That his real and whole Intention in calling for the said Accounts was, to inform himself, in the best manner he was able, of the State and Condition of the several Offices; and thereby to be the better able to make proper Regulations concerning the same: And therefore, though the said Article seems to insinuate as if the Calling for the said Accounts was dropped, as soon as the Masters were prevailed on to contribute, the said Earl saith, That afterwards, and without any regard thereto, he still continued to call for the said Masters Accounts; and, not finding them brought in as he expected, he did, about the Beginning of November following, cause another Letter to be sent to them, requiring them to bring in their Accounts; and, by both the Letters sent to them on that Occasion, he directed the particular Method in which he would have their Accounts made up: But the said Earl, being afterwards convinced how difficult and tedious a Work it would be, and what Obstruction it would give to the Business of the Court; and that at last it could not be depended upon with any Certainty; was forced to lay aside that Design, and to content himself with going on in the same Road which his Predecessors had done; and humbly begs leave to observe, That what has been lately done with respect to the Accounts of the said Masters, plainly shews the insuperable Difficulties of such an Undertaking.

XVIII.

To the 18th Article; the said Earl saith. He never knew how the Masters kept, or disposed of the Money and Effects belonging to the Suitors of the Court; and as he believes, that, after Dr. Edisbury's Failure, the then Lord Chancellor, so he knows, that after Mr. Dor± mer's Misfortune, the said Earl thought of several Methods to prevent any Inconvenience upon the.like Accident for the future; but they had both the same Misfortune, not to bring any of them to such Perfect tion as to venture to put them in Practice:

That several Proposals were made to him by the Persons he consulted upon that Occasion, but none that he believes it will be held criminal not to have then established: Some things were proposed that he thought impracticable, some insufficient, some inconsistent with that complete Regulation he hoped to make: The Objects be proposed to himself were, to provide for whatever Deficiency might happen in the Office late of Mr. Dorvier, to secure the Suitors from any future Loss, and to make several Regulations relating to the Offices of the Masters; and he thought these would be best done together; nor had he perfected the Scheme of any one of them, to his own Satisfaction; he remembers no Proposal that he thought would take it totally out of the Power of the Masters to dispose of the Securities or Effects, or effectually secure the Cash:

XIX.

To the 19th Article; the said Earl saith, That upon g*eat Consideration of Mr. Dormer's Deficiency; and of the Danger there might be of farther Inconveniences, frith relation to the Money and Effects in the Hands of the Masters; and of several Disputes and Differences that had arisen tit the Court of Chancery; and of some Applications of the said Masters for establishing them in their just Rights; and of some Practices of the Masters, frhieh the said Earl thought ought to be reformed; he fras convinced, that the same was a work of too great Consequence.for him singly to attempt; and, being highly sensible of his most Sacred Majesty's paternal Goodness to his People, did presume humbly to beseech ftis, Majesty, as the Fountain of Justice, to depute some of his most honourable Privy Council to take the Matters aforesaid into Consideration, in order to the establishing such Regulations, as might tend to the Honour of that high Court, and to the Advantage of his Majesty's Subjects, being Suitors there; which Request his Majesty, out of his wonted Goodness, was pleased to receive very graciously; and named several Lords, and htlier honourable Persons, of his Privy Council, to be a Committee to take the same into Consideration; and, pursuant to his Majesty's Command, the said Committee fret, and‘began with the Accounts of the said Masters; wherein the said Earl begs Leave to appeal to such of your Lordships who attended in that Committee, whether he did not contribute, to the utmost of his Power, to have every thing done which the said Committee thought expedient: And the said Earl saith, That hemade all such Orders as were by them judged requisite; and so pressed the Execution thereof that not only the Accounts of all the Masters, then in being, were brought in, but all the Securities in all their Hands, and the Cash of most of them, were actually lodged in the Bank of England; and therefore the said Earl is greatly surprised to find himself charged with obstructing the taking those Accounts, which he had thus desired might be taken, and contributed to the taking of them with all his Power.

And the said Earl saith. That he never thought of preventing a Parliamentary Enquiry, any otherwise than by making it unnecessary, and procuring to the Suitors a full Redress of all their Grievances, and rectifying whatever he found amiss: And that he looked upon to be his Duty; and begs Leave to say it here, once for all, in Answer to all the several Insinuations of that kind contained in the Articles:

To the Twentieth Article, the said Earl saith, That it never entered into his Thought to make use of, nor did he ever make use of, any of the Money belonging to thfe Suitors of the Court, for his own private Advantage^ but believes, that in December > 1720, having Occasion for the Sum of £. 1,500. and asking his Secretary, Mr. Cottirtgham, whether he would lend him the same, he said, He could not; but would procure it for him; and accordingly borrowed the same from Mr. Godfrey, Onfe of the Masters of the said Court: And the said Earl gave his own Note for Payment thereof to the said Mr.

Godfreys and, in February following, repaid £\ 1,000.

Part of the said principal Sum; but in the same Month of February 1720; upon a fresh Occasion, borrowed again Part of the said £. t,oooo. so paid back; and a Note or Notes were given for the Payment thereof; and some time after the said Earl ordered the whole Money, borrowed of the said Mr. Godfrey, to be paid, with all the Interest due for the same; and the said Godfrey received the Principal, but would not be prevailed upon to take the Interest, or any Part thereof: And the said Earl saith, That all the said Money was repaid within the Compass of a Year after it was borrowed: And the said Earl declares, that he never received or borrowed any Sum or Sums of Money whatsoever of any of the Masters of the said Court, except as above set forth.

To the One-and-twentieth Article; the said Earl saith. That, upon the strictest Review of his own Behaviour, during the time he had the Honour of serving his most Sacred Majesty, in the Office of Lord Chancellor, he is not conscious to himself, that he ever did, in any illegal or arbitrary manner extend his Power, or the Power of the Court, beyond their lawful and just Bounds; or that he did arbitrarily or illegally assume to himself, as Lord Chancellor, or by Colour of his Office, any unjust and unlimited Power of dispensing with, suspending, or controuling, the Laws or Statutes of this Realm; or that he any ways oppressed the Suitors of

the Court; or was guilty of any Breach or Violation of ' the Rights or Liberties the Subject, or of his own Oath, as Lord Chancellor: And with regard to the particular Complaint against him in this Article, the said Earl saith, That Rachel Tyson, in the Article named, as the Earl is informed, caused a Bill to be exhibited in the Court of Chancery, in the Name of her Son and Daughter, in the said Article likewise mentioned, by their prochein Amy, against herself, and the said John Tyson, and others, to have the Trusts in the Will of her late Husband duly performed; and the same was brought to Hearing at the Rolls, the Seventh Day of Jnty 1718; and, by the Decree then made, it was, amongst other things, ordered, upon the Prayer, as the said EarJ^hath heard, and believes, of the Counsel employed by the said Rachel Tyson, That a Receiver should be appointed of the Rents and Profits of the real Estate; who was to have a Salary allowed to him, and Power to lett and set the said Estate, as there should be Occasion, with the Approbat ion of the Master to whom the Cause was referred: And the said Earl saith, That in Execution of that Part of the Decree, which directed a Receiver to be appointed, the Master having certified, that he had appointed John Nicholas Esquire to be the Receiver of the Rents and Profits of the said Estate, the said John Tyson, thinking himself aggrieved thereby, did, in the usual Course of Proceedings in the said Court, cause Exceptions to be filed against the same: And, upon the Arguing thereof, before the said Earl, by Counsel of both Sides, Affidavits were read to shew, that the said John Nicholas was an improper Person; that the said Testator had declared in his Life-time, that the said John Nicholas, by Name, should not have any thing to do with the Management of his Estate; and that a considerable Part thereof consisted in old Houses, and Water-works: And the said Earl, upon a full Hearing of both Parties, was of Opinion, That the said John Nicholas ought not to be appointed the Receiver; and, upon the Proposal of the said John Tyson, then in Court, ordered Robert Doyley Esquire to be Receiver, he giving Security, to be approved of by the said Master; which Order was made, as he believes, on the 15th of January in the Year ^718; and affirmed, upon the re-arguing the said Exceptions, on the Sixth of March in the Year 1718; since which time the Parties interested have never thought fit to complain thereof to your Lordships by Appeal, in order to have it reversed, as mistaken or unjust; though, now, the Making thereof is complained oFas a Crime: And the said Earl is not ashamed to own, that he was very well acquainted with the said Robert Doyley, for some Years before the said Order; and believed him to be a Person of great Honour and Integrity, Application and Exactness; and believes there are several Persons of Distinction, to whom he had the Honour to be known, who had the same Opinion of him: But the said Earl did not appoint him Receiver because of his own Respect for him, but because he was named by the said John Tyson, who was Uncle of the said Infant, and Executor of his Father's Will, in Trust for him; and, by the same Will, appointed his Guardian, in case of his Mother's Death or Marriage; and to whom the said Testator had devised the said Estate, in ease of the Death of the said Infant without Issue Male; iind whose Interest it therefore was to take Care of the Infant's Interest in that Particular: And the said John Tyson, and Sir Casar Child, whose Daughter the said John Tyson had married, had such Confidence in him, the said Robert Doi/Uy, that, upon the 18th Day of 'March 1718, they entered into a Recognizance, together with him, in the Penalty of Seven thousand Pounds, for the said Robert Doyley s duly accounting for, and paying, the Money lie should receive out of the said Infant's Estate: And the said Earl saith, That no Complaint was ever made to the said Earl against the said Robert Doyley, to the time of his Death: But he owns, "that lie hath heard, that, upon the Master's stating the Account since Christmas last, there does appear due from the said Robert Doyley about £. 2,500. ovJJ.zfio o.;

but believes there is not any Fear or Donbt but that the same is very well secured by the said Recognizance: 1

And the said Earl saith. That he does not remember the particular Expressions used by the Counsel, or him* self, upon arguing or re-arguing the said Exceptions:

But he cannot believe, that any Counsel, of great Ability and Experience in the said Court, would have thought what the said Earl did extraordinary; much less wrould have used such an Expression to the said Earl, as in the Articles, which is an indecent Censure of hisProceedings:

And here being a Decree, in this Case, approved of by all Parties, That a Receiver should be appointed to receive the Rents and Profits of the Infant's Estate, the said Earl is at aLoss to understand how the Fixing on the Person to be the Receiver, upon good Security, to account for and pay the same for the Infant's Use, is reviving the Court of Wards; whose Business it was to take the;

Rents and Profits of the Infant's Estate,.for the King's Use, without accounting for any of them to the Infant; but barely providing a Maintenance for him, at the Discretion, perhaps, of some Grantee of the Custody.

Thus the said Earl has laid his Case before your Lordships; and doth farther, for Answer to all the said Articles, say, That he is not guilty of all or any of the Matters contained in the said Articles, or any of them* in Manner and Form as they are therein charged against him: And the said Earl doth further insist upon the Benefit of his Majesty's most gracious and general free Pardon, granted to all his Subjects (not therein excepted), in and by an Act of Parliament, for that Purpose made, in the Seventh Year of his Majesty's Reign,' in Bar of, and in his Defence against the said Impeachment, and the said Articles exhibited in Maintenance thereof, and all and every the Proceedings thereupon, so far as the same extend to any Neglect, Offence, or Misdemeanor, or supposed Neglect, Offence, or Misdemeanor, or any other Act, Matter, or Thing, suffered, done, or committed, or omitted, by him, the said Earl, before the 24th Day of July in the Year 1721; and doth humbly insist, That no Evidence ought to be given against him, for or concerning any of the Matters ot Things aforesaid, in and by the said Act pardoned, or any of them; and doth aver, That he is not within any of the Exceptions in the said Act contained.

Macclesfield.

Wm. Cotvper, Cler' Parliamentor'.

The Counsel for, the Sitting Member insisted, That the Evidence offered of Bribery did not affect him in this Election: And they objected Bribery, to induce the Electors to invite the Petitioner to be a Candidate, and to vote for him; and they called, Thomas King: Who said, That Mr. Isaac Tomkins, an Agent for the Petitioner, solicited him, and other Voters, to sign a Paper,'inviting the Petitioner to be a Candidate at this Election; and promised-to give theni as much as any others had, without naming any Sum: And,

That Thomas Vale told him, Tomkins had publickly promised the Voters Fifteen Pounds a Man; and bid those present tell as many others as they could, iHht they should have the same; upon which Promise many signed the Paper.

John Lock said, That Mr. Tmnkins invited him to the Three Horseshoes, to sign a Paper of Invitation of the Petitioner; and told him, He should have Five of Six Pounds to sign it: That he went and found about Sixty Voters there; and several of them told him, They had the same Promiseffrom Mr. Tomkins: That the Witness askinguponwhatTertusthey should invite the Petitioner, Mr. Tomkins answered, That they should be satisfied to their own Contents; or might vote1 as they pleased: Being cross-examined, he said, That the Petitioner declared publickly, he would give no Money; and when those Voters met again, upon the Evenin g of the Election, he never Went near them: This Witness also said, That he did not know, that any cne had any thing fur signing that Paper.

William Poicell said, That Mr. Tomkins came to the Three Horseshoes, when about Six of the Voters were there; and asked, Upon whose Account they drank; they answered, They spent their own Money; ‘ upon which he said, That he understood Mr. Cooke' would give Seven Pounds a Man; and then Tomkins declared, That tire Petitioner would give Ten Pounds, and, If that would not do, Fifteen, and, if that would not do, Twenty Pounds, a Man:

Being cross-examined, he said. He voted singly for the Sitting Member; and did not give his other Vote, because a Person did not come, as promised, on behalf of the Petitioner.

To invalidate the Testimony of Mr. Nelme;

Michael Stephens said, That, after this Election, Mr. 'Nelme and he, coming together from the Petitioner's House, fell into Discourse, upon the Road, concerning the Election, and the Nature of the Evidence to be given here touching it; Nelme saying. He was to be a Witness, and asking if the Evidence was to be upon Oath, the Witness answered, No; but great regard was to be had to the Truth -. Whereupon Nelme replied, That he might I ve to sell a little Flannel or Cloth in his'Shopw, and it would be no Harm to tell a Lye to serve his Friend: This Witness also said. That, at the time before mentioned, the Petitioner offered him great Rewards' to vote for a Person in his Interest, to be the next Bailiff.

The House being moved, That an Act, made in the Fourth Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for enforcing, and making perpetual, an Act, of the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Preserving of all such Ships, and Goods thereof, which shall happen to be forced on Shore, or stranded, upon the Coasts of this Kingdom, or any other of her Majesty's Dominions; and for inflicting the Punishment of Death on such as shall wilfully bum or destroy Ships; might be read;

The said Act was read accordingly.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill to continue several Acts, therein mentioned, for preventing Frauds committed by Bankrupts; for Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom; for preventing the clandestine Running of Goods; and for making Copper Ore, of the British Plantations, an enumerated Commodity; is committed; That they have Power to receive a Clause for explaining and amending the said Act.

Alexander Urquhart Esquire, a Member of this House, acquainting the House, in his Place, That he did not insist on his Privilege, in relation to any Demands of such Persons as had petitioned this House, in relation to his Privilege; which Petition is referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections;

Ordered, That the said Committee be discharged from proceeding on the said Petition.

Whereas an Act of Parliament was made, and passed, in the Seventh Year of our Reign, intituled, An Act for raising a Sum, not exceeding y£.f,oo, oooo. by charging Annuities, at the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, upon the Civil List Revenues, till redeemed by the Crown; and for enabling his Majesty, his Heirs or Successors, by causing such a Deduction to be made, as therein is mentioned, to make good, to the Civil List, the Payments which shall have been made upon the said* Annuities; and for borrowing Money upon certain Lottery Tickets; and fordiseharging the Corporation for Assurances of Part of the Money which they were obliged to pay to his Majesty; and for making good a Deficiency* to the East India Company: And, to the end we, our Heirs and Successors, might be enabled to reimburse oursel ves such Sum and Sums of Money, as, in pursuance of the said Act, shall have been issued, or furnished, out* of our Civil List Revenues, during our Life; or out of the Hereditary Revenues, therein after-mentioned, after our Demise; for or towards the Payment of the Annuities to be purchased or obtained thereupon; or for or towards the Redemption of the same; it is thereby enacted, That it should and might be lawful to and for us, our Heirs and Successors, by any Warrant, under the Great Seal, Privy Seal, or Royal Sign Manual, to cause a Deduction to be made, not exceeding Six Pence in the Pound, out of all Monies, w'hich, from and after the First Day of August 1721, shall be paid for or upon all Pensions and Annuities charged upon any of the said Hereditary or temporary Duties; and for and upon all Salaries, Fees, and Wages, payable for, and in respect of Offices of Profit, granted by, or derived from, the Crown* and for and upon all other Payments, from the Crown, whatsoever; or for or upon any Arrearages of them, or any of them, incurred, or to be incurred, except as therein is excepted; the same Deductions to be made for the Use of our Heirs and Successors, for the Benefit of our or their Civil Government, so long as the said Annuities, shall, by virtue of that Act, be payable out of the Revenues charged therewith; and until the same Annuities shall be redeemed, pursuant to the same; as by the said Act, relation being the reunto had, may more fully appear: Our Will and Pleasure nowr is, and we do, by tins Warrant, under our Royal SignManual, direct, authorize, and command. That a Deduction be made, after the Rate of Six Pence in the Pound, out of all Monies, which, after the said First Day of August 1721, shall be paid for Pensions and Annuities; and for Salaries, Fees, 6 L 9t

20° Aprilis.

A. 1715

Warrants for or Wages, payable in respect of Offices of Profit, granted Sixpenny by, or derived from, the Crown; and out of all other Deductions, payments whatsoever, which, after the said First Day of August 1721, shall be made out of any of our Revenues of Excise, or Duties under your Management; or for Arrearages of the said Pensions and Annuities, Salaries, Fees, and Wages, or any of them, incurred, or to be incurred; by the Hands of you, our said Commissioners, or of any Receiver, or Receiver General, Cashiers, Collectors, or other Officers and Ministers, of our said Revenues and Duties respectively, to whom it shall appertain to make any such Payments and Deductions out of the same, for the Time being; other than, and except, such Payments dS are to be made upon Exportation of exciseable Liquors, or for Drawbacks, Premiums, or other Allowances, upon Exportation of Malt, Leather, or other Commodities, for which, special Provision is, or shall be, made by an Act or Acts of Parliament concerning the same; and other than, and except, all other Payments to be made, out of our said Revenues, into our Exchequer, or otherwise, which by any Act or Acts of Parliament, are, or shall be, exempted from Payment of any Taxes or Imposition; and other than, and except, the Salaries, Fees, or Wages, of such particular Offices, where the Salaries, Fees, or Wages, together with all the lawful Perquisites, and other Advantages, or Profits, to such particular Officesseverallyand respectively belonging, do not altogether, in the Whole, exceed Fifty Pounds per Annum; and other than, and except, such Part or Parts of the yearly Sums, amounting to One hundred thousand Pounds, granted to our dearly beloved Son the Prince of Wales, during the joint Lives of ourself, and the said Prince, as are charged, or chargeable, upon the said Revenues of Excise, or any of them; and other than, and except, such Part or Parts of the yearly Sums, amounting to Fifty thousand Pounds, granted to our dearly beloved Daughter the Princess of Wales, or to any Person or Persons in Trust for her, to commence immediately after the Death of our said Son the Prince of Wales; and are charged, or chargeable, upon our said Revenues, or any of them: And our Pleasure is, and we do hereby direct and command, That you and every of you, in yourrespectivePlaces and Stations, do take especial Care, that the said Deduction, of Six Pence in the Pound, be made out of all the said Payments, except as before is excepted; and to cause all the Monies, so deducted, to be reserved for the Purpose above-mentioned, according to the true Intent and Meaning of the said Act of Parliament: And, for so doing, these Presents, or a Copy thereof, attested under the Hand and Seal of the Secretary of you, the Commissioners of Excise for the Time being, shall be to you, and every of you, and all others herein concerned, a sufficient Warrant in this behalf.

Given at our Court at Kensington, the 25th Day of September, in the Eighth Year of our Reign.

By his Majesty's Command, v R. Walpole,

Geo. Baillie,

Cha. Turner,

To our trusty and well beloved our Commissioners for managing, and causing to be collected and managed, our Revenues of Excise; and to our Receivers General,

Cashiers, and other Officers thereof, for the Time being; to whom, in their respective Places and Stations, these Presents do or shall appertain.

George R.

Whereas by a Warrant, under our Royal Sign Manual, bearing Date the 25th Day of September last, in pursuance of an Act, passed in the then last Session of Parliament, for raising a Sum, not exceeding^.500,000. by charging Annuities, after the Rate of £.5. per Centum per Annum, on the Civil List Revenues, fife, we signified

to you, our Royal Will and Pleasure, That a Deductioi should be made, after the Rate of Six Pence in the Pound out of all Monies, which, after the First Day of Angus 1721, should be paid for Pensions and Annuities; anc for Salaries, Fees, and Wages, payable in respect of Of fices of Profit granted by, or derived from, the Crown, and out of all other Payments whatsoever, which, aftei the said First Day^of August 1721, should be made out of any of our Revenues of Excise, or Duties under your Management; or for Arrearages of the said Pensions and Annuities, Salaries, Fees, and Wages, or any of them, incurred, or to be incurred; except as ip our said Warrant is excepted: And whereas we have thought fit, that the Monies, which have been, or shall be, paid fot the particular Services hereafter mentioned, should be excepted from the Paj^ment of the said Six Pence in the Pound, as well as those excepted by our said Warrant; that is to say,

For the Monies paid for the Rents of the Houses, wherein the General Excise Office is kept; and of the several Chambers in the several Divisions within the Weekly Bills of Mortality; and the Parish Duties charged on, and paid by you for, the said Houses; and the Workmen's Bills for the necessary Repairs thereof;

For the Monies paid by you, and the Officers under you, for Portage of Letters, Carriage of Parcels, Messengers, and other petty Incidents;

For the Petty Incidents charged and claimed every Round by your Collectors, Supervisors, and Officers, in the Country, for small Sums, which are very numerous, being for the most Part, paid to Persons officiating for sick and absent Officers, Letters, Messengers, and other Necessaries;

For the Riding Charges allowed to the Collectors, Supervisors, and Officers, whilst they are upon the Rounds;

For the several Bills of Law-charges of our Solicitor for the said Revenues, and of others occasionally employed Jby him in the Country, for Management of Causes there; consisting principally in Counsellors Fees, and Fees of Officers, actually paid by him;

For the Monies paid, or payable to such Persons as enjoy Grants of Pensions, payable out of our said Revenues, which were established by any of our Royal Predecessors:

Our Will and Pleasure, therefore, is, That you cause the several and respective Payments aforesaid to be made, without deducting the said Six Pence in the Pound from them, or any of them: And whereas we have thought fit, that the Monies, which you have or shall pay to the Stationers, who furnish your Offices with Books, Papers, and other Stationary Wares, for the Town and Country, and with whom you are under Contracts, as you inform us, for the same, at low Rates; and the Money paid to Tradesmen, and others, who furnish your Offices with Candles, Coals, or other Necessaries; shall be subject to the Payment of the said Six Pence in the Pound; but that the same shall be repaid by you, and placed to your Account of petty Incidents; our Will and Pleasure, therefore, is. That you cause the said Six Pence in the Pound to be deducted from the said last-recited Payments; but that you make the same good out of our said Revenues, and place the same to your Account of Incidents accordingly: And we further direct. That all Salaries, of Fifty Pounds a Year, and upwards, be charged with, and liable to, the said Deduction of Six Pence in the Pound, only from Michaelmas next: And this shall be, as well to you, as to all others herein concerned, a sufficient Warrant.

Given at our Court at Saint James*s, this Fourth Day of May 1722, in the Eighth Year of our Reign.

By his Majesty's Command,

JL Walpole,

R. Edgcumbe,

That he hadreceivedhis Majesty'sCommands to acquaint this House, That the Petitioner had, Seven Years since, made his humble Application, and Submission, to his Majesty, with Assurances of Duty, Allegiance, and Fidelity; which his Majesty so far accepted, as to give him Encouragement to hope for some future Marks of his Majesty's Grace and Goodness; and that his Majesty is satisfied, that the Petitioner's Behaviour has been such, as convinces his Majesty, that he is an Object of his Majesty's Mercy; and his Majesty consents, that this Petition be presented to this House;

Vol. 20.

After which, the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner is truly concerned for his Offence, in not having surrendered himself, pursuant to the Directions of an Act of the First Year of his Majesty'sReign, whereby the Petitioner was attainted of High Treason, and forfeited all his real and personal Estate; and, by reason thereof, hath suffered very great Losses: That, upon the Petitioner's Marriage, in 1700,

Sir Walter St. John Baronet, and the Right honourable the Lord Viscount St. John, the Petitioner's Grandfather and Father, together with the Petitioner, made a Settlement of their Family Estate in the Counties of Wilts,

Surrey, and Middlesex; all whichPremisses, except a very small Part thereof, are now in the Possession of the Petitioner's Father; and the Petitioner cannot become intitled thereto, for his Life, until after his Father's Decease:

That the Petitioner hath, in most humble and dutiful manner, made his Submission to his Majesty; and given his Majesty the strongest Assurances of his inviolable Fidelity, and of his Zeal for his Majesty's Service, and for the Support of the present happy Establishment; which his Majesty hath been most graciously pleased toaccept:

And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Petitioner, and the Lleirs Male of his Body, notwithstanding his said Attainder, to take and enjoy the said settled Estate, according to the Limitations of the said Settlement, or other Assurances therein mentioned; and for enabling the Petitioner to hold and enjoy any personal Estate, or Effects, whereof he now is, or hereafter shall be, possessed; and to invest the same in the Purchase of any real or personal Estate within this Kingdom.

The Commons have considered the Answer of Thomas Earl of Macclesfield to the Articles exhibited against him by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses* in Parliament assembled; and observe, That the said Earl hath industriously avoided giving a direct and particular Answer to several Matters positively and certainly alleged against him, in the said Articles; fthich, from the Nature of the Facts themselves, must necessarily lie in his own Knowlege; and hath attempted to disguise and cover the real Crimes laid to his Charge, by immaterial and evasive Insinuations of Facts of a different Nature; and that many Parts of the s^id Answer are contradictory to, and inconsistent with, each other; upon which they might demand your Lordships immediate Judgment:

Yet the Commons, being able to maintain the Truth and Justice of their Accusation, are willing to enter into the due Examination thereof; and to aver their Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against the said Thomas Earl of Macclesfield to be true; and that the said Earl is guilty, in such manner as he stands impeached; and that the Commons will be ready to prove their Charge against him, at such convenient time as shall be appointed for that Purpose.

Mr.Speaker acquainted the House, That since he came into the Chair, he had received a Letter from Alexander Urquhart Esquire, a Member of this House, acquainting him, That, as the said Mr. Urquhart was coming to the Service of the House, he was arrested at the Suit of one of the Petitioners that he wayed his Privilege to: And the House, being informed, That there were Two Persons at the Door, who could give the House some Account of the said Arrest;

They were severally called in; and examined at the Bar.

Resolved, That the Arresting of Alexander Urquhart Esquire, a Member of this House, as he was coming to attend the Service of this House, is a notorious Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That the said Mr. Urquhart be discharged out of the Custody of the Bailiff who arrested him.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do go, and demand, that the said Mr. Urquhart be discharged out of the said Custody.

Resolved, That Pocklington, Attorney at Law, in causing the said Mr. Urquhart to be arrested, is guilty of a notorious Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved!, That Daniel Harrod> Bailiff, in arresting the said Mr. Urquhart, is guilty of a notorious Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That the said Pocklington be, for the said Breach of Privilege, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House.

Ordered, That the said Daniel Harrod be, for the said Breach of Privilege, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House.

In ib66; The Lord Viscount Mordaunt, being impeached of High Crimes and Misdemeanors, was allowed by the Lords to have Counsel to plead his Cause; and his Lordship to sit on a Stool, within the Bar, uncovered:

To which the Managers for the Commons objecting, divers Conferences were had between the Two Houses thereupon; and the Commons acquiescing as to the allowing Counsel to his Lordship, but not agreeing to his Lordship's Sitting within the Bar, with his Hat off, during the Time of his Tryal, several other Conferences were had in relation thereto; and the Lords adhering to their Resolution for such Sitting within the Bar, and the Commons adhering to their Resolution against it, the Session ended abruptly, without further proceeding on that Impeachment. Die Luna, 26° Aprilis 1725;

A Message was sent to the House of Commons, by Mr. Holford, and Mv.Lighthoun, to acquaint them, That the Lords have appointed Thursday Sevennight, being the Sixth Day of May next, at Eleven of the Clock, in the Forenoon, for the Tryal of Thomas Earl of Macclesfield, at the Bar of tins House, for the High Crimes and Misdemeanors whereof he stands impeached; and that their Lordships will order Conveniences to be prepared theie, for the Managers of the said Impeachment.

Die Martis, 27® Aprilis 1725;

Ordered, That Tomorrow Sevennight this House shall be called over; and that all the Lords do then attend.

Ordered, That Letters be writ, by the Lord on the Woolsack, to the absent Peers and Prelates, to require their Attendance on Tomorrow Sevennight, being the Fifth Day of May next; and to signify to them, That they who, through, Sickness, cannot come, do prove the same by Two credible Witnesses, upon Oath, at the Bar of this House; and that no other Excuse will be admitted; and that Notice be given, in the same Letter, of the Time, appointed for the Tryal of the Earl of Macclesfield; and that their Attendance is expected on the Service of the House during the said Tryal.

Ordered, That proper Conveniences be made for the Managers of the House of Commons, their Agents and Witnesses, at the Tryal of Thomas Earl of Macclesfield; and that the Lord Great Chamberlain be desired to give Directions to the Officers of his Majesty's Works for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the Committee appointed to inspect the Journals of this House, in relation to the Proceedings on Impeachments for High Crimes and Misdemeanors, be revived; and that the said Committee do meet on Thursday Morning next; and report to the House the Precedents they find of the Proceedings of this House upon the Tryal of Impeachments.

Die Sabbati, 1* Maxi 1725;

The Lord Delawarr reported from the Lords Cc mittees appointed to inspect the Journals of this Hoc in relation to the Proceedings on Impeachments for H Crimes and Misdemeanors; and who were directed to port the Precedents they found of the Proceedings of t House upon the Tryal of Impeachments: That the Coi mittee have inspected the Journals of this House, w relation to the Proceedings upon such Tryals; andobsen that, on the Tryal of Peers upon Impeachments for Hi Crimes and Misdemeanors in this House, the Baro Bench next the Bar has been taken away, and a Sto placed, in the room thereof, within the Bar, on which tl Lord impeached sits uncovered; but whether the Lori have, on such Tryals, always sat in their Robes, does n appear by the Journals: And the Committee, on this Oi casion, think proper to acquaint your Lordships, Tha on perusing the Proceedings of this House upon sue Tryals, they do not find any Methods usually prescribet with respect to the Lords Sitting with, or without, thei Robes; but the Journals being silent, touching this Mai ter, the Committee apprehend the most usual Methoc upon the Tryal of Lords impeached, has been for tli Lords to sit in their Robes, and in their due Places:

Which Report being read by the Clerk; the following Order was made;

Ordered, That the Barons Bench next the Bar be taker away; and a Stool placed in the room thereof, on whicl the Earl of Macclesfield is to sit, during his Tryal, un* covered, and w ithout his Robes; but that all the other Lords of this House are to sit in their Robes, and in their due Places.

Ordered, That the Committee appointed to inspect the Journals of this House, in relation to the Proceedings on Impeachments for High Crimes and Misdemeanors, be revived; and meet on Monday Morning next, at Ten a Clock; and that the Surveyor General, and other the principal Officers of his Majesty's Works, do then attend the said Committee.

Die Luna, 30 Mail 1725;

The House being moved to dispense with that Part of the Order made on Saturday last, upon the Report of the Lords Committees appointed to inspect the Journals of this House, in relation to the Proceedings on Impeachments for High Crimes and Misdemeanors, relating to the Lords sitting in their Robes during the Tryal of Thomas Earl of Macclesfield;

Whereupon the said Report and Order were read;

And, several Leads representing the great Prejudice it may be to their Healths, by reason of the Warmth of the Weather, to sit, during the whole Tryal and Examination, in their Robes, it is ordered, That so much of the said Order as directs the Lords to sit in their Robes, be dispensed with until the time of giving Judgment; and that then their Lordships do sit in their Robes.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords' have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better Regulating of Buildings, and to prevent Mischiefs that may happen by Fire, within the Weekly Bills of Mortality, and other Places therein mentioned, without any Amendment. And also,

Linlithgow, r A PETITION of William Frazer Esquire was pre-&c. Election. sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the District of Burghs of Linlithgow, Selkirk, Lanerk, and Peebles, in the room of Daniel Wiery deceased, the Petitioner was duly elected by a Majority oflegal Votes, and ought to have been returned; but the Clerk of the presiding Borough did make up the Minutes of the Election partially; and has taken upon him to Return the Sheriff of Selkirk, John Murray Esquire; in Prejudice to the Petitioner; and there were many illegal Practices used in the Election of the pretended Commissioners, for the Sheriff of Selkirk: And praying, That the House will take the Merits of the said Election hnd Return into Consideration, and give the Pe* titioner such Relief as shall be just.

- Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of JUnlilhgotv was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the District of Burghs of Linlithgow, Selkirk', Lanerk, and Peeblesy the Delegate from the Petitioners, with the Delegate from Lanerk, voted for Wm. Frazer Esquire; and the Borough of Linlithgow being the presiding Borough, he had thereby a Majority, and ought to have been returned: That certain pretended Counsellors of Lanerky who had not qualified themselves as such by taking the Oaths, took upon them to grant a Commission to John Ballantine to be their Delegate: That the Petitioners are highly apprehensive of the bad Consequences that must attend such a Precedent: And praying, That the House will take the Merits of the Election and Return into Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to Consideration of the Committee of Privileges of El tions: And that they do examine the Matter there and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, the House.

AM E S S A G E from the Lords, by Mr. Baron Page and Mr. Justice Denton:

Mr. Speaker,

The I^ords have commanded us to acquaint this House, Vol. 20.

That their Lordships are ready to give Judgment against Earl of Thomas Earl of Macclesfield\ if this House, with their clnsrield' Speaker, will come and demand the same. peachm*

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That this House will demand Judgment of the Lords against Thomas Earl of Macclesfield;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now' put;

The House divided.

The Noes go forth.

Tellers for the Yeas,

Tellers for fbe Noes,‘ CMm- } 65.

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That this House will demand Judgment of the Lords against Thomas Earl of Macclesfield.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the Thanks of Managers this House be given to the Members who were appointed thanked, the Managers.of the Impeachment against Thomas Earl of Macclesfield', for their faithful Management in their Discharge of the Trust reposed in them.

And Mr. Speaker gave them, they standing up severally in their Places, the Thanksof the House accordingly; as follows; viz.

Gentlemen,

It is with the greatest Chearfulness that I obey the Commands of the House on this Occasion; and yet I w as never, on any Occasion, more sensible of the Difficulty of performing them as I ought; but I have this Satisfaction, in this Motion's being* made when I least expected it, that my not being prepared may be some Excuse for those Defects, which I should not have been able to have supplied, had I had never so long a Time for Consideration.

Gentlemen,

You have maintained the Charge of the Commons with that Force of Argument, Beauty of Expression, and Strength of Reason, as would have gained you the highest Applause in the most flourishing of the Grecian Commonwealths; and, I may add,

----- --- Nec dignius unquam

Majestas meminit sese Romana loquutam:

But I shall not enlarge farther on this Part of your Praise, being sensible that I am not able to express myself in a manner suitable to the Dignity of the Subject: Your own Tongues are only equal to' such an Undertaking; and, were I able to do it, your Modesty would not permit it:

I shall therefore proceed in obeying the Commands of the House, in such a manner as you yourselves may hear it, not only without Offence, but, I hope, with Satisfaction, by endeavouring to set in their proper Lights the great and lasting Benefits your Country will receive by your faithful Discharge of your Duty.

You have stopped the Cries of Orphans, and dried up the Tears of the Widow; even those who must ever be insensible of the Benefits they receive, Idiots and Lunaticks, and such only can be insensible of them, will be Partakers of the Fruits of your Labours:

But you are more particularly intitled to the Thanks of this House, by having made the Prosecutions of the Commons against great Offenders practicable: The Power of Impeachment, that Sword of Vengeance, which the Constitution has put into the Hand of the Commons, and which, when drawn by Party Rage, w hen directed by the Malice of Faction, or weilded by unskilful Hands, has too often wounded that Constitution it w^as intended to preserve, has now, by your able Management, turned its Edge to its proper Object, a great Offender; and if the Wound it has given should not be so deep as many may expect, yet you may be very sure it never can be imputed to the Want of Strength in your Arm: And I hope and trust, from your prudent Conduct through the w hole Progress of the Tryal, that this great Privilege of the Com-

Ordered, That a Message be sent to the Lords, toac-‘ quaint them, That this House, with their Speaker, doth intend, immediately, to come to the House of Lords, to demand Judgment against Thomas Earl of Macclesfield', and therefore do desire, That the Painted Chamber, and Passages to the House of Lords, may be cleared.

Ofittred/lhat Sir William Gage do carry the said Message to the Lords.

Sir William Gage reported, That he had delivered the Message to1 the Lords; and that the Lords had directed, That the Painted Chamber, and Passages, should be cleared immediately.,

Then the House, with Mr. Speaker with the Mace, went up to the Bar of the House of Lords; and, by their Speaker, demanded Judgment against Thomas Earl of Macclesfield, for the High Crimes and Misdemeanors of which he was impeached by the Commons.

-And, being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That lie had, in the Name of the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, and of all the Commons of Great Britain, demanded Judgment against Thomas Earl of Macclesfield, for the High Crimes and Misdemeanors, of which he was impeached by the Commons; and that the Lords had given the following Judgment; viz.

" That Thomas Earl of Macclesfield be fined in the " Sum of Thirty thousand Pounds unto our Sovereign " Lord the King; and that he be imprisoned in the Tower " of London, and there kept in safe Custody, until he shall " pay the said Fine."

Memorandum: The Proceeding of the Commons-to demand Judgment against the Earl of Macclesfield was in this manner:

Mr. Speaker went with the Mace before him; the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod meeting Mr. Speaker at the Bottom of the Painted Chamber, and conducting him from thence to the Door of the House of Peers:

And Mr. Speaker w^ent with his Mace on his Right- hand, to the Bar of the said House; the Serjeant at Arms attending the House of Commons standing at the Bar, on Mr. Speaker's Right-hand, with the Mace on his Shoulder, all. the time Mr. Speaker continued at the Bar of the House of Peers.

Then the Lord Chief Justice of the Court of Common Pleas, being the Speaker of the House of Peers, sitting on the Wool-sack, directed the Black Rod to bring the Earl of Macclesfield to the Bar; which w as done accordingly.

The Black Rod being at the Bar, at some Distance from Mr. Speaker, on his left Hand, and the Earl of Mac* clesfield on the Left-hand of the Black Rod, the Speaker of the House of Peers directed the Earl of Macclesfield\ at his first coming to the Bar, to kneel: Which he did accordingly, in the Presence of the Commons, till the Speaker of the House of Peers bid him rise.

Then the Speaker of the House of Commons demanded Judgment, in the following Words; viz.

-My Lords,

The Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, in the Name of themselves, and of all the Commons of Great Britain, did, at this Bar, impeach Thomas Earl of Macclesfield of High Crimes and Misdemeanors; and did exhibit Articles of Impeachment against 1

i* Maii. 172

him; and have made good their Charge: I do there] in the Name of the Commons in Parliament assemt and of all the Commons of Great Britain, demand Ji ment against the said Earl, for the said High Crimes Misdemeanors.

Then the Speaker of the House of Peers pvonour the Judgment:

And then the House of Commons, with Mr. Spej with the Mace, returned to their own House.

And then the House adjourned till Moh Morning, next, Nine of the Clock.

A PROCLAMATION.

IV. Cant. King C. Kingston C. P. S. Dorset, Holies Neucastle, Harcourt, R. Wafpole.

WHEREAS this present Parliament stands prorogued to the Sixteenth Day of this instant De-combei': We, with the Advice of his Majesty's Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Sixteenth Day of December, to Thursday the Twentieth Day of January next: And that we have given Order, That a Commission be prepared for proroguing the same accord-

ingly: And we do hereby further declare his Ma Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on th< Twentieth Day of January, he held, and sit, for the patch of divers weighty and important Affairs: Ar Lords Spiritual and Temporal; and the Knights, zens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners of Shire Burghs, of the House of Commons; are hereby req and commanded to give their Attendance accord at Westminster, on Thursday the Twentieth Day 0 nuary next.

A MESSAGE from his Majesty, by Sir William Sanderson, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod;

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And, being returned;

Several Members took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, pursuant to the Laws made for those Purposes.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had rc-. ceived a Letter from Mr. Edward Stables, the Clerk Assistant of this House, acquainting him, That he is, at present unfortunately disabled, by Rheumatism, to attend the Service of the House; and humbly desiring, That, by the Indulgence of the House, One may be permitted to officiate for him, during his Indisposition.

And Mr. Michael Aislcew being proposed;

Ordered, That Mr. Michael Aiskew do attend, to assist the Clerk of this House, during the Indisposition of Mr. Stables.

A Bill to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attci his Majesty in the House of Peers: And that his jesty was pleased to say, That he had ordered the 1 Chancellor to declare, in his Name and Words, the 1 sons of his Majesty's meeting his People in Parliamei this time: And thereupon the Lord Chancellor acquai both Houses, That he had received a Speech from Majesty on the Throne; which the Lord Chanc< read; and of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to pre Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the Hoi and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have had such frequent Experience of the Wist and Zeal of this Parliament, on many important Ot sions, that it is with Pleasure I now meet you again;

I make no Doubt but that your Endeavours for Good and Service of your Country will be as sucees as they have hitherto been.

The distressed Condition of some of our Protest Brethren abroad, and the Negotiations and Engagemt entered into by some foreign Powers, which seem to h laid the Foundation of new Troubles and Disturbance Europe, and to threaten my Subjects with the Los: several of the most advantageous Branches of their Tra obliged me, without any Loss of Time, to concert, v other Powers, such Measures as might give a Check the ambitious Views of those who are endeavouring render themselves formidable, and put a Stop to the 1 ther Progress of such dangerous Designs: For these En I have entered into a defensive Alliance with the m Christian King, and the King of Prussia, to which sevc
