Laws; and express their utter Abhorrence of the Disobedience thereto, that has of late been shewn in several Parts of Scotland, on putting in Execution the late Act imposing a Duty upon Malt: That the Petitioners, upon the First Appearance of those Disorders, did, when met in a Convention, exert themselves to prevent the se-veralTumuIts which happened thereupon; as was manifest by an Act, passed in the said Convention, and sent to all the Boroughs of Scotland; and are firmly resolved to shew their Duty, at all times, to his Majesty; yet humbly observe, that the Poverty of the Country, and the Quality of the Grain is so very mean, that a Duty upon Malt for the ensuing Year will not only render the Brewers unable to continue brewing, but utterly ruin the Trade of the Country: And praying such Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ditto. A Petition of the Heretorsand Freeholders of the Shire

of B a niff] whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, of this Parliament, for continuing the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, a Duty of 3 d. per Bushel is laid upon all Malt made in Scotland; and, if tjiat Duty did not raise £. 20,000. net in one Year, the Deficiency should be made good by a Surcharge. 011 every Maker: That Scotland is unable to pay the said Duty, not only by reason of the Badness of Barley this Year by the excessive Rains, but the Scarcity of Money, Decay of Trade, and Poverty of the Inhabitants; besides, this Duty will lessen the Revenue, of the Excise more than the Sum for which it is given; for that the Brewers will lay down their Trades, as many have -already done, because they cannot make any Profit thereby; and so also the landed Men will be greatly prejudiced, because there will not be the usual Consumption of Barley; there being already heavy Taxes upon Ale and Beer in Scotland: And praying, That Scotland may not lie liable to pay the Duty upon Malt.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Malt Tax in \ PETITION of the Provost, Bailies, Town Scotland. Council, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Elgin,

.in the County of Elgin, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, of this present Parliament, for continuing the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, a Duty of 3 d.per Bushel is imposed on all Malt made in Scotland for One Year; and if the Duties shall not amount to, £. 20,000. net Money, the Deficiency shall be made good by a Surcharge on all Makers of Malt: That Scotland is utterly unable to pay the said Duty, not only by reason of the Badness of Bigg, or Bariev, there, :but also by the Scarcity of Money, Decay of Trade, and Poverty of the Inhabitants, who are disabled to consume Beer and Ale at a lower Price than the Brewer can afford to sell it; which will, force them to leave off brewing, as many have already done; and thereby the Revenue of Excise will be lessened more than the Sum intended, by the said Duty on Malt, to be raised, will amount unto; and the Rents of the Heretors will be also thereby much impaired; and, besides, the Excise upon Beer and Ale in Scotland will be higher, in Proportion, than the Excise i\\ England: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises; and that Scotland may be exempt from the Duties on Malt.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the principal Owners and Proprietors of Lands within the North Division of the great Level of the Fens called Bedford Level, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Owners and Proprietors of Lands within the same Division, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act of Parliament, 150 Car. 2dl, for settling the draining the great Level of BedfordYens, the Adven-turers and Participants in that Undertaking were made a Body Politick and Corporate; and being entitled to 95,000 Acres, as a Recompence for draining the same, by Agreements with the Country, 83,000 Acres were vested in the said Corporation; with Power to lay Taxes upon the same, and upon the remaining 12,000 Acres, for the Preservation of the whole Level; and to levy the same, with Penalties for Non-payment: That the Level is divided into Three Parts; viz. the North, Middle, and the South, Levels; and the Outfals were sufficient for draining the Waters into the Sea at the time of their Making; but now, particularly, the Waters of the North Level, for some Years past, have been so choaked by the Sands thrown up by the Tides, that they cannot be discharged as formerly; by which means many Thousand Acres in that Level have, for several Years, been frequently overflowed, to the Petitioners great Damage; and by the great Rains and Floods this Year they are totally drowned; and must remain so, untiianewand better Outfal can be obtained; to procure which there will be occasion to cut through the Lands of several' Proprietors without the Boundsof the North Level; which the Petitioners are advised, the said Corporation cannot do by virtue of the said Act, without the Aid of Parliament; and, being satisfied the whole 95,000 Acres ought not to be charged with the Expences of such new Undertaking, which will b& only for the Petitioners Benefit, they are desirous, that the said Corporation may be enabled to prosecute all necessary Means to obtain anew Outfal, for the future Preservation of the Petitioners Estates in the North Level: And, to that End, T the'Petitioner, the Duke of Devonshire's Guardian to the Duke of Bedford, a Minor, for the immediate Relief and Preservation Of the said Minor's Estate* being several Thousand Acres in the said North Level, now . wholly drowned) is willing to hear arid p sty a proportionable Part of the Charge of the said

A Petition of the poor and miserable Prisoners now lying in the Prison of White Chappel, in the County of Middlesex, on behalf of themselves, and others, their fellow Prisoners, being about One hundred and Twenty in Number, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are imprisoned for very small Debts; the Charges of the Arrest, and Fees of Confinement, generally amounting to more than the Debt; which mostly have arisen, from the Necessity of their Families, Vo l, 20,

to Tallymen, Pawnbrokers, and others, who will not allow them time to pay their Debts by their Labour; and the Petitioners are now as Men buried alive, having no Allowance but Water; and some have been reduced to the Extremity of eating Horse flesh: And praying the till Tomorrow House to take their most lamentable Condition into Consideration, and afford them such Relief as shall be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests, shall be read a Second time.

A Petition of Harry Waller Esquire, was presented to chepping the House, and read; setting forth, That at the Election Wicnmb of a Burgess, on the 3d Instant, to serve in Parliament for kiectiou. the Borough of Chepping ll'icomb in Com' Bucks, in the room of Charles Collyear, Esquire, whose Election had been declared void by the House, the Petitioner, and Mr.

Collyear, stood Candidates; and, upon calling over the List of all the Voters by the Town Clerk, an undoubted Majority appeared and voted for the Petitioner; who ought to have been returned; but Richard Shrimpton, Mayor of the said Borough, partially admitted several Persons to vote for Mr. Collyear, who never pretended to have any Right of voting at any former Election; particularly Two Persons w'hose Votes were expressly ordered by the Mayorto be entered for Mr. Collyear, although they owned they had no other Authority to vote, than by the illegal Charter of King James the 2d: That the Mayor was desired by the Petitioner to order the Poll to be immediately castup, and declare who had the Majority; but Mr. Collyear desiring a Scrutiny, the Mayor said, The Candidates should have it; but did not cast up the Poll, nor declare the Majority; and immediately withdrew' himself; and soon after, before any Meeting for the Scrutiny, declared, He was resolved to return Mr. Collyear; and afterwards, on the same Day, the Mayor appointed a Scrutiny; and it was agreed, that each Candidate should be assisted with Three Persons, which were named, to take the Scrutiny; and, soon after meeting, the Mayor was desired, on the Petitioner's behalf, to produce the Town-books, in which the Names of all the Electors were entered, as the only proper Foundation upon which any just Scrutiny could be taken; but the Mayor absolutely refused to produce those Books;

Mr. Collyear insisting, That the Mayor was the only Judge who were the Electors; and thereupon no Scrutiny was made; upon which the Mayor, with Mr. Collyear, and others, went back to the Town-hall, and there signed a Return of Mr. Collyear: And, at the same time, one Marshall, the Postmaster, was ordered by Mr. Collyear to redd the Proclamation against Riots; which could be done with no other Intent but to disperse the Electors who were there assembled, pursuant to his Majesty's Writ, in a legal manner: All which arbitrary Proceedings of Mr. Collyear, and his Agents, are not only injurious to the Petitioner, but a manifest Violation of the Freedom of Elections: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put,

That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House;

The House divided.

That the Committee, in pursuance of the several Orders made by the House, have examined the Matters of the said Petitions:

That the Petitioners laid before the Committee the Act of Parliament passed in the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of King William the 3d, for repairing the Highways between the City of London, and the Town of Harwich in Com Essex, and several other Roads, as in the Act mentioned; and also the subsequent Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for enlarging the Term, granted by the said former Act, for the further Term of Fifteen Years; which said Act expired the 24th Day of February last.

John Sparr<m\ Surveyor, being examined, delivered in to the Committee an Estimate of the Charges, which he made, pursuant to the Order of General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the said County, for repairing and amending the said Roads; and the whole amounted to the Sum of £.1,310. 6s.: And said, If the same were put into good Repair, a much greater Sum must be expended for that Purpose:

That he likewise surveyed the Road from Chelmsford to Colchester, and all the Roads in the said last Act of Parliament mentioned; and that the same, in several Parts, is very bad; particularly the Road from Stanwich to Harwich; and that the Statute-work is not sufficient to repair them: And they are obliged to fetch Gravel Three Aliles distant from some Parts of the Road to amend the same.

Richard Dighton said, That the Alonies, arising from the Toll granted by the said Acts, have been received by the Trustees annually, and applied in Repairing of the said Roads; and a Rate of Six Pence in the Pound has been also raised upon the Inhabitants of the several Parishes

lying between the Town of Brentwood and Hanvich, for repairing the said Roads; yet the same has been insufficient.

Wm. Say well, Carrier, said, That he constantly travelled through the Roads from Colchester to Harwich; and they are very bad; particularly the Road to Dower Court.

The said Witnesses all severally said, That several Parts of the said Roads yet remain unrepaired, and are in a very ruinous and dangerous Condition; and that a consider^ able Sum is yet wanting to complete the Repairs thereof; and that the same cannot be done, unless the said Act of Parliament be continued, and enlarged, for a longer Term.

Charles Gibbs said, That the Road from Chelmsford to Sudbury is, in most Places, very bad; which is near 24 Aliles; and but 2 Aliles thereof are amended by the Alo- ney arising by Essex Road Turnpike.

Malt Tax in A Petition of the Heretors and Freeholders of Ayr,

Scotland. whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act of this present Parliament, for continuing the Duties on Malt, &c. a Duty is laid upon all Malt made in Scotland in One Year; and if the Duty thereon shall not produce JO.i 0,000. net Money, the Deficiency shall bemadegood by a Surcharge on the Makers thereof: That the Taxes already laid on landed Men are more than other Taxations; the yearly Produce of Money far exceeding what Heretors can raise from their Ground; and yet the Land Tax, Excise, and other Duties, directly affect them; which makes them the more unable to bear the Malt Tax: Besides, the Duty on Malt will lessen the Revenue of Excise more than the Sum intended to be raised by it; for several Brewers will give over their Trades, as many have already done; and the People of Scotland sere so poor, that they cannot advance the Price of Beer and Ale to make it worth the Brewers while to brew; and the Duty of Excisein Scotland is already higher than the Excise in England, if compared with the Strength betwixt one and the other; aadalsothereisa further Duty of Two Vo x. *0.

Peny Scots, upon every Pint of Ale brewed in the Royal Burghs of Scotland-, which is near, if not equal, to the Malt Tax; and is an additional Charge above what is paid in England: And praying the House to consider the Premises, and relieve them as shall be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Committee had examined the Mattel of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; arid afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; v «.

That, pursuant to an Order of the House, the Committee proceeded to examine into the Matter of tlj.e sa d Petition:

That it appeared to the Committee, by an, Act of Parliament, made in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for settling the Draining, of the great Level of the Fens called Bedford Level, the Adventurers and Participants therein Avert! made a Body Politick and Corporate, with Power to lay a Tax. upon the said Level, for draining and preserving the ' same, as in the said Petition is set forth:

That the said Level is divided into Three Parts; and distinguished by the Names of the North Level, the Middle Level, and South Level.

That, to prove the North Level under Water, the Petitioners called,

Mr. Tho. Eldred: Who produced aMap of the North Level, Middle Level, and South Level; and said, That last Siniday was Sevennight, he went over in a Boat from Thorny Town to The Dog and Doublet Sluice, which is above Two Miles; and most of the Towns were covered with Water, not the Twentieth Part dry Ground, that he could observe in his Passage thither.

Mr. Robert Wright said, That the North Level is almost drowned; and a very small Part thereof but what is under Water.

Stephen Recount said. That the North Level is almost all under Water, very little uncovered; all the flat Part is covered with Wa.ter.

Anthony Culing said, That the North Level hath been under Water ever since Michaelmas last; and still continues to be so: That he rents 500 Acres in the said North Level; and not an Acre but what is under

Water a Foot and a Half; and has been forced to carry his Corn from the said 500 Acres to higher Lands.

Colonel Armstrong surveyed the Level in 1723, and found the Sands Ten Feet higher in the Chanel of Wisbech, than the Sole, or Bottom, of Gunt hr of Sluice, which is the Outfal for the SI lire Drain: That Wisbech River*

He answered* No; and he thought none could be made hearer to the old Outfal than the Place before-mentioned; and that the same can be no Prejudice to any of the Lands thereabouts, but a Benefit to all the said Lands; and that at present there is no other Outfal to drain the the North Level, but the old Outfal at Gunthrop Sluice, which is insufficient; and, in his Opinion, can now be made capable of draining the said North Level.

Mr. Thomas Badeslade, Surveyor, said. That the Outfal called Gunthrop Sluice, at the time of the Undertaking for draining, was a proper and sufficient Outfal for draining the said North Level; bnt, since that time, the Wisbich River is so choaked with Sand, that the said Outfal has been useless from the time of his being acquainted with it, which is above 3 Years; and must remain so, for that the Low-water Mark of the Chanel of . Wisbich Ri ver, opposite to Gunthrop Sluice, is more than One Foot higher than the Surface of the Lands of the North Level; notwithstanding the great Floods, within this Year, have considerably scoured out the Sands, and deepened the Chanel:

So that it is impossible ever to drain the North Level through Gunthrop Sluice:

That there is such a Fall to a Place above Three Miles below Hills, and Gunthrop Sluices, that a Drain, made from Hill Sluice to the said Place, distant above Three Miles, near Westmear Creek, will as effectually drain the North Level as it was at first drained by the Corporation*, and will bring the Waters of that Level, now Two Feet and a Half above the Surface of the said Lands, at least 4Feet under the Surface of the same Lands, if requisite; and that he does believe there is no other Drain that can do it effectually:

That the whole new intended Cut, for carrying Shire brain Waters to Sea, must be through Lands without the Bounds of the Levels.

Mr. Eldred, being asked what he knew of the Petitioners, said, He believes that the greatest Part of them are Owners, and the rest Occupiers, of the said Level; and that they are desirous the same should be done in the Method intended; and at their own proper Ex-pehces, without burthening any other Persons.

Navigation, the Petition of the Master, Wardens, Searchers, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Corporation of Cutlers in Hallamshire, in the West Riding of the County of York, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Workmen and Traders in the Iron Manufacture, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz. '

That the Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Petitioners called,

JViltiam Palmer\ Surveyor: Who produced a Plan of the River; and said, The River is navigable; except in fvery dry Seasons, from the River Ouze to Doncaster; and, by a Flash of Water, small Vessels may navigate^ at any time:;

That it may be made navigable from Doncaster to the utmost Extent of Tinsley Westward, without making any new Dams, and only by Cuts; and without raising any old Dam higher:

That the Cuts may be made without flooding any of the Proprietors Lands: That from Doncaster toSprad-bo rough, the Water is already sufficient:

To make a new Lock at Spradboimgh, at Mrs. Copleys Mill, on the North Side of the River, as she desires:

That from thence to Coningsborough is navigable: To make a small Cut, by the End of Coningsborough Dam, to pass it:

That she River is already navigable from Coningsbo-rough to a little below Mexborough; whence a Cut about a Mile and a Half must be made, and a Lock at each End of it: That it will not overflow any of the Lands thereabouts, but be a Means of draining the m:

A long Cut below Kiln hurst River, and passes Kiln-hurst and Timber Works, to go into Thriber Dam: That the new Cut will not drain the old River: That where Necessity is for Bridges, the Undertakers are to build them:

The River is navigable from Thribery to about a Quarter of a Mile below' Old-icork; and from thence to make a Cut on the South Side of the River, being opposite to Mr. Fotjamb's House; over which Cut must be a Bridge, and a Lock at the End of the Cut, to pass the Mill-dam.

That, from OUl-work to Eastwood, it is navigable, except some few Shoals to be deepened, in the said Sliver:

That, from below' the Shallows at Eastwood, a Cut must be made on the North Side of the River, to Rotherham Mill-dam:

And, from below the next Shallows, a Cut must be made, on the South Side of the River, into Ides Mill-dam:

Thence from the Shallows near Dcadmens Ford, to make a Cut, on the South Side of the River, to Jordan Dam, from whence the River is already navigable to Tinsley Common:

That the River may be made navigable, in this Method, without making any new- Dam cross the River, or heightening any old one; and that it is practicable, without flooding any of the Lands adjacent.

Mr. George St ear said, That the making the said River navigable, will be very advantageous to the Town of Shes-jei/d, and also to the adjacent.Town, by Carrying of Goods at a cheaper Rate: That this Year they paid Thirty Shillings a Ton for Carriage of Goods from Sheffeild to D(m* caster, when, in former Years, they used to pay but Fifteen Shillings per Ton.

Mr. John Smith confirmed what Mr. St ear said: And said further, That the last Year the Roads were so bad, that Carts could not go; but w ere forced to fetch Iron, and other Commodities necessary for their Trade, on Horseback:

That the Navigation of the River will save above Half what they pay for. Land-carriage: That the Town of Shffeild, ancj Towns adjacent, return, at least, £. 120,000. a Year, in Jthe Iron and Cutlery Trade:

That, - according to the best Computation he can make, there w ill about 13 or 14,000 Ton be Water-borne, coming tip, and going down, the said River, every Year; and he believes it rather w'ould increase.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making she River Dunn, in the West Riding of the County of York, navigable, from Holmes tile, in Doncaster, up to the utmost Extent of Tinsley Westward, a Township within Two Miles of Sheffield: And that Mr.

said Mr. Hampden, during his being Treasurer of the Navy, became indebted, in a very great Sum, to the Crown; whereby his w'hole Estate, subject to the said Settlement, became chargeable with the said Debt: That, in May last, her said Husband did settle, in Trust, for her, Three hundred Pounds per Annum, clear, over and besides the said Sum of Two hundred Pounds per Annum: That the Petitioner is necessarily involved in the Misfortune of her said Husband, though having no-ways conduced thereunto: And therefore praying the conf-passionate Regard of the House to the Hardship of her Case ;by securing to her, until she shall come to the Possession of her said Jointure, such a sufficient Provision for her Support and Maintenance, as the House shall think fit.

Richard Cooksey Esquire: Who said. That the Trustees have, upon the Credit of the said Act, raised, and laid out, the Sum of £. 600. over and above the Toll, or Monies, collected at the Turnpike; and that the same still remains due, and owing, upon the Credit of the said Act; and that the Trustees generally passed their Accounts monthly.

liichard Cooksey, Wentworth Clifford, John Hall, and Gilbert Tolly, said, That, by reason of the great and many Loads and Carriages of Salt, and other Goods, which daily pass through the said Road between the said Borough of Droitivich and the Quay of the City of Worcester, the Road, and the Pavements of the Streets in the said City, from a Place called The Tithings of Whist on, through Foregate-street to the cross broad Street, Rain-street, and from the upper Slip to the lower Slip of the Quay, are very bad, and in a ruinous Condition, and much out of Repair: And said, That the Streets in the Borough of Droitwich, from a Place called Nether-tvich Bridge to the Chapel on a Bridge, and from thence to Dyers Bridge, are also become very bad and ruinous, by reason of such Loads and Carriages frequently passing through the same:

That the said Road and Streets are become much worse than formerly, by reason that the Carriages of Coals are, of late Years, very much increased; and though, by the said Act of Parliament, they are obliged not to carry above One Ton and Half of Coals for One Load; vet they now carry upwards of Three Ton; the said Act of Parliament giv ing no Power to the Trustees to weigh the same Loads:

That it will cost upwards of £. 500. to get Timber to make a Foundation for laying of Stone and Gravel to repair about Four Miles and a Half of the said Road; and that Part of the Pavement through the Borough of H itch is so much broke, that it must be all new-paved; and most of the Inhabitants are very poor, and not able to repair the same: The said Witnesses all severally said, That the Inhabitants, as they believe, have constantly done their Statute-work; and that Four Shillings in the Pound will not be suflicient to repair and amend some Part of the said Road and Streets.

with divers Remainders over: That the Petitioner's said Wife is since dead, and has left One Daughter, now an Infant, and no other Issue; who, by the last mentioned Settlement, is intitled to the respective Sums of One thousand Five hundred Pounds, and Two thousand Five hundred Pounds, for her Portion, to be paid after the Petitioner's Death: That the Petitioner has since intermarried with Henrietta Vesey; and hath Issue by her, now living, Three Sons, who, by-virtue of the said Settlements, will be successively intitled to Estates Tail in all the Premises, which are now charged with Six thousand Six hundred Pounds; Part of which: carries Interest at Ten Pounds per Cent, and the rest at Eight Pounds per Cent.: That the Petitioner has contracted severaL Debts; and, being only Tenant for Life, cannot otherwise* raise Money to pay the same, than by cutting down Timber; the preserving of which will be of much greater Advantage to the Persons in Remainder, than the raising Money by Sale or Mortgage, of Part of the Premises, for Payment of the Petitioner's said Debts, can be a Prejudice: That the Petitioner is willing to be barred from committing Waste on any. Part of the Premises, so as sufficient may be sold*;or mortgaged, for; raising Money to pay the Petitioner's Debts, and the Monies charged on the Premises: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Petitioner, and his Trustees, by Sale, or Mortgage, of a sufficient Part of the Premises, to raise Money to pay the Sums charged thereon, and the Petitioner s Debts; and that the Trustees may stand seised of such Part as shall remain unsold, and the Equity of Redemption of such as shall be mortgaged, to the Use of such Persons, and for such Estates and Trusts, as they would be intitled unto, by virtue of the said Settlements, or either of them.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House,

That his Majesty, having been acquainted with the Contents of the said Petition, had been pleased to command him to acquaint this House, That, as tar as there is any Interest in the Crown, his Majesty consents, that the Prayer of the said Petition may be granted.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr.* Sloper and Mr. Himgerford do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Campbell's Losses by Riot.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, tti whom the Petition of Daniel Campbell Esquire, was referred:

And the said Report was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioner called,

Captain Francis Bu shell: Who, being examined, said, That, on the 23d of June last, he was sent to Glasgow by General JVade, with Two Companies of Foot, with Orders to assist the Civil Magistrate in keeping the Peace; and to protect the Officers of his Majesty's Revenues ill the Execution of their Duty;

He arrived there on the 24th in the Evening 1 On his Way thither, at a Bridge which was almost down, some Miles distant from the Town, a Crowd of People Were gathered together; who called out to him, saying, That King George had better order the building up the Bridge, than send them to levy the Malt Tax 1 That, as he entered the Town of Glasgow, a Mob of Men, Women, and Boys, followed and crouded upon him, and his Men; reproaching them with opprobrious Names; cursing the m; and saying, They would be but a Morsel to them: That they threw Stones and Dirt at them; by which he, and several of his Men, were hurt: This he did not resent; but endeavoured to appease them, by giving them good Words: At his Arrival in the Market-place, the Officer he had sent into the Town before him, acquainted him, that lie had got Billets for his Soldiers; but could not get Access to the Guard-room, the Keys being taken away by the Mob: He, soon after, waited on the Provost, desiring he might be putin Possession of the Guard-room, to enable him to prevent Disorders, by keeping his Men together: That the Provost at first agreed to break open the Door, but a Gentleman, who stood by, telling him there was Danger of the Mob's being enraged by it, he told the Captain he could not do it that Night: The Captain thereupon desired, he would give him any House where His Men might lie all Night on their Arms, not thinking it safe to have them dispersed: To this the Provost answered, "I cannot do it this Night; you must make good your €i Quarters, and lodge your Men the best way you can; "and To-inorrow I shall take cate of them:" That he, the said Bushel\ thereupon sent his Men to the Quarters allotted them; with Orders to lie on their Arms all Night: That, about Ten or Eleven at Night, some People came into the House where he was, telling him there was a very numerous Mob breaking into the House of Mr. Daniel Campbell, their Member of Parliament; whereupon he sent to the Provost to tell him, he would come with his Men to assist him in dispersing the Mob, if he desired it; but had for Answer, That it was not in the Power of the Two Companies to disperse them; and that, when he saw it convenient, he would send to him: That, soon, after, he was informed* That the Mob had actually broke into the Petitioner's House; pillaged and' destroyed every thing within it; and threatened, after they had done there, to go and destroy his House in the Country also:

That, the Day following, he was obliged to retire to Dumbarton; from whence he returned to Glasgow about a Fortnight after; and was, with the Men Under his Command, lodged in the Petitioner's House: That he then saw the House, and the Summer-house in the Garr den, in a most- rumpus Condition; all the wainscoting pulled down; the Floors much damaged; the Statues in the Garden all broke to-pieces; the Trees* some of them pulled up, and others split to the Grouad; and th$t he heard it commonly reported, that the Reason of their committing this Violence was, That the Petitioner, apd his Brother, had farmed the Malt Tax.

Mr. Thurloe, being examined, confirmed Captain BushelTs Evidence: And further said, That he saw . some of the Mob, on the 24th Day of June, beat the Officers of the Excise; and heard thenusay, the Reason

of their doing so wris, Upon the Account of the Malt Tax.

Mr. James Bogle, said, That, bn Friday Night, the 23th Day of June last, he, being in Glasgow, saw great Numbers of loose and disorderly People got together; and the general Cry was* That the Petitioner had a great Hand in promoting the Malt Tax; and therefore they had pulled do\Vn his Housei

There were two Letters produced, and laid before the Committee, which were sent to the Petitioner while the Mob were destroying his House; one of them from Mr: Miller, the then Provost of Glasgow, and the other from Colline Campbell Esquire, a Justice of Peace of the said Town.

In the Letter from ProVost Miller, which is dated at Oile in the Morning, are the following Words; " This " comes with the melancholy and sad Account, that the r£ Rabble, this Evening, has fallen on your Lodging; " and has broke it up; and is just now destroying, and " carrying off, all your Effects; it's such a Mob as the " like was never in this Place: I cannot now give you " Account of the Treatment they gave to the Tw o Companies of Men, that came to this Place this Afternoon: 41 They threaten, after they have have done with your " House, to fall upon Provost A infs, Collector Gordons, " and others: God krtows where it will end: I am " afraid the Two-thirds of the Place will fit and see theif " Neighbours rabbled."

Mr. Campbell's Letter is to the same Effect.

It was proved to the Committee, That the First Letter was the Hand-writing of Provost Miller \ and the Second of Colline Campbell.

The Petitioner informed the Committee, Thai the building and finishing the House, wl>ereof now only the Shell remains, together with the Fitting-up of the Garden, cost him between Four and Five thousand Pounds Sterling; yet he states his Loss, on that Article, only at £. 2,000. Sterling.

As a Proof of this Article;

Geo. Drummond Esquire, Lord Provost of Edinburgh^ being examined, said, That there was a general Clamour in the Country against the Malt Tax; and particularly against the Petitioner, as if he had a more than ordinary Concern in promoting it: And that it was reported at Edinburgh, some Days before the 24th of June last, That the Petitioner's House w*as actually pulled down on account thereof:

He sadd, That he had been often in the Petitioner's House: The last time he was there was about a Year before the Riot happened; and that the House w as 60 Foot in Front, and 48 Foot in Depth, built all of Freestone; that most of the Rooms were wainscoted, and finely furnished; and that he verily believed, the Damage which is done to the House and Gardens only, cannot be' repaired for £. 2,000. Sterling.

This was confirmed by the Testimonies of other Persons,

The Petitioner further informed the Committee, That his Pictures, Looking-glasses, Household and Kitchen Furniture, exclusive of Table and Bed Linen, Plate and China, cost him about £. 2,500.; but, having had the Use of them for some time, he only states his Loss, on that Account, at £. 1,500. Sterling.

To prove this Article;

Mr. Campbell junior said, That he was at the Petitioner's House at Glasgow, about Four Days before the same was rifled by the Mob: That the House was very well furnished with Pictures, Looking-glasses, Silk Beds, Hangings, Chairs, and other rich Furniture, mostly new; and that, he verily believes, the Furniture of the House, if disposed of by Auction, would have sold for much more than £. 1,500. Sterling: That the Cellars were we\\ stored, with Variety of Wines, and other Liquors, which were all destroyed.

Mr. Alexander Hamilton said, That, in Anno 1723, he was at the Petitioners House: That the same was faiely built; and that the Furniture thereof, to the best of hie Judgment, was worth £. 1,500. Sterling:

This was also confirmed by the Testimonies of other Persons.

The Petitioner also informed the Committee, That lie lost in Gold, Silver, and Bank Notes, about £. 1,640. Sterling; whereof he had sent to him from Edinburgh by Mr. James Nimmo % some Days before, £. 540 Sterling; and that he received from his Estate in Ilay, the Week before, £.450. by Alexander McMillan; and that he had lying by him, besides these Sums, £. 650; which, in all, amounts to £. 1,640.

To prove this Article;

Mr. Campbell junior said* That he had brought to the Petitioner, from Mr. Ninrmoi in Edinburgh, the Week before his House was robbed, ^.540. Sterling, which he saw him lock up in his Scrutoir: And that Mr. M'Millan told him, That he had delivered to the Petitioner, about the same time, the Sum of £. 450.: That the Petitioner usually had a large Sum of Money by him; and that, he was well informed, the Scrutoir, in which he kept his Money, was broke to pieces, and all the ready Money carried off, by the Mob; which, he verily believes, amounted to above £. 1,600.

George Drummond Esquire said, That, on the 25th of June last, Mr. James Nimmo, of Edinburgh, told him; That he had sent to the Petitioner, the Week before, by the Hands of Mr. John Campbell, a Sum of above £. 500.: And Mr. Alexander M'Millan told him the same Day, That he paid to him from Ilay, about the same time, about £400. Sterling.

The Petitioner further informed the Committee, That Mrs. Campbell's Jewels, carried off by the Mob, were a large Breast Jewel, Two Pair of Diamond Ear-rings, Two Diamond Buckles, Three Diamond Rings, a Diamond Necklace, and a Pearl Necklace; which, besides other Stones, Seals and plain Rings, cost £. 1,140.; the Diamond Necklace, and a small Piece of the Breast Jewel, he is informed, are recovered, in Value about £. 400.; the Remainder lost is £. 740. Sterling:

To prove this Article;

Mr. Campbell junior said, That, about Four Days before the Petitioners House was robbed, he saw Mrs. Campbell's Jewels, which, lie verily believes, were to the Value of about £. 1,140. Sterling; and believes the «ame were in the House when it was rifled.

Mrs. Sommei'vcll, the Petitioner's Lady's Woman, said, She had often seen the Jewels above-mentioned: That her Lady usually kept them in a fine strong Box, in her Closet: and always left them there, when she at any time went into the Country: That the last, time she saw them was about a Fortnight before the Mob happened; and is very sure, that the said strong Box, and all the Jewels, were in the House on the 24th of June last, when it was robbed; for that, after hearing of the Mischief that had been done to her Master's House, she went into Glasgow on the 25th of June, about Eigfyt in the Morning; and went through all the House, while a great many of the Mob were in it; and, at that time, she saw this strong Box, and her Master's Scrutoir, lying, broke and empty, in One of the Rooms.

The Petitioner further informed the Committee, That Mrs. Campbell had in her Cabinet, or strong Box, when his House was robbed, a Purse or Two of Gold, consisting of Medals, Five Guinea Pieces, broad Pieces, and some foreign Gold, to the Value of above £. 200.;

To prove this Article;

Airs. Scmmerccll said, She had often seen her Lady's Two Purses of Gold and Medals: That she saw them last in her strong Box about the 10th of June last; she verily believed the Gold in them was, in Value, between 2 and ^.300.; and that they were carried off by the Mob.

The Petitioner also informed the Committee, That he had lost almost all his Table and Bed Linen; his own, Mrs. Campbell's, and the Children s, Linens, Laces, and Wearing-apparel; all his China, and Tea Equipage of r Plate; all the Liquors in his Cellars; his own, and his Son's; Library; his Coach; his Book^ of Account's, and Vql. 2X>.

a great many Papers of Importance; which being of an uncertain Value, he could put no Estimate on his Loss, on that Account.

Mrs. Sommeixcll said, That her Lady, who left Glas-genv the 23d of June, proposing to return back thither on the Monday following, carried only some few Changes of Linen for herself, Mr. Campbell, and the young Ladies, along with her; and no Wearing-apparel, but what they had on; leaving all their Laces, Linen, and other Wear* ing-cloaths, in the House in Town: That she also left in it all the Household Furniture; all their fine Table and Bed Linen; a great Quantity of China and Plate; and great Stores of Wines, and other Liquors, in the Cellars.

That, upon the Whole, it appeared to the Committee, That the Loss sustained by the Petitioner is as follows; viz*

In Money and Bank Notes -

In Gold and Medals of Mrs. Campbell's -

And that he lost considerably in other Articles, on which he did not put any particular Estimate.

Resolved\ Nemine contradicente, That it appears to this House, That the said Riot was in Opposition to, and to prevent the Execution of, the said Act in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland\

Resolved\ Nemine contradicente, That it appears to this House, That, during the said Riot, the House of Daniel Campbell Esquire, a Member of this House,.was broken into, and ransacked; and all the Money, Plate, Jewels, Furniture, and other Things of Value, in the said House, were pillaged; and likewise the Garddn, Summer-house, Trees and Statues, thereunto belonging, were destroyed > which several Damages were done on account of the Concern the said Mr. Campbell had, or was supposed to have had, in promoting the said Act for laying a Duty on Malt.

Resolved, That Satisfaction ought to be made to the said Mr. Campbell, for his said Damages, Losses, and Sufferings.

Sir Richard Hopkins reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Society or Company of Freemen, and of the Art and Mystery of Tilers and Bricklayers, of London, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as follows; viz.

That, pursuant to an Order of the House, the Committee proceeded to examine the Allegations of the said Petition:

That, to prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Petitioners called,

Mr. John Broum: Who said. That the Brick makers do not dig the Earth, and let it lie so long as they ought to do: That the Earth to make Bricks'ought to be dug between the Beginning of November and February; laud ought to be turned once, at least; and not to be made into Bricks till the Beginning of March:

That he has gone out a searching; and the Brick-makers have. threatened him: That he has seen them digging Earth in the Summer-time, to make Bricks: That the Bricks and Tiles made with the Earth dug iii Summer, are not so good as if the Earth was dug between November and February: That they used to burn GreyStocksin Kilns; but now they burn theta in Clamps, and set them round with Place-bricks; which makes the Place-bricks good for nothing*

That they use a great deal of Spanish, in making Bricks: That they have a By-law of their ow n; blit that there is no Act of Parliament that gives them any Power over the Brickmakers: That, about Fifteen Miles oft', thfey make good Bricks, because they do not use so much'Spanrsh: That the Site bf Bricks ought to be Two Inches Three-quarters thick, Four Inches and a Quarter Wide, and Nine Inches long, when burnt': That those Bricks are proper for Building: That schfcy generally want an Inch in Length, and a Quarter of aril Inch in Breadth: ^That Pan-tiles ought to be Thirteen Inches and a Half long, Nine Inches and a Half broad, and Half an" Inch thick. J

John Moreton said, He was appointed, by the Company, to search whether the Brickmakers dug their EartJi in due Season: That, the Beginning of he saw several digging of Earth, which was made into BricKs sooii after- which, when burnt, were good for little: That they use a great deal of Spanish with their Earth: That he agreed with- Mr. Brown, as to the Dimensions of the Bricks and Tiles! '

That an Agreement between the Bricklayers artd Bricktfiakers was read:

That Clamp-plate Bricks are sold for 11 s. aTho us and, and Kiln-bricks are sold for £. 1. 6s. a Thousand.

Mr. Moreton, Bricklayer, said, That one Mr. Long had made Bricks Nine Inches long; and that they are as good as any; and are most beautiful in building; and are as strong to build, with as any: That some Earth requires more Spanish than others.

.. John Brown said, That the biggest Bricks are the best; butmiddle Bricks have been used for these Twelve Years past: That he has measured Several under Eight Inches.

Thomas Fox, Brickmaker, said, That the Brickmakers generally make Bricks Eight Inches and a Half long. Two Inches and a Half thick, and Four Inches broad: That Nine Inches would be too long, and cannot be burnt well.

John Hudson, and Mr. Porter, Bricklayers, said. That Bricks Nine Inches long, Four Inches and a Quarter wide, and Two Inches and Three-quarters thick, are best for Service: That they have had very good Bricks of that Size.

James Barrat and Tho. Waxham said. They think the best Size of Bricks are those in the Agreement mentioned: And Barrat said, That old Spanish makes the bfest Bricks; and that the Mixing of Spanish saves Fuel, in the Burning: That they use Eight or Nine Chaldron of Coals, without Spanish, to burn One hundred thousand of Bricks, when Five Chaldron will do, with Spanish: That the most durable Bricks are mixed with Spanish: That Sand, instead of Spanish, will make them rotten: That Bricks burnt with Spanish, of the same Dimensions, do not weigh so much as those without.

Thomas Tunstall, of Brentford, Brickmaker, said. That Two Inches and Three-quarters thick are not so sound as those of Two Inches and a Half: That those of Eight and a Half in Length are best; can't be burnt well, when longer, or thicker.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinio^ oif this Committee; That the best Assize of Bricks, for Sale, is Nine Inches long. Two Inches and a Half thick, and Four Inches and a Quarter wide, when burnt.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion'of this Committee; That the Earth to make Bricks ought to be dlig between the First of November and February, and ought to be turned once, at least; and Hot to be made into Bricks until the Beginning of March.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no more than Twenty-fivg Load of Spanish, sifted (not exceeding Forty Bushels in eaCh Load) through & Sieve Half an Inch, be allowed to the quantity of Brick-

earth for making One hundred thousand of Bricks,

r 4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Pan-tiles, for Sale, ought to be made to contain 13 Inches anda Half in Length, Nihe Inches and an Half in Breadth, and Half an Inch in Thickness, when burnt.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the ‘Corporation of Tilers and Bricklayers, of the City of London, ate the proper Persons to inspect the Making of Brieks add Tiles, and the Materials whereof they are made, within Fifteen Miles of London.

The First and Second of tfaie said Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, Upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors confined in Debtors his Majesty's Gaol in Newgate, within the Town arid Petitions. County of Newcastle, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners were Prisoners before the 29th of September 1724, the time appointed by the late Act for Relief of insolvent Debtors; arid hoped to have had the Benefit thereof; but were defeated, by the Scruple of the Gaoler's Oath concerning their Confinement; they having, through his Indulgence, been permitted to go out of the Liberties of the said Gaol, upon some extraordinary Occasions: And praying. That the House will provide some Remedy, for their Enlargement* as shall be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of such of the insolvent Debtors, confined in the County Gaol of Salop, as were Prisoners to the Gaol on or about the Twenty-ninth of September 1724, and so continued undischarged by Law, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners are truly sensible of the good Intentions the House had to them in passing the Act for Relief of insolvent Debtors, although, by the Letter of the Act, the Petitioners could have no Benefit by it, by reason, many of them having long lain in Gaol, the Keeper has, out of Pity, suffered them to go out of Gaol to work for their Bread, on giving Security for their forthcoming, paying weekly, for Liberty, some Twelve Pence, some Eighteen Pence; which weekly Charge has been incumbent upon some of them for Six, Tight, , and Ten Years; and pays not the Creditor, but fobs their Families; so that the Gaoler, out of a tenderCon-science, or in respect to his Weekly Reception, refused to swear to the Petitioners Confinement, as the said Act requires; and thereby they have had no Benefit thereof, which Prisoners in Execution had; and so

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in Wood-street Compter, in the City of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and several Thousands under the same deplorable Circumstances, in the other Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That notwithstanding many Prisoners were discharged from that Prison by the late Act for Relief of insolvent Debtors, yet more were left behind; and many since reduced to the same Calamities, through the merciless cruelty of their Creditors, who will not accept of all they have, hut will have their Bodies confined, without allowing them any thing to live upon: That it is the Custom of other Nations to make the Prisoner an Allowance suitable to his Quality before Imprisonment; and this

.....Two Years ago passed a Bill for that Purpose;

but the House of Lords had not time, as it is apprehended, to go through the same: And praying, That their Creditors may be obliged to give them such Allowance, for their Maintenance in Prison, as the House shall think fit; they making, to their Creditors, all the Satisfaction in their Power.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill to prevent frivolous and vexations Arrests, was committed, be received.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and prin- ' cipat Inhabitants, of Ripple, Strensham, Earles Cromb, Desford, and Besford, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Tewkesbury, in Glo' stershire, is the chief Market to which they resort for buying and selling Corn; and their direct and only Road thither is through Tivyning, in the Road leading from Boiobridge to Tewkesbury; which Road is in very good Repair: That the Inhabitants of Tewkesbury have petitioned the House for aTurnpike to amend their Itoads from their Town to the Top of Stamvay-hill; which Road i$ on the other Side the River and Town of Texckesbury, and quite contrary from Tivyning Road; whereon they have likewise prayed aTurnpike: That there is no Occasion for a Turnpike on the Tivyning Road; and, if one should be erected there, it will be a great Imposition upon the Petitioners, and many other Townships on that Side the Country: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairing the several Roads leading into the Town of Tewkesbury, in the County of Gldster, is committed.

A Petition of the Landholders, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the Parishes of Breeden, Kerrimerton, Beckford, Overbury, in behalf of themselves, and others,

was presented to the tlouse, and read; setting forth!, That there is a Bill depending in the House, for amending several Roads leading into Tewkesbury in Glo'stershire $ which Bill will greatly prejudice the Petitioners; for that the Road leading from Teivkesbury to Stairway-hill, Eastward, is Ten Miles in Length, and a very deep and foun-' derous Road; and there is very little, if any, Materials'to be had for Two-thirds of the said Way, but what must be fetched from Ereeden-hitts, which lie Four Miles Northward of the said Road; and must be carried in Carts, or Waggons, through the Parishes of Breeden, Kemmerton.

Overbury, or Beckford; whereby the lower Roads and Fields of those Parishes will be very much damaged, unless fetched at a proper Season of the Year: That there is butTwo Mile6of thev Roadbetween Breeden and Teivkes-bury intended tobe repaired by the Bill, which isalready in as good Repair as the last Summer-season would admit; and the Inhabitants are able, and willing, to put and Veep the same in sufficient Repair, without further Assistance from Parliament; but if a Turnpike should be erected on the said Road, not only the Petitioners, but great Numbers of other Persons coming to Teivkesbury Market, will be obliged, under Pretence of repairing a Road that does not want it, to pay a Toll for re-e pairing a Road that they have not the least Benefit by, and do not use; which will be a very great Oppression upon the Petitioners: And praying. That they may be heard, by Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairing the several Roads leading into the Town of Tewkesbury, in the County of Gloucester, is committed:

A Petition of the Rector, Inhabitants, Freeholders, and Tewkesbury Landholders, of the Parish of Upton upon Severn, in the Roads. County of Worcester,' was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners understand a Bill is brought into the House for repairing the Roads leading into Tewkesbury, Coni Gloucester, which is the Petitioners next Market Town; and which was first intended to amend the Road from Tewkesbury to Stanxcay-hill; but the Bill also extends to amend the Road from Texckesbury to Bowbridge, in the Parish of Twyning, about Two Miles in Length, through which Way lies the Petitioners ordinary Way to Texckesbury; and there to erect a Turnpike, and take Toll for the Cattle coming that Way; which needs no Repair; and, if it does, the Inhabitants are able and willing to put and keep it in good Repair; and the Petitioners think it unreasonable to have a Tax laid upon them to repair a Road in another County, wherewith they have no Communication: And praying, That no Turnpike may be erected in their Way to Texckesbury; but that they, and their Cattle, may pass, without Obstruction, as usual; and that they may be heard, by Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairing the Roads leading into the Town of Texckesbury, in the County of Gloucester, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard before the said Committee, by their Counsel, if they think fit.

Hudson: Who, being severally examined, said, That the Road between Stockton and Dar/iifgton, which is Ten Miles in Length, is become so bad and ruinous, and several Parts so deep, in the Winter-season, that the same are dangerous to all Passengers: That the Inhabitants of the Parishes through which the said Road doth lead, have constantly clone their Statute-work; and, if they were to do and pay twice as much as they are by Law required to do and pay, the same would not be sufficient to repair the bad Parts of the Road.

Kensington The Lord Carpenter reported from the Committee, Roads. to w horn the Petition of several Gentlemen, Fanners, and other Inhabitants, of the Parishes of Kensington, St. George, Ilamver Sjuarc, St. Margaret, Westminster, Chelsea, and Fulham, in the County of Middlesex, in behalf of themselves, and others, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing. Date the 21st of March instant, the Committee proceeded to examine the Allegations of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners called,

John Jones, and Colonel Howard: Who, being severally examined, said, That most Part of the Road between Fulham and London is so bad, that the Commissioners for the Land Tax have been obliged to go through a private Way: That the Inhabitants have constantly done their Statute-work, and a Pound-rate hath been raised; yet the same hath not been sufficient to repair that Road.

John Birchctt, of Chelsea, said, That the Roads from Fulham to London, through Utile and Great Chelsea, Vol. 30:

and Kensington, are very ruinous; which has been occasioned by many heavy Loads of Bricks and Tiles, and Drays, passing through the same: That although the Statute-work hath been constantly done, and Six Pence in the Pound raised; yet that hath not been sufficient to put the Roads into Repair.

Abraham Odell, Christopher Grey, and ThmasWrench, being severally examined, said, That the Road from Fulham to Knightsbridge is so bad, that a great deal of Mischief has been done to Persons that travelled that Road: And Thomas Wrench further said, That, some time since, he had a Horse smothered in that Road:

That Six Pence in the Pound has been raised; and the Inhabitants of the several Parishes have constantly done their Statute-work; and, if a Bridge should be built between Fulham and Putney, Two Shillings in the Pound will not be sufficient to repair the said Roads.

John Sutton and Robert Turber said, That the Roads from Counters Bridge to Kensington, and from Kensington to Chelsea Church, and from Kensington to Knightsbridge, are so very bad, that they are almost impassable in the Winter-season: That the Statute-work hath been done, and a Rate of Six Pence in the Pound raised.

Reginald May riot Esquire, being examined, said, That if One Shilling and Six Pence in the Pound was raised, towards repairing the Roads, it would not be sufficient to put the Road from Fulham to Knightsbridge into such Repair, as that Passengers might pass through the same with Safety.

iniliam Birchctt said, That the Road from Chelsea Ferry' to Hyde-park-corner, in the Winter-season, is, in many Places, dangerous: That the Statute-work hath been constantly done: That, if Six Pence in the Pound was raised, it would not keep the Road in Repair: And said further, That the Persons, wrho did usually drive Brick-carts, and other Carriages, from Hammersmith to London, through the high Road, now drive the same through a Bye-road, to avoid paying Toll at the Turnpike at Hammersmith.

Peter Algood said, That the Road from Wansdown Green to the Turnpike at Hammersmith, North End, is very bad; and almost impassable, in the Winter-time: And said,

He lost a Horse in the Road by the Badness thereof.

Mr. Treasurer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from his Majesty to this House, signed by his Majesty; and he delivered the same to Mr. Speaker; who read the same to the House:

And the said Message is as follows; viz.

George R.

I]is Majesty, having nothing more at Heart than an earnest Desire to secure to his own Subjects the full and free Enjoyment of their Trade and Navigation; and, in the best manner, to prevent and frustrate such Designs as have been formed against the particular Interest of this Nation, and the general Peace of Europe; has found it necessary, not only to augment his Maritime Force, but to concert such other Measures as may most effectually conduce to these desirable Ends: And, as these Services will require some extraordinary Expence, his Majesty hopes lie shall be enabled, by the Assistance of Parliament, to increase the Number of Seamen already voted and granted for the Service of this Year; and to enter into, and make good, such Engagements as the Circumstances and Exigency of Affairs may require.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, take his Majesty's most gracious Message into Consideration.

Address. Majesty, on Saturday last, with their Address; to which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I return you my Thanks for this loyal and affectionate Address: And you may be assured, I shall make no other Use of the Confidence you repose in me, hut for preserving the general Tranquillity; and in Support of the Trade, Honour, and Interest, of my people.

Frauds in A Petition of the Wardens and Commonalty of the Silver \Vart*. Mystery of Goldsmiths, of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by several Acts of Parliament, they are empowered to assay and mark wrought Wares, of Gold and Silver, to prevent Frauds; and have, for some Hundred Yearspast, kept an Office at Goldsmiths-hall, for that Purpose: That, of late Years, the small Works of Gold and Silver very much increasing, the Petitioners are at a considerable yearly Charge, over and above the Prices allowed for such Assaying and Marking: That the Petitioners are also impowered, by Act of Parliament, and severalCharters, to search try, and regulate, all wrought Wares of Gold and Silver, and to punish Offenders; but have met with great Opposition, in the Execution of such Powers, from several Persons, who frequently work and sell Wares of Gold and Silver, which they do not bring to the said Office to be assayed; and that also, of late, great Quantities of Brass Works have been silvered over, and sold, having Marks thereon resembling the Marks appointed to ascertain the Standard of wrought Plate; to the Deceit of the Subject, and the great Diminution of the Duty on Plate: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to provide such Remedies therein, as the House shall think fit.

Orr/cm/, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

Where

Combination of Workmen in Woollen Manufactures.

648 31

Where the same was read; and the Report, and the Resolution, of the Committee, are asToIloweth; viz.

That the Committee have, pursuant to the Order of this House, of the Third of this Instant March, examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find the same, upon the Examination of Witnesses, to be as followeth; viz.

Mr John Voider: Who said. That the Weavers havb many Clubs in several Places in the West of England, particularly at Exeter, where they make Bye-laws; some of which he has seen; which Bye-laws are, among divers other things, to appoint Places of Meeting, fix their Officers, make Allowances to travelling 'Workmen, and to ascertain their Wages:

That several Weavers have brought home their Work, and durst not go onto serve their Masters, for fear of other Weavers of the Club, who have deterred them therefrom: And he believes, one of the Occasions of the late Riots, that have happened, has been, that the Masters have refused lo raise the Workmen's Wages to what Price they pleased:

That he was present at a great Mob in the Town of Crediton, inZ>am^/rc, consisting of Weavers, and others concerned in the WToollenManufacture; who were headed by a Captain, who threatened their Masters, iftheyrefused to raise their Wages; and carried about with them a Chain of Serge cut off from a Loom; and declaring the y would do the like to the Pieces of Serge of the otherMa-sters, who refused to comply with their Demands: That, when the Constables had seized some of the Ringleaders, and brought them before Two Justices of Peace, the Mob beset the House, insulted the Justices, threw Stones at them, and forced them to fly, and rescued the Prisoners: That at Calling ton, on another Riot, he has seen a Master carried about on a Coolstaflf, for refusing to comply with their Demands; and that others have been threatened with the like Usage:

That most of the Masters do pay their Workmen in Money; but some of them do pay by way of Truck; which is not so satisfactory; however, he believes, the Masters would all willingly be obliged to pay the Whole in Money.

Mr. William Pike said, That he has seen the Weavers at their Clubs, where none but Weavers are admitted; and that they have their Ensigns and Flags hung out at the Door of their Meetings:

That they go about, in Parties, to Looms; and demand Twelve Pence, or some other Sum of Money, towards supporting such of their own Gangs as are now in Prison; and has seen several Looms cut within these Eight Months past, and the Work carried away for the Non-payment of the Money, and because some would work cheaper than others; and that Pieces of Serge are frequently cut on the Racks:

That the Weavers complain of paying them in Truck; but believes, that is not the cause of their Riots; for that they generally begin in the Spring, w hen there is the greatest Demand for Goods, and most Plenty of Work: That his own Weavers would willingly have worked for him at fheWages hegave; but that theClubthreatened, if they did so, to pull them out of the House, and cool-staff them; upon which, he was forced to pay them the Price demanded, to save his Work from being cut; and has known several that have been coolstaffed: That he is willing to pay his Workmen in Money; and, believes, all the other Masters would willingly be obliged to do the same.

William Blake said, That, upon the last grand Riot at Taunton, several Warrants were issued for apprehending the Rioters; and he, and about Thirty more, went to serve them; hut a body of about a Thousand got together, and cried, One and all; and came up into the Hall, and fell upon William Gartvay Constable, and beat and wounded him very much; and so wounded Mr. John Coggin with a Brickbat, that he was not Well in three Months after: That Mr. Justice Catby sei2ed

ib Aprilis. 1726.

One of the Mob; and the Mob came about him, and struck him, and took away the Mah; and that several were seized, but rescued again:

That the Town Clerk read the Proclamation for dispersing the Mob; but they pulled off his Hat and Wig, and put Dirt upon his Head:

That he saw a Man carried upon a Coolstaff because he fetched Mr. Myner's Work contrary to the Orders of the Club; and that he has seen several Letters, which have been dropt in Master Weavers Houses, threatening That if they would not comply with their Workmen's Demands, they would burn their Houses, kill their Horses, and cut down and deface their Orchards.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee, having considered the respective Petitions referred to them, relating to the said unlawful Clubs and Combinations, came to the following Resolution;

656 7° ApriliA. 17

Fnwds in That the Act of the 28th of King Edward the First, Gold and Sil- Chapter the 20th, was read; whereby it is enacted, That ver Wares. 110 Ye^ei of Silver shall depart the Workers Hands till assayed by the Wardens of the Craft, and marked with the Leopard's Head; and that none work worse Gold than of the Touch of Paris.

The Act of the 18th of Queen Elizabeth, Chapter the 15th, was read; That no Goldsmith shall work any Gold less in Fineness than Eleven Ounces Two Penyweight: And that if the same be allowed by the Wardens, and after found faulty, they to forfeit the Value.

The Act of the Eighth and Ninth of William the Third, Chapter the 27th, was read; That no Silver Plate be made less in Fineness than Eleven Ounces Ten Peny-weight; nor sold, or exchanged (unless small Things un-capable of receiving a Mark), until marked as is therein particularly mentioned.

Humphry Hctherington, Clerk of the said Company, said, That he found, by the Books of the said Company, that they have, for about Four hundred Years, kept an Assay Office; and, particularly, by an Entry dated the Ninth of December 1633, that it hath been the ancient Custom of the said Company, Time out of Mind, to take an Allowance of Four Grains per Pound Weight, on all Silver Plate, for marking thereof; which Custom is still continued as to large Plate; and that, of late Years, the small Works of Silver much increased; and, about the Year 1717, the Workmen had Meetings, and attended the Company, or a Committee thereof; and delivered a Petition, and a Representation, signed by great Numbers of them; which Petition and Representation were produced, and read: And the Workmen thereby prayed to have their small Works marked; and said, they had a Proposal to offer, to defray the Charge:

That they afterwards agreed to pay Three Pence apiece for Snuff-boxes; Two Pence a Pair for Spurs; and proportionally for other small Wares: And, to vouch the Truth of this, he appealed to Affidavits made by Win. Fiskt Maurice Boheme, and others.

Joseph Ward, the Assay-master, said, The Company always took Four Grains per Pound Weight for large Silver Plate; and, oFlate Years, for Gold Watch-cases, from One to Four together, One Shilling; and all above Four, Three Pence apiece; and so proportionably for other Gold Works.

And the said Humphry Hctherington produced an Account of the Receipts and Payments, for Six Years, for assaying and marking Plate; and the Total of the Receipts is 1,615. l3s- 1 lid.; and that the Total of the Payments is £.2,074. 3$. 8d.; so that the Company are out of Pocket, for those Six Years, viz. from May 1717. to May 1723, £.458. 19s. 8id.; besides an Increase of the Assayers Salary £.30. a Year; and £. 50. a Year for Rent of their Assay Office, and Assayers House; and £.20. a Year, which the Clerk deserves for keeping the Accounts:

That Part of the Act of the 28th Edward the First, Chapter the 20th, was read; That the Wardens shall go from Shop to Shop to try Gold, whether it have the right Touch.

The Act of the 6th and 7th of William the Third was read; That a Warden with Two Assistants, may, within the Bills of Mortality, enter Houses, or Shops, to search for unlawful Bullion:

That the Company's Charter was produced, and read; dated the 4th Day 0\ January, in the 18th Year of King Charles the Second; being an Inspeximus Charter: The Kings does thereby grant, That the Wardens of the said Mystery, for the Time being, shall for ever have the Search, Inspection, Trial, and Regulation, of all wrought Gold and Silver in and about London, and elsewhere, in this Kingdom; and to correct Defects:

That the Wardens have frequently, in their Searches, been opposed, insulted, and threatened; and, particularly, he finds, by Entries in the Company's Books, that, in the Year 1700, Mr. Jennings, Goldsmith, in the Strand, refused to let them see his Goods; and said, if Mr. Snell,

one of the then Wardens, sent for a Constable to break open his Glass, he would shoot him through the Head; and, in the Year 1712, Mr. Fleming threatened to shoot Mr. Robert Cooper, one of the then Wardens, through the Head: And he said, the Wardens had been opposed, in Searches, above One hundred times:

That several Pieces of Gold and Silver were produced, which Mr. Hethei'ington said were brought by Order of the Company: And Mr. Ward said, some of the Gold was Two Carracts, Three Grains, and a Quarter, worse than Standard; and some of the Silver was Three Ounces,

One Penyweight, worse than Standard:

That Mr. Hethtrington shewed the Committee a Tankard, which the Company bought for Fifteen Shillings, which had been pawned for about Seven Pounds; being silvered over, and having Marks very much like the Company's Marks.

William Warner said, His Mother had lent divers considerable Sums of Money upon Silver Tankards, and other Things pawned to her by a Woman that used to come to her often, and sometimes in Company with a Lady in a Coach; and afterwards the Woman who pledged the Plate said, it belonged to Persons of Quality; therefore she, at several times, took it away; and, instead thereof, brought Tankards, and other Things, of Copper, Brass, or other base Metal, silvered over, very much like the Plate she took away; and he shewed some of the false Metal, with Marks thereon, to the Committee; and said he had great Quantities of it; and concluded, That lie believed his Mother might lose between 1,600, and £. 1,800. by the same.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Mr. Waller Bacon reported from the Committee, who Expiring were appointed to inspect what Laws are expired, or near Laws, expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House which of them are fit to be revived, or continued; That they had inspected the Laws accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Than an Act, made in the Eighth Year of her inte Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act to regulate the Assize of Bread; which Act was to continue for Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and was further continued for Three Years, by an Act made in the First Year of his present Majesty's Reign; and by an Act, of the Fifth Year of his Majesty's Reign, was further continued for Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and will expire at the End of this present Session of Parliament; is fit to be continued.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Than an Act, made in the Ninth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for the more effectual punishing wicked and evil-disposed Persons going armed, in Disguise, and doing Injuries and Violences to the Persons and Properties of his Majesty's Subjects; and for the more speedy bringing the Offenders to Justice; which Act was to commence from the First Day of June 1723, and to continue for Three Years, and from thence to the

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerics Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, a Sum, not less than One Pound, nor more than Six Pounds, yearly, be paid to his Majesty, by every Victualler, and Retailer of Beer and Ale, in the Cities of LjondomwA Westminster, and within the Weekly Bills of Mortality; in Consideration that no Beer, or Ale, to be sold out of their Houses, shall be sent out in any Pot, Bottle, or other Vessel, belonging to such Victualler, or Retailer, less than a Gallon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That One hundred additional Hackney Chairs be added to the present Number already licensed; and be subject and liable to the Payment of the same yearly Rent, on Licensing thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Seven thousand and Forty-six Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Eight Pence Three Farthings, remaining in the Receipt of his Majesty's Exchequer, on Arrears of former Land Taxes, be applied towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty for the Service of the Year 1726.

Fulham A Petition of the several Watermen, whose Names are

Bridge* thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Watermen, being about One hundred, who have a Right to the Sundays Foot-ferry between Fulham and Putney, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, and their Predecessors, have, Time out of Mind, claimed and enjoyed the said Foot-ferry, exclusive of all others; the Income whereof amounts to above One hundred Pounds per Annum: That in case the Bill, depending before the House, for building a Bridge cross the River of Thames from Fulham to Putney, should pass as it now stands, the Petitioners would lose the said Foot-ferry; which is their Freehold: And prayin:r, That they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, what they have to object against the said Bill; and that the same may not pass, unless Satisfaction be made to the Petitioners for the said Foot-ferry; and the Petitioners be further relieved, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for building a Bridge cross the River of Thames from the Town of Fulham, in the County of Middlesex, to the Town of Putney, in the County of Surry, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, if they think fit.

ed to the House and read; setting forth, That he is Tenant, by Lease for Years, of the Ferry, or Passage, over the River of 'Thames, from Chelsea to Battersea, and of the House and Ground belonging, at a reserved Rent, which lie is obliged to pay; for which Lease the Petitioner paid a valuable C onsideration; and he has expended a considerable Sum in improving the Premisses; and he is obliged to preserve and keep the same in Repair, during hL Term: That in case the Bill, depending before the House, for building a Bridge cross the said River of Thames from Fulham to Putney, should pass, the Petitioner will be greatly affected and injured in his Property: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill, for giving him such Recompence and Relief as the House shall tmnk fit; and that he may be heard, by himself or Counsel, before the Passing of the said Bill.
