The Lord Finch reported from the Committee, to w'hom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, residing in the Parishes of Newport Pagnellj Moidesoe, Broughton, Middleton, Keynes, and JVavendon, in the County of Bucks, and also of several Waggoners and Stage Coachmen, in behalf of themselves and others, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same w?as read; and is as follows; viz.

That, pursuant to an Order of the House, the Committee examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Petitioners called,

John Norman, a Carrier, and Thomas Williamson: Who, being severally examined, said, That they knew the Road between Wooburn, in the County of Bedford\ and Newport Pagnell, in the County of Bucks, being the great Road leading from Newport Pagnell to the City of London; and that the Road is so bad and founderous, that the same is dangerous to Passengers travelling that Way: That although the Statute-work hath been constantly done, and Six Pence in the Pound raised; yet the same hath not been sufficient to put the said Road into Repair.

John Head, of Milton, being also examined, said, That he knows the Road between Wooburn and Newport Pagnell: That the same is so bad and founderous, in the Winter-time, that all Passengers that travel that Way, are in Danger of their Lives: That the Inhabitants have done Nine or Ten Days Statute-work; yet the same hath not been sufficient to repair the said Road: He further said, That once, the last Winter, his Waggon, loaded with Wool, was stuck in the Wooburn Road; and although he bad Two Team of Horses, of Seven in each Team, yet the same was not sufficient to draw his Waggon out Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to w hom the Bill for enlarging the Term granted by an Act of Parliament, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highway between Hockley and Woburn, in the County of Bedford; and for making the said Act more effectual; is committed; That they have Power to make Provision, in the said Bill, for repairing the Road leading from Woburn, in the County of Bedford, to Newport Pagnell, in the County of Bucks.

Twenty-first Day of March 1725, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That if the Bill depending before the House, for the more effectual Draining and Preservation of the North Division of the great Level of the Fens called Bedford Level, should pass, the Consequences thereof would be to the inestimable Damage of the Paris of South Holland, in the said County of Lincoln; more particularly to the Towns of Tyd St. Marys, Sutton St. Marys, Lulton Sutton, St. James Sutton, St. Edmund's, Gedney Fenn, Gcdney Fleet, llolbeach, and JFhaplode, in the said Parts and County: and would deprive them of the Benefit of the Law's, as they now* stand; and the necessary Powers in the Commissioners of Sewers, to order proper Defences and Drains, from time to time, as the uncertain and mutable Circumstances of the Lands in the Parts aforesaid require, for the Preservation of the Estates there, as well against the Flux of the Sea, as the Inundations from the Hill Countries: And therefore praying. That if any Bill shall pass, affecting the Premises, Provision may be made therein for the Preservation and Safety of the said Parts of South Holland, which are entirely out of Bedford Level; and that they may not be subjected to the Authority of the Corporation erected by an Act of the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for settling the Draining of the great Level of the Fens called Be(tf 'ord Level; or that Corporation be, in anywise, impowered to interfere with the Authority of the Commissioners of Sewers for the County of Lincoln.

A Petition of the Commissioners of Sewers, Gentle- Bedford men, Inhabitants, Land Owners, and Occupiers of Lands, within the Parts of South Holland, in the County of Lin- L)ruinil&e* coin, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a Bill is now depending in the House, for the more effectual Draining and Preservation of the North Division of the great Level of the Fens called Bedford Level, by a new Outfal to the Sea: That the Petitioners are fully apprised of, and have considered, the said Bill; and had the Opinion of several able Surveyors, and Persons skilled in the Works of Draining; who are of Opinion, That the said intended Outfal will not only carry off' the Waters within the North Level, but also will drain several Thousands of Acres within the said Parts of South Holland, which are now intirely, and for many Years have been, destitute of any Outfal for their Waters to Sea: But the Petitioners are apprehensive, that they may be disappointed of the good Intentions of the said Bill, unless the Commissioners to be thereby appointed be impowered to determine Differences which may arise amongst the Proprietors: And praying, That the Commissioners to be named in the Bill for the more effectual Draining and Preservation of the North Division of the great Level of the Fens called Bedford Level, by a new Outfal to the Sea, may be impowered to determine all such Differences as may arise amongst the said Proprietors and Occupiers of Lands, concerning the Manner of conveying them Waters into the new-intended Cut and Outfal.

Mr. Gybbon, according to Order, reported from the Liulitbgow Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it County Elec-appeared to them, touching the Election for the Shire oftl0Q' Linlithgmo, with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the Report and Resolution are as follows; viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir James Cuninghame, of Milner aig, Baronet, complaining of an undue Election and Return of George Dundass, of Dundass, Esquire, to serve for the Shire of Linlithgow:

That the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of this Petition:

The Petitioners Counsel alleged, That the Petitioner had the Majority of legal Votes; and, in order to prove it, offered an Extract of Minutes of the Proceedings at the Election, signed by John Cunynghame, as Clerk of the Meeting:

To which the Sitting Members Counsel objected,

That the said Extract, so signed by John Cunynghame only, ought not to be admitted in Evidence, because, as they alleged, he was not legal Clerk of the Meeting; and that he was objected to; as was also Mr. Stuart, as not legal Prases of the Meeting; and that such Extract, signed by the said John Cunynghame only, was in Nature of a Certificate, by himself, of his own Election; and could not be admitted as Evidence, when that Election was disputed, as in this Cose:

They also insisted, That Mr. Hamilton was the legal Freeses of the Meeting, and Mr. Bell the legal Clerk:

That the Act of Parliament, made in Scotland, September 17th 1681, concerning the Election of Commissioners for Shires, was read to shew, that the First thing to be done, at the Meeting of the Freeholders to make such Election, is to choose a Prases, and a Clerk, to the Meeting; and, till such Choice made, the First, or Second, Commissioner last elected, or, in their Absence, the Sheriff, or Stewart Clerk, is to ask the Votes, Who shall preside, and who shall be Clerk to the Meeting

It was admitted, by the Counsel, That at the Convening of the Freeholders of this Shire, to elect a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament, Sir James Cunynghame, as Commissioner last elected, presided; and that the Sheriff' Clerk attended:

It was also admitted, by the Counsel, That the Merits of this Election turned upon the Question, Who was legal Frases, and who legal Clerk, of the Meeting? And that the C lerk of the Meeting, and no other, is the proper Officer to take the Poll of the Electors of a Commissioner to Parliament.

The Petitioner's Counsel offered the before-mentioned Extract of Minutes of Proceedings at the Election:

But, the said Extract being no otherwise signed than by the said John Cunynghame, the Committee did not think fit to admit it to be given in Evidence.

The Petitioners Counsel alleged, That the whole Number of Freeholders inrolled, present at the Election, was Fifteen: That Eight of them voted for Mr. Stuart to be Prases, and Mr. Cunynghame to be Clerk; and that the other Seven, though the Minority, separated from the Meeting, and pretended to choose Mr. Hamilton Prases, and Mr. Bell Clerk; against which Separation, and Proceeding, the Petitioner protested, and took Instruments:

And, to prove this, they offered an Instrument signed by a publick Notary:

But the Sitting Member s Counsel objected, That such Notorial Instrument was no Evidence of Fact, and ought not to be admitted to prove Proceedings at the Election; of which the Minutes were not proved, nor any Evidence of Fact offered:

And the Committee not thinking fit to admit the said Notorial Instrument to be given in Evidence, to prove such Proceedings; 4

Mr. Gybbon, according to Order, reported from the Linlithgow, Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the uoa* District of Burghs of Linlithgow, Selkirk, Lanerk, and Peebles, with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report and Resolution were read ;and are asfollows; viz.

Upon the Petition of William Fraser Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of John Murray Esquire to serve for the District of Burghs of Llinlithgow, Selkirk, Lanerk, and Peebles:

That the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of this Petition.

It appeared, by the Minutes of the Election, That James Glen, Delegate for Linlithgow, the presiding Burgh, voted for the Petitioner:

And that William Wauch, Delegate for Selkirk; John Bannatyne, Delegate for Lanerk; and John Ramadge,

Delegate for PeebUjs; voted for the Sitting Member.

The Petitioner's Counsel alleged, That they should disqualify some of the Sitting Member's Votes; and establish the Vote of William Inglis, who tendered his Commission as Delegate for Lanerk, and appeared for the Petitioner; but his Commission was rejected by the other Delegates, as illegal: And,

That they should make a Majority for the Petitioner.

They objected to John Bannatyne, who voted a9 Delegate for Lanerk, that he was not the legal Delegate; and alleged, that William Inglis was the legal Delegate for that Burgh:

And they offered to produce Evidence, of their Objection:

Which was opposed by the Sitting Member's Counsel, because such Objection Was not made at the time of the Election to Parliament.

That the Committee did not think fit to admit the Petitioner's Counsel to produce Evidence, to disqualify Persons who voted in the Election of a Delegate for Lanerk, and were not objected to at the Election of the Burgess to serve in Parliament for this District of Burghs.

That the Petitioner's Counsel also objected to the Delegate for Peebles; but were likewise opposed in giving Evidence of their Objection, because not made at the time of the Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament: And,

Thereupon, they acquainted the Committee, That they had no other Evidence to offer against the Electors:

But they objected, that the Sitting Member was, at the time of the Election, hereditary Sheriff of Selkirk; and therefore, by the Nolumusm the Writ, incapable of being elected to Parliament;

To which the Sitting Member's Counsel answered.

That the Common Clerk of Linlithgozo, the presiding Burgh, was the Returning Officer; and not the Sheriff of Selkirk; besides, that the Objection was of no Weight.

And the Petitioner's Counsel declaring. That they had nothing farther to offer;

The Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That John Murray Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the District of Burghs of Linlithgow, Selkirk, Lanerk, and Peebles.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That this House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That John Murray Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the District of Burghs of Linlithgozo,

Deficiency of A Petition of Richard Manley Gentleman, and Eli-

Choice*m *abeth his Wife; Thomas Case and James Casey In^ ancei^‘ fants; Joseph Cranmer, John Beare, Margaret Pyne, Widow; Anne Pyne and KatHei'inePyne, Infants; Lewis Thomas; June Lloyd, an Infant; Sarah Howard, Thomab Cromp, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; for and on the behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Suitors of the Court of Chancery; was presented to the House, and read, setting forth. That they ate interested in several considerable Sums of Money, which were, by Orders of the said Court, brought ' before Fleetwood Dormer and John Borrett Esquires, deceased, late Masters of the said Court; and Richard Godfrey and Edward Conway Esquires; Two of the present Masters; or some or One of them: it appears

by several Reports, made by other Masters of the said Court, That the Deficiency in the Offices of the afore- mentioned Masters amounts to Eighty-two thousand Three hundred and One Pounds Nineteen Shillings and

# Eleven Pence Farthing: That a Sign Manual having

been obtained from their Excellencies the late Lords Justices, directing the Thirty thousand Pounds Fine, paid by the Earl of Macclesfield, to be issued to Mr. Holford and Mr. Thurston, Two of the Masters of the said Court, to be applied towards making good the Losses of the Suitors, occasioned by the Deficiencies of the Masters of the said Court; the same was lent out on the Land Tax, in the Names of the said Mr. Holford and Mr. Thurston, in order to be applied as aforesaid: That the said Thirty thousand Pounds, with the Interest thereof, when applied, will reduce the said general Deficiency to the Sum of Fifty-one thousand Eight hundred Fifty-one Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Eleven Pence Farthing: That besides the said stated Deficiency, there are several other Claims, which have been reported specially, for the Judgment of the Court; which, if allowed, will greatly Increase the said Deficiency: That many of the Petitioners are Widows and Orphans; and their whole Substance is included in the above-mentioned Deficiency; and they are reduced to Extremities: And inasmuch as such Difficulties have happened to them by the Means aforesaid, and not by their own Acts, or Defaults; the Petitioners pray, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and give them such Relief as the House shall think proper. Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ditto. Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to

his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to give Directions, That the several Reports made, relating to the Claims and Demands of the Suitors of the Court of Chancery, upon the deficieut Masters of the said- Court, may be laid before this House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council.

Ways and Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the

Means. Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred

to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards deliveredin at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Imposition of two Penies Scots upon each Pint of Ale and Beer brewed and sold in the City of Glasgow; which, by several Acts passed in the Parliaments held in Scotland, were granted to the Magistrates and Town Council of the said City for severalTerms of Years, since expired; and which, by an Act of Parliament passed in the First Year of his Majesty's Reign, was continued until the First Day of Novehiber 1738; be vested in his Majesty, for raising the Sum of Six thousand and Eighty Pounds, granted to him, to make Satisfaction to Daniel Campbell Esquire, a Member of this House, for the Damages by him sustained in the late Riot at Glasgow, on account of the Concern the said Mr. Campbell had, or was supposed to have had, in promoting the Act for laying a Duty upon Malt, for the Service of the Year 1725.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty of Three Shillings per Pound on Snuff granted to her late Majesty by an Act passed in I lie Eighth Year of her Reign, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Rate of all Snuff imported in British Ships from the British Plantations, or the Spanish West Indies, be Two Shillings and Six Pence for every Pound Weight Avoirdupois; and in that Proportion for a greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of Jhi3 Committee,

That the Rate of all Snuff imported from Italy, Spain, l*ortugal, and all other Parts, except France, be Five Shillings for every Pound Weight Avoirdupois; and in that Proportion for a greatecor less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, on the Exportation of any Snuff all the Duties be drawn back, except the Old Subsidy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That any of his Majesty's Subjects may import Whale-fins, Oil. or Blubber of Whales, taken and caught in St. David's Straits, or in any other Parts of the Seas thereto adjoining; as also the Skins, Oil, Blubber, or other Prodifce whatsoever, of Seals, and other Creatures, caught in the Greenland Sea, St. David's Straits, or any other Parts of the Seas adjoining; ‘AfittoottPpay-ing any Custom, Subsidy, or other Duties,1 for the Hattie, during the Term of Five Years, front the Twenty-fourth Day of December 1726. r

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of Richard Macgwirc and Josiah Poole Gentlemen, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they are Lessees, or Farmers, under the Right honourable James Earl of Derby, by Indenture, dated the Ninth of February 1721, of the Duties and Customs of the Isle of Man, for a Term of Twenty-one Years, commencing from the First of March 1721, under the yearly Rent of One thousand and Fifty Pounds: That, should the Bill, depending before the House, for the better preventing collusive Seizures, pass, as the same is now drawn, the Petitioners, and many other fair Traders to the said Island, must be deprived of their Properties, and be ruined in their Fortunes: And pray ing, That, they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, so far as the same concerns the said Island, and the Petitioners; and that they may have such Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petitionbe referred to the Cori-^ideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better preventing collusive Seizures of foreign Goods; and for Improvement of his Majesty's Revenues of Customs, Excise, and Inland Duties; is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, if they think fit.

MR. Wyld reported from the Committee, to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for the Sale of several Estates of Henry Grey Esquire, in the County of Southampton and for settling other Estates, of equal Value, in the Counties of Berks and Wilts, to the same Uses; was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consents to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Bill to the House, without any Amendment: And he delivered the Bill in at the Clerk's Table.

of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several of the same Trades in other Parts of the Kingdom, and of many Thousand Families depending upon, and employed, in the said Occupations, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Trade of Gilding hath been practised for some Hundred Years; and the Petitioners have served Apprenticeships thereto; and exercise the same in the several Branches thereof; such as Gilding and Silvering of Furniture for Horse-harness and Bridles, the Inside of Watches, Watch-chains, Sword-hilts, Buttons, several Sorts of Toys, and many other Manufactures of Brass, Copper, Tin, Sc., and if the Bill, now in the House, for the better preventing Frauds and Abuses in the Manufacturing Gold and Silver Wares; wherein is a Clause prohibiting the gilding with Gold, or silvering over, any Manufacture of Brass, or other base Metal; should pass; the Petitioners conceive the same will totally deprive them of their said Trade, to the utter Ruin of themselves and Families; and their Art is so necessary, that, without it, a Watch cannot possibly be made to answer the Purposes designed; and it will also hinder very great Quantities of gilded Manufactures from being yearly exported; which are, at this time, a considerable Branch of the Traffiek of the Nation; and the Petitioners apprehend the said Clause doth not at all affect the Interest of the Goldsmiths Company, nor relate to the general Purport, for which the Bill seems calculated; to which the Petitioners have no Objection, but only desire the free Exercise of their Trade, as usual: And praying, That they may be heard, by Counsel, against the said Clause in the said Bill; or be otherwise relieved as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the better preventing Frauds and Abuses in the manufacturing Gold and Silver Wares, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard for the said Bill.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards Satisfaction of the Debts and Demands of the Suitors of the Court of Chancery from the deficient Masters of that Court, there be laid an additional Duty of Six Pence upon every Piece of Vellom, or Parchment, Or Piece of Paper, upon which any original Writ, except such Original on which aW rit of Capias issues; Subpoena; Bill of Middlesex; Latitat; Writ of Capias quo minus-, Writ of Dedimus potestatem, to take Answers, examine Witnesses, or appoint Guardians; or any other Writ whatsoever; or any other Process, or Mandate, that shall issue out of, or pass the Seals of, any the Courts at Westminster, Courts of the Great Sessions in Wales, Courts in the Counties Palatine, or any other Court whatsoever, holding Plea, where the Debt, or Damage, doth amount to Forty Shillings, or above; or the Thing in Demand is of that Value; shall be ingrossed, or written; Writs of Covenant for levying Knes, Writs t>f Entry for suffering common Recoveries, and Writs of Habeas corpus, excepted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, ThfU, towards Satisfaction of the Debts and Demands of the Suitors of the Court of Chancery from the deficient Masters of that Coart, there be laid an additional Duty of Six Pence upon every Piece of Vellom, Parchment, or Paper, upon which any Entry of Action in the Mayor's and Sheriffs Courts of I^ojidon, and in Courts in all Cor-

?orations, and other Courts whatsoever, out of which no Vrits, Process, or Mandates, issue, holding Plea, where the Debt, or Damage, doth amount to Forty Shillings, or above, shall be ingrossed, or written.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thtf, towards Satisfaction of the Debts and Demands of the ftiitors of the Court of Chancery from the deficient Masters of that Court, there be laid an additional Duty of Six Pence upon every Skin, or Piece, of Vellom, or Parchment, or Sheet of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, or written, any Citation, or Monition, made in any Ecclesiastical Court, or the Courts of Admiralty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duties be laid for the Term of Sixteen Years.

A Petition of Edward Coirway Esquire, one of the Masters in Ordinary of the High Court of Chancery; and also of Margaret, Wife of the said Edward Conway, and Whitmore Conway, their eldest Son; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner Edward, being, upon the Resignation of John Orlebar Esquire, on the Tenth of January 1720, admitted into the Office of Master in Chancery, Mr. Orlebar was ordered to pay, and deliver over, to him, all the Money and Effects of tl»e Suitors of the Court then in his Hands; but Mr. Orlebar retained, out of the Suitors Money, Six thousand Pounds, which was never paid to the Petitioner:

That, on the Petitioners Admission into the said Office, he paid, out of the said Suitor's Money, to the Earl of Macclesfield, then Lord Chancellor, or for his Use, the further Sum of Fifteen hundred Pounds; and Five hundred Pounds more of the said Suitors Money, which was to have been paid to the Petitioner, was stopped, to be applied towards making up the Deficiency of Mr. Dormer, formerly a Master of the said Court: That, by Mr.

Holford's Report, now lying before the House, the Petitioner is reported to be deficient in his Account of the Money and Effects of the Suitors of the Court, in the Sum of Twenty thousand Five-hundred Fifty-three Poun Is Four Shillings Three Pence Halfpeny; in which the several Sums before-mentioned are included, though he received no Benefit thereof; That the Petitioner Edward, in order to make good the Deficiency w herewith he is charged, hath conveyed all his real Estate, being upwards of Five hundred Pounds per Annum, to Mr. Holford; and the other Petitioners have joined in a Fine and Recovery

yoo I J° — 16° Maii. A. 1726.

very thereof; a,nd the said Estate, having been exposed to Sale, appears to be of Value sufficient to answer the said Deficiency, if the Sums before-mentioned may be allowed: That the Petitioners Margaret and Whitmore, in order to free the Petitioner Edward, having joined in the said Fine and Recovery, have thereby given up all their Estate, and Interest in the said Estate, towards making good the said Deficiency; without which, the Whole must have remained a Deficiency; and they are thereby stripped of all Provision for their Subsistence, in case of Death, or Disability, of the Petitioner Edward: And therefore praying the Consideration of the House, and such Relief as the House shall think fit.

And his Majesty was afterwards pleased to say;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The King's I have ordered my Lord Chancellor to declare to you, peec in my JJame and Words, the Reasons of my coming this Day to Parliament.

Aryl the Lord Chancellor acquainted both Hbrises, That he had received fVoiiihis Majesty'sHands, from the Throne, his Majesty's Speech to both Houses of Parliament: Which the Lord Chancellor tead;1 and is as follows:

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Icannot, in Justice to you, put an End to this Session without returning you my hearty Thanks for the many

Instances youhave givenmeofyour Duty and Affection to my Person and Govenment; andofvourZeal to maintain the Honour, and true Interest of this Kingdom.

The Spirit and Resolution you have shewn on this important Occasion, when our most valuable Rights and Privileges have been struck at, are highly becoming the Weight and Authority of a British Parliament; and the Steps which have been taken abroad, in Support of the Measures entered into against this Nation, must convince every body of your Wisdom and Prudence, in endeavouring to put an early Stop to the further Progress of them:

I hope the Precautions you have enabled me to take, will be sufficient, in Conjunction with my Allies, to defeat the Designs which have been formed against us; and that the Promoters of them, when they have fully weighed their own Circumstances, and better considered those of the several. Powers united in Defence of the Tranquillity and Liberties of Europe, will find it their own Interest to preserve the Peace, and think it most safe and prudent to desist from*their dangerous Schemes.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my particular Thanks for the Supplies which you have So chearfully and effectually raised; and you may be assured, that they shall be faithfully applied to the Uses for which yo>i intended them.

My Lords, and-Gentlemen,

The constant Employment of my Thoughts, and the most earnest Wishes of my Heart, tend wholly to the securing to my Subjects their just Rights and Advantages; and to the preserving to them, and to all Europe, the Enjoyment of a safe and honourable Peace:

And I must not conclude without giving you the strongest Assurances, that the particular Confidence you have placed in me, shall he made use of in such manner only, as may most effectually conduce to the attaining those good and great Purposes.

Then the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty's Command said;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

A PROCLAMATION. GEORGE R.

Proclamation TJI WHEREAS our Parliament stands prorogued to P&rUamln8 Thursday the Eighth Day of December next: We, ar menu with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Eighth Day of December next, be further prorogued to Tuesday the Seventeenth Day of January next ensuing the Date hereof; to be then held at Westminster: And we have given Orders to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same, accordingly: And we do hereby further declare our Plea-

sure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Seven- teenth Day of January next, be held, and sit, for the Dis^ patch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal; and the Knights, Citizens* and Burgesses, and Commissioners of Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons; are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance, accordingly, at Westminster, on the said Seventeenth Day of January next.

Given at our Court at Kensington, the Twenty-ninth Day of November 1726; and in the Thirteenth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the King.

reported.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the Housh had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; and that his Majesty was pleased to say, That he had ordered the Lord Chancellor to declare, in his Name and Words, the Reasons of his Majesty's meeting his People in Parliament at this time; and thereupon the Lord Chancellor acquainted both Houses, That he had received a Speech from his Majesty, on the Throne; which the Lord Chancellor read; and of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as folio wet h; viz.

*My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I acquainted you, last Year, with the Treaties of Peace and Commerce concluded between the Emperor and the .'King of Spain. As that sudden and unaccountable Con junction gave, at the first Appearance, just Grounds , of Jealousy and Apprehension to the neighbouringPow-ers of Europe; the subsequent Proceedings and Transactions in thoseTwo Courts, and the secret and offensive Alliances concluded between them about the same time, ^bave laid the Foundations of a-most exorbitant and for*

'. VOL. 20.

jnidable Power; and are so directly levelled against the most valuable and darling Interests and Privileges ofthig Nation, that we must determine, either tamely to submit to the peremptory and unjust Demands of the King of Spain, in giving up Gibraltar, and patiently to acquiesce in the Emperor's usurped and extended Exercise of Trade and Commerce; or must resolve to be in a Condition to do ourselves Justice, and to defend our undoubted Rights, against these reciprocal Engagements, entered into in Defiance and Violation of all national Faith, and the most solemn Treaties.

I have likewise received Informations, from different Parts, on which I can intirely depend, That the placing the Pretender upon the Throne of this Kingdom is one of the Articles of the secret Engagements: And if Time shall evince, that the giving up the Trade of this Nation to one Power, and Gibraltar anc| Portmahon to another, is made the Price and Reward of imposing upon this Kingdom a Popish Pretender; what an Indignation must this raise in the Breast of every Profestant Briton I

Nor were these fatal Combinations confined to those Parts of the World alone; but they extended themselves into Russia: And had not the Designs of that Court against some of their Neighbours been prevented by the seasonable Arrival of our Fleet in those Seas, a Way bad been opened for invading these Kingdoms, and giving a powerful Assistance to any Attempt to be made from other Quarters.

Such Circumstances would not suffer me, and my Allies, among whom there has been, and is, the most perfect Harmony, Union, and Concert, to be idle Spectators, and regardless of our own Safety, and the common Cause of Europe: For which Purpose, his most Christian Majesty has been at a great Expence, this last Year, in augmenting his Forces; and the States General, sensible of the imminent Danger, have not only acceded to the defensive Alliance concluded at Hanover, but have come to strong and seasonable Resolutions for an extraordinary Augmentation of their Forces, both by Sea and Land: The Accession of the Crown of Sweden is in such a Forwardness, and the Negociations with the Crown of Denmark are so far advanced, that we may reasonably depend upon the Success and good Effect of them.

ifhifr

708 170 Januarii. 1726.

This short View of the present Posture of Affairs will,

I am confident, not only secure to n\e the Support and Assistance of my Parliament in carrying on this great and necessary Work, in Conjunction with my Allies, but justify the Measures hitherto taken, and the Expences already made.

The Confidence you reposed in me last Year, has been made use of for the Benefit of the Publick: And as the chief Article of Exceedings has, by my equipping, and sending to Sea, Three considerable Squadrons, fallen upon the Head of the Navy, I am persuaded the Necessity of the Services, and the Security, Advantage, and Glory, that has accrued to this Nation from those Squadrons, will sufficiently speak for themselves, as long as both Friends and Foes, with Joy or Concern, confess they have seen and felt the Effects of the naval Power of Great Britain.

It is not to be wondered at, that the Princes engaged in these Enterprizes arc very much disturbed to see their Projects rendered abortive: The King of Spain, impatient of the Disappointments he has met with, can no longer disguise that Enmity to us, which for some time he has only waited for a favourable Opportunity to declare: He has now ordered his Minister residing here to depart immediately from this Country, leaving a Memorial that islittle short of a Declaration of War; wherein he again demands, and insists upon, the Restitution of Gibraltar: He does not himself deny the offensive Alliance, nor his Engagements to support the Ostend Company: He makes my recalling those Squadrons, which his Conduct had put me under a Necessity of sending to the If'cst Indies, and the Coast of Spain, the Condition of any further Correspondence between the Two Crowns; and, supposing the Continuance of my Fleets Abroad to be actual Hostilities, threatens to repel them with Force, to the utmost of his Power:

Blit, not content with these Menaces, Insults, and Infractions of Trcaties, his Catholick Majesty is now making Preparations to attack and besiege Gibraltar; and, in order to carry on that Service, or to cover another Design, has assembled a great Body of Troops in that Neighbourhood: But as the present State and Condition of that Garison,\vith the Reinforcements I have ordered thither, give me little Cause to apprehend, or my Enemies to hope for Success in that Undertaking; the certain and undoubted Intelligence 1 have, that it is now resolved to attempt an Invasion upon these Kingdoms, in favour of the Pretender, by an Embarkation from the Coasts of Spain, gives me reason to believe, that, though the Siege of Gibraltar may probably be undertaken, the publick, avowed, and immense, Preparations for that Purpose are chiefly calculated to amuse the World, and to disguise the intended Invasion; which, I am surely informed, has been for some time agreed to be the first Step and Beginning of the long-premeditated Rupture.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

These Considerations must awaken in you all such a Sense of our common and immediate Danger, as will,

I doubt not, inspire you with a Zeal and Chearfnlness in raising the Supplies necessary for the Defence of your Country, and for making good our Engagements with our Allies.

I received too much Satisfaction from the Happiness of my People in their full Enjoyment, and future Prospect, of Peace, Ease, and Prosperity, not to be sensibly affected with these new Convulsions; and the unavoidable Necessity I am under of asking larger Supplies of my People, and of desiring to be enabled to make such an Augmentation of my Forces, by Sea and Land, as the present Exigency of Affairs requires.

I will order the proper Estimates to be laid before yon, and such Treaties as i have made with foreign Princes for the Hire of foreign Troops: And as the Expence I was, last Year, in a particular manner, entrusted to make, has amounted to no considerable Sum, and the publick Utility may again require the likeSeryices to be performed, I

hope you will again repose the same Trust and Confidence in me.

It is with great Pleasure that I see the Time so near approaching, when such a considerable Addition will be made to the Sinking Fund: Let all that wish well to the Peace and Quiet of my Government, have the Satisfaction to see, that our present Necessities shall make no Interruption in the Progress of that desirable Work of gradually discharging the National Debt: I hope therefore you will make a Provision for the immediate Application of the Produce of the Sinking Fund to the Uses for which it was so wisely contrived, and to which it now stands appropriated.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have had no Thoughts of making any Acquisitions to any Parts of my Dominions: My whole C^re and Concern has been, to preserve and maintain the undoubted Rights and Privileges of my People: And therefore all my Measures have been preventive and defensive: But, such Endeavours being now rendered impracticable, vigorous Resolutions, and a speedy Execution of them, can alone put an effectual End to the Dangers that surround us: However hazardous and desperate the Enterprizes formed against us may appear to be; your being assured, that they are resolved upon, will, I am persuaded, be sufficient to prevail upon you to put yourselves in a Condition to resist and defeat them.

If preserving a due Balance of Power in Europe; if defending the Possessions of the Crown of Great Britain, of infinite Advantage and Security to ourTrade and Commerce; if supporting that Trade and Commerce against dangerous and unlawful Encroachments; and if the present Establishment, the Religion, Liberties, and Properties, of a Protestant People; are any longer Considerations worthy of the Care and Attention of a British Parliament; I nee,d say no more to incite my loyal and faithful Houses of Parliament to exert themselves in the Defence of all that is dear and valuable to them.

A Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to his *lie Majesty, to return him the Thanks of thia House for k ne his most gracious Speech from the Throne; to acknow-lege his Majesty's Goodness in acquainting his Parliament with the several Proceedings and Alliances entered into between the Emperor and the King of Spain, giving such just Cause of Jealousy to the neighbouring Princes and States, so formidable, and destructive of the true Balance of Power in Europe, and striking at the Foundation of the most valuable Privileges and Interests of the Subjects of his Majesty, and those of his Allies; to declare the Resentment of the Commons of Great Britain at the unjust Demand of the King of Spain for the Restitution of Gibraltar, and the unwarrantable Usurpation of the Emperor in erecting and carryingon th eOstend Trade, and their mutual Obligations to support each other in these unjustifiable Attempts and Undertakings; but, above all, to express our highest Indignation at the Resolutions and Engagements entered into for attempting to place the Pretender on the Throne of these Kingdoms; to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House for his great Care in strengthening his Alliances, and for employing his Royal Fleets so usefully for the Security, Advantage, and Glory, of this Nation; and, as this House cannot but look upon the Measures and Resolutions taken in Opposition to, and in Defiance of, most solemn Treaties, as tending to an immediate Rupture, humbly to desire his Majesty, That he will forthwith give the necessary Orders for putting this Kingdom into a Posture of Defence; and to assure his Majesty, That this House will not only chearfully and effectually raise the Supplies necessary for the present Exigency of Affairs, but will stand by, and support, his Majesty in making good his Engagements with his Allies, in preserving the BalanceofPower in Europe, in defending the Possessions of the Crown of Great Britain, in supporting the Trade of this Nation against all unjustifiable Encroachments,

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm, hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be fyvolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, in case it shall appear any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices; this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof; this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any l^ord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is sitting: And that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker's Cham-

ber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House; and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Anns attending this House, do take care to clear the Speaker's Chamber, every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is sitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning to Four in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and JPest minster-hall, shall be kept free and opipi; and that no Obstruction be made, by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passages of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster: And that he do see the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House: And that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Beverley A PETITION of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Ca-Creek, Arc. pital Burgesses, of the Corporation of Beverley,

in the East Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Town of Beverley hath heretofore had a considerable Trade, by means of a Creek, or Cut, called Beverley Beck, formerly made from the said Town to the River Hull, which runs into the Humber, for the Passage of Ships, or other Vessels, to and from the said Town; and that, likewise, there bath been divers publick Staiths, or Landing-places, adjoining the said River and Beck, for the more easy and convenient Lading and Unlading of all Sorts of Godds, Wares, and Merchandizes, to the great Benefit and Advantage of the said Town, and Country adjacent: And that the said Creek, or Beck, for want of a sufficient Fund to defray the necessary Expences thereof, cannot be kept open; but is choaked up, and the Staiths very much out of Repair, and thereby rendered useless for the Purposes aforesaid: And also, that the several Roads, or Ways, leading to the River Hull, are unpassable, to the great Decay of the Trade of the Town; notwithstanding the Corporation, in Ease of the Inhabitants, have expended great Sums of Money in cleansing and repairing the said Becks, Staiths, and Roads; w hereby the Revenues of the Corporation are so exhausted, that they are unable to defray the necessary Expences of the same: And praying, That the House will give Leave to bring in a Bill to impower the Petitioners to raise Money to enable them to cleanse, scour, deepen, and w iden, the said Beck; and to repair the said Staiths, Roads, and Ways, in such manner as to the House shall seem proper.

Mr. Onslow reported from the Committee appointed Address cm Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to his the K,nos Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address *peec accordingly; which they had directed him to" report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our humblest Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

The Communication which your Majesty has been pleased to make of the Proceedings and Transactions in Europe for some time past, and of the Engagements entered into between the Emperor and the King of Spain, is an Instance of your Majesty's singular Goodness, in being as desirous to give your People all reasonable Satisfaction, as you have ever been solicitous for their Good and Welfare.

We are very sensible of the fatal Tendency of the sudden and unaccountable Conjunction between those Two Crowns: And as this Nation has always looked with jealous Eyes upon the very Beginning of every Attempt made by their Neighbours to establish a Commerce, at the Hazard, and to the Prejudice, of our undoubted Rights and Privileges; we cannot but he greatly alarmed to see these Encroachments upon our Trade, and notorious.

71$

180 — 190 — 20° Januarii. 1726.

rious Infractions of Treaties, accompanied with a Scheme of Greatness that lays the Foundation of a most exorbitant Power; which, if not timely opposed and withstood with Vigour and Resolution, may become formidable to all Europe, and enable the Aggressors, without Control'll, to maintain their unwarrantable Attempts:

Nor can we at all doubt of the Spirit and Design of this new Friendship and Alliance, when we see it cemented, by mutual Obligations, for supporting#one of the contracting Powers in the unjustifiable and usurped Exercise of the Ostend Trade, at the same time that a peremptory Demand is made, and insisted upon, by the other, for the Restitution of Gibraltar; a Place of such Importance to the Trade of this Kingdom:

Hut the Consideration that creates the highest Resentment in your faithful Commons, is, to see that, whenever the Ambition of foreign Princes leads them to aspire and grasp at exorbitant Power, or to acquire, and possess themselves of, any valuable Rights and Privileges belonging to the Subjects of your Majesty, and your Allies; all Guarantees, and the most solemn Engagements of Faith and Gratitude to your Majesty, purchased by the Blood and Treasure of this Nation, are cancelled, and forgot: And it is vainly imagined, that your Majesty must either tamely submit, and patiently acquiesce under the greatest Indignities and Injuries to your Crown and People, or be insulted with Menaces and Projects in favour of a Popish Pretender:

But your Majesty's loyal, faithful, and affectionate, Subjects the Commons of Great Britain, sensible of the inestimable Blessings they enjoy under your Majesty's most gracious and happy Government, have too great a Regard to the Honour and Dignity of your Crown, and too much Abhorrence and Detestation of the abjured Pretender, to suffer these vain Threats and Terrors to have auv ill Effect upon their Minds, or Deliberations.

It is with Indignation that we see this injurious Treatment, and these provoking Insults; and it is with an unshaken Fidelity and Resolution that we are determined, with our Lives and Fortunes, to stand by and support your Majesty against all your Enemies.

We must, at the same time, with all Gratitude, acknowledge your Majesty's Wisdom and Vigilance, in strengthening yourself with the Alliance of Powers united in Interest, and best able to withstand the impending Danger, and to support the common Cause of Europe: We see, with the greatest Satisfaction, the Naval Power of Great Britain appearing, in distant Regions, in its proper Lustre; so usefully and wisely employed to carry Safety and Protection to your own Subjects, and to your Allies; and to curb and restrain the boasted Projects of the Disturbers of the Peace of Europe:

And as we cannot but look upon the Measures and Resolutions concerted and taken in Opposition to, and in Defiance of, the most solemn Treaties, as tending to an immediate Rupture; we humbly beseech your Majesty, That you will be pleased forthwith to give the necessary Orders for putting this Kingdom into a Posture of Defence; and we assure your Majesty, That we will not only chearfully and effectually raise the Supplies necessary for the present Exigency of Affairs, but will support your Majesty in making good your Engagements with your Allies; in preserving the Balance of Power in Europe; id defending the present Possessions of the Crown of Great Britain; in supporting the Trade of this Nation against all unjustifiable and pernicious Encroachments; and in defeating and confounding all Attempts that shall be made in favour of the Pretender, and for the Destruction of our Religion, Liberties, and Properties:

And that all, who wish well to the Peace and Quiet of your Majesty s Government, may have the Satisfaction to sec,1 that our present Necessities shall make no Interruption in the Progress of that desirable Work of gradually discharging the National Debt, we will consider of the most proper Methods for immediately applying the Produce of the Sinking Fund to the Uses for which it was so wisely contrived, and to which it stands now appropriated; and will repose such a Trust and Conti-

denccVm your Majesty as the publick Utility shall require, and as your Majesty shall find reasonable and necessary for carrying on the great Work in which your Majesty is engaged, for the Interest and Security of your People, and the common Cause of Europe.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Gentlemen,

I return you my Thanks for this very dutiful and loyal Address. The just Sense you have expressed of the present Posture of Affairs in Europe, and the hearty Assurances you have given me of your Support, in detending my Possessions, and the Rights and Privileges of my People, as they are Evidences of your known Zealand Affection to my Person and Government, I am persuaded they w ill confirm the Spirit and Vigour of my Allies; ^nd convince my Enemies how vain and ill-grounded all their Expectations arc, of being able to succeed in ^ny Attempts to disturb the Peace of Europe, and in offering Injuries and Insults to this Nation.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Farrer took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Farrer reported from the Committee, That they had come to some Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Mr. farrer also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, That they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Copies of Four Instruments belonging to the Accession of the States General to the Treaty of Hanover, all dated at the Hague, Ninth of August 1726; with the Translations of them:

And the Titles of the said Translations were read.

The said Translations are as follow; viz.

WHEREAS their Majesties the King of Great Britain, the most Christian King, and the King of Prussia, have thought fit, as well for tying closer the Bands of that strict Union which subsists between them, as for the Security of their Kingdoms and Dominions; and likewise for the Preservation of the publick Peace and Tranquillity, to make an Alliance together;whereof the Treaty was concluded at Hanover, the Third Day of September of the Y'ear 1725 last past; together with Three separate Articles; all which have been communicated to their High Mightinessss the Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, by the Marquis De Fenelon, Ambassador of France; by Mr. Finch, Envoy Extraordinary of Great Britain; and by Monsieur De Meynertshagen, Envoy Extraordinary of the King of Prussia; who jointly, in the Name of the Kings their Masters, invited the said Lords the States General to accede to that Treaty, and the separate Articles, in conformity to what they had agreed upon in the Seventh Article of the same Treaty; which, with the separate Articles, are here inserted, Word for Word:

Their Majesties the King of Great Britain, the most Christian King, and the King of Prussia, having observed, with Pleasure, howr much the strict Union subsisting between them has contributed not only to the Happiness of their ow n Kingdoms and Subjects, but also to the publick Good and Tranquillity; being likewise persuaded, that there is not a more proper Means of secu ring and strengthening the said Advantages, against all Events ;*]iat may happen, than to cultivate the said Union more and more, and to make it indissoluble; and having maturely considered all the Treaties that subsist betw een their said Majesties, from which they declare that they do not intend anyway to derogate by this present Treaty; they have thought lit to take, beforehand, new Measures, in Case any Disturbances should arise in Europe, by agreeing among themselves, upon what may be necessary, not only for the

Second separate Article.

If, out of Resentment on account of Succours which his most Christian Majesty may furnish to his Britamiick Majesty, and to his Prussian Majesty, to secure them from the Disturbance which they might suffer in the Territories they possess, Jthe Empire should declare War against his said most Christian Majesty; as, in this Case, such a Declaration would not less affect the most Serene King of Great Britain, and the most Serene King of Prnssia} whose Interests would be the Occasion of such a War, than his most Christian Majesty; they not only will forbear to furnish their Quota in Troops, or in any other kind of Succours whatever; even though their said Bri-tannick and Prussian Majesties should not be comprehended and named in the Declaration of War that the Empire should make against France; but they will even act in Concert with his most Christian Majesty, until the Peace disturbed on that Occasion he restored; his said Britan-mick Majesty expressly promising, moreover, to execute, in Such Case, as in all others, the Treaties he has concluded vrith his most Christian Majesty, who, on his Part, promises faithfully to observe the same.

This separate Article shall be of the same Force, as if it had been inserted, W ord for Word, in the Treaty concluded and signed this Day: It shall be ratified in the same manner, and the Ratifications of it shall be exchanged at the same time, as the Treaty.

In Witness whereof, we whose Names are subscribed, by virtue of the full Pow ers this Day communicated to each other, have signed this Article; and have set thereto the Seals of our Arms. Done at Hanover, the 3d of September 1725.

Third separate Article.

If it should happen, that, notwithstanding his most Christian Majesty's firm Resolution to observe exactly all his Treaties with regard to the Empire, in those Things In which there has been no Derogation therefrom by the present Treaty, if it should he attempted on the Part of the Empire, to take any Resolution against France, to the Prgudice oftlie General Guaranty of Possessions, as it is stipulated by the Treaty signed this Day; his Bi'itanniek Majesty, and his Prussian Majesty, promise, in such case;, to employ their good Offices, Credit, and Authority, the most effectually they shall be able, either by their own Votes, and those of the Princes in Friendship with them, at the Diet, or by all other proper Means, to prevent any thing being done contrary* thereto: Arid if, against all Expectation* and notwithstanding all their Endeavours, War should be declared ‘against France, on the Part of the Empire; although, in this case, the same being no longer a defensive one, they might not, by its Constitutions, be obliged to furnish any Quota; yet* to remove all Doubt among their said Majesties, if they should think they could not be dispensed with from performing their Duty, as Members of that Body, their said Britdmnick and Prussian Majesties do reserve to themselves the Liberty of furnishing their Quotas of Foot, or of Horse, of their own Troops, or of such as they shall take Into their Pay from any other Prince, at their own Choice: Yet their Britannick and Prussian Majesties shall not, on account of Such furnishing ‘ their Quotafe, be Vol. 20.

deemed to have acted contrary to the Treaty signed this Accession of Day; which shall continue in all its Force: Their Bri-tannick and Prussian Majesties do promise not to furnish, of Hanover/ in such Case, any other, or greater, Number of Troops against his most Christian Majesty, than w hat they are obliged to find for their Quota; and that they will, iu other respects, perform, in the Cases foregoing, their Engagements to his said-most Christian Majesty; who, on his Part, shall not, on account of the said Quota, exercise any Hostility against the Territories and Subjects of the said most Serene King of Great Britain, and the said most Serene King of Prussia, in the Empire, or elsewhere; nor demand, or pretend to, any Contributions, Forage,

Quarters, Passage, or other Things, at the Charge of the said Countries and Territories, on any Pretence whatsoever: In like manner it shall also not be lawful for the said Territories, Places, Countries, and Subjects, to furnish any of the said Things to the Enemies of his most Christian Majesty; who does also oblige himself, and promise, on his Part, that if, in the Empire, Resolutions should come to be taken, like to those that are mentioned in this Article, to the Prejudice of the Kings of Great Britain and Prussia, his most Christian Majesty will openly take their Part; and will not fail to assist them, with all necessary Vigour, in pursuance of this Treaty, until the Disturbances, Wrongs, and Infractions, shall entirely cease.

This separate Article shall be of the same Force, as if it had been inserted, Word for Word, in the Treaty this Day concluded and signed: It shall be ratified in the same manner, and the Ratifications of it shall be exchanged at the same time, as the Treaty.

And whereas the said Lords the States General, after having seen and examined this Treaty, and these separate Articles, have shewn themselves extremely sensible of the Honour which their said Majesties have done them by so ready and obliging an Invitation to accede to thisAlliance; and as they acknowledge, at the same time, the Care they have taken in making this Treaty, as well for the Preservation of the publick Quiet in general, without w'hich that of their Repeblick cannot be secured, as, in particular, for the Maintenance of their Commerce, without which it cannot subsist; and as they have added, that they are fully convinced, that the Aim of this Alliance does not at all tend to the hurting, in the least, any preceding Treaty, or Alliance, contracted either between the high Contractors hereof, or between them, or any one of them, with other Princes, or States, but that the Intention rather is to maintain and corroborate them; and that the grand Aim of this Alliance tends only to the binding themselves more closely together, without offending any one wrho* soever* for the Guaranty, Protection, and Maintenance^ of all the Territories, Countries, and Towns, as well within Europe as without, which each of the Allies shall be actually in Possession of at the time of the signing this Alliance ;* and likewise of the Rights, Immunities, and Advantages, and, particularly, of those which relate to Commerce, both within Europe also, and without, which edeh of the Allies enjoys at the time of the signing this Accession:

Moreover, the said Lords the States General, being firmly persuaded, that, by acceding to the said Treaty of Hanover, that it is not required of them to charge themselves with the general Guaranty of the Treaties of Westphalia and Oliva, -whereof mention is made in the 5th Article of the Treaty of Hanover, and in the First of the separate Articles; in which general Guaranty they never were engaged; but that their Guaranty, in this respeefy extends only to the Rights and Possessions which the high 8 X Allies,

sion of Allies, or any one of them, have acquired by those Trea-Stales Gene- an(j wf1jc[1 they enjoy at the time of signing, and of Ilanovtr!^ *n Case of being troubled in the said Possessions and Rights; and that this is the intention of their said Majesties:

As to the Business of Thorn, whereof mention is made in the First of the separate Articles of the Treaty of Iiam-ver, they engage themselves only to employ, jointly with the high Contractors, their friendly Offices for obtaining a reasonable Satisfaction and Reparation of the Infractions which might he made in the Treaty of Oliva; and in case that these friendly Offices should be without Effect, and it were found necessary to do something more, then they shall, in that Case, have a full Liberty in their Deliberations, without being obliged to any thing more than good Offices; unless they give a new Consent thereto.

In fine, since this Alliance has for Aim, among others, the establishing an entire Confidence between the contracting Parties, the Lords the States General suppose, that the Allies will mutually communicate, in all Confidence, their Thoughts concerning the Ways and Means, which shall be judged the most effectual, in case of Need, for preserving and maintaining the Possessions and Rights above mentioned* as well with respect to Commerce, as otherwise, both within Europe, and without.

And whereas, upon a firm Persuasion and Confidence, that this is the true Aim and Intention of their said Majesties, the said Lords the States General, to give a Mark of their Desire of uniting themselves strictly with their Majesties, and of the high Esteem they have for their Friendship and Alliance, have resolved to accede to the Treaty, and to the separate Articles here above inserted; and to that Purpose have named the Sicurs ChristianCharles Baron of Lintelo, Lord of Eshe, Bailiff of Lockum, and ^. That the Lords the States General shall accede, as the said Deputies and Plenipotentiaries have declared that they do accede, in their Name, and on their Part, to the said Treaty, and separate Articles, obliging them, towards their said Majesties, to every thing contained therein, entirely in the same manner, as if they had contracted with them from the Beginning:

And that their said Majesties, owning their Aim and Intention to be such as is before expressed, shall accept the Accession of their High Mightinesses; so as the said Ambassador, and Ministers Plenipotentiaries, have declared, that they accept this Accession in the Name, and on the Part, of their said Majesties, obliging them, towards their High Mightinesses, to every thing that is contained inth e said Treaty, and separate Articles, entirely in the same man-

As the Succours, which their High Mightinesses are to give in case of Need, could not be regulated in this Treaty; it is agreed, that they shall be Four thousand Foot, and One thousand Horse.

For explaining the Sixth Article of the Treaty; it is declared, That after the Expiration of the Fifteen Years therein mentioned, the Whole shall return to the Terms of the preceding Treaties which shall subsist between the high Contractors; and, particularly, to the Terms of the Tripple Alliance of the Year 1717.

This present Treaty, for the Accession of the States General, shall be approved and ratified by their Majesties the King of Great Britain, the most Christian King, and the King of Prussia, and by the Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, and the Ratifications shall be delivered, here at the Hague, in the Space of Two Months, from the Day of the Signing of these Presents; or sooner, if possible.

In Witness whereof, we, the underwritten, appointed Plenipotentiaries for the Purpose of these Presents; and provided with full Powers from their Majesties the King of Great Britain, the most Christian King, and the King of Prussia, and from the said Lords the States General; have signed the present Treaty; and have set thereunto the Seals of our Coats of Arms. Done at the Hague, the 9th of August 1726.

Separate Article concerning the Commerce from the

Austrian Lore Countries to the Indies.;

Though it be clear and uncontestable, that their High Mightinesses the Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries have, by the 5th and 6th Articles of the Treaty 0iMunster, of the Year 1648, between Spain, and the Republick.of the United Provinces, acquired a Right, that excludes the Subjects of the Austrian Low Countries, as likewise those of every other Country, which then made a Part of the Spanish Monarchy, from the Navigation and Commerce to the Indies, within the Limits of the Privileges, or Grants, which the said Lords the States General have given to their Companies of the East and West Indies; and consequently, that this RighJ; is plainly comprehended in the Guaranty iof Rights, ,tp which the Allies have mutually bound themselves by the Second Article of the Treaty concluded at Hanover ~ the Third of September 1725; nevertheless, to remove all Occasion of Doubt and Scruple thereupon, the under* written Ambassador, and Envoy Extraordinary, and Plenipotentiaries, of their Britamuck and most Christian Majesties, at the Requisition of the underwritten Deputies, and Plenipotentiaries, of their High Mightinesses, have willingly declared, as they do declare, by these Presents, in the Name, and on the Part, of their said Majesties, That the abovesaid Right, resulting from the 5th and 6th Articles of the Treaty of Mwister, is comprehended among the Rights which the Allies guaranty in the Second Article of the Treaty of Hanover', and that on account of the Use of this Right, or in Hatred of this Alliance; any Disturbance should happen, and that his Imperial Majesty, contrary to all Expectation, would suspend, or retain, the Payment of the Subsidies due to the Republick for the Maintenance of their Troops in the Places of the Barrier, or the Payment of the Interest and Principal placed by Mortgage on divers Funds assigned by his Imperial Majesty for the Security of that Payment, pr would make use of any other kind of Reprisals, or Ways of Force; The Deputies of the Lords the States General of the United Provinces having communicated to the Ministers of their Majesties the King of Great Britain, the most Christian King, and the King of Prussia, the Resolution taken by their High Mightinesses to accede to the Treaty of Hanover, upon the Invitation which had been made them, for that Purpose, by the said Ministers, on the Part of their said Majesties; and having likewise added, that they, the Deputies, were provided with a full Power; and that they were ready to proceed to the concluding and signing the Treaty, and separate Articles, made upon this Accession; Mr Fim h. Plenipotentiary from his Britarmick Majesty, and the Marquis de Fenelon, Plenipotentiary from his most Christian Majesty, declared, That they likewise were provided with full Powers; and that they were ready to conclude and sign: But the Sieur de Meynertzhagen, Minister from his Prussian Majesty, having said, That he had not yet received the Orders, nor the full Power, from the King his Master, for the same Purpose, the Ministers Plenipotentiaries from their Britannick and most Christian Majesties, as also the Deputies Plenipotentiaries of the Lords the States General, considering that there was no more time to be lost; and that all further Delay, which should be given to the perfecting the Accession of the Republic^ to the Treaty of Hanover, could not but be dis* advantageous to the Aim proposed in this Treaty; and, at the same time, having no room to doubt but that his Majesty the King of Prussia will likewise authorize his Minister to sign the Treaty of Accession, and the separate Articles; it is on this Consideration, and in this certain Hope, that they have proceeded to sign, the Treaty of Accession, and the separate Articles, leaving a Plage open for the Minister of his Majesty the King of Prussia toiign in the same manner, as soon as he shall have received his full Power: However, it has beep agreed and determined, by this separate Article, That if, contrary to all Expectation, his Prussian Majesty did not take that Resolution, the said Treaty of Accession, and the separate Articles, should, nevertheless, have their Effect, and be executed by the contracting Powers, in all their Clauses, in the same manner as it has been stipulated; and that the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged at the time appointed.

Declaration.

WHEREAS, in the Fourth Article of the Treaty signed at HanoVer, the 3d of September 1725, between their Majesties the King of Great Britain, the most Christian King, and the King of Prussia, among other Cases therein mentioned, there is something said concerning the examining w'hat may be proper to maintain the Balance of Europe, which it is so necessary to preserve, for the Good of the General Peace; the Deputies of the States General of the United Provinces, with the Consent of the Ministers Plenipotentiaries of the Three contracting Powders, have made a Reserve, that their Majesties finding it necessary to concert together, and with the said Lords the States General, upon such Points* whose Objects should be the maintaining the Balance in Europe, the Lords the States General shall continue to have the same Liberty, with respect to every thing that might be proposed to them upon that Head, as t$ey bad before, their Accession to the said

7H ^4° — 2 5° — 2 A. 1716*

said Treaty; without being bound, by their Accession* to take part in the Measures which they should not consent to.

This Declaration shall be ratified in the same manner, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged at the same time, with those of the Treaty.

In Witness whereof, we, the Underwritten, being appointed Plenipotentiaries by virtue of the full Powers from their Majesties the King of Great Britain, the most Christian King, and the King of Prussia, and from the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, have signed the present Declaration; and have caused the Seals of our Coats of Arms to be set thereunto. Done at the Hague, the 9th of August 1726.

Resolved, That is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight hundred eighty-five thousand Four hundred Ninety-four Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the (jlharge of the said Twenty-six thousand Three hundred Eighty-three effective Men, for Guards, Garisons, and other his Majesty's Land Forces in Great Britain, Guernsey, and Jersey, for the Year 1727.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding One hundred fifty-seven thousand Six hundred Thirty-seven Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Five Pence Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining his Majesty's Forces, and Garisons in the Plantations, Minorca and Gibraltar; and for Provisions for the Garisons at Annapolis Royal, Placentia, and Gibraltar; for the Year 1727.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirteen thousand Seven hundred and Fifty Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Five Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying several extraordinary Expences and Services incurred, and not provided for by Parliament.
