Treaties with the Land-

Air. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had received his Majesty's Commands Cawct Ac*6 ,fty before t'1*s House, Copy of a Convention between

' his Majesty and the La*ndgrave of Hesse Cassel, dated

the 12th of March 172^:

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer likewise acquainted the House, That the said Convention referring to a former Convention between Great Britain, the States General, and the Landgrave of Ilesse Cassel, dated the Thirteenth of February 170L his Majesty had commanded him to lay the same before the Ifouse:

And he presented the said Conventions to the House, together with Translations of them:

And the Titles of the said Conventions were read.

The Translations of the said Conventions arse as fol- lows; viz.

WHEREAS the underwritten the Alajor General de Diemar had, on the Twelfth of the Alonth of January last past, N. S. made and signed at Hclvoet Slays, a Declaration, in the Name of his Highness the Landgrave of Hesse Cassel, concerning a Body of Troops to be furnished, in case of Need, to his Majesty the King of Great Britain, of the Tenor following:

His most Serene Highness Monsigneur the Landgrave of Hesse Cassel, my Master, has impowered me to sign, and give, a Declaration, whereby he obliges himself to hold in Readiness a Body of Troops, of Twelve thousand Men, for the Service of his Britannick Majesty; that is to say, of Eight thousand Foot, and of Four thousand Horse; to be employed, when his said Majesty shall require it, in all Places where there shall be Occasion, and w here the Case of the defensive Alliance, lately concluded at Hanover, shall want it: But, as his most Serene Highness actually, and at present, has not a Body of Troops of Twelve thousand Men effective; and as therefore, to have that Number complete, he will not only be obliged to raise more than Three thousand Foot, and above Two thousand Horse, and to furnish Horses for the Troopers, who really have none at all, but likewise to maintain the abovesaid Body of Troops, at his own Expence, for the Space of Two whole Years; his Britannick Majesty not being willing, at this present time, to take upon himself the Charge of Subsidies, and of the Pay of these Troops; iiis most Serene Highness promises himself, That his said Britannick Majesty will furnish him with the Money which he shall want for the said Levies, and Horses to remount the Troopers; that is, with the Sum of One hundred and twenty-five thousand Pounds Sterling; of which Sum his most Serene Highness expects that Seventy-five thousand Pounds shall be paid when this Declaration shall besigned; and the other Fifty thousand Pounds in the Alonth of February 1727, unless the said Body of Troops shall be wanted before: I11 that Case, the said Sums shall be paid to his most Serene Highness, at the least, Two Months before the said Troops are to begin their March.

When the abovesaid Troops shall enter into the Service of his Britannick Majesty, they shall be under his Cora-Vol. 20.

"Which^Declaration having been afterwards accepted and approved, the 25th of the said Month of January, at Cassel, by his Highness the said Landgrave; his Majesty the King of Great Britain, approving the Conditions specified in the above-mentioned Declaration, has ordered his underwritten Privy Counsellor, and Principal Secretary of State, the Lord Viscount Tcncnshend, to enter into a Negotiation with the said Alajor General Dicmar thereupon; and to draw up a Convention, in due Form, on the Foot of the said Declaration; who, having conferred together, have, in the Name of the said King and Landgrave, agreed upon the following Articles:

His Highness the Landgrave of Hesse Cassel shall hold in Readiness, for the Service of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, a Body of Troops, of Twelve thousand Men; that is to say, of Eight thousand Foot, and Four thousand Horse; which Body shall be employed, when his said Majesty shall require it, in all Places where there shall be Occasion; and whenever the Case of the defensive Alliance, concluded at Hanover the Third Day of September last, shall want it.

IE

As his said Highness has not a Body of Troops, of Twelve thousand effective Men, at present on Foot, he shall raise immediately what is wanting to make such a Body complete, and in a Condition to march: He shall likewise maintain the said Body of Troops, at his ow n Expence, for the Space of Two whole Years, to be always ready to take the Field at all times, when his said Majesty shall require it, during the said Term.

As the Alinister of the said Landgrave has represented, That his said Highness, his Alaster, to make the said Body complete, as abovesaid, must raise more than Three thousand Foot, and above Two thousand Horse; and must also furnish Horses for the most Part of the Troopers, who are not provided with them; his Majesty the King of Great Britain, in Consideration of the very great Expences which the said Landgrave must be at to make the Levies, and buy the Horses for remounting the Troopers, as abovesaid, and for the Maintenance of the said Body during the time that it is not employed in his Service, will pay the said Landgrave the Sum of One hundred and twenty-five thousand Pounds Sterling, at Two Payments; that is to say, Seventy-five thousand Pounds Sterling after the Ratification of this present Convention, and the other Fifty thousand Pounds Sterling in the Month of February 1727.

IV.

But, in case his Majesty the King of Great Britain should have Occasion for the said Body of Troops before the abovesaid Month of February, his Majesty will pay his Highness the Landgrave the said Sum of Fifty thousand Pounds Sterling, at least, Two Months before the said Troops are to begin their March.

When the abovesaid Troops shall enter into the Service of his said Majesty the King of Great Britain, they shall be under his Command, and intirely at his Disposal, to be employed where the Necessity of his Affairs, and w'here

VIII.

This Convention shall be ratified, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged, on each Side, as soon as may be after the Signing of these Presents.

In Witness whereof, we the underwritten Ministers of the said King and Landgrave, being sufficiently authorized for that Purpose, have signed this present Convention; and have put the Seals of our Coats of Arms thereunto. Done at Westminster, the 12th Day of March 172^.

Convention made between his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High Mightinesses the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, on One Part; and his most Serene Highness the Landgrave of Hesse Cassel\ on the other Part; concerning a Body of Nine thousand Men, which his said Highness has promised to give for the Good of the common Cause.

I.

vr:

In time of War, the said Six thousand Men shall be paid in Money, for Waggons, and other Equipages, what is paid by their High Mightinesses to their own Troops; and, besides, they shall enjoy all the same Advantages in general, which the said Troops of their High Mightinesses enjoy.

VII.

In case that after an Accommodation, or a Peace made, his Majesty of Great Britain, and their High Mightinesses, design to send back the said Six thousand Men, his said Highness shall have Notice thereof Two Months before they begin their March to return home.

yin.

In case, as abovesaid, that the said Troops are sent back, or recalled; his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High Mightinesses, shall pay the said Troops what shall be due to them as well on Account of Pay, as of Waggon-money.

IK.

It shall be left to the Disposal of his Highness, in case of any great and evident Danger, or if he should be attacked in his own Dominions, thereupon to recal the said Troops; and they shall be sent back to him immediately, and without any Contradiction.

X.

When his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High Mightinesses, after the War is ended, shall send back the said Six thousand Men; in that case, they shall have the Pay of One long Month for their Return, and their Carriage; but, in case his Highness recals them before the Ratification of the Treaty of Peace, they shall not be paid any more than the Remainder of the Pay of that Month w herein they are recalled.

Sir Charles Hotham reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Capital Burgesses, of the Corporation of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table 2 Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition: And,

To prove the Allegation thereof, the Petitioners called Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Christopher Northern and Mr. John Codgell: Who were severally examined; and said, That the Town of Beverley had formerly a considerable Trade by means of a Creek, or Cut, called Becerley-beck, made from the Town to the River Hull, which River runs into the Humber, for the Passage of Ships and Vessels to and from that Town; but the said Creek is now choaked up, and cannot be cleansed, and kept open, for want \>f a sufficient Fund to defray the Expences thereof:

And they said, That there hath been divers publick Landing-places, or Staiths, adjoining to the River and Beck, for the convenient lading and unlading of Goods and Merchandizes, for the Advantage of the Town, and Country adjacent; but the said Staiths are now so much out of Repair, that they are rendered useless:

The same Witnesses, being examined as to the Condition of the Roads leading to die River Hull, said, That they are very bad; and, in the Winter-season, impassable:

That the same Witnesses gave Evidence, That the Corporation, in Ease of the Inhabitants, had expended great Sums of Money in cleansing and repairing the Creek, or Beck, and Staiths; and in amending the Roads aforesaid; and although they had been at so much Expence, yet the said Beck cannot be cleansed, deepened, and widened, so as to be useful; nor can the Staiths and Roads be effectually repaired, and made commodious; without some other Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for cleansing, deepening, and widening, a Creek called Beverley-beck, running into the River Hull; and for repairing the Staiths near the said Beck; and for amending the Roads leading from the said River to the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York: And that Sir Charles Hotham and Sir Michael Newton do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the ancient Freeholders of the Borough of Pcttrsfield, in the County of Southampton, whose N dines are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others of the said Borough, was presented to the Home, and read; setting forth, That, at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, Edmund Miller, of the said Borough, Serjeant at Li v, and Joseph Taylor, of London, Esquire, were Candidates; and the Election came on the 27th of January 1726, and from thence was unusually adjourned till the next Day; when Serjeant Millet was duly elected by a great Majority, and ought to have been returned; but Mr. Taylor, being supported in a violent and illegal manner by Mr. Edward Gibbons, One of the late South Sea Directors, having, by split Votes, false Votes, Bribes, and other illegal Practices, by himself, and Agents, obtained a pretended Majority, hath procured himself to be icturncd; the Mayor, who is the Returning Officer, being elected at the said Mr. GySbons' Court Leet. he being Lord of the Manor of the said Borough; besides, other Proceedings, as well before as at the Election, were altogether unjust, and in Violation of the Freedom of the Rights of the said BoroughAnd praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do hear the Matter of the said Petition at the same time they hear the Matter of the Petition of Edmund Miller, Serjeant at Law, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough.

Day of this instant February, on the Petition of the Weavers referred by his Majesty to the said Committee of Council, might be laid before this House, had been presented to his Majesty; and that his Majesty had been pleased to command biin to lay the same before this House;

The said Report is as follows;

At the Council Chamber, the 4th Day of

February, 1720.

By a Committee of the Lords of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council.

Your Majesty having been pleased, by your Order in Council, of the 16th of last Mouth, to refer unto this Committee the humble Petition oiseveral Weavers, whose Names are thereto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of their oppressed Brethren, in the Counties of Wilts and Somerset, complaining of the Combinations of their Masters, the Broad-clothiers, residing within the said Counties; whereby the Petitioners allege they have been reduced to the utmost Necessity, Want, and Despair:

First, by their lengthening the Warping-bars from 12 Quarters Three Inches to 14 Quarters and upwards, by which means, the Petitioners allege, they have been compelled to weave Three Y ards and an Half for Three Yards, contrary to Usage and Custom; and, in the next Place, by making illegal Deductions out of their Wages, upon Pretence of Damages; and when the Petitioners have applied to the Justices of the Peace for Redress, as the Law directs, and that the said Justices have, upon a full Hearing of all Sides, given Judgment in favour of the Petitioners; yet, notwithstanding such legal Determinations, the said Clothiers have commenced vexatious Law-suits against the Petitioners, on account of the said pretended Damages so heard and determined by the Justices; by means w hereof they have been intimidated, and forced to fly from their Families, to avoid a Gaol; and therefore the Petitioners humbly implore your Majesty's Mercy and Pardon towards them, and such of their Brethren as have of late unlawfully assembled themselves together; and that your Majesty will be graciously pleased to recommend their deplorable Circumstances to Parliament;

The Lords of the Committee, in pursuance of your Majesty 's said Order, have met, and taken the said Petition into their Consideration; and were attended by some of the Petitioners, and also by some of the Clothiers, and liUidanll-hall Factors: And, having fully heard what was alleged on all Sides;

It ap|>enred, from the Confession of the Clothiers, That the Length of their Warping-bars had hitherto been very uncertain, some lieing several Inches longer than others; and that the fixing a certain Standard, for the future, would be of mutual Advantage both to the Clothier and W eaver: And it also appeared, as to the other Part of tfxe Complaint, That, although the Justices had Power finally to determine all Matters in Dispute between the Petitioners and Clothiers, relating to Wages; yet, on Pretence of Damages, or any other Matters, except only Wages, the Petitioners were liable to be prosecuted at common Law; the Apprehension of which bath proved greatly terrifying to them.

The Lords of the Committee, therefore, thought it proper to recommend to both Sides, to agree among themselves upon proper Articles for fixing a certain Standard for the length of their Warping-bars; for submitting all Matters, that shall hcreaftt/ be in Dispute between them, to the final Determination of the Justices; and also for adjusting whatever else might be in Difference amongst them:

And the Petitioners, with the Clothiers, having accordingly drawn up some Articles of Agreement for the aforesaid Purposes;

The lairds of the Committee agree to offer the same to your Majesty; with their humble Opinion, That the said Y'ot. 20.

747

Articles of Agreement may be established and confirmed Report ot to them, in such manner as to your Majesty's great Wis* Council on dom shall seem most proper; which, their Lordships humbly conceive, will be the most effectual Means to preserve Peace, and good Order, between the Parties, and to prevent any the like Complaints for the future.

And their Lordships beg Leave further to report to' your Majesty, That, as it appeared in this Examination, the Clothiers had, in some Instances, given Grounds for the Complaint of the Weavers, their Lordships thought proper to take Notice thereof to the Clothiers, that they might not impose any such Hardships upon them for the future; and likewise to reprimand the Weavers for their assembling themselves in so unjustifiable a manner ih order to obtain Redress: And their Lordships also admonished them, for the future, to lay their Grievances in a regular Way before your Majesty, who would be always ready to grant them Relief suitable to the Justice of their Case; at the same time declaring to them, That, if they should hereafter attempt to right themselves in an illegal manner, their Lordships should think themselves obliged to advise your Majesty to cause the Laws to be put ii Execution against them with the utmost Rigour:

Whereupon they acknowledged their Offence; and expressed their great Thankfulness for your Majesty's Mercy and Indulgence towards them; and promised their good Behaviour for the future.

Articles of Agreement between the Clothiers and the Weavers of the Counties of I Fitts and Somerset.

1st. That no Manufacturer in the Woollen trade, shall for the future, give out, or take in, any Work to or from any of his Work-people, by any Weights exceeding Sixteen Ounces to the Pound, under the Penalty of

2. That, for the future, the Warping-bars, to be made use of by Manufacturers of Woollen-cloth, shall contain in Length Three Yards and Three Inches, and no more J each Yard to contain Six-and-thirty Inches; the Three Inches being allowed for the Over-measure, which is always given in Cloth; and that the Thruinbs, at the End of such Bars, shall not exceed Eighteen Inches in Length; and that, for the future, the Weaver of such Manufacture shall be paid by the Length of the Bars, and no otherwise, under the Penalty of

3d. That there shall be no future Demand of any Arrears, or pretended Arrears, of the Weavers, nor any Action brought, Claim or Demand made, by the Clothiers, for any Damages done to their Goods by the Weavers, to Christum last past.

4th. That no Clothier, Manufacturer, or Maker of Goods, of any kind whatsoever, shall, for the future, use, or cause to be used, any Ends of Yarn, Flocks, Wests,

Short Yarn, or other Refuse of Cloth, Drugget, or other Woollen Goods, or Goods mixed with Woollen, by working the same into Goods again, of any sort or kina whatsoever, on Pain of forfeiting such Goods so made, and a Penalty to be levied, <$r.

5th. That if any Disputes shall happen, for the future, between Clothier and Weaver, concerning Wages, Damages, Stoppages, Arrears of Wages, or other Disputes whatever, any-ways relating to the manufacturing Woollen Cloth, that the same, on Complaint made to Two of his Majesty's Justices of the County, §c. where such Matter in Controversy ariseth, shall be by them heard and determined; who must be impowered to summon, and, on Oath, ex. <$r.; And if any Person shall think himself aggrieved by any Judgment, or Order, of such Justices, it shall be lawful for such Person to appeal to the Justices in their next Quarter Sessions for the County, <§r.; who are to be impowered to summon/ and, on Oath, ex. and finally determine and award such Costs to either Party, as to them sha.ll seem meet; and that no Action at Law shall lie, or further or other Appeal be had, against the Adjudication of such Justices in their Quarter Sessions.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Then Witnesses were called to prove the Condition of the said Highways; viz.

Mr. Reddall and Mr. Willoughby: Who, being severally examined, said, That, altliough the Money collected by the Tolls hath been duly applied, and accounted for, as the Act directs; yet several parts of the Highways are still very much out of Repair; and that they cannot, by the ordinary Course of the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, be effectually amended, without some further Provision be made for raising Money to be applied for that Purpose; Materials fit for repairing the Roads.being at a great Distance from the same.

Then the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House of the Second of February instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the Second Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof, several Witnesses were called; viz.

John Preston, being examined as to the Condition of such Part of the Road between Woburn and Newport Pagnell, as leads through the Parish of Broughton, said, That the same is very bad; and that the doing the Statute-work, and laying out Six Pence in the Pound, which Work hath been constantly done in the said Parish, and Six Pence in the Pound raised, will not near be sufficient to amend such Part of the Road as lies in the said Parish, and keep the same in Repair.

Roger Norris and Thomas How: Who said, That such Part of the Road between IVoburn and Newport Pagnell, as lies in the Parishes of Midleton, Keynes, and JVaven-don, is very bad* notwithstanding the Inhabitants of the said Parishes have constantly done their Statute-work, and last Year collected, and laid out, Fourteen Pounds, over and above their Statute-work.

John Norman, Waggoner, said, That the Road from Minchcdge to Tickford Bridge in, Newport Pagnell is very bad, and some Part of it worse than any other Part of the Road between IVoburn and Newport Pagnell: And he said further, That, if the Inhabitants were to do, and pay, much more than they are obliged to do, and to raise, by Law, the same would not effectually repair that Road.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Rill for the more effectual amending the Highway between Hock-lisse and Woburn, in the County of Bedford; and for repairing the Road leading through IVoburn to Tickford Bridge in Newport Pagnell, in the County of Bucks: And that Mr. Leigh, Sir Jiowland Alston, and Mr. Chapman, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir Henry Hoghton reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the High Sheriff, Grand Jury, Justices of the Peace, and Gentlemen, of the County of Lancaster, at the Assizes held for the said County at Lancaster, the Twenty-fifth Day of August 1726, relating to the Highways between the Towms of Warrington and Wigan, in the said County, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee had, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition; and, upon the Examination of Witnesses, find the same to be as followeth; viz.

Wm. Middlehurch, of Warrington, in the said County, said, The Roads between Warrington and Wigan are so founderous, that in many Parts Carriages cannot pass; and that, the Causeway for single Horses being under a

Yard wide, loaded Horses cannot pass each other when they meet:

That the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, wherein the said Roads do lie, have done their Days Works, and laid out the 6d. in the Pound required by Law, and expended several other large Sums, in the Repair of the said Roads: That, if they are not repaired, it will be to the manifest Prejudice of the Trade of that Country; That it is the great Western Road between England and North Britain: That the several Inhabitants are not able under the Provision of the several Laws, to put them in sufficient Repair.

Wm. Wood, of Asheton, Gentleman, said, He had surveyed the Road leading from Warringlon to Wigan; and that the same is so bad, that Carts, and other Carriages, cannot pass; and that the Road for single Horses loaded is so narrow, that Two cannot pass each other without unloading:

That the Inhabitants of the several Townships have all done the Statute-work; and some of them even expended 11 d. and 12 d. in the Pound: That it is the great Western Road between North Britain and London.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing, widening, and amending, the Roads leading from ffarrington to Wigan, in the County of Lancaster:

And that Sir Henry Hoghton and Sir Roger Bradshaigh do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Brereton reported from the Committee, to whom Wigan the Petition of the High Sheriff, GranS Jury, Justices of Roads, the Peace, and Gentlemen, of the County of Lancaster, at the Assizes held for the said County at I^a?icaster, the Twenty-fifth Day of August 1726, relating to the Highways between the Towns of Wigan and Preston, in the said County, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee had, pursuant to the Order of this House, examined the Matter of the said Petition; and, upon Examination of Witnesses, find the same to be as followeth; viz.

Wm. Wood, of Ashton, in the said County, says, He has several times surveyed the Road from Wigan to Preston: That the same was hardly passable for Carriages, and, in some Parts, very difficult for single loaded Horses to pass each other when they meet; and, if the same be not repaired, it will be to the great Prejudice of the Trade of the Country:

That the Townships have done the Statute-work; and even expended several large Sums, over and above what is required by Laws: That the Inhabitants are not able, under the Provisions of the Laws in being, to put them in sufficient Repair.

Wm. Midlchurst, of Warrington, in the said County, says, He has surveyed the Road leading from iVigan to Preston: That the same is in a very bad and founderous Condition; and, in some Parts, so narrow, that Two Carts cannot pass:

That the Inhabitants of the several Townships have done the Six Days Work, laid out the 6d. in the Pound, required by Law; and have expended several large Sums, besides, in the Repair of the same: That, in some Parts, two Pack-horses cannot pass without being unloaded;

That it is the great Western Road between North Britain and London.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing, widening, and amending, the Roads leading from Wigan to Preston, in the County of Lancaster:

And that Mr. Brereton, and Sir Thomas Lowther, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir Richard Hopkins reported from the Committee, to Relief of

whom the Petition of several Merchants, whose Names British Subjects in Tuscany.

/3 Geo. I. 2 2° Februarii. 765

are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others trading to Leghorn, in Italy, in the Great Duke of Tuscany's Dominions, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the if>th February instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and, to make good the Allegations of the same, called the several Witnesses following; vte.

Christopher Crow Esquire, formerly Consul at Leg-home: Who said, That a Duty of One Livre per Ton, which is about yd. Sterling, on all Tonage Goods, and f of a Livre per Pale, or Parcel, which is about 3 d. Sterling, on all Bale Goods, imported into the Port of Leghorne in British Shipping, was settled, about 20 Years ago, by general Agreement of the British Factory there, and approved of by the Traders thither, and paid all the time he was Cpnsul there, by E?/glish, and all Foreigners; and the Money, so collected, was applied towards the Maintenance of a Minister; and the Relief of Mariners, Seamen, and other distressed Persons.

Mr. Craw, Mr. Heames, Mr. Blackwell, Mr. Yeates, and Mr. Godfrey, being examined, said, That the small Contributions, collected for the Uses aforesaid, have been paid for many Years last past; and the Goods imported into Leghorn, in British Shipping, were generally consigned to the British Subjects there; but, of late, some Persons have consigned Goods, in British Shipping, to Foreigners, to avoid the Payment of the said small Duties; which is a Discouragement to our Merchants and Factors there:

And also, That, if the said Duties were laid on all Goods imported into Leghorn in British Shipping, all Merchants trading thither would be equally liable to the said Duty.

That it appears to this Committee, That, for want of a Law to recover the said Duties, some Persons decline to pay the same; unless a Law can be obtained to receive and recover the said Duties equally on all Persons having Goods consigned to them in British Shipping; it being no more than w hat is practised by other Nations.

Mr. Croze said, That Mr. Xacton, her late Majesty's Envoy at Florence, informed him, the said Mr. Crozv, that he had received Orders from her said Majesty, that she was desirous that the Factory at Leghorn should have a Chaplain, and to know what Allowance they were willing to make him; upon which, Mr. Crow summoned the Factory together; and, by them, it was unanimously resolved to settle the small Duties afore-mentioned; out of which they agreed to allow a Chaplain £. 200. per Annum; and the Remainder of the said Duties to be applied to other publick and pious Uses, as Occasion should require:

That, during the time Mr. Crow was Consul, after the Duties were settled, it was a Means of preserving, at least, 1,500 British Subjects and Seamen from entering into foreign Services; without which they would have been lost to this Nation, as Numbers were before this Contribution was collected.

Mr. lleames, Mr. Blackwell,\ and Mr. Godfrey, were all Treasurers for receiving the said small Duties, in their Turns, during their Residence at Leghorn; and the said Duties were collected upon a!l Goods imported in British Shipping, without Interruption; and the Monies, so collected, were constantly applied to discharge the publick and pious Uses aforesaid.

Mr. Yeates, who resided at Leghorn Eight Years, and came from thence about a Year since, during his Stay there, never heard the Payment of the said Duties refused; except by Mr. Huygens, some Mouths before he, the said Mr. Yeates, came from thence; and the said Huygens endeavoured to dissuade other Foreigners from paying the same, on Pretence it was to maintain a Protestant Minister, contrary to their Religion.

Vol. 20.

Mr. Croze, Mr. Heames, Mr. Blaclcwell, Mr, Yeates* and Mr. Godfrey, said, That the French and Dutch Nations, residing at Leghorn, collect Monies for their national Expences; and, if British Merchants import Goods in their Ships, they subject them to their Regulations and Duties:

That the said Duties, when collected by the Merchants and Factors residing at Leghorn, are applied to the Uses following; viz. £. 200. per Annum for the Minister; about £. 120. per Annum to Doctors, Surgeons, and the Hospitals at Leghorn and Florence, for the Cure of the Sick and Wounded: The Remainder is applied to the sending home such Persons as want to return; and for other national Exigences.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for more equal paying, and better collecting, certain small Sums for the Relief of shipwrecked Mariners, and distressed Persons, his Majesty's Subjects, in the Dominions of the Great Duke of Tuscany, and for other pious and charitable Purposes, usually contributed to by the Merchants trading to Leghorn: And that Sir Richard Hopkins, and Mr. Barnard, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Digbij reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Tow n of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick; and also the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Tradesmen, and Inhabitants, of the Market-town of Dudley, in the County of Worcester; and also the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, in and about the Market-town of Wednesbury, in the County of Stafford; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Orders of Reference upon the several Petitions, proceeded to examine the Matters thereof.

To prove the Allegations of the First Petition;

John Ward Esquire was called: Who said, That the Road lying between the Town of Birmingham, and the Town of Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford, is about Ten Miles; and that the same is, in the Winter-season, in a very ruinous Condition, and, in some Places, almost impassable; and this very great Decay of the Road has been by the great Number of Carriages constantly passing, laden with Iron, and Iron-wares, from Wolverhampton, and thereabouts, to Birmingham, and from thence to London, and by carrying great Quantities of Coals for the Use of the Town of Birmingham, and other Places in Warwickshire, Northamptonshire, and Oxfordshire; and, the said Road being so bad, the same cannot be effectually repaired and amended, without some further Provision for that Purpose.

Mr. Samuel Stuart was called; and, being examined, spoke to the same Effect as Mr. Ward had: And also

said. That the King's Carriages, for the Use of the Soldiers going that Way, could not pass through that Road this Winter; and it being so bad, that no Carriages can pass, he had threatened to indict the Inhabitants of some of the Towns.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine the Allegations of the Second Petition, praying, That the Roads from the Great Bridge to Dudley, and so to St azeerbridge and Kingman ford, may be repaired:

And, to prove the Condition of those Roads;

Mr. Richard Keeling was examined: Who said, That the same are so very bad, that Waggons and Carriages cannot pass through either of the said Roads, in the Winter-time; and that the Inhabitants of the several Parishes through which the said Roads lead, are not able to amend the same by the ordinary Course of the Laws now in Force.

Mr. Ward and Mr. Gevern, being severally called, confirmed the Evidence Mr. Keeling had given in relation to these Roads.

That, to make good the Allegations of the Third Petition, praying. That the Road leading through Wednesbury Town, by the Market-house, to Birmingham, may be repaired;

Mr. John Gevern w as called 1 and, being examined, said*, That, by reason of many heavy Loads of Iron-w ares and Coals carried that M ay, the said Road is become so very bad, that it impassable for Carriages; and that the carrying of such great Weights of Iron, Iron-wares, and Coals, has occasioned such great Ruts, in such Part of the Road as lies in the Town of Wednesbury, that the Foundation of some of the Houses there has been very much damaged: And further said, That the Inhabitants of the Town of Wednesbury have constantly done their Statute-work; and that it would require much more to put the Road into such Repair, as that Passengers may pass and repass with Safety.

Mv.Samuel Stuart confirmed what Mr. Gevent had said.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing kite several Roads leading from the Town of Birmingham, through the Town of Wednesbury, to a Place called High Bullen; and also to a Place called Great Bridge; and from thence to the several Towns of Wolverhampton, Dudley, Kingswinford, and Stourbridge, in the Counties of Warwick, Stafford, and Worcester: And that Mr. Dig by and Mr. Leveson Gower do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other principal Inhabitants, of the County of Hereford, in behalf of themselves, and many others of the said County, and other Counties trading thereto, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That an Act was made, in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for making navigable the Rivers Wye and Lugg, and die Rivers and Brooks running into the same, in the Counties of Hereford, Gloucester, and Monmouth; whereby certain Persons, therein named, were impowered, upon the Terms in the said Act mentioned, to carry on, and perfect the said Navigation; which Persons, so impowered, did not perform the same effectually; and that the Locks and Passages, by them made, are now utterly decayed and ruined: That another Act was made, in the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for making navigable the said Rivers Wye and Lugg; v\ hereby the Commissioners therein named were impowered to pull down and demolish all the Weirs upon the said Rivers, rendering Satisfaction to the Proprietors; in pursuance of which Act, large Sums of Money were laid Out in purchasing Weirs and Mills on the said Rivers, and in demolishing the same; which was at that time apprehended would very much tend to the Making of the said Rivers perfectly navigable; but the Shoals, and other inconveniencies, since discovered, by the Demolition of the said Weirs, have obstructed the Navigation of the said Rivers, and rendered the said Acts inef* fectual: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the said Acts; and to make the same more effectual.

Sir Thomas Lee reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace of and for the County of Bucks, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in nis Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House of the 17th Day of February instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof, Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. Hillium Hay ton junior, Clerk of the Peace for the said County: Who, being examined, said, That, there being no County Gaol, a House in Aylesbuty, which is a Market-town situate about the Middle of the County, was rented for that Purpose; for which the County paid Twenty Pounds per Annum; and for many Years had been at great Charge in Strengthening and Repairing thereof; but that the same was never taken for a publick Vo L. 20.

Gaol: That the sdid House was Very inconvenient, and so small, that the Sheriff was frequently obliged to keep Debtors and Felons together; and wm$ so much out of Repair, being neither large or strong enough fora County Prison, that several Prisoners had made their Escapes; and the present Under Sheriff now is under a Prosecution on that Account:

That the Petitioners being obliged to purchase the Ground whereon to build anew County Gaol, with proper Conveniences for the Use of the County, and to den fray the Expence and Charges thereof, an Assessment of One Peny in the Pound was made outlie County; which being found insufficient, the Sum of Two Pence in the Pound was afterwards assessed; which likewise not being, sufficient for completing the said Building, the further Sum of Two Pence in the Pound was also assessed on the County: All which several Assessments appeared to the Committee to amount to about £.4,900.

That it appeared to the Committee, by the Evidence of the said Mr. Hay ton, Mr. Gamham Edwards, Under Sheriff of the said County, and other Persons, That the Place where the Judges of Assize, and Justices of the Peace, usually sat, for the Holding of the Assizes, General Quarter Sessions, and Transacting of other publick Business, of the said County, was in the common Market-house of the Town of Aylesbury aforesaid; which belongs to Sir John Pakington, or his Sod, arid made use of by their Leave; was not only much out of Repair, but very inconvenient for that Purpose; and that several Disputes had arisen relating to the electing a Court of Nisiprius for the Sitting of the Judges: YVhe'refore the Petitioners are desirous, that a convenient Court-rcom, or Shire-hall, might be built for the Use of the County; and, that a proper Place should be provided, for the more commodious Dispatch of the publick Business thereof, iri building the said Gaol, have designed a large Room, in the Body of the said Gaol, for that Purpose.

That it also appeared, That a considerable Progress i3 already made in the Building of the Gaol, with the Court-room, or Shire-hall; and that there is due to the Workmen employed, the Sum of £.1,800. for their Work already performed; which, with the further necessary Charges of completing the said Building, the Petitioners could not effectually raise, and levy on the said County, without the Assistance of Parliament.

A Motion being made, and the Question being pot, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Justices of the Peace for the County of Bucks, to finish a Gaol, and Sessions-room, for the Use of the said County;

The House divided.

Anno 130 Georgii Regis, 1726. Prayers.

to the unfortunate Subjects of this Kingdom, when they have been penned up in Prison, till almost rotten and starved, by their merciless Creditors, that they can be heard, and relieved, by their Representatives in Parliament; and though an Act lately passed for Relief of insolvent Debtors, to which Benefit the Petitioners were in* titled, as they apprehend; yet so hard is their Fate, that it being the Custom of every Gaol to permit a Prisoner to go out with a Tender; and it being not according to the Construction of these Words of the Act, viz. " unless out " by due Course of Law;M therefore the Gaoler refused to put Twenty of the Petitioners into his List, because he could not swear for them, according to the Form of his Oath; but if the House shall think fit to insert a Clause in the Bankrupts Act, or any other, for the Prisoners Maintenance, or Deliverance, it will procure a Quietus to the House, by stopping aTorrent of Petitions of this Nature: And praying the Consideration of the House, and such Relief as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor and miserable Prisoners confined for Debt in White-chapel Gaol, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That all the late Acts for insolvent Debtors have been with Limitation of a Sum; whereby those Persons that have been most considerable in Life are now most miserable, remaining still in Gaol: That the Acts of Bankruptcy are near expiring: And praying, That the Petitioners may have the Benefit of those Laws, delivering up their All to their Creditors; or that they may be obliged to maintain them in Prison.

Ordered, That the said Petition dolieupon the Table.

A Petition of the poor confined Debtors in the Poultrey Compter, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they have done and offered all they have to their Creditors, for their Satisfaction; yet they are deaf to their Petitions, andIntreatiesof their Families starving abroad for Want; and take more Pleasure in the Insolvent's Confinement, though at the Expence of that Substance which they might share the Benefit of, than pity his Misfortune, or his Desire for Liberty: And praying. That they may be put on the same Footing with Bankrupts, by delivering up their All to their Creditors; or be otherwise relieved, as the House shall think fit. South Sea Company's Trade in Negroes.

A Petition of the Court of Directors of the South Sea Company was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Transportation of Negroes from Madagascar, and the South-east Coast of Africa, within the Limits of Trade granted to the East India Company, to Buenos Ayres in America, within the Limits of Trade granted to the Petitioners, may become a very beneficial Branch of the Trade of Great Britain; and that the Petitioners are desirous to undertake the said Trade, under Vo L. 20.

the Licence and Permission of the East India Company; but all Ships trading from the East Indies being, by several Acts of Parliament, obliged to come to some Part of this Kingdom, without breaking Bulk, the said Trade will be impracticable, without some Provision be made by Parliament: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be enabled to exercise the Trade of transporting Negroes from Madagascar to Buenos Ayres, under the Licence of the East India Company.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas to take hi Negroes, with the Consent of the East India Company, within their Limits of Trade; and to deliver the same at Buenos Ayres: And that the Lord Mayor of London,

Mr. Budge, and Mr. Ilungcrford, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are there- claims unto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all other Smith Sea Creditors of Robert Knight Esquire, late Treasurer, or Company. Cashier, of the South Sea Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Trustees for the South Sea Company having disallowed Two several Claims of the said Company upon the Estate of the said Mr. Knight, amounting to Seven hundred thousand Pounds, the Court of Directors of the said Company, not being satisfied therewith, declared by aResolution of the said Court, That the said Claims ought to have been allowed; which, with another Claim of the said Company, amounting to One hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds, allowed by the said Trustees, will be much more than the Amount of Mr. Knight's whole Estate; and, consequently, nothing will be left towards making any Satisfaction for the Petitioners just Debts, which have beon allowed by the said Trustees, and liquidated and ad justed between the Petitioners, and the Court of Directors of the said Company: And this being a case so circumstanced, that the Petitioners are ,not relievablo, but in Parliament; therefore praying the Consideration of the House, and such Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report of the Trustees for the South Sea Company shall be taken into considers.: ion.,

Mr. Hugh Williams reported from the Committee, to Tenby iiur-. whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, hour, of the Town of Tenby, in the County of Pembroke, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House of the 22d Day of February instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to make good the Allegations of the same, they called,

Mr. William Williams, of Tenby: Who said. That there is a Pier and Harbour, or Haven, at Tenby, and very commodious, safe, and of great Advantage to many trading Towns and Places situate on, or near, the River Severn, and Bristol Channel; and that it is the only Pier in the whole Extent of South Wales; and is capable of receiving and preserving Ships in Stress of Weather, and from Enemies in time of War; and is also of great Advantage and Conveniency in Exporting and Importing of great Quantities of Coal, Culm, Com and other Wares, Goods, and Merchandizes:

That he further gave Evidence, That, of late Years, great Quantities of Sand hath been driven into the Harbour, by the Sea; which hath almost filled up, and rendered the same useless; and, in order to cleanse the g M Harbour,

e

jjS — 28

Marboilr, the Towft have lately expended large Sums of Money in erecting a Bason within the Harbour, with several Sluices in the Bason wall; which, in a great measure, have answered the End proposed, and thereby deepened the Harbour considerably; but, the Sand being high at the time of making that Bason, the Foundation of great, and the most useful. Part of the Bason-wall, could not then be laid on the Rock; by which means the said Wall is now so much shattered and cracked, that the same is in danger of falling; and the said Harbour of being filled with Sand, as it was before.

That it appeared to the Committee, That Ships and Vessels in the Pier oftentimes, in bad Weather, do Injury to themselves, and to one another, by rolling and svvad-ling, which is occasioned by the Rebound and Surge which the Sea makes; but, if the old Pier-head was rebuilt, the same would he effectually prevented, and the Pier and Harbour be restored to their ancient Goodness:

That, in carrying on the Works mentioned in the Petition, the Town have exhausted their Stock of Money; and, by their present Revenue, are not able to repair the said Bason-wall and Sluices, and to rebuild the said old Pier-head, without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the effectual cleansing, scouring, and deepening, the Harbour of Tenby, in the County of Pembroke; and for repairing the Bason-wall, and Sluices there; and for rebuilding the old Pier-head; and for regulating Shipping in the said Harbour: And that M r. Hugh Williams, and Sir Arthur Owen, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A PETITION of the poor insolvent Debtors in the Debtors iv Sheriff's Ward for the County of Somerset, at titious. Ivelchester, whose names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners arc ready and willing to surrender up whatever they have, for their Creditors Satisfaction, so that they may have their Liberty; but such is their Cruelty, that, notwithstanding several late Acts have been made for the Petitioners Liberty, their Creditors have found means to elude the same, although some of their Debts have not amounted to Twenty Shillings: whereby the Petioners are likely to starve in Gaol, having no Allowance: And praying such Relief as th

House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors of the Prison of Ludgate, in behalf of themselves, and all other insolvent Debtors in the several Prisons of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Miseries they labour under arc almost inexpressible, and too many to enumerate; and that little Substance they had, when imprisoned, and which should have been applied towards Satisfaction of their Creditors, is spent in the very Necessaries of Life to support them; so that Death is more preferable to them than a lingering starving Life; and great Numbers of them are willing, au*l able, to serve their King and Country: That the Petitioners have not wherewithal to satisfy their Creditors; so expect no Mercy from them, having been applied unto, although the Petitioners have offered them their All; and desire that a Bill may be brought in for that Purpose, under the severest Penalties; or that their Creditors may maintain them in Gaol: That, by the late Act for Relief of insolvent Debtors, out of 300 Prisoners, then in the said Gaol, not above 70 could receive any Benefit thereby, by reason of the strict Oaths required to be. taken by the Keeper and Prisoners, in respect to Liberty given to Prisoners in going out with a Keeper, which was sometimes absolutely necessary: And praying, That a Bill may be brought in for the Petitioners. Enlargement, upon their surrendering all their Estates and Effects to their Creditors, under such Penalties as the House shall think proper; and that such Persons as were Prisoners at the time of passing the said late Act, may now be discharged; or that the Petitioners may-have such other Relief as shall he thought meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Mary O'Gqra Widow, One of the O'Garai Daughters of Randal late Lord Baron of Shine, in the Kingdom of Ireland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, on the Death of her First Husband, Bichard Fleming Esquire, in 1689, she became intitled to Lands in Ireland, then of the Value of Two hundred Pounds per Annum, as her Jointure; and was soon after outlawed for High Treason, on account of the War in Ireland, being then under the Age of One and twenty Years: That the said Outlawry was procured by the Contrivance of her said Husband's Relations; who have, for Thirty Years past, received the Profits of the said Jointure-lands; and have hitherto refused to allow her any Subsistence, on Pretence they may be called toi an Account by the Crown for the said Profits: That the Trustees for Sale of the Irish Forfeitures, not beingap-prised of the Title, could not sell the said Estate; and the same, being a Forfeiture undisposed of, is, by Act of Parliament, vested in his Majesty, subject to such Disposition as shall be made thereofin Parliament: That she is ready to make out the Title in the Crown: And, having committed no Crime of a treasonable Nature, but accompanying her late Husband, Oliver O' Gar a Esquire, into France; therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable her, or Trustees on her behalf, to sue for the said Jointure lands, with the mean Profits thereof.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That, the Petitioner's Case having been represented to his Majesty, his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, That his Majesty gives his Consent, that this House may do in this Case as they think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir George Oxenden, and Mr. Palmer, c!o prepare, arid bring in, the same.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House of the 12th of this instant February, proceeded to examine the Matter of the sai l Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations of the same, they called the following Witnesses: viz.

Mr. John Clark: Who said. That the Level of Iladdenham is under Water; and has been so for about 6 or 7 Years: That the same cannot be drained, but by throwing the Water over the Banks; which must be done by Mills, or some other Engine: That theije is about 6 or 7,000 Acres under Water.

Mr. James For try: That the Level is inti rely drowned; and there is not any Outfal whereby to drain it: That the Rivers, into which the Waters should discharge themselves, lie higher than the Lands: That she Rain waters often drown the said Level: That the Level is capable of being drained by Mills, or some other Enginesand ii will be no Damage to the neighbouring Parts.

Mr. Walker; Who said the Level hath been drowned 2 Poot deep for about 6 or 7 Months in the Year: That the Water was not all off the last Summer: That there is no other Way to drain the said Level, but by Mills, or other Engines, to throw it into the River Owze.

Mr. John Kent: Who, being examined, said, That the said Level is very much drowned, and has been so for many Years: That that Part that lies near Sutton is Four Foot under Water; and those Parts that lie towards the Delves is Two Foot under Water: That several Parts of the said Level is not worth Two Shillings and Six Pence an Acre at present; but, when drained, will be worth Twenty Shillings an Acre, as he believe*.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the effectual Draining and Preservation of Iladdenham Level, in the Isle of Ely: And that Mr. Shcpheard, Mr. Robert Lloyd, and Mr. 7 ho mas Bacon, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

the Clerk's Table: Where the Report and Resolution of the Committee were read; and arc as follows; t iz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 20th of February instant, proceeded toexaminetheMatter of the said Petition:

Aiul, to prove the Allegations of the same, they called,

Mr. Micajah Perry, of London, Merchant: Who appeared in behalf of the Legislature of Pcnsilvania, in America; and informed the Committee, That he had resided there some time; and that the said Province is commodiously situated for Fishing; and abounds with several Sorts of Fish in the River, Bay, and Coast, of the said Province:

That Salt is very difficult and scarce to begot there; which oftentimes occasions them to fling great Quantities of their Fish away: That, ifthey were impowered to import Salt from Europe, it would be a means of their carrying on a considerable Fishing-trade: That, for want of Encouragement in their Fishery, they arc scarce able at present to purchase Goods from Great Britain, to supply their Wants withal: That formerly the said Province was comprehended under the general Name of New Eastland: That there is a Liberty already granted to New England and Newfoundland to import Salt from Ew* rofye, for the Use of their Fishery; but, since the erecting that into a distinct Province by the Name of Pensilvania, it is doubted whether or not an Act, made in the 15th Year of King Charles the 2d, Cap. 7. intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of Trade, extends to them.

There was also produced to the Committee a Petition from the Legislature of Pensilvania, to the Lords of the Treasury; which was referred to the Commissioners of the Customs; and, upon their Report back to their Lordships, they had no Objection to the carrying Salt from Europe to Pensilvania; afterwards the Lords of the Treasury were pleased to refer the said Petition, with the Report of the Commissioners of the Ctistoms, to the Commissioners of the Salt-duty; and they reported back to their Lordships, That they had no Objection to the granting them the Liberty they desired.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioner hath proved the Allegations of the Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for importing Salt from Europe into the Province of Pensilvania, in America: And that Sir Richard Hopkins, and Mr. Barnard, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Michael Stephens, and others, That, in pursuance of the last mentioned Act, large Sums of Money have been laid out, in purchasing Weirs and Mills upon each of the said Rivers; which have been pulled down, and demolished; but it has been found by Experience, that the Demolition thereof, instead of conducing to perfect the Navigation of the said Rivers, which at that time it was apprehended it would, it has occasioned great Shoals, and other Inconveniencies, whereby the Navigation of the said Rivers is much obstructed:

That there has been little or no Work done upon the River Lugg; so that the same is in a very bad ^Condition; but is capable of being made navigable:

That there are now remaining in the Hands of some Persons, several Sums of Money, that were collected for the Use of the said Rivers; but the same cannot be applied, there not being a sufficient Number of the surviving Trustees to put the said Acts in Execution.

Sir Richard Hopkins reported from the Committee, to importing whom the Petition of the Master, Wardens, and As- foreign sistants, of the Company of Silk-throwers, on behalf of dirjwn Silk, them selves, and the Commonalty of the said Company, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as follows j

That the Committee had, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition That it appeared to the Committee, by an Act, made 2d Wm. and Mary, Cap. 9. Page 1569, intituled, An Act for discouraging the Importation of thrown Silk, all Silk was prohibited to be imported into this Kingdom, except from Italy, Naples, and Sicily and by another Act, made 5th and 6th Wm. and Mary, Cap. 3.

Page 1663, intituled, An Act for the Importation of fine Italian, Sicilian, and Naples, thrown Silk; giving Liberty to import fine Italian thrown Silk, not coarsen than a Sort known by the Name of Third Bolognia,

Second Orsoy, or any Sort of Silk commonly called Trains:

That, by One other Act, made i* Anna, Cap. i*]°.

Page 2203, intituled, An Act for the Importation of fine Italian thrown Silk, Persons were impowered* during the then War, and Three Months after, to import from Italy fine thrown Silks, not coarser than Third Bolognia, or any Sort of Silk called Trams:

Which Acts, being temporary, are expired, and no Provision hath been made since to restrain the bringing in of any coarser Sorts of the thrown Silks and Trams aforesaid.

Tho. Teaton, Alexander Weller, and John Russell, said, That, during the Continuance of the above-recited Acts, the Petitioners employed upwards of Forty thousand People, consisting chiefly of the Wives,

Children, and Widows, of Mariners and Seamen; but, since the Expiration thereof, several Persons have imported very great Quantities of the said foreign thrown Silks, coarser than 3d Bolognia % 2d Orsoy, and Trams; which are commonly made Use of, instead of the raw Silks imported from Turkey, and elsewhere: \

That, by reason of the Importation of such coarse thrown Silk, and Trams, the Petitioners, for several Years last past, have found their Trade very much decline > and, at present, it is so much reduced, that they do not employ above Sixteen or Seventeen thousand Persons therein:

That the Silk-manufacture in Great Britain is very much increased; and that, if the Importation of the coarse thrown Silks were restrained, the Petitioners would be able to employ, at least, Fifty thousand Persons in Throwing, Twisting, and Winding, of raw Silks:

That, before the Importation of the said several Sorts of thrown Silks, the Petitioners used, instead thereof, the raw Silks imported from Turkey and Persia and, if the Importation of these coarse thrown Silks were restrained, they should use much greater Quantities of Legee and Sherbaf' Silks from Turkey, of which, at present, there is very little Consumption; and that, of late, several Persons do import single-drawn Legee Trams from Italy, to the great Prejudice of the Silk-throwsters Trade.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the effectual preventing the Importation of foreign thrown Silks, known by the Names of Third Bolognia,

Second Orsoy, and all Trams, into this Kingdom, from Italy, Milan, Naples, and Sicily 5 and for the better employing the Poor, and preserving the Silk-throwing Trade in this Kingdom: And that Sir Richard Hopkins, and M r Thomas Bacon9 do prepare, and bring in the same.

That by an Act, of the 5th Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for continuing certain Duties on Coals and Culm; and for establishing certain Funds to raise Monies, as well to proceed in the Building of new Churches, as to complete the Supply granted to his Majesty, and to reserve the Overplus-money of the said Duties for the Disposition of Parliament; and for more effectual suppressing private Lotteries; a particular Fund of £. 21,000. per Annum, to arise out of the Duties thereby granted; and to have Continuance for the Term of Thirty-two Years, from the Feast of the Annunciation of the blessed Virgin Mary 1719; was appropriated for the Purposes aforesaid; and in lieu of the Duties granted by the said former Acts:

That Five or more of the Commissioners appointed by his said Majesty, pursuant tolhe said Act of the First Year of his Majesty's Reign, having purchased all that ancient Chapel, sometime called the Church, or great Chapel, situate within the Precinct or Site of the late House, or Priory, of St. John of Jerusalem, near Clerkenwell, in the County of Middlesex, did, in pursuance of the said Acts, by an Instrument in Writing on Parchment, under their Hands and Seals, bearing Date the 11 th Day of December 17 23, and in rolled in Chancery the 16th Day of the same Month, declare and appoint, That the said Chapel, from, and for ever after, the Inrolment of the said Instrument, and Consecration of the said Chapel, should be converted into and made a Parish Church; and did thereby describe and ascertain the District and Division of and for a new Parish to the said Church:

That the said Church was consecrated by the Lord Bishop of London on the 27th of December 1723; and, in the Act of Consecration, named the Church of St. John, Clerkenwell, in the County of Middlesex:

That the new Parish, allotted to the said Church, was a District taken out of the Parish of St. James, Clerkenwell, in the said County, and contains about 800 Houses; but, although large in Extent, is very much burthened with Poor; inso much that 349 Houses, containing therein about 400 Families, are not charged to the Poors Rate; and those Rates for many Years past have been, and still are, is. 6d. in the Pound, and amount to £.620. per Annum, or thereabouts; and the Parish is incapable of any Improvement by new Buildings; and above 400 Houses are under the Rent of £.8. per Annum each:

That Divine Service hath been constantly performed in the said Church, ever since the Consecration thereof, by Adam Batty Clerk, Master of Arts, Rector of the said Church, as being the Morning Preacher usually officiating therein for the Space of One Month next before the Consecration thereof; but no Provision hath been yet established for the Rector of the said Church.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making Provision for the Rector of the Parish of St. John, Clerkenwell, in the County of Middlesex, and his Successors: And that Mr. Freman, Mr. North, and Mr. Drew, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir Richard Hopkins reported from the Committee, to Copper and whom the Petition of the Master, Wardens, Court of Assistants, and Livery of the Company of Armourers ac m and Brasiers of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and others, dealing in Goods and Wares made of Copper and Brass, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report and Resolution of the Committee were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee had, pursuant to the Order of the House of the 17 th of February last, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

That, upon such Examination,

It appeared to the Committee, by an Act of Parliament 190 H. 7. Cap. 4. intituled, Pewterers walking,

That the Pewterers and Brasiers were in One Company; and thereby several Powers were given them for regulating the Working and Selling of Goods made of Pewter, Copper, and Brass; and to prevent Persons from going from Town to Town to cheat People; and to restrain all Persons from selling Pewter and Brass-wares, but in open Fairs and Markets, or in their Dwelling-houses only, unless desired by the Buyers; and Searchers were thereby to be appointed, in every City and Borough, to enquire into the Goodness of the Metal, with Power to recover the Penalties:

That by an Act, 40 Hen. 8th, intituled, An Act made for Pewterers, and true Weights and Beams, the said Statute of Hen. 70 was confirmed; and by several other Acts, particularly 25° Hen. 8th, Cap. 9th, intituled, A Bill concerning Pewterers; and 33° Hen. 8th, Cap. 4.

12 intituled

9

13 Geo. I. 6°-f i

intituled, The Pewterers Bill; several other Powers were granted to the said Company:

That, since the said Acts of Parliament, the said Company of Pewterers and Brasiers have been separated into Two distinct Companies; and the Brasiers have now little or no Benefit by those Laws:

That, by Charter granted 7°Ann<e, the Armourers and Brasiers were incorporated into One Company, with divers Powers for the better regulating the said Company; andaPowerto appoint Persons to inspect all manner of Goods, or Wares, wrought of Copper, or Brass, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Five Miles round the same; and to make Bye-laws, and impose Fines on Persons acting contrary thereto.

Then the Petitioners proceeded to prove the Frauds and Abuses committed by the Manufacturers: And called,

Thomas Piggott: Who said, It was a common Practice with some Workmen, to put a leaden Collar round the Top of their Pots, instead of an Iron Wire one; and likewise to make the Handles of their Pots and Kettles hollow, and fill them with Lead, and weigh them with the Pots as Copper, or Brass; and produced a Pot with such Lead, instead of an Iron Collar; by which means, in a Pot of 185. Price, the Buyer is imposed upon 1 os. or thereabouts.

Richard Walker said, It was customary with some Workmen, to turn thin Plate Iron hollow for Rings to their Pots, and fill the Hollow with Lead; so that it is notdiscernable even to another Workman; and produced such an Handle, which he bought with an old Pot.

Seagrave said, That he had frequently done so by the Direction of the Master whom he served his Apprenticeship with, who is since dead; and *tis usual to put large heavy Iron Wires and Handles, containing at least Three times the Quantity useful and necessary 3 and likewise large Ears of cast Iron, instead of Brass or Copper, as they ought to be; which are weighed with the Pots, and sold as Copper, or Brass; to the Prejudice of the W ear thereof; and to the great Abuse of the Buyers.

Benjamin Wall said to the same Effect; and that he bought a Kettle, the Iron about which weighed more than the Brass: That it is a common Practice to affix a Quantity of Lead to their Copper-work, and colour it over so, that it is difficult to distinguish it from Copper: That he once bought about Sixty Pounds Weight of Copper, as he thought, in which was at least 15 L. of Lead so coloured; and produced a Copper Indigo-mill, at the Bottom of which was about 27 Pounds of Head so coloured, besides 8 L. of Iron; and but 20L. of Copper.

Wm. Warner and Thomas Westall being examined, 6aid, They had worked in several Places in the Country; and that the Custom of putting large heavy Handles, and cast Iron Ears, to their Work, had obtained greatly amongst the Country Masters; and that, even to a small Sawce-pan it was common to find a thick Iron Handle of One Pound and a Half, or Two Pounds Weight.

Mr. Appleby said, That the Company have commenced Suits against several Persons, in pursuance of their Charter and Bye-laws, who have been guilty of the Frauds and Abuses above-mentioned; but, for want of sufficient Authority to prosecute the same, the Company have been nonsuited.

And that upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent Frauds and Abuses in the Working up of Goods and Wares made of Copper and Brass, within that Part of Great Britain called England .* And that Sir Richard Hopkhis, Mr. Recorder ot' London, and Sir Jtoger Bradshaigh, do prepare, and bring in* the same.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the 24th Day of February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition: And to prove the Allegations of the same, they called the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Wm. Martin: Who said, That there has been upwards of £. 45,000. laid out in making the said Navigation, and other Works incident thereto: That, in some Cases, the Proprietors are without Remedy to recover their Tolls and Duties, there being only Two Remedies granted by an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for making the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Nezcbury, in the County of Berks; the one by Stoppage of the Goods in Barges, the other by Action or Suit at Law: As to the First, they cannot make Stay of any Goods, until the Barge has made her Voyage; and, if she never returns, the Remedy is at an End; and if the said Barge should return, and the Proprietors should make Stay of any Goods, yet the Proprietors, by the said Act, have no Pow er to make Sale thereof: And, as to the Second Remedy, no Action can be maintained, butby the joint Action, and in the Names, of all the Proprietors; and if any one of them release, or refuses to join in that Action, the rest of them can have no Benefit by that Remedy. Mr. cry an Philpof, being examined, said. That he has been employed as chief Accomptant, and Receiver of the Duties, for 7 Years last past; he also produced an Account of £. 40,403. 5s. 11 d. expended by the Undertakers, in making the said Navigation, and the Works incident thereto: Thathe declared, That the Proprietors laboured under the same Difficulties that Mr. Martyn had before mentioned; and that divers Sums of Money has been lost by the Proprietors on that Account:

That one Orpzcood, a Barge-master, having run *£\8o. in Debt to the Proprietors for their Riverage, has not returned to work upon the River ever since: That the said Act is eluded by divers Millers; who, as often as a Barge comes loaded up or down, let the Water run waste to lay them aground: That 3 Millers, Occupiers of Sheffield Mills, interrupted the Navigation for the Space of 6 Weeks, in the Months of July and August 1725; and declared, That no Barge should pass up or down the River again:

That when the Undertakers endeavoured to make Works to pen up the Water for making good the Passage for the Barges, the Millers joined with upwards of -200 Persons at one time, and 300 at another, and cajne

and cut to Pieces the Undertakers Works: That they have threatened to cut through the Undertakers Banks:

That Persons unknown, by drawing the Sluices of the Undertakers Locks in the Night-time, let the Waters run to Waste; whereby they are subjected to satisfy Damages to the adjacent Millers: That divers Laud-owners refuse to let the Undertakers bring any Timber, upon any Ground adjacent, to mend their Works;

That the said River, within the Town of Readings which has been immemorially navigable, they have hindered the Undertakers Workmen from removing a Scour, or Shoui, brought down by the late Floods, though the same hath been done by the Wharfingers adjoining, as often as there hath been Occasion for it, by imprisoning their Men on frivolous and vexatious Suits in the Corporation Court.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making more effectual Two several Acts, passed in the First and Seventh Years of his present Majesty's Reign; the one intituled, An Act for making the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Nezcbury, in the County of Berks; and the other intituled, An Act for enlarging the time for making the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Nezcbury, in the County of Berks; and for the more easy recovering the Duties appointed by the said Acts; and for the better preventing Frauds and Abuses, and other Damages done to the said Navigation; And that the Lord William Pozclett, and Mr. Parsons, do prepare, and bring in the same.

Mr. Farrer reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of that Part of his Majesty'sSpeech, which relates to the discharging the National Debt, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards lessening the publick Debts and Incumbrances, the Annuities, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, payable for, or in respect of, certain Tallies of Sol, struck in pursuance of an Act of Parliament of the Third Year of his present Majesty's Reign, and which are charged on the General Fund, and are a Joint Stock of Annuities transferrable at the Bank of England; other than and except such of them as have been subscribed into the Capital Stock of the South Sea Company; be redeemed, and paid off.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Annuities, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, payable for, or in respect of, certain Army Debentures, certified before the Twenty-first Day of March 1719, which are charged on the General Fund, and are a Joint Stock of Annuities transferrable at the Bank of England; other than and except such of them as have been subscribed into the Capital Stock of the South Sea Company; be redeemed, and paid off.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Annuities, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, payable for, or in respect of, the Sum of Five hundred thousand Pounds, charged on the Aggregate Fund, by virtue of an J±ct of Parliament of the Fifth Year of his Majesty's Reign, and raised'for discharging a like Sum of Exchequer Bills, erfeated before the Twenty-fifth Day of December 1716,whifcli are a Joint Stock of Annuities transferrable at the Bank of England'; other than and except such of them as have been* subscribed into the Capital Stock of the Smith Sea.Conv pany; be redeemed, and paid off at Michaelmas 1727.
