MR. Packer reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Farmers, and Traders, in the County of Berks, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in, at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report and Resolution were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 27th February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to make good the Allegations of the same,

The Act of Parliament, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled, An Act to prevent the Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Weirs upon the River of Thames, Westward; and fot ascertaining the Rates of Water-carriages upon the said River; whereby the Rates of the said Locks and Weirs are ascertained; was read:

Then Witnesses were called; viz.

Geo. Bay ley and John Greenway: Who, being severally examined, said, That, since the Expiration of the said Act of the 6th and 7th of King William, the Occupiers of the said Locks and Weirs have exacted such Prices from the Masters of Barges, as amounts to treble the Sum that they were entitled to, by virtue of the Order of the Justices of Peace, at their Quarter Sessions for their respective Counties made, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act, who were empowered to put the said Act in Execution: That the Proprietors of several of the said Locks and Weirshave given the Barge-masters Notice, That they intend to raise the Prices which now they exact from them; which is a very great Discouragement to the Navigation, and a great Diminution to the Trade of the several Counties through which the said River passes; and also to the Trade of the City of London, and Parts adjacent: That the Erection of the several Locks and Weirs was first intended for the Use of private Mills, and not intended for the Benefit of the Navigation; yet, as they being of some Use for the Passage of larger Vessels, the Barge-masters are willing to submit to moderate Prices for passing through the same: That, during the Continuance of the said recited Act, the Lightening-boats attending on the said Barges, and taking Goods out of them, for their Passage through the several Locks, Weirs, and Shoal-waters, were excused from any Payment; but, since the Expiration of the said Act, they make them pay for all their Lightening-boats attending the said Barges: That, of late, the Navigation is put to great Charge and Expence for Towing-paths for Horses; which the Barge-masters had always a Right to tow with Men; which used to be Forty or Fifty Men to each Barge; and, instead of Men, they use from Three to Six Horses to each Barge; which Horses do much less Damage to the Ground than the Men; and yet the Occupiers of the Lands exact much greater Prices for the Passage of the Horses than they ought to do; when, if the Barge-masters used the Number of Men before specified, they would pass free; all which is a very great Prejudice to the Trade and Navigation of the said River.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be mpvedjThat Leave be given to bring in a Bill for reviving, Explaining, and amending, an Act, passed in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act to prevent Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Weirs on the River of Thames, Westward; and for ascertaining the Rates of Water-carriage upon the said River; and for making the same perpetual; and also for setting out Towing-paths upon the Banks of the said River, either for Men or Horses; and for ascertaining the Damages occasioned thereby.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for reviving, explaining, and amending, an Act, made in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act to prevent Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Weirs upon the River of Thames, Westward; and for ascertaining the Rates of Water-carriage upon the said River; and for making the same perpetual; and also for setting out Towing-paths upon the Banks of the said River, either

13 Geo. I. 8°

That the Statute-work hath been constantly done, and a Rate raised for amending the Road 5 yet the same hath not been sufficient to repair the same.

Benedict Brown Esquire, Rogers Holland Esquire, and George Duckett Esquire, being severally examined, said, That some Parts of the Road now'desired to be repaired are so very bad and ruinous, that Wheel-carriages cannot pass, in the Winter-season; and many Parts of the Road are dangerous to Passengers:

That, although the Inhabitants of these veral Parishes, wherein the said Road lies, have constantly done their Statute.-work, and collected a Rate; yet the same hath not been sufficient to repair the Road: And the same Witnesses added, That if the Inhabitants of the Parishes were to do, and raise, much more than is required by Law, it would not effectually repair and am^nd the Road.

Dyeing Sir Richard Hopkins reported from the Committee, to

Trade. whom the Petition of the Company of Dyers of the City of London, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report and Resolution were read; and are as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 27th of February last, proceeded to examine the Matter thereof:

To make good the Allegations of the Petition, Captain Hodges was called: Who said, That he had been several times requested to dye Bays Black, in a false Way, in Imitation of true Mather-blacks, and to put a red Rose, being the Mark of a true dyed Mather-black, to the same; and that he himself had once dyed Twenty Pieces in that false Way, being pressed by a Customer so to do; and that, he believes, they were exported into foreign Parts:

That the Consequence of the Dyeing of those 20 Pieces in that falseWay, gave him so muchDisreputation VoL io.

Mdrtii. 791

with a Merchant that was his Customer; for whom lie used to dye Goods iu a true Way, that he lost the taking £. 500. a Year by him:

That Twenty-two Shillings a-piece is paid for dyeing Bays true Mather-black, and Ten Shillings per Piece for the false ones:

That Bays dyed in the false Way will soon lose their Colours; and that the true Mark might be put upon the said Bays, not only by the Dyers, but by Drawers, and other Persons.

Then a Sample of Bays, taken off a whole Piece truly dyed, and another off a whole Piece Talsely dyed, with the same marks fixed to each of them, were produced to the Committee,

Samuel Pugh Esquire said. That he never dyed Bays in the false Way; but that he has been a considerable Loser, by refusing to dye them in a false Way, knowing it to be a Fraud.

Wm.Mandrell said. That he had worked with one Mr. Thomas Marryott, Dyer; and that he used, by his Master's Order, to boil the Corners of the Bays, and afterwards mather them at that Corner, and make a red Rose to it; and used to wrap it up, and dye the rest of the Piece this false Way, without using Indigo, Woad, or Mather; which Ingredients fix the Colour, and make it permanent; and that a trueMather-black cannot bedyed without these Ingredients: And further said, That this Fraud had been committed for several Years last past.

John Willis confirmed what Captain Hodges, Samuel Pugh Esquire, and Wm. Mandrell, had said; and likewise made an Experiment before the Committee, by putting a Piece of false, and a Piece of true, dyed Goods, into the same Liquor; and the true Goods retained its Colour, when the false one was quite lost.

Walter Wid?noresa\d, That he was desired by a Draper to dye some Cloths without Woading, and to put the blue Rose, which is the Mark of a true woaded Black, to the same, and by which the true woaded Black is distinguished from that which is dyed without Woad and Indigo: And further said, That 45 s. per Piece is paid for Cloth dyed with Woad and Indigo, and 305*. for that which is dyed without it:

That he has known long Ells and Bays, and other Woollen Goods, dyed with Woad and Indigo; and has done it for his Master, with such blue Mark fixed to them, as if they were woaded throughout, when it was only woaded at the Corner.

Wm. Fowler said, That he had seen Bays, and other Woollen Goods, dyed black, with a blue Mark put to the Corner of each Piece; and no other Part of the Piece had been woaded.

Wm. Cock said. That he had seen the same thing done in coarse Cloths; and had been concerned in doing of it himself.

John Willis, being further examined, said, That he had seen Woollen Goods dyed blue, with Logwood, without Woad and Indigo; which will not hold; it presently fades by the Air.

Captain Hodges, being further examined, said. That he several Cloths, which had been dyed false Blues in L>n-don, and else where, and which were intended for Exportation, had been sent to him to be dyed over again, as not being fit to be exported; and, at other times, that he has had false Blues, which had been actually exported, and which were returned back to the Merchant, and sent to him to be dyed over again.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there are several Frauds and Abuses committed in the Dying-trade; and that the same ought to be remedied.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Sir Richard Hopkins reported from the Committee, to whom tin- Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and principal Inhabitants, of the several Hamlets of How, Poplar, Spiff Itfelds, Wapping, Stepney, and Limehnuse, in the Parish of St. Duns tan Stebunhcath, n\v<\$Slepimi, in the County of Middlesex, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 24th of February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And to make good the Allegations therein, relating to the new Church at Stratford, Bow;

Doctor Warren, Minister thereof, Sajnuel Summer, Churchwarden, and John Hughes, were called: Who, being severally examined, said, That the Church was formerly a Chapel; but has been upwards of Seven Years converted into a Church, by the Commissioners of the 50 new Churches, who have appointed the Ham-

1726.

let of Bow. a District for a new Parish to the same; and the said Church has been consecrated; and Divine Service is performed therein; but the certain Provision, at present, for the Minister thereof, appeared to be only £. 10. per Annum.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine such Part* of the Petition as relates to the Chapel of Poplar, in the Hamlet of Poplar, and examined Vigerus Edwards Esquire, DoctorLa/nfo/z, and Mr. Wnu Hoa r, Churchwarden for the Hamlet of Poplar; by whose Evidence it appeared, That the said Chapel belongs to the East India Company, and that the said Chapel at Poplar is fit to be converted into a Parish Church, and to have a District of a Parish appointed for the same; and in order thereto it is agreed between the said East India Company and the College of Brazen-nose, who are Patrons of the old Parish Church, and the Commissioners of the new Churches, that the said Chapel, and the Cemetery thereto belonging, shall be vested in the said Commissioners; and he converted into a Church; and have the Hamlet of Poplar appointed for a Parish to the same; and the Presentation thereto, being in the said College, is to be settled in the College and Company, who are to present by Turns; and this Agreement is intended to be made effectual by the Bill prayed by the Petition.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine that Part of the Petition, which relates to a Church built in the Hamlet of Spit tie fields; and examined Mr. Reuben Fox-well, and Josiah Tidmarsh: Who said. That the Commissioners of Churches have erected a newChurch there; and that the same is finished, and ready for Consecration, and to have Divine Service performed therein: And a Deed Poll, under the Hands and Seals of the said Commissioners, 5 or more of them, inrolled in Chancery, was produced to the Committee; whereby a District, being the Hamlet of Spittle fields, is appointed and ascertained for a new Parish for the said new Church

Then the Committee proceeded to examine that Part of the Petition which relates to a Church built* in the Hamlet of Wapping, Stepney, and examined Alexander Dickes, the present Churchwarden of the Hamlet of Wapping, Stepney; and John Breese, the late Churchwarden thereof: Who said. That the Commissioners have erected a new Church in Wapping, Stepney; which is finished, andready for Consecration, and fit to have Di-vineService performed therein; and that a District, being the Hamlet o Wapping, Stepney; is appointed and ascertained fora new Parish to the same: And another Deed Poll of the Commissioners, inrolled in Chancery, was produced to the Committee, to make the same appear.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine that Part of the said Petition, which relates to a new Church built by the Commissioners in the Hamlet of Limehouse -, and examined Joseph Woodward, late Churchwarden for that Hamlet; zxi&Richard Stanton, the presentChurch warden for the same: Who said, That the new Church built at Limehouse is finished, and ready for Consecration; and that a District, being the Hamlet of Limehouse, is appointed for a new Parish to the said new Church: And another Deed Poll of the Commissioners was produced to the Committee, for making out the same:

That the said Witnesses gave. Evidence, That no Provision is already made for the Ministers of any of the said new Churches, except j£. 10. per Annum for the Minister of Bow.

And the Committee find, That no Division or Apportioning, of the Tythes and Dues belonging to the old Church of Stepney, can be made to the Ministers of the said 5 new Churches, but by Agreement with the College of Brazen-nose, the Patrons of the said Church, which is a Rectory, divided intoMoieties, or Two Portions; to which they used to present Two Portionists; the one called the Portionist of Ratcliffe, Stepney; and the other the Portionist of Spit tie fields. Stepney; and that the said Portion called SpittlefieIds, Stepney, as now vacant.

Mr. Treasurer reported to the House, That their Address of Wednesday last, That his Majesty would be graciously*pleased to give Directions, That an Estimate of the Rebuildings and Repairs of his Majesty's Ships of War, for the Year 1727, might be laid before this House, had been presented to his Majesty; and that his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, That he will give Directions for laying the same before this House.

Mr. Treasurer also reported to the House, That their Address of Wednesday last, That his Majesty would be graciously pleased to give Directions, That the Memorial presented to his Majesty on Thursday the Second Day of March instant, by Monsieur de Palm, the Imperial Resident^ might be laid before this House, had been presented to his, Majesty; and that his Majesty had been pleased to command him to lay a Copy of the said Memorial before this House, together with a Translation of it:

And Mr. Treasurer presented the said Copy of the said Memorial, together with a Translation of it, to the House accordingly:

And the Title of the said Memorial was read.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, take the said Memorial into Consideration.

The said Memorial is bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

Sir Charles Turner, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to enforce the Laws for Transportation of Felons; and for preventing their Return to Great Britain; was committed; the Amendments the Committee had made to the Bill; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the said Amendments were once read throughout; and then a Second time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were, with some Amendments to One of thorn, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, for making it a temporary Act:

And the same was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next, Nine of the Clock.

De Palm's The Lord Fitz William reported from the Committee

Memorial, appointed to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, pursuant to the Resolution Yesterday, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was re&d; and is as follows; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE your Majesty's most dutiful and faithful Subjects, the

Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, think it our indispensable Duty to express the highest Resentment at the Affront and Indignity offered to your most Sacred Majesty, by the Memorial delivered by Monsieur De Palm, the Emperor's Resident; and at his Insolence in printing and dispersing the same throughout the Kingdom.

This audacious manner of appealing to the People against your Majesty, under the pretext of applying to you for Redress and Reparation of supposed injuries; and turning a Memorial, presented to your Majesty, into a seditious Libel; is a Proceeding that creates in us the utmost Abhorrence and Detestation.

The endeavouring to instil into the Minds of any of your faithful Subjects the least Distrust, or Diffidence, in your Majesty's most Sacred Royal Word, or to make a Distinction between your Majesty and your People, is an Attempt as vain as presumptuous; for, by your Goodness, the Interest of your Majesty, and your People, is but one; and as inseparable, as their Duty, Affection, and Confidence, in your Majesty, are most justly and deservedly unalterable; and, if Time has not effaced the Memory of the glorious Exploits, and important Succours, confessed to have been received from Great Britain, Gratitude, Affection, and Esteem, for this Nation, will be best manifested by doing Honour to the King, whom the People honour; arid Justice to the People, whose Rights and Privileges the best bf Kings is now defending against the Invasions and Incroachments made upon them.

We return your Majesty our airreerest Thanks for your Care and Vigilance in discovering the secret and periii-cious Designs of yoilr and our Enemies; and for yOnf-Goodness in communicating to your1 Parliament the Dangers that threatened this Kingdom: *

And we beg Leave to allure your Majesty, That no Amusements, by artful or evasive Denials, shall lead us into a false security; or divert us from exerting ^ourselves in Vindication of your Majesty's Honour;' afleb in defending and supporting your Majesty againfct all your open and secret Enemies, both at home and1 abroad: '

And if any, among your own Subjects, have been sb wicked as to countenance, encourage, or abet, the Dis^ turbers of the publick Tranquillity, in this extravagant Insult upon your Majesty; or flattered tlierri with Hopes, that an obstinate Perseverance in their destructive Measures could stagger the Firmness of the British Nation1; we are resolved effectually to defeat all such groundless Expectations; and to convince the World, that the Intrigues of a few cannot, in any Degree, abate or slacken that Vigour and Resolution, with which a true Love and'

Concern lor our Country, a just Sense of its Interests, and an unshaken Loyalty to your Majesty, have inspired us.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to his Ma-jesly.

Resolved, That the Concurrence of the Lords be desired to the said Address. *;

Mr. Speaker reported, That both Houses did Yesterday attend his Majesty with their Address; To which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Your unanimous Concurrence in this dutiful and affectionate Address gives me the greatest Satisfaction: The just Concern you express for my Honour, and the Dignity of the Crown, is very becoming a British Parliament; and this fresh Proof of your Confidence in me will convince the World, that all Attempts to divide our Hearts and Interests will be vain and ineffectual.

A Petition of Charles Cholmonddty, of Vale Royal\ in the County of Chester, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That he, being seised of an ancient Salt-work and Brine-pit at IVinsford Bridge, near the River Weaver, hath annually sent a great Part of the Salt made there to Ireland, and other foreign Parts, by Sea; and, by carrying the Navigation of the said River to IVinsford Bridge, as was intended by art Act of the Seventh Year of his Majesty's Reign, he would still be enabled to send his Salt to Sea, upon an Equality with other Works; which lie will be deprived of, if the said Act should be repealed: And praying, That a reasonable Satisfaction may be made him for the Loss which he must suffer by carrying the said Navigation no further than Northwich only; and that he may be heard, by his Counsel, touching the same, before the Bill, depending in this House, for repealing an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of his Majesty's lleign, tbr making the River Weaver navigable from Frodsham Bridge to IVinsford Bridge, in the County of Chester.; and for the more speedy and effectual carrying on, and perfecting the Navigation of the said River, from Frodsham Bridge to Noi'thwick, in the said County; do pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for repealing an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of his Majesty's Reign, for making the River Weaver navigable from Frodsham Bridge to IVinsford Bridge, in the County of Chester; and for the more speedy and effectual carrying on, and perfecting, the Navigation of the said River from Frodsham Bridge to Northwich, in the said County; is committed: And that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, if he think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard for the said Bill.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, for preventing the Taking and Destroying of Salmon, and other Fish, at any Wear, or Mills, that shall be erected or built upon the River IVye, by virtue of this Act:

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, That, in case the Owners of Lands lying.near the Rivers shall refuse to agree for Sale thereof with the Trustees, the Trustees may issue their Warrants to the Sheriff of the County of Hereford, to impanel a Jury qualified, which, 5

on their Oath, shall esquire and assess the Damages, and the Recompence to be made; and the Judgment*of the Trustees thereupon shall be binding to all Parties; but no Trustee shall sit, or act, where he is concerned in Interest:

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

Complaint being made to the House, That several Post Orders re-Letters, directed to Members, of the House, have been *Pectlus intercepted, and taken out of the Boxes appointed for the Letters.1* same at the Door of the House;

Ordered, That, to prevent the Intercepting of Letters belonging to the Members of the House for the future, the Person appointed to bring them from the General Post-office do constantly attend Two Hours, at the least, after the Rising of the House, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to w hom they shall be directed, and no other.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, give such Letters as shall remain undelivered to One of the Servants belonging to the House; who shall take care to deliver the said Letters to the several Members to whom they are directed, their known Servants, or to such Persons who shall produce a Note under the Hands of the Members who shall send for the same.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Commissioners for executing the Office of Postmaster General.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Kinaston and Mr. Mashctm:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Manors, Lauds, and Hereditaments, in the Kingdom of Ireland, the Estate of Sir Redmond Eve-rard Baronet, in Trustees, to be sold, for raising Money to discharge Incumbrances affecting the same; and for other Purposes; To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House. And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for making the Will of Sir John Cass Knight, deceased, effectual: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House. And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing a Power of Revocation in the Settlement made on the Marriage of Francis Goulston Esquire; and for establishing and vesting a new Power, instead thereof: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House. And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for Sale of Part of the Estate of Valentine Brown Esquire, commonly called Lord Kenmare, in the Kingdom of Ireland, for Payment of Debts and Incumbrances, affecting the same: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House. And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting the real Estate, late of Elihu Yale Esquire, deceased, in the County, of Denbigh, in Trustees, to be sold; and applying One-third Part of the Monies arising by Sale thereof, according to the Will of Ursula Yale, his Daughter, deceased; and the Two-thirds for the Benefit of his Two other Co-heirs: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House. And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act to vest the Manors of Great Hallingbury and Little Hailing-bury, JVallbury, and Monk bury, and the Forest or Chace in the Parish of Hatfield, in the County of Essex, and also the Manor or Lordship of Bluntshall, in the County of Suffolk, and the Manor or Lordship of TVintcrton, in the County of Not folk, in Trustees, to be sold, for the Payment of the frebts to which the same are subject, by virtue of the Will of Sir Edward Tumour Knight, deceased; and for laying out the Surplus of the Money, if any, arising by such Sale, in the Purchase of Lands, to be settled to the Uses mentioned in the Will of the said Sir Edward Tumour: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House. And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of the Reverend Doctor Maxwell, and Ft'ancis Lucas Esquire, Hector Graham and Peter Mason Gentlemen, on behalf of themselves, and many other Protestants in Ireland, who are Lessees and Creditors of Sir John Fleming Knight, deceased, and of Michael Fleming Esquire, his Son and Heir, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by a Petition presented to the House by Mary GGara Widow, she pretends to be intitled to Lands in Ireland\ of £. 200. per Annum, on the Death of her First Husband, Richard Fleming Esquire; and that soon after, she being outlawed for High Treason, her Estate for Life vested in the late King IVm. and Queen Mary; and was afterwards, by the Act of Resumption, vested in Trustees appointed for Sale of the Irish Forfeitures; but that they could not Find out any Title to the Estate; so it remained undisposed of; and is now vested in his present Majesty by an Act of Parliament; and that she is ready to make out his Majesty's Title; and therefore prayed, That Leave might be given to bring in a Bill to enable her to sue for her Jointure-lands, with the mean Profits thereof; which Allegations, the Petitioners conceive, cannot be proved: That Sir John Fleming Knight, deceased, had Issue the said Richard Flemings and Michael Fleming his only surviving Son and Heir; add Sir John, being adjudged within the Articles of Limerick, enjoyed his whole Estate during his Life; and, being reputed absolute Owner thereof, the Petitioners, and others, were induced to V o l. 20.

lend him considerable Sums, and to take long Leases, and improve the same out of their own Fortunes; and became Purchasers for valuable Considerations; and, for many Years, have quietly enjoyed their several Interests; and never heard of any Claim made by the said Mary O Gar a, before that set up by her said Petition:

That a Bill being brought into the House, upon her Petition, she is not only thereby enabled to sue for her Jointure, but also her Outlawry is thereby to be reversed, and she enabled to use alb such Process and Means, as the King might have used; and so she will be in a much better Condition than if she never had been outlawed; which may tend to the Disquiet and Ruin of the Peti* tioners, and other Protestant Lessees and Creditors:

And praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill; or be otherwise relieved, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill to enable Mary O Gara, Widow, to sue for her Jointure-lands, be read a Second time: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second time upon Wednesday come Sevennight.

Buckingham A Petition of several Freeholders, and other Land-Gaul. holders of the County of Bucks, was presented to the

House, and read; setting forth, That there is a Bill in th£ . Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, for charging the Inhabitants of the Parishes and Places liable to repair the great Read, in any of the Three Divisions mentioned in the Bill, with a Pound-rate:

And the said Clause was once read, with Blanks:

And a Debate arising in the House thereupon;

Ordered, That the Debate be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill for enlarging the Times for hearing and determining Claims by the Trustees for raising Money upon the Estates of the late Directors of the South Sea Company, and others; and for Relief of the Creditors of Robert Knight Esquire, late Cashier to the said Company.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Gyles Earle took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Gyles Earle reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Tuesday Morning next.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Clause contained in an Act, made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the Reign of the late King WUliqrn the Third, intituled, An Act to settle the Trade to Africa, for allowing, during a limited Time, a Draw back of the Duties upon Exportation of Copper Bars imported; and which Clause, after Expiration thereof, was, by an Act of the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty's Reign, revived, and continued for Fourteen Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is fit to be further continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act made in the Fifth Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for the better preventing Frauds committed by Bankrupts; which Act was to continue in Force for Seven Years from the Twenty-sixth Day of May 1716, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the Eleventh Year of his Majesty's Reign, was continued for One Year, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is fit to be further continued.

Resohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act made in the Tenth Year of his Majesty'? Reign, intituled, An Act for the better viewing, searching, and examining, all Drugs, Medicines, Waters Oils, Compositions used, or to be used, for Medicines, in all Places where the same shall be exposed to Sale, or kept for that Purpose, within the City of London, and Suburbs thereof, or within Seven Miles Circuit of the said City; which was to be in Force for Three Years, and from theuce to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is fit to be further continued.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon agreed unto by the House.

Mr, Gybbon, according to Order, reported from the Petersfield Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it Election* appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Petersfield, in the County of Southampton, with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: And the Report and Resolutions of the Committee are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Edmund Miller, Servant at Law; and also the Petition of the ancient Freeholders of the Borough of Petersfield, in the County of Southampton, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others of the said Borough; complaining of an undue Election and Return of Joseph Taylor Esquire to serve for the said Borough:

The Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

The Petitioners Counsel alleged, That this is a Borough by Prescription; and that the Right of Election is in such only as have Freeholds within the Borough, in Lands, or in ancient Dwelling-houses or Shambles, or Dwelling-houses built upon ancient Foundations.

The Sitting Member s Counsel alleged, That the Right of Election is in the Freeholders in general, without any Distinction of ancient Houses, or Houses built upon ancient Foundations.

The Petitioners Counsel called,

Mr. Alexander Robinson, Thomas Breaker, md Thomas Hughes: The First of which spoke for Forty Years, the next for Fifty, and the other for Nineteen Years; and they gave Evidence, That they always took the Right of Election to be in the ancient Freeholders of the Borough; those having Freeholds in Lands, or in ancient D welling-houses, or ancient Shambles, or Houses built upon ancient Foundations:

That Quit-renters had no Right of Voting: And Mr.

Robinson Added, That there are 15 Shambles in the Market-place, which had been anciently divided, and &lwfitys voted for.

Reasons for the Commons disagreeing to the Amendment, made by the Lords, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the more effectual amending the Highway between Hockliffe and JVoborn, in the "County of Bedford; and for repairing the Road leading through IVoborn to Tickjord Bridge, in Newport Pagnell, in the County of Bucks.

Your Lordships having, in the said Bill, made the following Amendment; vis.

Press 5. L. 27. Leave out from " notwithstanding" to " Provided," in the First Line of the next Press

The Commons cannot agree to the said Amendment;

1 st, Because very few Persons, if any, except the Inhabitants of the Three Hundreds of Newport, and die Hundred of Mansliead, come to the Markets of Newport and IVoborn; the exempting the said Inhabitants from Tolls, on those Days, can be no Prejudice to any; but the imposing Tolls on them may be a Prejudice to those Towns, and to the Lords of diosc Two Manors, by lessening the Tolls of their Markets, if the Inhabitants of those Hundreds should go toother Markets, in the Neighbourhood, which they may do, and, it is highly probable, they will, without passing die new Turnpikes to be erected by this Act:

2dly, That, there being a considerable Trade of Lacemaking in the said Hundreds, which is the Work of the very poorest of the People, and with very little Profit, die Toll will be grievous to them; and, since the Lace-buyers must pay the Toll, if the Sellers pay Toll also, it

Mail. A. 1727.

will be a double Toll for the same Commodity, which already scarce affords Bread to the Makers.

The Commons decline, at this time, offering any odier Reasons; believing these may be sufficient to prevail with yonr Lordships not to insist upon the said Amendment, that a Bill so necessary may not be lost.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That a Conference be desired with the Lords, upon the Subject-matter of the said Amendment.

The Lord Finch reported the Conference; and that the I-ords do insist upon their Amendment to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the more effectual amending the Highway between Hockliffe and IVoborne, in the County of Bedford; and for repairing the Road leading through IVoborne to Tickford Bridge, in Navport Pagjiell, in the County of Bucks: For which they gave their Reasons; which he reported to the House.

The said Reasons were read; and are as follow; viz.

The Lords having taken into Consideration the Rea-2 sons

13 Geo. I, 1.50

sons given by the Commons, at the last Conference, for their disagreeing with the Amendment, made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the more effectual amending the Highway between Hockliffe and IVobum, in the County of Bedford; and for repairing the Road leading through IVoburn to Tick ford Bridge, in Newport Pagnell, in the County of Bucks; their Lordships do insist on the said Amendment;

1st, Because the exempting the Three Hundreds of Newport, and the Hundred of Manshead, from paying Toll; which Exemption is very rarely, if ever, found in Bills of this Kind; will considerably lessen the Produce of the said Toll; and, in consequence, will prevent the Roads being speedily and effectually amended; which must be the mam Design of this Bill;

2dly, Because this Exemption would establish a Precedent of dangerous Consequence to all future Turnpike Bills; since the Argument used in behalf of Lace-buyers, and Lace-sellers may be insisted upon, with more Reason, for the Dealers in all other marketable Commodities; and, were this way of Reasoning to prevail, those who have the greatest and most constant Benefit from those Roads being kept in good Repair, and who are already, by Law, obliged to repair the same, would be free from paying the Tell; whilst Travellers, and others, who use them but seldom, must bear the whole Burthen and Expence:

For these and other Reasons, which the Lords decline entering upon at this time, they do insist upon their Amendment; and their Lordships cannot imagine the Commons will lose a Bill they think so necessary, by disagreeing to an Amendment so justifiable in every respect, and so consistent with the Nature of the Bill.

Resolved, Kemine contradicente, That this House doth insist upon their Disagreement with the Lords to the said Amendment

Ordered, That the Managers who managed the last Conference, do withdraw immediately into the Speaker s Chamber; and consider what may be proper to be offered to the Lords, at a free Conference upon the Subject-matter of the last Conference: And that they do make their Report to the House with all convenient Speed.

After which his Majesty was pleased to say;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have ordered my Lord Chancellor to declare to you, in iny Name and Words, the Reasons of my coming this Day to Parliament.

And thereupon his Lordship received from his Majesty's Hands, from the Throne, his Majesty's Speech to both Houses of Parliament; which he read; and is as followed]; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I acquainted you, at the Opening of this Session, with the Dangers which threatened this Kingdom, and die Peace and Liberties of Europe: I am now to return you my Thanks for the Zeal and Dispatch, with which you have proceeded upon the several Points I then recommended to your Care; for die Confidence you have reposed in me; and for the Assurances you have given me of your Support and Assistance in Vindication of my Honour, and in the Maintenance and Defence of the undoubted Rights and Privileges of this Nation, so openly and notoriously invaded and attacked:

The Siege of Gibraltar proves, beyond all Dispute, the End and Design of the Engagements entered into by the Emperor, and the King of; but the Preparations

I had made for the Defence of that Place, and the Bravery of my Troops, will, I doubt not, convince them of the Rashness and Polly of that Undertaking: However, the Love of Peace has hitherto prevailed upon me, even under this high Provocation, to suspend, in some measure, my Resentments; and, instead of having immediate recourse to Arms, and demanding of my Allies that Assistance which they are engaged, and ready, to give me,

I have concurred with the most Christian King, and the States General, in making such Overtures of Accommodation, as must convince all the World of the Uprightness of our Intentions, and of our sincere Disposition to Peace; and demonstrate to whose Ambition, and Thirst of Power, the Calamities of a War are to be imputed, if these just and reasonable Proposidons are rejected: in the mean time I have the Pleasure to acquaint you, That the Crown of Sweden has acceded to the Treaty of Hanover; and that the Convention between me, his most Christian Majesty, and the King of Denmark, is actually signed.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Vigour and Chearfulness you have shewn in raising so effectually, and upon such' easy Terms, the necessary Supplies for the Service of the current Year, are not only instances of your Zeal and Affection to me, but demonstrate the established Credit, Power, and Strength, of this Kingdom.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It would have been a great Satisfaction to me, if, before your Separation, I had been able to speak to you more positively, and with greater Certainty, upon the present Posture and State of Affairs: But as you have now dispatched the publick Business, and as the Season of the Year requires your going into your respective Countries,

I choose rather to put an End to this Session, than to keep you any longer together unnecessarily: The Provisions you have made, and the perfect Union and Har* mony between me and my Allies, will, I hope, enable me, by the Divine Assistance, either to withstand and defeat the Designs of our Enemies, if their Conduct should bring upon us the Necessity of a War; or to improve the Blessings of Peace, if Peace can, with Justice, Honour, and Security, be obtained.

And afterwards the Uord Chancellor, by his Majesty's P»r1i#rm Command, said; prorojuti

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Tuesday the Twenty-seventh Day of June next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the Twenty-seventh Day of June next.
